Friends buy a new car on credit, colleagues fly off to the islands. You calmly choose a road trip around old towns, and your wardrobe still has room: every new thing replaces an old one. You have no debts and no clutter, but you do have a reserve and a habit of not envying. **Your wealth lies in a sense of measure that frees you from the race.**

The balance breaks when each holds one pan of the scales. One saves, the other spends, and both believe they balance each other, though in fact they pull apart. Sometimes one lives on the other's money and is embarrassed to ask. Or envy creeps in after all: why do they have it and we don't? Temperance needs both of you to hold the measure, not one on behalf of two.

items.title: Hungry for big money

captions.C: Earn with zest and stay honest

items.meaning: You have a knack for money: hard, well-paid work, ambitious goals and an honesty without which the thrill is dangerous.
text: You have a real appetite for money. The Devil gives you both a firm grip: you are not afraid of hard work if it pays well, you take on extra projects, you invest and you count. Your goals are ambitious and shared, you don't live on credit, and you spend what you earn with pleasure — on yourselves and on those who need help.

For two years one of you works rotating shifts in the far north, and the other holds down two jobs in the city. It is hard, but you both have a figure on the wall before your eyes: the deposit on a house. When the sum is reached, you celebrate at the best restaurant in town, and part of the first “free” pay packet goes to a charity that sends children to summer camp. **Your grip serves a shared goal rather than greed, and that is why it lasts.**

Appetite becomes hunger when there is never enough money. One is forever unhappy with the other's earnings, compares, pushes, demands more. The temptation of quick money appears — “everyone does it” — and one nudges the other towards a dubious decision “for the family's sake”. The Devil is honest about one thing: dishonest money holds you tighter than any chain. Your grip remains a strength as long as you both know where the line is.

items.title: A building site, not a safe

captions.C: Build together and keep a reserve for bad weather

items.meaning: Your money goes into building: big joint investments, rules made up by the two of you and a reserve in case of collapse.
text: Your money turns into walls. The Tower runs the household through building: a joint budget, big investments — a house, a renovation, a plot of land — and strict discipline by rules the two of you devised. You look after things, mend rather than throw away, and know that system and patience are more reliable than any luck.

You build your house over five years — a floor a year, without loans. Every spring you sit down with the estimate; every autumn you close another stage. When one of you is suddenly made redundant, you don't abandon the build: you switch to “winter mode”, finish the interiors with your own hands and a year later pick up the pace again. **Blows don't bring your house down, because it is built to a shared plan, not on a single income.**

A sudden blow hurts more when you are not ready for it. Losing a job or a home reshapes your whole life, and it turns out you grew up with different attitudes to money: one is used to “there's never any money”, the other to “it'll all work out somehow”. Fear of change makes you expect the worst and cling to the old, even when it is time to rebuild. The Tower asks for a foundation: a cushion you never touch, and an agreement on what to do if things collapse.

items.title: Savings for a shared dream

captions.C: Invest in each other's dreams and talents

items.meaning: You make money work for a dream: you invest in each other's talents, and after spending, new chances come your way.
text: You spend on a dream — and the dream pays you back. The Star runs the household with hope: money goes on projects, study, tools for a talent, a shared wish you have long wanted to fulfil. Yet you are rational about it: there is always a side job or a reserve, and after a big expense new opportunities somehow open up.

One of you dreams of a photo studio of their own. For two years you save for the equipment, and the other takes on the website and the first clients. In the first month the studio brings in nothing, by the third it covers the rent, and to celebrate you buy not equipment but a cake. **Your shared purse is a piggy bank for a dream, and you both know what you are saving for.**

A starry purse springs leaks when a picture takes the place of the dream. Spending on the good life, impulse buys to feel better, faith in easy money — and having paid off one debt, you take on another. Or the reverse: talents gather dust because investing in them feels frightening. The Star needs balance: dream widely and count soberly.

items.title: Income from an odd idea

captions.C: Earn from your own venture and your instinct

items.meaning: Money reaches you by unusual roads: your own venture, a creative project, instinct — and it needs clear accounts.
text: Money comes to you by untrodden paths. The Moon runs the household by instinct: a business of your own, a shared creative project, an unusual profession that suddenly starts paying. You work honestly, don't mix friendship with money and dislike debts — taking or giving. Your intuition in money matters rarely lets you down, as long as clear accounts back it up.

One of you has a hobby — candles with scents you can't find in shops. The other takes them to a fair “just to see”, and by evening not one is left. That night you sit over the empty box and for the first time seriously work out what the wax costs, and to both your surprise the figures are kept by the one who at first only chuckled. **Your income grows where one partner's instinct meets the other's sober head.**

The money fog thickens when nobody sees the figures. It is unclear how much was earned and where it went, nobody thinks about the future, and debts appear as if by themselves. One keeps a secret stash from the other, the other lives in the hope that “it'll work out somehow”. The Moon in your wallet needs light: shared accounts, open figures and no secrets from each other.

items.title: Prosperity with an open door

captions.C: Earn honestly and live generously

items.meaning: Your prosperity is bright and honest: you both thrive in your work, plan years ahead and are generous to everyone.
text: You know how to live well and not hide it. The Sun brings you both strong fulfilment at work: each succeeds in their own field, income grows, and success is honestly earned. You like to plan and to count, you keep a reserve, you invest in the future — education, a home, travel — and at the same time you are generous: to your own, to guests, to anyone who needs help.

You make the last mortgage payment and that same evening invite friends to a party: a long table, music, a cake shaped like a key. A week later you sit down to a plan for the next five years — a country cottage, study abroad for one of you, a fund for your parents' old age. **Your prosperity shines but does not dazzle: it is there to warm you and those around you.**

The Sun scorches when money becomes the measure of everything. Status, the make of your car, the size of your house — the race for visible success eats up time and joy. Or one decides to save on everything and turns the home into an accounts department, while the other spends without looking out of spite. Prosperity that was meant to warm you becomes a field for competing over who matters more in this family.

items.title: Wealth that gets handed down

captions.C: Build together with an eye to family and legacy

items.meaning: Your prosperity grows with the family: a joint budget, your kin's support and things that pass to those who come next.
text: Your household is closely tied to the family line. Judgement runs it the family way: prosperity grows once you have become one family, opportunities come through relatives, and you plan the budget together, talking through the risks. You look after things inherited from your elders and think about what you will pass on.

A grandmother's flat in an old building comes to you with its 1950s decor. You don't sell it; for six months of weekends you scrub the parquet, keep the oak sideboard and leave the notches on the door frame where your parents' height was once measured. **Your prosperity is not just money but what you received from your elders and managed to make your own.**

An inheritance becomes a bone of contention when relatives come for it. Disputes over shares, grievances, lawsuits — and money that was meant to support you divides you instead. It can happen between the two of you too: one does not want to keep a joint budget, the other squanders what generations have saved. Judgement needs honesty: family money is agreed on in advance and out loud, or the past sends its bill at the worst possible moment.

items.title: A budget written by two

captions.C: Agree on money and think years ahead

items.meaning: You write your money rules together: savings, a long horizon, careful spending and an easy attitude to earning.
text: Your money rules are shared — written by the two of you and suiting you both. The World runs the household with a wide horizon: savings, investments, income that works while you travel, care for things and for what you will leave behind. You earn responsibly but without strain, and you need money to live more broadly, not to worry.

Every year, on the first evening of your holiday, you hold a “finance council”: somewhere on a terrace, with wine and a notebook. How much did we put aside, where did we invest, what do we want in five years. One of you loves figures, the other loves dreams, and by the end of the evening you have a plan with room for both. **Your joint budget is an agreement between two equals, not one partner reporting to the other.**

The horizon narrows when thrift turns into fear. “Old is better than new”, any change at work seems a threat, every purchase demands an account. Suspicion grows: who spent how much, is something being hidden. The World rests on trust, and once that cracks, the joint budget splits into two wallets keeping an eye on each other.

items.title: A wide-open wallet

captions.C: Spend easily and start from scratch just as easily

items.meaning: Money doesn't stay with you, but it doesn't hold you either: you spend easily, give generously and can start from zero.
text: Things and money don't hold you. The Fool runs the household travelling light: you spend a lot, give generously, don't cling to what you have bought and, if everything collapses, will calmly start again from scratch. You can find a way out where others see a dead end — a side job, a swap, an unexpected idea — and being poor frightens you less than being bored.

You sell nearly everything you have gathered in five years and move to another city for a year — just to try it. Friends are shocked, parents phone every day. You come back with empty pockets, three new skills and an idea for a business of your own, which you both laugh at and have both already started costing. **Your capital is not savings but the lightness with which you start again.**

Lightness turns into a hole in the pocket when nobody thinks about tomorrow. Money is borrowed “for a couple of weeks”, bills pile up, the salary is gone in three days, and the plan “we'll manage somehow” works less and less often. Sometimes parents bail you out, and that becomes a habit too. The Fool needs no bookkeeping, but even the freest people need a jar put by for a sudden turn.

items.title: Generosity and a quiet chest

captions.L: Generous spending with no reserve
captions.R2: Growing what's shared and multiplying it
captions.R: Hiding prosperity and skimping on joy

items.meaning: Your generosity becomes abundance when you grow what's shared — and isn't lost unless you then hide it in a quiet chest.
text: The Empress opens your line twice: first as generosity with no reserve — home, gifts, comfort, sometimes on credit — then as a path: growing what's shared, multiplying, investing in family and the future. The threes add up to six, and the Lovers trail behind to remind you that abundance is a decision for two. The Hermit at the exit hides the harvest in a chest.

The money that used to go on presents you one day decided to “plant”: every month part goes into a fund, part towards a small flat to let, part into education. Ten years on you have two flats, and you give presents to loved ones out of the returns rather than your salary. **Abundance began to grow when you started planting money, not only giving it away.**

Here the harvest goes into the shadows. When prosperity has come, one of you starts hiding it: skimping on pleasures, not saying how much is saved, keeping a separate secret account. The old generosity disappears from the home. Let the harvest be visible to both: a shared account, shared plans and a celebration after every big goal.

items.title: Double abundance and a shadow

captions.L: Feast or famine, and parents' help
captions.R2: Shared goals and patient multiplying

items.meaning: Your abundance doubles when shared goals grow from generous spending — and melts when parents' help is taken in secret.
text: Generosity is your nature, and at first it backfires: feast or famine, money flies off on comfort and presents, and in a hard month parents bail you out. The Empress stands both at the entrance and in the middle: the same love of abundance that creates the difficulty becomes the path once it turns into shared goals. A home of your own, investments, each one's growth — abundance that increases by itself. The Moon casts a shadow of things unsaid over this garden.

Every January you hold a “family harvest council”: you sum up the year and decide what to plant in the next — repairs, study, savings, a trip. After a few such councils you have a flat without debts, each has work they love, and the parents now come to you for advice. **Your generosity began to multiply once it had a planting plan.**

The shadow comes from an old habit. In an empty month one of you still calls the parents “till payday” and doesn't tell the other: it's awkward, now that you have a harvest council and a plan. The help adds up, and with it a debt only one knows about, and resentment when the other learns of it from relatives at a family dinner. Abundance loves the light: if help is needed, agree on it together, and give it its own line in your plan — with a sum and a date for repayment.

items.title: Abundance chosen together

captions.L: A lavish life not backed by income
captions.R2: Work you love and people around you
captions.R: Giving the harvest away before it's in

items.meaning: Your generosity brings income when it becomes shared work you love — and won't melt unless the harvest goes out too soon.
text: Generosity, comfort, a love of the good life — you have them twice over: the Empress opens your money line and closes it too. At first income can't keep up with generosity. Two threes make six, and the Lovers at the centre of the line suggest how to turn generosity into earnings: choose work you love and people you want to do it with. Then abundance starts to come back.

For many years dancing was your shared evening — just for yourselves. When friends asked you to teach them for their wedding, you gave three lessons in your living room. Now you have a wedding-dance school, and couples come recommended by those you've already taught. **Work you love, chosen together, gave your generosity back its price.**

Here the harvest is given away before it's gathered. The first good money goes on presents, celebrations, helping family and a beautiful home — generously and at once. When it runs short, the credit card steps in. And if one of you rises in the business, the other in time becomes the staff of their own home. Be generous from what's gathered, and let both of you have a field of your own.

items.title: Generosity that comes back

captions.L: Living large and relying on family help
captions.R2: People, connections and work you both enjoy
captions.R: Sacrificing your own, depending on the other

items.meaning: Your generosity to people comes back as income, as long as neither dissolves in the other or lives on credit.
text: You love to live large: a house full of guests, presents, comfort you don't stint on. The Empress is generous, but at first that generosity often leans on someone else's shoulder — parents, credit, whichever of you earns more. The Lovers lead to prosperity through people: acquaintances, joint decisions, work you both enjoy that gathers around you people willing to pay. The Hanged Man marks where generosity starts to cost too much.

Your parties have always drawn half the town, and one day friends ask you to organise their father's milestone birthday — for a fee, since you're so good at it. A year later you have a small family-events agency: one dreams things up and greets guests, the other deals with caterers and musicians. Clients come through people who once sat at your table. **The warmth you gave away for free came back to you as orders.**

The costliest thing in this line is sacrifice. One of you leaves their own job to carry the shared business and gradually loses what was theirs: no money of their own, decisions made by the other. Or you lend to anyone who asks and wait years for repayment. Savings go on others' needs, and your own are put off “for later”. Generosity is good when it comes from plenty: each should have their own income, and help to others stays within limits agreed in advance.

items.title: Generous hosts of an open house

captions.L: Spending widely and waiting for help
captions.R2: People, company and shared work you love
captions.R: A home that became only a business

items.meaning: Your generosity to people comes back as income through shared work you love — until the bill replaces hospitality.
text: Living generously and openly is your style: the Empress doesn't stint, and at first spending outruns income. The Lovers turn generosity into a business: people you like, company that grows into orders, joint decisions. Your open house becomes a source of prosperity. The World at the exit likes everything accounted for — and can turn the home into a hotel.

For years friends came to your country cottage at weekends — staying over, with a sauna and talk till morning. One day you decided to charge strangers for it: weekends in the country for small groups. Today you have three guest houses, and guests come back as if to old friends. **Your hospitality turned out to be a craft people pay for.**

An open house risks becoming only a business. Weekends are booked for guests, your own friends are invited “in the off-season”, every bottle and towel is counted, and evening talk is only about occupancy. The World at the exit likes everything accounted for, and quietly makes you hotel keepers rather than hosts of a home. Keep at least one house where no places are sold, and a couple of weekends a month that cost nothing at all.

items.title: Generous table, quiet workshop

captions.L: Lavish spending and leaning on family
captions.R2: Study and mastery without haste
captions.R: Spending from the heart, comparing incomes

items.meaning: Your generosity rests on mastery you grow without haste, and doesn't leak as long as spending doesn't serve emotions alone.
text: The Empress makes you generous: the house is full, the table laid, the presents dear. Only at first generosity outruns income. The Hermit shows a source that can bear it: mastery grown unhurriedly, knowledge that's valued. The Lovers decide how you spend — and you spend from the heart.

Weaving was rest for you, not work: for years you mastered old patterns. When a neighbour asked to buy a rug, you named a price shyly. Now interior designers order your rugs, and at weekends students come to you. You're no longer shy of naming the price: behind every rug are months of work. **Unhurried mastery became the source that can bear your generosity.**

The heart spends faster than the hands earn: presents, restaurants, celebrations and surprises eat a month's income in a week. Comparisons come too: “others have more”, “you could earn better”. Spending from the heart is fine when you can afford it: set aside a share of income for it and enjoy it without guilt.

items.title: Abundance through mastery

captions.L: Spending on comfort more than comes in
captions.R2: Deep knowledge and unhurried growth
captions.R: Pressing the other “for the family's sake”

items.meaning: Your comfort rests on mastery, not spending: prosperity grows until one pushes the other too far “for the family”.
text: You love abundance: a beautiful home, a generous table, presents. That's the Empress, and the difficulty starts with her too: more goes out than comes in, and when it runs dry, parents bail you out. The Hermit in the middle teaches another abundance — the kind that grows from within. Knowledge, mastery, an unhurried pace, a reserve: through these comes prosperity that doesn't depend on anyone's help. The Devil at the end of the line lures with big money — sometimes in the voice of care.

Your home is always full of guests and pies, and one day a friend asks if you'd teach her to bake like that. For years you'd perfected the recipes for yourselves, and now that knowledge becomes a business: classes in your kitchen, then a recipe book, then courses. **Your abundance became income when mastery grew out of a generous table.**

The Devil speaks in the voice of care. The one who manages the money persuades the other to take on one more course intake though they're already exhausted, or to give the recipes to someone else's name for a good advance: “it's for us, after all.” Refusing sounds like betraying the family, agreeing like betraying yourself, and comparisons with friends who earn twice as much only add fuel. If the work demands something one of you dislikes, the decision lies not with the sum but with the one who has to do it.

items.title: Abundance after waiting

captions.L: Generosity on credit, leaning on parents
captions.R2: Patience and investing in the family
captions.R: Stinginess, each silent about their own

items.meaning: Your abundance comes slowly: patience and investment in the family grow it — until thrift turns into stinginess.
text: The Empress loves abundance, but at first yours is borrowed: generous spending, parents' help, a life a little wider than income allows. The Hanged Man teaches something else — patience. Put off what you want, invest in the family, work for the future, give up debts. Abundance comes later, but it's your own. The Hermit shows how easy it is afterwards to tip into stinginess.

For three whole years you lived more modestly than you were used to: no loans, no help from parents, one car between two. Friends didn't understand. In those three years you paid off every debt and saved a deposit. You furnished the flat gradually, a room a year, and every item in it was chosen with pleasure. **The abundance you waited for proved sweeter than the borrowed kind.**

The Hermit can turn patience into a habit of skimping on everything. Prosperity has come, but you're afraid to enjoy it: every expense is questioned, each has their own stash, and you discuss plans less and less. The house is full, but there's less warmth. The Empress in you expects abundance to be used: leave room in the budget for joys and share your plans with each other.

items.title: A harvest with no hiding places

captions.L: Generosity beyond your means
captions.R2: Patience and investments for years
captions.R: Wealth that exists only on paper

items.meaning: Your generosity becomes abundance through patience and long-term investment — and is lost in wealth that's only on paper.
text: Generosity beyond your means is your starting difficulty: the Empress loves living lavishly, and income can't keep up. The Hanged Man suggests a different rhythm: patience, the ability to postpone joy, investments that ripen over years. The harvest comes later, but rich. And the Moon sets up hiding places at the end, where abundance can quietly leak away.

Instead of the long trip you'd saved two years for, you put the savings into a tiny studio flat to let, and the relatives were baffled. Five years later there were three flats, and now you travel on the income from them without touching your salaries. **One postponed celebration turned into a dozen future ones.**

The Moon paints an illusion of wealth. Three flats look like capital, but you have less free money than it seems from outside: repairs on one, interest on the second, tax on the third, and any month without tenants punches a hole in the budget. Meanwhile the Empress's generosity spends as if it all paid for itself long ago, and trips are bought against rent that hasn't come in yet. Count not what the flats are worth but your free money each month, and keep a reserve to last six months without a single tenant.

items.title: Abundance seized with grip

captions.L: Generosity that outruns income
captions.R2: Ambition, zest and well-paid work
captions.R: Spending all that comes in, growing apart

items.meaning: Your generosity finds support in ambition and hard work — and doesn't leak as long as spending doesn't become extravagance.
text: The Empress holds the first and last points of your money line: you're generous, love comfort, presents, abundance. At first this abundance leans on someone else's shoulder or a credit card. The Devil in the middle gives it grip: ambition, zest, readiness to work a lot and hard when it pays well, extra earnings, investments. The wish to live richly becomes an engine rather than a hole in the budget.

You always wanted a beautiful life, but for a long time lived on credit. One day you decided to earn it yourselves: one became a site foreman with bonuses for deadlines, the other set up a mobile kitchen for parties. Two years without days off, but then a flat, a car and a holiday paid for to the penny. **The grip you aimed at your dream of a beautiful life is what paid for it.**

The second Empress pulls towards extravagance. Once money starts coming, you want everything at once: a renovation, presents, restaurants, help for all the relatives. Money earned hard goes easily. There's also a risk of unequal growth: if one works flat out while the other keeps the home, dependence and resentment appear in time. Spend generously, but to a plan, and make sure both have their own fulfilment.

items.title: Grip that wasn't sacrificed

captions.L: Generosity that income can't cover
captions.R2: Thrill, ambition and a grip on money
captions.R: Giving away what you earn and losing your own

items.meaning: Your generosity gains a grip and brings money — and it leaks away when earnings are given away out of guilt.
text: Your generosity runs ahead of income: the Empress loves giving, having guests, living beautifully. The Devil gives it teeth — ambition, a taste for risk, a readiness to take on the hard and well-paid, a second income, bold investments. That's how generosity starts to feed itself. The Hanged Man waits where earnings are again handed out to anyone who asks.

For years you helped friends find flats for free — simply because you were better at it than anyone. Once you admitted it was work, you got an estate agent's licence and took your first commission. Now your agency has five staff, and friends still get a discount. **The grip you allowed to take money turned generosity into income.**

Awkwardness about earnings pushes you to give it away: loans to relatives with no deadline, discounts for friends, money for others' troubles. Sometimes one carries it all while the other endures and stores up resentment. Generosity is wonderful until it becomes sacrifice: decide how much you give, and don't be ashamed to keep the rest.

items.title: Generosity with grip and a lock

captions.L: Spending lavishly and on credit
captions.R2: Grip and the thrill of big earnings
captions.R: Miserly order and fear of the new

items.meaning: Luxury you charge a real price for brings big money — until what you've earned is put under lock and key.
text: A generous life suits you: the Empress loves comfort, gifts, abundance, even when there's no money for them yet. The Devil teaches you to charge a real price for beauty: not to be shy of the expensive, to set the value of your work and to work as much as it takes to justify it. Luxury you gave away becomes luxury you sell. The World closing the line tends to lock your earnings in a fortress with suspicious guards.

The wedding dresses one of you sewed for friends were lavish and almost free. When you decided to charge a real price and opened a bridal salon, the relatives gasped at the price tag. The brides didn't: appointments are booked a year ahead, and the salon dresses weddings in three counties. **The luxury you finally charged full price for became your wealth.**

The World at the exit loves to lock things up. Earnings sit under lock and key, the new collection is put off — “what if nobody buys?”, trial fabric has to be accounted for, and the friends you once sewed for almost free are now shy even to ask a price. The generosity everything began with leaves the home, and the salon starts to look like a safe. Remember that wealth came to you through generosity and daring, and leave room for them in the budget now too.

items.title: Comfort dreamed up at night

captions.L: A generous home on credit
captions.R2: Creative work found by intuition

items.meaning: Your love of comfort becomes income when it finds creative work by intuition — if orders aren't chosen by heart alone.
text: You love comfort and don't stint on it, only at first the Empress's generosity outruns income, and the home is furnished on credit. The Moon shows another way: work grows out of a love of beauty — creative, found by intuition, sometimes strange to others. Your taste starts to feed you. The Lovers, though, choose orders with the heart — and not always profitably.

Guests first praised the lampshades one of you sewed for the bedroom, then asked to buy them. You started making them at night, choosing fabrics on instinct. Now the lampshades sell in two interior design shops, and clients wait a month for their turn. **The beauty you made for yourselves became your income.**

The Lovers choose orders with the heart, and that's expensive. A fabric you love gets bought even if it eats half the price, a lampshade for a friend is made at cost, and a dull but profitable order from a hotel is put off because it's “not about beauty”. Beauty grows in the workshop but the till doesn't, and every rent bill reminds you of that hotel order. Decide together how many orders a month you take for money — and let the rest be for love.

items.title: Beauty out of the dusk

captions.L: Spending on beauty on credit
captions.R2: Night-time inspiration and an unusual trade

items.meaning: Your love of beauty becomes income through a venture found on instinct — until success awakens greed.
text: Beauty around you matters to you, and you don't begrudge money on it — even money you don't have yet. The Empress is generous to comfort and things. The Moon suggests how to turn this love into earnings: trust your imagination, find a trade that's strange and beautiful, born at night, in quiet. But success wakes the Devil — with his thirst for more and his habit of measuring everything in money.

The dried flowers you gathered in summer and arranged in frames at night at first decorated only your own flat. Then friends' flats, then coffee shops. Now you have a botanical-art studio, and interior designers order whole series for their projects. **A night-time passion for beauty turned out to be the most beautiful way to earn.**

Appetite grows with the takings: you're tempted to push prices up shamelessly, to take on orders where you're asked to pass your work off as someone else's, to sit in the studio round the clock. Money starts distributing power at home, and generosity turns into leverage. Agree what sum you need and what for, and check every profitable deal for cleanness.

items.title: Abundance without borders

captions.L: Generous spending and parents' help
captions.R2: The wide world, savings and shared rules

items.meaning: Your generosity becomes prosperity in the wide world and under shared rules — if modesty doesn't then put a ceiling on it.
text: Abundance is your element, and at first the Empress keeps it going on generous spending and parents' help. The World shows where real abundance lies: in the wide world, where many people need your work, in savings that grow by themselves, in budget rules the two of you drew up. The Hermit reminds you that modesty can put a ceiling even on what's growing.

For years your knitted toys went to friends as presents. One day you put them on an international marketplace — and orders came from twenty countries. Now three knitters work in your workshop, and you put part of the income into funds that work by themselves. **Generosity grown from a circle of friends found a whole world of buyers.**

The Hermit puts up a ceiling: “we have enough.” A shop in Japan asks for a thousand toys for the holidays — you refuse, because you'd have to hire people and do the sums; a factory offers to license your patterns — too much bother. Modesty passes itself off as wisdom, and the generosity it all began with goes to everyone except your own business. Before refusing, work out together what you're losing: sometimes “enough” is just fear of more.

items.title: Abundance across the map

captions.L: Spending generously, relying on relatives
captions.R2: Distant markets and money that grows by itself

items.meaning: Your generosity found buyers all over the world and brings prosperity — if presents don't eat the earnings.
text: Abundance is dear to you, but you don't know how to keep it: the Empress spends generously, and at first relatives bail you out in hard months. The World widens the source: your taste, your skill, your generosity are needed not only by relatives and neighbours, and what you earn can grow by itself — in savings and in income that doesn't need you present. And the Moon brings a fog in which what's gathered is easily lost.

A visitor from Germany once saw the painted wooden spoons you gave all your relatives and ordered fifty for her shop. A year later orders come from five countries, and for the first time part of the income has gone into savings that grow by themselves. **The presents you shared so generously found buyers all over the world.**

The Moon confuses generosity with income. You send spoons to buyers abroad without prepayment, put an extra one in every parcel as a gift, pay delivery yourselves “for regulars” — and by the end of the year neither of you can say how much you actually earned. The business seems to be growing, yet no spare money appears. Work out what one spoon costs by the time it reaches the buyer's door, and decide together which generosity you can afford and which you no longer can.

items.title: Teachers of order

captions.L: Tight control and slow decisions
captions.R2: Mentoring, knowledge and family ways

items.meaning: Your strictness earns money when it becomes knowledge you share, and fails you when hoping for luck replaces it.
text: You're strict with money: everything under control, decisions slow, no exceptions. The Emperor gives order, but also heaviness — income grows reluctantly and life becomes dull. The Hierophant shows how to turn order into prosperity: teach it to others, pass on knowledge, build a way of life people are drawn to. The Wheel of Fortune waits to see whether you'll let go of the wheel once things get easier.

“You talk about money so calmly,” a friend said once after dinner. “Teach us.” In an hour you told them what you've done for years: envelopes, savings pots, a rule against borrowing. A month later six couples were sitting in your kitchen, then the meetings moved to the library. Today it's a paid course for families, and the words heard most often are “and we thought it was complicated”. **Your order began to feed you as soon as you started teaching it to others.**

The most dangerous moment is relief. When everything is running, strictness slackens: “we know how, we can relax.” A loan against a good year, an investment on someone's tip, spending you'd never have allowed yourselves before. The wheel turns, and order has to be built all over again. Keep your own rules in good years too: it's especially galling for a teacher to be caught out by what they warned their pupils about.

items.title: Order to be proud of

captions.L: Strictness and slow decisions
captions.R2: Knowledge, tradition and elders' recognition

items.meaning: Your strictness earns money through knowledge and tradition, and money leaks when success makes you arrogant.
text: The Emperor has accustomed you to strictness: considered decisions, firm rules, not a penny wasted. This protects but doesn't grow. The Hierophant shows how strictness turns into income: through knowledge, mentoring, tradition, a profession where order is respected. The Sun brings success — and the temptation to be proud of it.

Every Friday you have the same ritual: you phone the learners who took their test that week and write the result in a thick notebook. The town teases you for your strictness, but the notebook speaks for itself: almost everyone passes first time. One day the head of a neighbouring driving school leafs through it — and asks you to train his instructors. From that day you have a second job, and it pays better than the first. **The strictness you pass on to others became your best advertisement.**

The Sun and the Emperor easily make the best arrogant. Learners pass first time, other schools ask you to train their instructors, and you start talking down about colleagues, turning away “unpromising” learners and raising prices to weed out “the wrong ones”. The respect you earned through strictness goes faster than it came: recommendations are your main income, and people give them to those who are pleasant to deal with. Be proud of the result, not of yourselves.

items.title: Strictness shared fairly

captions.L: A habit of deciding alone
captions.R2: An honest agreement and accounts for two
captions.R: Two commanders fighting over the budget

items.meaning: Two strict people grow rich when their strictness becomes an honest agreement, not a fight between two commanders.
text: The Emperor greets you at the entrance to money and sees you off at the exit: you're both used to deciding, keeping rules and not giving way. Two fours add up to eight, and in the middle Justice shows how two strictnesses turn into income: an honest agreement where roles, contributions and rules are written down and clear to both. Then firmness serves the shared cause, not the argument.

For its first two years your joint wholesale business crackled with disputes: each considered themselves in charge. The way out was found on paper — a partnership agreement setting out areas of responsibility, profit sharing and how disputes are settled. The disputes ended, and turnover doubled. **An honest agreement between two commanders brought more than any victory in an argument.**

The second Emperor doesn't like sharing power. Even with an agreement, one of you pulls the budget their way: “leave this to me”. The other now gives way, now resists, and money is spent on the struggle. Go back to the agreement whenever an argument starts, and revise it when life changes.

items.title: Order that knows how to change

captions.L: Rigid rules and slow decisions
captions.R2: Accounts, contracts and always a plan B
captions.R: Fear of changing jobs, and one partner's growth

items.meaning: Your order earns money when it is honest and flexible — and fails you when it's used to change nothing.
text: With money you're serious: “measure twice, cut once”, not a penny borrowed, decisions slow and final — that's how the Emperor runs the household. Sometimes this seriousness becomes narrowness: one way of earning, one opinion for two, no experiments. Justice turns strictness into an honest system — with contracts, accounts and a plan B. Death closes the line: every system demands change one day.

Friends envy your document folder: contracts, warranties, receipts, a five-year forecast. When one of you is offered a move to another company, you don't argue on emotion but open the folder and calculate: what you lose, what you gain, where you'll be in three years. The decision takes an evening, not six months. **Honest figures became your way of deciding, not an excuse for standing still.**

Letting go is hard for you. A job that stopped growing but is a pity to leave; a business that should be closed. Sometimes one of you grows while the other sees it as a threat to the order you built so carefully. And debts — when a stage ends, they're easily shifted onto the one who stays. Review your system once a year: what still works, what should be closed, who needs support right now.

items.title: Strict books, a merry loophole

captions.L: A hard hand and rigid decisions
captions.R2: Honest accounts and agreements on paper

items.meaning: Your strict order brings money when it becomes an honest system — and loses it when a careless hole opens up in it.
text: Strictness is your way of holding on to money: firm decisions, hard rules, and sometimes not enough flexibility — that's how the Emperor rules. Justice makes this strictness honest: accounts, contracts, a plan B, a clear price — and the system starts to feed you, not only to forbid. And at the very end the Fool laughs at all the rules.

Your building crew hands over each job with a folder of paperwork thicker than the contract itself: every estimate, every sign-off, every receipt. A big client, burned by previous contractors, chose you precisely for that folder and brought three more. **A folder of honest paperwork has won you more work than any advertising.**

The Fool creeps up unexpectedly — in the strictest system. One of you suddenly breaks loose: an expensive purchase without discussion, a trip on all the savings, work dropped because they're fed up. Strictness that leaves no room for freedom breeds such outbursts. Give freedom a lawful place in the budget — a small sum with no rules — and the outbursts will stop.

items.title: Firmness with a gentle grip

captions.L: Being categorical, deciding for years
captions.R2: Flexible strength and the art of agreement
captions.R: Racing for first place and reckless loans

items.meaning: Your firmness earns money when softened by flexible strength, and fails you when it becomes a race to be first.
text: You don't lack firmness: you make decisions for the long term and set rules once. The Emperor makes you reliable but inflexible — whatever doesn't fit the plan is rejected at once, and good opportunities with it. Strength teaches another firmness: gentle but tenacious. Negotiate where you could have commanded, find a way round, hold out through long bargaining. The Chariot kindles rivalry.

Talks over renting new premises had reached a dead end: the landlord wouldn't give an inch. Before, you'd have slammed the door. This time you offered something unexpected — to renovate the frontage at your own expense in exchange for three years at a fixed rent. The landlord agreed, and you saved more than the renovation cost. **A gentle grip got you what no amount of rigidity would have.**

The danger lies in competition. Once business takes off, you both want to be first: whose decision, whose project, who leads. The Chariot speeds the argument up into a race, and in the heat of it you might take a loan for a dash just to prove you're right. Money starts serving the argument. Divide the field: each has their own line of work, and big shared decisions are made only together and without haste.

items.title: A fortress with a back door

captions.L: Strictness that won't let you risk
captions.R2: Endurance and an unconventional move
captions.R: A sudden loss and a row mid-crisis

items.meaning: Your strictness becomes prosperity when flexible strength joins it, and a reserve takes the fear out of the sudden.
text: The Emperor builds your financial life like a fortress: strict rules, slow decisions, no debts. The difficulty is rigidity: a fortress can't turn, and good opportunities pass it by. Strength in the middle adds flexibility: find an unconventional solution, wait things out, save stubbornly, use what others overlooked. The Tower at the end of the line tests the walls.

When cuts began in your industry, you didn't wait your turn. One of you mastered a related speciality within six months, the other proposed to management that the department go remote and save on rent — and got a promotion. You lost less than others and came out of the crisis with two incomes instead of one. **Flexible strength inside solid walls — that's what feeds you.**

The sudden is this fortress's main exam. A market crash, a big client leaving, an unexpected expense — and the familiar order cracks. The Emperor inside you wants to keep everything as it was, which is sometimes impossible. A row in the thick of trouble is dangerous too: each pulls the wheel their way, and you lose time. Keep a separate pot for the unexpected, and agree in advance what you'll do if the walls shake.

items.title: Strictness softened by measure

captions.L: Commanding the budget and not giving way
captions.R2: Compromise, balance and living within means
captions.R: Money rows going round in circles

items.meaning: Your strictness becomes prosperity when softened by compromise — if the compromise holds through a quiet season too.
text: The Emperor makes you serious about money, but stubborn too: each is sure they know the right way and won't give way. The budget becomes a battlefield, and income grows slowly. Temperance shows the way: compromise, the middle ground, living within your means without fuss, joint decisions you both agree with. The Wheel of Fortune rocks your income and tests whether you'll keep your measure.

You stopped arguing about money after one rule: any decision bigger than a month's income is made only when each can explain the other's position better than their own. At first it took evenings, now minutes. Your purchases are rarely mistakes, and friends ask how you manage to live so evenly. **Compromise turned out to be the most profitable decision in your couple.**

The Wheel rocks not only your income but the peace between you. In a good season your rule works and there's nothing to argue about, but in a quiet one the old stubbornness returns: every expense becomes a reason for “I told you so”, and money talks go round the same circle. A compromise that's easy to keep in good months is tested in bad ones. Agree in advance how you decide in a downturn, and remember the rule before the mutual grievances.

items.title: Firmness that learned to yield

captions.L: Stubbornness and one opinion for two
captions.R2: Compromise, measure and patient growth

items.meaning: Your firmness earns money when it learns to yield — and doesn't stifle the growth of whoever is in the shade right now.
text: Giving way is hard for you: the Emperor makes each of you firm, and with money you often hear two “I've decided”s. Temperance teaches another language — compromise, the middle way, patient growth without dashes. Once you've learned to agree, income starts to grow. And the Sun, promising success, tests whether it will make you quarrel.

For two years you couldn't decide where to put your savings: one wanted a flat, the other a business. At last you split it: half into a flat to let, half into a small recording studio. Five years later both halves bring in income, and you laugh about the argument. **An argument split down the middle brought you two incomes instead of one.**

The Sun shines unequally. The recording studio has become well known, written about, while the flat to let is quiet income looked after by the other. The one in view starts speaking for both: “what do you need that for”, “we've got everything already”, when the other wants to study or start something of their own. Firmness returns disguised as care that confines. Share not only the income but the right to grow: each should have a stage of their own.

items.title: A star between two walls

captions.L: Rigid limits and slow decisions
captions.R2: Freedom for talent and recognition
captions.R: One controls everything and decides for two

items.meaning: Your strict order flanks talent on both sides and brings money when it lets it breathe, not when it keeps it framed.
text: The Emperor stands on both sides of your money line: strictness, rules, firm decisions — first as a difficulty, then as a habit that's hard to give up. Between them stands the Star: talent, inspiration, work people can see. That's exactly where money comes from, if the walls leave a window. The two fours add up to eight, and Justice trails behind to remind you of an honest division of power.

Calligraphy was one partner's hobby, while the other ran the family budget with an iron hand. When you dared to open a lettering studio for weddings and shop signs, strict accounting proved the best helper: estimates to the last decimal, deadlines met to the day. Today people come to you from other towns. **A strict frame helped your talent shine instead of locking it in.**

The second Emperor may take everything into his own hands. The order that helped the business becomes power: one decides how much to spend, where to invest, when to rest, and the other is left to create to a timetable. Inspiration dislikes that. Divide power no less honestly than profit: each with an area of decisions, and shared rules agreed together.

items.title: Strictness given a dream

captions.L: Rigid order with no room for dreams
captions.R2: Talent, inspiration and a name of your own

items.meaning: Your strict order earns money when it makes room for talent — and fails you when one is made to change.
text: Your order is strict: the Emperor holds the budget and decisions firmly, and there's little room for dreams in this system. The Star asks to be let in: talent, creativity, a name of your own, work that inspires. When order starts serving a dream, prosperity comes. Death warns that both order and roles will one day have to change.

Your strictness about contracts and money was once valued by creative people: you started keeping the books and handling contracts for artists and musicians who can't do it themselves. Today you have an agency protecting their rights, and one of you is finally writing the book they kept quiet about for twenty years. **Order in the service of others' talents woke your own.**

Death loves change, and the one who has just changed wants the same of the other. One is finally writing the book and says more and more often: “it's time you dropped your spreadsheets too, if I managed it.” The other's order is dear to them not out of fear but because it's their work. The pressure of “grow like me” costs more than any budget mistake: grievances, separate purses, quiet rivalry. Rejoice in each other's changes, but don't assign them.

items.title: Order for a free gift

captions.L: A rigid plan with no room for inspiration
captions.R2: A gift that's seen and valued
captions.R: Rules for one of you only

items.meaning: Your order helps talent bring in money — and you lose it when the rules are written only for the other.
text: Plan, budget and rules are your support: the Emperor is strict, and inspiration feels cramped in such a system. The Star asks for room: talent, creativity, a gift that can be shown to people. When strictness starts to serve talent, prosperity arrives. The Fool waits at the end of the line and laughs at the rules — even the ones you made up yourselves.

One of you has drawn comics since childhood, while the other worked in a bank all their life and loved spreadsheets. Together you drew up a plan: an issue a month, a subscription, sales at festivals, an account of every penny. Three years later the comic has ten thousand subscribers and a publishing contract. **One partner's spreadsheet and the other's fantasy earned more together than apart.**

The Fool laughs at the rules he made himself. The one who keeps the spreadsheet watches the other's every penny — a report on paints, a cap on festivals — while slipping their own “little things” past: a new laptop, a trip with friends “on business”, dinner on the project. The other notices and starts spending out of spite. The plan that got you out holds only while it's the same for both. Let the rules be shared, and exceptions apply to both at once.

items.title: A strict heir

captions.L: Commanding alone and not asking for help
captions.R2: A family business and the support of kin
captions.R: Cancelling a dream for the farm's sake

items.meaning: Your strictness brings money in a family business — until the family's cause cancels one of your dreams.
text: You don't ask for help: the Emperor decides alone and doesn't listen to advice. Judgement shows that strength isn't in solitude: kin, family, the elders' business with their experience and connections. Strictness that serves the family business brings prosperity more reliably than any independence. The Chariot demands full speed from the family business — and from both of you too.

You took over one partner's father's farm when he decided to rest. Order, accounts, contracts with shops — and three years on, the farm brings in a steady income for the first time, while the father proudly tells the neighbours about his “managers”. **The children's strictness with the accounts breathed new life into the father's farm.**

The Chariot demands that the farm run at full speed, and demands it of you both. The one who grew up there thinks it natural to give it every weekend and holiday, while the other once meant to pursue their own work and remembers it less and less. The father is pleased, debts aren't growing, but one dream in your couple has been quietly cancelled for someone else's. Expand out of profit, and write each of your goals into the farm plan on a par with the harvest.

items.title: A family fortress

captions.L: Rigid rules and solo decisions
captions.R2: Family, kin and a legacy that grows
captions.R: A sudden blow to the family business

items.meaning: Your strictness earns money when it serves the family and its business — as long as not everything is in one business.
text: Strictness is in your character: the Emperor decides firmly, keeps rules and dislikes advice. At first this makes the couple lonely with money — doing everything yourselves, without support. Judgement shows where to find support: the family line, a family business, a legacy you can not only receive but multiply. Order that serves the family brings prosperity. The Tower keeps the sudden in reserve.

The strict order you brought into the family greenhouses outraged the elders at first: “we've always done it the homely way.” Three years later the greenhouses turned a profit for the first time, and cousins adopted your spreadsheets and schedules on their own holding. **Order brought into the family business multiplied the family's legacy.**

The Tower strikes unexpectedly: a failed harvest, a breakdown, a key buyer leaving — and the family business is under attack. The Emperor in you reaches to restore the old order, but sometimes you need to rebuild fast. It's dangerous too that there's no reserve: everything is invested in the business. Put money aside separately for the unexpected, and agree within the family who does what if trouble comes.

items.title: Secured with three locks

captions.L: Fear of overspending and elders' advice
captions.R2: A system, stable income and savings pots
captions.R: Secret stashes and a tally of who paid what

items.meaning: Your money rests on three locks — tradition, system, honest accounts — as long as they don't lock you from each other.
text: Your money line is made of the most reliable energies. The Hierophant gives thrift and respect for tradition, the Emperor a system, Justice honest accounts. The difficulty at the start is fear: an extra expense seems a mistake, relatives watch that things are done “properly”, and for a long time the couple dares nothing new. Yet prosperity comes precisely through the system: reliable income, separate pots for goals, decisions taken once and for a long time.

Your budget is like a small state: a treasurer, a plan for the year, a separate account for every goal, a report at the end of each quarter. Friends chuckle, then come for advice when they can't afford a holiday. Ten years on there are no debts, there's a flat of your own and a second one you let. **The order your friends laughed at made you the best-off of the lot.**

The weak spot is locks hung against each other. Honest accounts become a ledger of grievances: who put in how much, who spent more on themselves. Stashes appear — not from need but from mistrust. Or one decides not to work because “that's fair”, while the other pulls the load and silently seethes. Keep the order shared: a transparent budget, personal sums for both, and a conversation when contributions are unequal.

items.title: A fortress too small for dreams

captions.L: Living “like everyone” and fearing spending
captions.R2: Systematic income and clear savings pots
captions.R: A dream breaking out in a splurge

items.meaning: Your order builds solid prosperity if it has room for talent and dreams — otherwise they break out in costly splurges.
text: You live “like everyone else”: the Hierophant taught caution, elders' advice and fear of overspending. The Emperor carries this into practice: a stable job, systematic income, an account for every purpose, not a penny borrowed. Prosperity is built solidly, like a fortress. The Star at the end of the line reminds you what the fortress lacks — dreams and talent.

Your budget spreadsheet is a source of pride: five pots, a ten-year plan, a monthly report. The flat was paid off early, and there's a year's cushion in the account. When the neighbours across the landing take out a loan for a holiday, you go on your savings and come back with no debts. Friends ask you to teach them. **The system you built holds your prosperity more firmly than any luck.**

The fortress hides what the Star speaks of. Talents lie idle, dreams are put off “until retirement”, and then they break out in a splurge: one evening one of you spends half a pot on a synthesiser and recording the songs they kept quiet about for ten years, and the other doesn't know whether to be angry or glad. A splurge is a dream that found no legitimate place. Set up a separate pot for the dream in your system — then it won't break the others.

items.title: From the rulebook to the road

captions.L: Keeping to rules until they slow you down
captions.R2: Getting several ventures moving at once
captions.R: Carrying everything and holding the purse

items.meaning: Prosperity comes to you on the move, when rules serve the road instead of keeping you at the gate.
text: Your first money comes carefully, by the rules: an official job, a clear position, the elders' “don't take risks”. The Hierophant gives the couple support but also holds you at the gate: you're afraid to spend too much, afraid to leave a job the family approved. Prosperity comes when the Chariot rolls out through the gate — ventures, travel, several projects at once. And Strength decides who drives this cart and whether they'll overstrain themselves.

For years one of you has kept the books at the same firm, while the other mends the neighbours' bikes at weekends. One day you count: there are more bike jobs than weekends. Six months later you have a van, a pitch by the park and a summer rental service, and the bookkeeping now serves your own accounts. Knowing how things work becomes the map, and the Chariot drives along it. **Money comes to you on the road: the more roads you open together, the fuller the till.**

The leak starts with the reins. Once business picks up, one of you takes full control: works without days off, decides alone what to spend on, and hands the other money by the rules — “this much for the household”. It looks like care and strong character, but a quiet rivalry grows at home: who's in charge here and whose contribution counts more. It's better to drive together and sometimes let go: a shared day off without client calls costs less than lost respect.

items.title: Your own road, no family feud

captions.L: Waiting for the elders' approval at every step
captions.R2: Your own business, the road and many projects
captions.R: Inheritance quarrels and a squandered reserve

items.meaning: Money comes to you on a road you chose yourselves, and leaks into family disputes over who is owed what.
text: The Hierophant taught you to consult your elders: what job to choose, how much to save, what's “right”. While you wait for approval, income stands still. The Chariot pulls you out of this waiting: your own business, moves, several projects, speed. Prosperity begins where you drive your own road. Judgement at the end of the line holds a family past that knows how to make itself felt.

The uncle who scolded you loudest for “throwing away a good position” comes into the workshop on a Saturday, walks between the workbenches for a long time, runs his hand over the worktops and finally says: “Will you make me a kitchen? For money, like everyone.” You laugh all the way home: for two years you worked without days off — orders by day, exhibitions in the evening, trips for materials to neighbouring counties on Saturdays — and never once went to the relatives for approval. **Your speed became income when you stopped asking permission.**

An inheritance, the division of a flat, grievances over help someone got and someone didn't — strength and savings go into wrangling. And within the couple a reluctance to keep a joint budget may appear: each has “their own”, and nobody knows how much you actually have. Settle family matters by the law and calmly, and keep your own budget joint and transparent.

items.title: Family ways meet a lucky break

captions.L: Spending only “the way it's done”
captions.R2: A chance, a change, a lucky turn
captions.R: Managing your partner's money out of care

items.meaning: Your order keeps money safe, and change makes it grow — as long as family rules don't become control of the other's purse.
text: The Hierophant meets you at the entrance and waits at the very end of the line, so the theme of rules sounds twice over for the couple. You spend “as is proper”, save, listen to your elders, keep a joint budget. Two fives together make ten — and the Wheel of Fortune stands right in the middle: prosperity comes not from thrift in itself but from a chance that your order lets you take.

The owner of a farm shop happens to taste your jam, made to your grandmother's recipe, and orders a batch. You don't throw yourselves headlong into production: you keep to the recipe, work out how much the kitchen can handle, register everything properly. A couple of years later you have your own brand, and the family jars sell in three towns. **A lucky turn becomes yours because your family ways were ready for it.**

The same five at the end of the line shows its other side. Order easily turns into guardianship: one of you starts managing the other's money — “I know better what it's for”, “you don't need that”. Or relatives enter the couple's budget with their demands and disputes over inheritance, and your strength goes into family wrangling instead of earning. The rules of your family are written by the two of you; relatives can only advise.

items.title: Old rules, a new city

captions.L: Clinging to one secure job
captions.R2: A move and an unexpected offer

items.meaning: Prosperity comes with a turn of fate, and balance keeps it: neither partner lives as the other's dependant.
text: You are drawn to what is secure: one job for years, a clear salary, the elders' advice “leave well alone”. The Hierophant protects the couple from adventures but locks your income in one place. The Wheel of Fortune brings what wasn't in the plan: an offer, a move, an unexpected buyer. Temperance watches the scales — so that after the turn the couple doesn't end up with one breadwinner and one dependant.

One of you is offered a post in another city. Parents object, friends shake their heads. You weigh it for a week and decide to go, but in your own way: with a two-year contract, savings set aside and a plan for the other to find work within six months. A year later the salary is twice what it was, and the flat is one you couldn't have afforded before. **A turn of fate brings you money if you take your own order along for the road.**

The leak appears in an imbalance. After the move one earns everything while the other is still finding their feet — and a tally quietly begins: who supports whom, who spends how much, who has to ask permission. Or you start showing off your prosperity: a new car, holiday photos for the relatives back home. Keep the balance through deeds: each has their own money for their own needs and their own occupation, even if it earns little for now.

items.title: Leaving the family track

captions.L: Working where the family always has
captions.R2: Closing one stage and starting another
captions.R: A principle the other pays for

items.meaning: Money flows in when you leave the well-worn family track, and stays while the accounts between you are honest.
text: Your way into money was laid by your elders: a profession chosen for you, a job “like Dad's”, the certainty that no place is safer. The Hierophant gives support but keeps you in a track where income stopped growing long ago. Death opens the road to prosperity through a decisive ending: leave what no longer feeds you and start something else. Justice demands that the transition be honest — without debts or grievances.

For fifteen years one of you has taught at the same school where their mother and grandmother taught. The decision to leave ripens slowly but is taken in one evening: you sit down and honestly reckon what those fifteen years were worth and what the next ones could be. Six months later — your own exam-preparation courses, twice as many students and three times the money. **A new life cost you less than eternal loyalty to the old one.**

Justice at the end of the line tests the transition for honesty. While the courses were gathering students, the other carried all the bills, and the one who left the school refused any side work “on principle”: they hadn't left only to work for others again. A fine principle, but one person pays for it, and the tally of who put in how much grows louder. Agree on a date until which one carries the load, and on what the other does if by then the new venture still isn't paying.

items.title: A new life, no gilding

captions.L: Clinging to the accepted and approved
captions.R2: A bold end to the old stage
captions.R: One dream in the shadow of another

items.meaning: Prosperity comes when you dare to end what the elders approved — if one partner's dream doesn't eclipse the other's.
text: Your first money was earned “as is proper”: in a profession that was approved, by rules nobody questioned. The Hierophant holds you in that track, reliably and dully. Death opens the door: finish, let go, change — and that's where growth begins. The Star gives the new life a dream and a sparkle, but not always an affordable one.

On the day you were offered promotion at the bank where you'd spent twelve years, you turned it down and handed in your notice. Six months later you have a small school for adults learning to draw from scratch, and the students bring their friends. Income didn't rise at once, but it rose. **Leaving the approved path, you found one that pays more.**

The Star shows the other side of a dream too: not everyone gets room for theirs. The drawing school is the dream of the one who left the bank, while the other handles the timetable, advertising and accounts and remembers their own old wish — a pottery studio — less and less. Talking about it feels awkward: all your strength and money are in the shared business now. A dream built on the other's postponed dream will one day turn bitter. Find room in the budget and the timetable for the second one too, however small for now.

items.title: Rebuilding the family home

captions.L: Keeping the old even when it's in the way
captions.R2: Building, renovation and big shared investments
captions.R: Building on one, housework on the other

items.meaning: Your prosperity grows where the old stood — when you tear down what has outlived itself and chores don't fall to one.
text: You hold on to the tried and tested: your parents' old flat, a familiar job, the advice “don't touch what works”. The Hierophant protects but also holds you back. The Tower breaks this order — and it is through the Tower that prosperity comes: rebuilding, renovation, construction, a new life on the site of a collapsed old one. Strength tells you the price: a persistence that easily tips into overstrain.

You inherit an old house with a leaking roof, and relatives advise selling it for a song. For three years you build it yourselves: dismantling, relaying, learning from the carpenter next door, living on one salary and putting the other into materials. The house is now worth three times as much, and you let half of it. **You build wealth literally: from ruins, by hand and by rules the two of you invented.**

Strength goes entirely into the building. One of you spends every evening and weekend on the scaffolding, and everything else — cooking, bills, relatives, the job that pays — silently falls to the other. There's no help at home “because I'm building, aren't I”, and each new stage is paid for not only with money but with the other's exhaustion. Money goes in, respect leaks out. Write up not only the building budget but the chores for the duration — and share them fairly.

items.title: Break a rule, save the family

captions.L: Living by the family's old rules
captions.R2: Decisive rebuilding and a big project

items.meaning: Prosperity comes when you dare to rebuild what was established — and isn't lost as long as change breeds no family lawsuits.
text: Family rules are firm for you: how to earn, where to live, what counts as reliable. The Hierophant protects the couple and keeps it in the old ways. The Tower breaks the established order — and prosperity comes through the break: a move, a rebuild, a shared venture undertaken against habit. Judgement waits at the end and reminds you that changes touch the whole family.

Your parents' fabric shop in the town centre was quietly dying: fewer and fewer customers, higher and higher rent. You proposed something unthinkable to the elders — close it and open a made-to-measure tailoring studio in the same place. Six months of arguments, a year of renovation, and now clients book a month ahead. **A broken rule saved the family business.**

Changes in a family business don't pass without a trace. One relative feels their share has lost value, another recalls how much they once put in. Disputes over inheritance and the right to a say take both time and money, and within the couple a wish may appear to keep “family” money separate from shared. Put shares and agreements with relatives on an official footing before the money starts coming in.

items.title: Light within the family ways

captions.L: Being modest and doing “what's done”
captions.R2: Success, recognition and a shared business

items.meaning: Your way of life brings prosperity when it lets each of you shine, and fails you when there's still no joint budget.
text: The Hierophant stands twice on your money line, and tradition is in your blood: live honestly, modestly, “as is done”, consult your elders. This protects, but it also hides the couple in the shade. The Sun in the middle brings you into the light: recognition, success, a shared business where each is fulfilled, family prosperity you needn't be shy of. Two fives make ten — and luck follows those who've stepped into the light.

For many years you ran the family joinery workshop quietly: orders through acquaintances, prices like grandfather's. When you first show your tables at a city exhibition, they sell out in a day, and a design magazine asks for an interview. Now architects queue for you, and you set your own prices. **The family craft began to shine once you stopped hiding it.**

The second Hierophant keeps the old ways in the purse too. The workshop has long been yours, but money is still kept “like grandfather did”: takings in one box, personal money in another, each with their own savings, and no joint budget. Nobody knows how much you actually earn, and an argument over a big purchase becomes a dispute over whose money it is. Bring everything into one clear set of accounts, and leave each a sum to manage alone.

items.title: Modesty's time to shine

captions.L: Keeping your heads down, living “as is proper”
captions.R2: Each fulfilled, success in plain view

items.meaning: Prosperity comes when modesty gives way to each one's bright fulfilment — without showy glitter or lopsided spending.
text: You were taught to keep your heads down: work honestly, live “as is proper”, spend nothing extra. The Hierophant protects the couple by keeping it in the shade: you work conscientiously, but hardly anyone has heard of it. The Sun leads to prosperity through light: recognition, each one's fulfilment, work that can be seen. Temperance tests at the end whether you'll keep measure once things grow bright.

For seven years your bakery ran without a sign: “those who know will find it”. One day you take the plunge — a new sign, a shop window, a stall at the town fair, where your bread wins a prize. A month later there's a queue at the door and restaurants are asking for deliveries. **The light you were so shy of turned out to be the best advert for honest work.**

When things grow bright, you want to dazzle. A new car, a renovation you tell the relatives about, expensive presents for the holidays — prosperity starts being shown off. And a tilt appears in the couple: one wants to finally live a little, the other still saves every penny, and each thinks the other is wrong. Keep to the middle: part of income for joy, part for the reserve, and not a single purchase for others' eyes.

items.title: Free-range pupils

captions.L: Living by rules others chose
captions.R2: Unusual work and a bold beginning
captions.R: Loose ends: taxes, debts, settling up

items.meaning: You earn more when you turn off the prescribed path onto your own unusual one — and leave no debts behind you.
text: Your rules were once handed to you ready-made: a profession, a post, a career ladder. The Hierophant keeps the couple on this ladder, where everything is clear and income grows slowly. The Fool suggests jumping off: do what isn't done, start from scratch, turn what seemed a pastime into work. Justice meets you at the end of the road with the bill.

For years you ran negotiation trainings dully, by the manual. One day in a session you offer improvisation instead of a lecture, and the group laughs till they cry for the first time. You take the risk and open your own improvisation studio for companies. Two years later there are more orders than you can take. **The manual you set aside turned out to pay better than all the years of working by it.**

Freedom likes to leave loose ends. A tax you forgot, a contract you didn't put in writing, money borrowed from friends “for the start” and not repaid on time — Justice remembers it all. A tally can appear in the couple too: one took the risk, the other is still employed and pays for everything. Keep accounts from the very start of your freedom, and settle obligations before you spend on the new.

items.title: Skipping class for your own work

captions.L: Obeying the rules and avoiding risk
captions.R2: Freedom, lightness and an unusual path

items.meaning: Your income grows when you allow yourselves freedom instead of “as is proper” — and leaks into chasing easy money.
text: You were brought up on rules: study well, work in your profession, listen to your elders. The Hierophant keeps the couple in a frame where income grows slowly and predictably. The Fool suggests skipping class: try what nobody expected of you, start from scratch, live on your own schedule. The Star lights the end of the road — beautifully, and dangerously.

For a long time engineering degrees with honours defined your life: stable posts, a clear career. One day you take unpaid leave and build a wooden guest cabin on your plot in the country — just to try. The cabin is booked six months ahead. Now you have three such cabins, and you design them for others. **The freedom you allowed yourselves earned more than the rules.**

The Star lures with easy money. After the first success it seems it can always be like this: a course in “passive income in a month”, an investment in someone else's cabins at a “sure return” on an acquaintance's advice, a free project “for exposure” that eats half the season. The freedom you allowed yourselves doesn't promise a free lunch — it promises only your own work. Check every “quick and easy” as strictly as you'd check a drawing, and spend from what you've earned, not from the future.

items.title: A love that knows how to grow

captions.L: Choosing with your heart, then regretting it
captions.R2: Shared goals and patient growth

items.meaning: Your feelings become prosperity when they turn into shared goals and growth, not discontent with what you have.
text: Feelings colour your money from both sides: the Lovers open the line and close it. You choose work with your hearts, spend by mood, give generously. The Empress in the middle shows what this love can grow into: shared goals, a home, investments, growth in which each is fulfilled in their own way. Prosperity comes when feelings start to grow things, not only to spend.

You drew up your first joint budget on a café napkin, laughing — and on it you wrote three goals: a flat, studies for one, a studio of their own for the other. The napkin has hung on the fridge for five years. Two of the three goals are done, the third is under way. **Love written down as shared goals turned out to be the most reliable investment.**

The second Lovers are for ever unhappy with income. Two of three goals done, yet it feels as though you live worse than people you know: one couple's car is newer, another's holidays further away. “You could earn more” sounds like a joke at first, then in earnest, and any expense becomes a dispute over who brings in how much. The napkin on the fridge reminds you that the goals were yours, not other people's: check yourselves against it, not against the neighbours.

items.title: Abundance without a leash

captions.L: Spending for love, without counting
captions.R2: Shared growth and generous investment in the future
captions.R: Money as power, reproaches over earnings

items.meaning: Your love grows abundance, as long as money doesn't become one partner's power or a measure of who's worth more.
text: You spend for love: the Lovers don't count when they want to give pleasure.
