The Empress turns this generosity into growth: a shared home, investment in the future, plans, prosperity that increases year after year. The more you grow together, the less you need to count. And the Devil reminds you that abundance can turn into a chain.

In the early years your money went on presents and trips. Everything changed with the purchase of a small plot out of town — “just for weekends”. In five years a greenhouse, a guest cabin and a garden grew on it, and letting the cabin covers half your expenses. **Love invested in something shared began to bear a harvest.**

The Devil turns abundance into a lever. When there's more money, whoever brings in the bulk starts deciding for both and reminding the other of it. The other hears “you don't earn much” and feels in debt. The temptation of more — at any price — appears too. Agree that what's shared belongs to both, and that each one's contribution isn't measured in money alone.

items.title: Money likes a conversation

captions.L: Torn between work you love and a salary
captions.R2: Connections and decisions made together
captions.R: Shutting yourself away with a money worry

items.meaning: Your income grows from choices made together and dries up where one of you handles money matters alone.
text: The Lovers open your money line and lead it to prosperity, so everything hinges on choice. At first choice torments you: work you love or work that pays; spend now or save; say yes or wait for something better. Income jumps around because of it. But the same choice also leads to prosperity if you make it together. The Hermit shows where money leaks: into a silence in which each carries a worry alone.

A decision to change jobs ripens at your kitchen table: two people, a sheet of paper, two columns of pros and cons, and then a call to a friend who knows someone. Half your good money has come through people you both enjoy spending time with: shared dinners turn into orders, chatter at a friends' wedding into a new post. **Your best money is born in conversation: from “let's think it over together” and from friendships you don't trade on.**

The leak opens when the conversation stops. One of you has a bonus cut or gets an unpleasant letter from the bank and decides not to worry the other — they'll cope alone. For a week, a month, they tighten their belt, turn down outings that cost money, and grow quiet and prickly. The other feels the chill but doesn't know why. Have a simple rule: money trouble is talked about the same day, even if there is no solution yet.

items.title: Pretty, honest, nothing hidden

captions.L: Spending with your heart, not your head
captions.R2: Connections, taste and a shared passion
captions.R: Secret spending and illusions about money

items.meaning: Money comes to you through people and a taste for beauty, and goes into things unsaid: purchases nobody mentions.
text: You spend for love — of beautiful things, of friends, of each other: the Lovers stand both at the start of your line and in the middle. Hence the difficulty: decisions are made on impulse. But the same taste and the same sociability lead to prosperity: work where people and beauty matter, where clients come through acquaintances. The Moon casts a shadow: with money it's easy to start deceiving — yourselves and each other.

One of you has a gift for choosing clothes that make a person blossom, and the other knows half the town. You open a small vintage clothing shop, and the first customers are friends of friends. A couple of years later stylists and photographers come to you, and your fitting evenings have become a neighbourhood event. **Your taste and your people add up to an income that's a pleasure to earn.**

The Moon hides spending. Something bought on impulse is awkward to show, so the bag stays in the car and the receipt in a pocket. The credit-card debt grows quietly, and to the question “how are we doing for money?” comes “fine”. The illusion lasts until a letter from the bank arrives. There's no place for secrets here: each has their own sum for whims, and anything bigger is discussed in the light of day.

items.title: Mastery instead of dithering

captions.L: Trying everything, finishing nothing
captions.R2: Study and patient mastery
captions.R: A home used to buy off tiredness

items.meaning: Your income firms up when interest in everything becomes mastery in one, and time is left over for home.
text: Everything interests you — hence the difficulty: the Lovers pull you first to one pursuit, then another, and money scatters on courses, tools, unfinished projects. The Hermit suggests choosing and going deep — becoming masters people come to for quality. That's how prosperity comes. The Empress spends it on home and comfort — sometimes more than there is.

Out of your three passions — knitting, drawing and gardening — one day you choose one. The garden. Five years of study, a greenhouse of your own, rare varieties — and now people come to you for seedlings from neighbouring counties, and in spring you lecture at the botanical garden. Knitting and drawing haven't gone anywhere: they live in your weekends, not your budget. **You chose one thing — and that's what started to feed you.**

A garden that feeds you knows no days off. In spring the seedlings keep you both busy from morning till night, in summer there are fairs, in autumn lectures, and the house runs to the greenhouse's timetable: repairs are put off, meals eaten on the run, guests come only for seedlings. The Empress asks for comfort and time for two, and when there's none, money goes on buying off the tiredness: expensive furniture “so at least home is nice”, food deliveries, new clothes. Keep one day in the season when the greenhouse is closed to everyone, you included.

items.title: Choose one and go deep

captions.L: Grabbing at everything you like
captions.R2: Going deep into one thing and mastering it
captions.R: Sacrificing your own for another's purse

items.meaning: Prosperity comes when, out of many passions, you choose one and go deep into it, without sacrificing yourselves.
text: You like too many things, and money scatters because of it: photography courses, then pottery, then a part-time job in a café because the people there are nice. The Lovers make choosing hard — every road beckons. The Hermit leads to prosperity through depth: choose one thing and go into it for years. The Hanged Man marks the quietest leak: sacrifices nobody asked of you.

Out of a dozen passions the two of you keep one — antique books. One learns to restore bindings, the other gets to know editions and prices. Five years of slow work, and people start bringing you books from other cities, while collectors join a waiting list. **Curiosity that has chosen one road brings you more than ten open doors.**

You both know how to sacrifice, and it costs a lot. One of you puts their own plans aside for the other's business, quits their job to help, and quietly stores up resentment: “I gave everything.” Or you lend to friends and relatives who are in no hurry to repay. There's a third trouble too: savings lie as dead weight because you're afraid to use them. Let each have their own work and their own money, and help others only up to a sum you won't miss.

items.title: Depth instead of scatter

captions.L: Torn between desires
captions.R2: Study, depth and rare expertise

items.meaning: Prosperity comes to you from depth, not scatter, and lasts as long as you trust each other without demanding accounts.
text: You want this, and that, and something else besides: the Lovers pull you between desires, and money trickles away into everything at once. The Hermit calls you where it's dull at first: study, go deep, become an expert in one thing. That's exactly where prosperity comes. The World closes the line with a question of trust: will what you've gathered become a fortress where everyone watches everyone?

Coffee, travel and talk about food were long just spending for you. One day you decide to study seriously: one of you coffee roasting, the other the tea trade. Some years later you run tastings for cafés and companies, and friends ask you what to give as presents. **Your tastes became a profession when you stopped grabbing at everything and chose to learn.**

The order the World guards sometimes goes too far. Every expense must be explained, every new proposal meets suspicion, and “the old is better than the new” becomes the family motto. One starts demanding accounts, the other hiding purchases. Trust each other with at least part of the budget without checks, and once a year review the rules you set long ago.

items.title: The patience of two lovers

captions.L: Waiting for work you'll love at once
captions.R2: Patience, service and unhurried growth

items.meaning: Choosing with your hearts brings prosperity once patience joins in: money comes to those who know how to wait.
text: You want to work where you like it and spend on what's pleasant: the Lovers hold both ends of your money line. Two sixes make twelve, and in the middle stands the Hanged Man — patience. Prosperity comes not at the first wish but to those ready to serve their work for a long time, respect any job, and not borrow for a quick joy.

For its first three years your shoe-repair shop brought in exactly enough to pay the rent. Friends advised you to give up. You carried on: took any job, paid suppliers on the dot and never promised clients the impossible. In the fourth year there are queues, and a fashionable shop in the centre sends you all its repairs. **Patience that looked like stubbornness from outside was your capital.**

Impatience returns as soon as money appears: you want everything at once — a present, a trip, new furniture — and what was saved over years of waiting goes in a month. And in a hard season comes the grumble: “how long can we wait”. Agree what share of each income goes on joy and what on the future, and keep that ratio in any mood.

items.title: Serving the work, not a whim

captions.L: Spending and choosing by mood
captions.R2: Patience, service and honest work

items.meaning: Your income grows through patient service to your work, not whims, and leaks when people's trust starts being sold.
text: Choosing is hard for you and spending easy: the Lovers make earning a matter of mood, and income ebbs and flows with your feelings. The Hanged Man offers an unexpected path — patience and service. Work where people need you, discipline, payments on time, giving up quick joys for the future. And the Devil tempts with shortcuts.

For seven years you've run classes for older people learning to use phones and banking apps. The pay is small, but everyone comes — with neighbours, friends, grandchildren. One day a bank offers you a contract to train its customers across the region. **The patience with which you served people turned into your most generous order.**

The Devil arrives with the big order. The bank pays generously, but one day asks you, by the way, to recommend its savings accounts and insurance to your pupils, promising a percentage on every signed form. People trust you — everything you've built rests on that. The temptation looks innocent, and one of you is already working out what to spend the bonus on. Hold on to what brought you prosperity: you teach, you don't sell.

items.title: Passion turned into income

captions.L: Income that follows your mood
captions.R2: Ambition and hard, well-paid work

items.meaning: Your wish to live better becomes income when it turns into shared ambition, not nitpicking over spending.
text: For a long time your earnings depend on mood: you like the job — you try hard; you go off it — you leave, and the purse swings with your feelings. The Lovers at the start make money a matter of the heart. The Devil gives that heart grip: strong desire, ambition, readiness for hard work that pays well. The Hermit closes the line with a stern eye on the other's spending.

Tired of salaries that never rise, you take the plunge into selling country houses on commission. The first year is hard: viewings at weekends, refusal after refusal. Then the thrill takes over, and you start playing one game: one finds buyers, the other gets the houses ready to show. **Your ambition earns money when you share one “I want” and one game.**

The Hermit turns money into an excuse for nitpicking. The commission comes in, and each watches the other's purchases: “another takeaway coffee”, “why do you need a second jacket”, “do you know what that dinner cost”. The criticism sounds like care for the budget but lives on as quiet resentment, and the thrill you shared goes into a tally of trifles. Agree on a sum each can spend without comment, and discuss only big things — together and in private.

items.title: Passion with no dark corners

captions.L: Working only while you enjoy it
captions.R2: Strong desire and a grip on money

items.meaning: Your passion becomes income when it turns into clear ambition — and leaks into secrets and dubious deals.
text: For a long time your earnings depend on feelings: the Lovers let you work while you enjoy it and leave when you don't. The Devil turns feelings into grip: strong desire, readiness for hard and well-paid work, a second income, the thrill of growth. That's how prosperity comes. The Moon at the end of the line leaves dark corners where money disappears.

A passion for old motorcycles was long an expensive hobby for you. One day you decided it should pay its way: you restored two bikes and sold them to a collector for three times what you'd put in. Today you have your own workshop and a queue of clients, and work you love brings in more than your old salaries. **The passion you allowed to earn became your main income.**

Dark corners appear when the thrill leads to deals you'd rather not talk about: a dealer with no paperwork, payment off the books, a debt on a promise. One of you might keep spending or a loan secret, ashamed to admit it. A secret in money corrodes trust too. Let everything to do with shared money be transparent to both, even when it's unpleasant.

items.title: Instinct turned into a home

captions.L: Torn between jobs and desires
captions.R2: Your own work, found by instinct
captions.R: Hoarding beautiful things instead of money

items.meaning: Your income grows from work found by instinct, and melts away on shelves crammed with beautiful stock.
text: You dither between jobs as between two crushes: the Lovers won't let you choose, and money follows your mood. The Moon suggests leaning not on mood but on instinct — deeper, quieter, truer. Work of your own that you sensed, creative and unusual — that's where prosperity comes from. The Empress at the end of the line decides where it will flow.

After five jobs in three years, one day you noticed your best evenings were the ones spent sewing costumes for friends' parties together. You tried making some to order for a children's play — and three more theatres called. Now you have a costume workshop with orders booked a season ahead. **Instinct found what five jobs in a row hadn't.**

The Empress loves beautiful fabrics more than she counts them. Velvet “for the future”, lace too lovely to pass up, shelves stocked for three seasons — the workshop's money sits on racks, and in a month when theatres pay late you're asking your parents for the rent again. Keep the stockroom as strictly as the till: fabric is bought for an order, and “just beautiful” things come from a separate small sum.

items.title: Instinct instead of whim

captions.L: Choosing work by mood
captions.R2: A business of your own by intuition, and creativity
captions.R: Sacrificing yourselves and lending without count

items.meaning: Income grows when whim gives way to instinct: a quiet business feeds you until you give it away without count.
text: For a long time you choose work by mood: you like it — you take it on; you go off it — you leave, and the Lovers make income fickle. The Moon offers to lean on a deeper feeling — instinct. A business of your own found by feel rather than from a textbook; creative work; a quiet business grown from a present or a hobby. The Hanged Man closes the line and says where you give too much.

You started making candles as presents for friends — with scents chosen by instinct. Friends ordered for their friends, then cafés asked. Now you have a small workshop and an online shop, and you still devise new scents in the evenings, by instinct. **A present made on a hunch grew into a business that feeds you both.**

Here kindness easily becomes a leak. Discounts for friends, free for relatives, loans to anyone who asks, with no receipt and no deadline. Or one of you gives up their job to help with the other's business and quietly loses independence. Instinct will tell you where you're being used, if you listen to it. Set a price for your own people, and name each one's contribution aloud.

items.title: A choice made by instinct

captions.L: Torn between options
captions.R2: Trusting instinct and an unusual trade
captions.R: Freezing in success and shutting out the new

items.meaning: Your income finds its road when instinct, not mood, makes the choice — and doesn't freeze unless you lock up your success.
text: Choosing is torture for you: the Lovers offer several roads at once, and income goes where the doubts go. The Moon tells you what to trust — not mood but instinct: a quiet knowledge of which work is yours. The strange, the creative, the thing invented on a hunch — that's what feeds you. The World then gathers it all into a solid life and watches that it doesn't become a glass display case where nothing may be touched.

For three years you were torn between bank work and woodcarving classes. The answer came in a dream: one of you dreamed of a wooden mobile above a cot, and the next morning you sat down to carve it. Today your hanging mobiles sell in children's shops in three towns, and dreams still suggest the shapes. **Instinct chose for you better than all the lists of pros and cons.**

An established business tempts you to stop. The mobiles sell, the shops are happy, and when one of you dreams of a new shape again, the other replies: “they buy well as it is — why take risks?” Mocking the other's idea looks like caring for the budget, but it snuffs out the very instinct that feeds you. Give dreams their own line in the budget: a small yearly sum for trials that needn't be defended.

items.title: Love without borders

captions.L: Choosing work at the heart's bidding
captions.R2: The wide world and shared budget rules

items.meaning: Your feelings find income when they look wider than usual: the world gives you more if you don't spend it for others' eyes.
text: The heart decides a lot for you: where to work, what to spend on, whom to support. The Lovers meet you at the start of the money line and see you off at the end: your money is always a little about feelings. The World in the middle offers to widen their horizon: work without borders, a move, shared budget rules, investments that grow while you live. A heartfelt choice made broadly brings prosperity.

Your romance began by letter between two cities and continued with a move to a third — a shared one. There you both found work at an international company, and a few years later opened your own translation bureau for tourists and business people. Clients come from all over the world, and you write your budget rules together every autumn. **A love that outgrew one city opened up an income without borders.**

The Lovers look around. Other couples post their island holidays, and your year, in which everything is fine, suddenly seems modest: you want the same, or better. Spending starts being done for others' eyes, and at home comparisons are heard: who brings in more, who puts more into the shared life. The wide world demands a wide measure: look less at other people's shop windows and set goals the two of you actually need.

items.title: Choosing the world, not a window

captions.L: Restless, spending by mood
captions.R2: Borderless work and money that works by itself

items.meaning: Your choice leads to prosperity when it looks wide — at the world, not a shop window — and money doesn't become a leash.
text: “If we like it, we work; if we don't, we look for something new”: that's how the Lovers drive your money at the start, and it gets spent at the heart's bidding too. The World in the middle offers a wider choice: work without borders, other countries, people from all over the globe, investments that earn by themselves. The Devil at the end of the line tests whether that money will become a chain.

For a long time travel was your main shared expense: as soon as you'd saved up, you were off again. Then one of you started writing about routes, the other leading small groups. Today clients pay for your trips, and part of the fees goes into investments that feed you in the off-season. **The wide world you chose together began paying you itself.**

Money easily becomes a leash. As income grows, the temptation of more appears: a faster scheme, a more lucrative client, even if something about him is shady. And at home money can become power: whoever earns more starts deciding for two, and the other hears “you'd be nowhere without me”. Keep a joint account for shared goals and money of your own for each: the freedom for which you chose the world should stay in the budget too.

items.title: A cart on the family track

captions.L: Pulling up stakes at the first sign of boredom
captions.R2: A joint budget, family and a solid profession
captions.R: A career that takes you away from home

items.meaning: Your energy earns money on a shared track: family, profession and a joint budget instead of two separate races.
text: Between you, you have energy enough for four: the Chariot opens your money line and closes it too. The difficulty is the dashes: changing jobs out of boredom, rushing off to a new city, dropping everything before results come. The Hierophant in the middle lays the track: family as a shared goal, a profession you grow in over years, a budget you keep together. On this track your speed finally works for the home.

You changed cities three times and jobs five times before the first shared plan appeared: a house of your own in five years. You opened a joint account, both went on professional training courses and for the first time stayed in one place for more than two years. Promotions came almost at once, and the house was finished a year early. **Your wheels turn faster when they have a shared track.**

The Chariot at the exit calls you onto the road again, this time for work. Business trips came with the promotions, and the house finished a year early stands empty for months: one is travelling, the other on shifts. The joint account grows faster than you can live in what you saved for, and the argument over “whose work matters more” is heard more and more. Decide how many weeks a year you'll both be home before you sign the next lucrative contract.

items.title: The racer goes back to school

captions.L: Rushing into ventures and dropping them halfway
captions.R2: Learning from masters and living by rules
captions.R: A sudden collapse and a habit of expecting the worst

items.meaning: Knowledge and shared ways turn your speed into money, and you prepare for sharp changes in advance.
text: You pull up stakes easily: a new idea, another city, a fresh scheme. The Chariot starts well but drops what it has begun just as easily, and the couple's first money often goes on abandoned ventures. The Hierophant sits the racer down at a school desk: learn from those who have already travelled this road, live by clear rules, build a joint budget. The Tower reminds you that even a good road has landslides.

After two abandoned ventures you do it differently for the first time: before opening a coffee shop, one of you spends six months as a barista for a well-known owner in town, the other takes a bookkeeping course. You write a plan, take advice, ask that same owner to be your mentor. The coffee shop opens later than you'd hoped, but it is now in its fifth year. **Haste starts making money once it agrees to learn.**

The hole is sudden. Redundancy, a closed project, a client who walks away — and the familiar order collapses within a month. The Chariot then rushes straight into a new race, though it would be wiser to stop and recount. And once burned, it's easy to start expecting the worst and fearing every step. Six months' reserve and a “what we do if” plan agreed in advance turn a collapse into a rebuild.

items.title: A race with a contract in hand

captions.L: Dashing off without reading the terms
captions.R2: A contract, accounts and a fair price
captions.R: Borrowing on the crest of luck

items.meaning: Your speed turns into prosperity when each step is secured by a contract and luck isn't mistaken for steady income.
text: You start fast — and it's at the start that you lose. The Chariot charges ahead: a new venture, a second project, a move for work, a decision made in one evening. Speed itself isn't the trouble; the trouble is terms left unread. Justice puts the momentum on rails: a contract, a fair price, accounts, a backup plan. And the Wheel of Fortune reminds you that luck moves in circles, and even a straight road has bends.

You take your first big job as a pair, and for the first time you don't start work “on trust”: an estimate, deadlines, a deposit, signatures. The client winces but pays on time. A year later you have a folder of contracts and a reputation as people it's easy to deal with: everything's fair with them. New clients come by recommendation, and you no longer have to justify the price. **You grow richer where speed is backed by a signature.**

A good season is more dangerous than a bad one. When income is rising, you want to lock it in with something bigger: a car on credit, an expansion, a larger mortgage. Then orders go quiet for a while, but the payments remain. That's when “I told you so” is heard in the couple, and each recalls who insisted. Before a big debt, ask yourselves whether you could carry it in the worst season, and decide together, so there's no blame to share out later.

items.title: Champions by the rules

captions.L: Rushing ahead without checking the terms
captions.R2: Fair rules of the game and precise accounts
captions.R: Pride in success and spending on status

items.meaning: Your speed earns money when it plays by fair rules — and it goes on the glitter you use to confirm your success.
text: You're the first to grab the new and the first to trip over the small print: the Chariot gives speed but no patience for detail. Justice puts the game on rules: fair deals, accounts, a contract, a clear price. That's how speed starts to earn instead of only taking risks. The Sun at the end of the road brings success visible from outside, and with it the wish to show it off.

You opened a small web studio, and handed over the first orders in a rush, redoing them for free. One day you stop and bring in rules: a fixed estimate, a contract for each stage, a report to the client every Friday. Speed dropped, but the complaints vanished, and a year later you're recommended as the most honest in town. **Fair rules made your speed profitable.**

Visible success brings the temptation to show it. An office in the expensive centre, cars like your big competitors', bonuses that hit the budget — glitter costs dearly. And within the couple it's easy to start dividing the glory: whose name is on the poster, who's in charge. Spend on growth, not on the shop window, and don't forget to thank each other in front of people: the Sun shines more evenly when there are two in it.

items.title: Stamina instead of dashes

captions.L: A dash, a halt, and another dash
captions.R2: Endurance and long persistence

items.meaning: Your energy earns money when dashes give way to endurance, and leaks where one takes power over the budget.
text: You start at a gallop and then run out of breath: the Chariot accelerates faster than the road can pay off, and everything earned melts away on ventures begun and dropped. Strength changes the way you move: not in dashes but through stamina — holding a pace for years, enduring the dull stretch, not turning off. The Emperor closes the line and asks who in your couple commands the money.

You're training for a marathon — not a running one but a money one: you've decided to pay off the mortgage in five years instead of twenty. For the first months you're on fire, then you want to quit. So you agree not on dashes but on rhythm: the same sum every month, no heroics, no skipping. In the fourth year the bank sends a letter confirming the loan is closed. **Money yields to you not in a sprint but over distance.**

The danger is the commander. Once things are running, one of you easily becomes head of the budget: deciding, checking, handing out, and meeting disagreement with a flat “I've said so”. Order holds, but the other stops taking part — in money and in shared plans. The struggle for the lead takes strength the work needs. Divide the areas: each has their own part of the budget and the right to decide in it without consultation.

items.title: Speed that needs endurance

captions.L: Dropping things halfway
captions.R2: Endurance and an unexpected solution

items.meaning: Momentum earns you money when endurance tames it, and one partner's changes are met with joy, not jealousy.
text: You catch fire easily and cool down even more easily: that's how the Chariot drives the couple at the start. Ventures begun and dropped eat money, and the chase after the new lets nothing grow. Strength in the middle is endurance: see things through, wait out a hard year, find a solution where others gave up. With it your drive starts to pay. Death reminds you that every stage will end, and what matters is how you meet the change.

Three times you started an online shop and three times you dropped it after six months. The fourth time you agree in advance: two years without giving up, whatever happens. In the second year, when sales stall, one of you comes up with renting the goods out instead, and that is what takes off. **Money was waiting for you just past the line where you always used to quit.**

Sooner or later one of you will grow: change profession, leave the shared business, start earning more. The other may meet this warily, as if being left behind. Another danger is shifting one partner's debts onto the other when a stage ends. Greet your partner's growth as shared news, and keep a reserve that lets each of you change without panic.

items.title: Persistence versus carelessness

captions.L: Grabbing at everything and cooling fast
captions.R2: Endurance and a tamed thrill

items.meaning: Your thrill-seeking turns into money when endurance tames it, and leaks away when lightness becomes carelessness.
text: You don't lack zest: the Chariot easily fires you up with a new venture, a new city, a new project. You cool just as fast, and income jumps after your interest. Strength is the tamer: not to snuff out the zest but to lead it, not to quit in the third month, to endure the dull stretches. The Fool at the end of the line adds lightness — and carelessness too.

You worked as cycling guides now and then, and between seasons lived on whatever came along. One day you commit yourselves: for a whole year you'll run a club with a timetable, even when the groups are small. In winter you train indoors, in spring come the first rides out. By the end of the year the club has a hundred regular members. **Your freedom started earning money when you put it on a lead.**

The leak here is light and cheerful. The Fool doesn't like counting: money goes on trips, gear, friends, and there's still no reserve. One of you may decide that working for someone else is boring and quit with nothing else lined up. Freedom is good when it has a cushion: save while it's fun, and agree that bold steps are taken with at least three months' reserve.

items.title: Two drivers, one measure

captions.L: Rushing and grabbing at everything at once
captions.R2: Measure, pace and patient growth
captions.R: Each pulling the team their own way

items.meaning: You're both fast, and prosperity comes when speed finds a shared pace rather than turning into a contest.
text: The Chariot occupies both ends of your money line: you're energetic, quick to catch fire and in a hurry. Two sevens add up to fourteen — and Temperance in the middle suggests what to do with this speed. Not to damp it but to blend it: find a shared pace, keep spending level with income, grow patiently. Where you travel at one speed, there's more.

Long years in sales taught you to compete over who closes more in a month. When you opened a joint agency, the first months went on arguments. The turning point came when you split the road: one finds clients, the other looks after them, and you draw up the quarterly plans together and don't change them on the fly. The agency grows more slowly than you dreamed but doesn't dip in a single month. **The shared pace of two fast people is your prosperity.**

The second Chariot pulls to the side. Each wants their own project, their own car, their own decision, and the joint budget is pulled apart between two teams. The thrill pushes you towards loans and risky investments, and after a failure you hear “it was your idea”. A contest that was once fun starts costing money. Decide on big spending together and keep a rule: one dash at a time.

items.title: Speed diluted with measure

captions.L: Racing without stopping, and wearing out
captions.R2: An even pace and living within means
captions.R: Barbs in the thick of trouble

items.meaning: Your energy earns money when it finds an even pace — and isn't wasted on barbs when a sharp turn comes.
text: Speed is your normal mode: projects, travel, decisions on the move. The Chariot gives strength but wears out both you and the budget. Temperance teaches you to keep an even pace: work without strain, spend no more than comes in, grow gradually. That's when money starts to stay. The Tower keeps a sharp turn at the ready — better met with a reserve.

You used to take on everything: three projects, two side jobs, weekends on the road. One day you worked out that half of this bustle brought in less than it cost. You kept two lines of work, hired an assistant and brought in a rule: “no more than five working days”. Income didn't fall — it grew. **By slowing down, you started reaching the money for the first time.**

The Tower tests not only your reserve but your tone. A big client leaves — and on the very first evening comes the barb: “I told you not to rely on one client”, “you were the one who dropped the second line”. Irritation looks for a culprit faster than a solution, and in trouble you look in different directions. Keep a cushion for several months and agree a rule: the first three days after a blow are for a plan only, not for finding who's to blame.

items.title: Steering by your own star

captions.L: Rushing between projects for the money
captions.R2: Talent, inspiration and a public profile
captions.R: Living large in a fat year

items.meaning: Money comes through a gift you stopped frittering away on bustle, and leaves when a good year is taken for the norm.
text: You can work fast and a lot, and that's the trap: you take on anything that pays and race from project to project. The Chariot gives energy but not direction. The Star shows the direction: what you do best and what people can see — creative work, experience, a name. Money comes when the race turns towards that star. The Wheel of Fortune makes income swing and tests whether you can live without a lucky season.

For years one partner's writing went to other people's websites — fast, in bulk, and unsigned. One day the other says: “Nobody writes about food like you. Let's give it a go.” Together you launch a newsletter about local markets and farmers: the other takes the photos, the first writes. Two years later the newsletter has paying subscribers and an offer from a publisher. **You stopped racing and started shining — and from that moment the gift feeds you both.**

The leak is living large after a good year. A big fee comes in — and straight away a new laptop, a trip, a renovation, and the next year turns out quieter. The Star also likes to make promises: one debt paid off, the next one taken on, since a new project lies ahead. Set the ceiling on regular spending by your worst year, not your best; everything above goes into reserve and towards your shared dream.

items.title: A starry road, a shiny finish

captions.L: Racing from project to project
captions.R2: Talent, inspiration and a name
captions.R: Pride in fame and spending on glitter

items.meaning: Talent served by your speed earns money — and it leaks into glitter staged for social media.
text: Speed is your element: the Chariot drives you from one project to the next, and the race brings in less money than it takes strength. The Star shows the goal: your talent, your name, what you do better than anyone. When speed serves the gift, income grows. The Sun at the end of the line greets you with success — and a wish to show it off.

“Could you film not a wedding but us — our forty years?” asks an elderly couple after seeing one of your films. You film them for a month: old reels, letters, conversations in the kitchen. At the premiere in a café the whole family weeps, and a week later three more families call. That season, for the first time, you turn down half the weddings and triple your price — and nobody haggles. **By choosing your own and slowing down, you tripled the price of your gift.**

Glitter is the main temptation of the finish. You want expensive equipment, a studio in a prestigious spot, a life to show off on social media. The Chariot adds zest: more, faster. And between you an argument may flare up over who is the author of the success. There's plenty to be proud of, but spend on the work and on life, not on others' eyes, and call the success shared.

items.title: Family business, full speed

captions.L: Chasing other people's opportunities
captions.R2: Family, kin and a business with a history
captions.R: A hard hand on the family budget

items.meaning: Your energy finds its road in the family business — as long as order in it doesn't become one partner's power.
text: For a long time you're carried along by other people's opportunities: new projects, cities, offers — the Chariot knows no stops. Judgement opens a road home for this speed: into the family. A shared business with a history, the support of kin, an inheritance you can develop — that's where your energy starts to pay. The Emperor brings order to it and may overdo the power.

One partner's father's haulage yard carried goods around the county for twenty years. You came into it with logistics experience from a big company and within two years took it onto intercity routes. The father grumbles that everything has got too fast, and is proud all the same. **Speed found its best road in a business the elders started.**

The Emperor brings strictness into the family business — and can bring dictatorship. One of you takes over management completely: all the decisions, all the money, all the rules. The other and the elders are left as mere executors. A struggle for the lead in a family business hurts more than in someone else's. Write the roles down on paper and agree which decisions are made only together.

items.title: Back to your own, and richer

captions.L: Chasing along other people's roads
captions.R2: Family, kin and a shared family business
captions.R: Clinging to the outworn and mixing debts

items.meaning: Your speed finds direction in family: a shared business and the support of kin give more than racing along others' roads.
text: For a long time other people's roads seem shorter: new cities, new projects, work wherever it pays right now. The Chariot drives you on but doesn't bring you anywhere. Judgement brings you back to your own: to family, kin, the business your relatives already have, the support you hadn't noticed. Prosperity comes when speed serves the family. Death closes the line: something will have to end.

For ten years you lived the big-city life in rented flats, while one partner's parents had a printing works in a small town. One day the father asks for a month's help — and you stay. You bring to the old business what you learned in the city: a website, orders from all over the country, new presses. The printing works triples in size. **Your road to money went round in a circle and led home.**

Death asks you to let go. When the family business passes to you, it's hard for the elders to step back, and hard for you to change established ways. Or one of you grows faster, and the other feels superfluous. Mixing debts is dangerous too: the family's old obligations can land on the couple. Agree the handover with the elders honestly and on paper, and with each other that one partner's growth is a shared joy.

items.title: The road home, the free wind

captions.L: Speed without direction
captions.R2: Returning to the family and its business
captions.R: Dropping what works for a new freedom

items.meaning: Your speed finds meaning in a family business — and you lose money when the urge returns to drop it all for freedom.
text: You have speed but no direction: the Chariot races the couple through towns and projects, and money scatters along the road. Judgement shows where to drive: home — to family, kin, a business waiting for you among your own. There speed becomes prosperity. The Fool waits until everything's running smoothly, then whispers: “why not take off somewhere else?”

After years on the move you came back to the village where one partner's parents kept an old sauna on the shore. You renovated it, added guest cabins and a cold plunge pool, and now townspeople book weekends a month ahead. **The road that brought you home turned out to be the most profitable.**

Settling down comes hard to you. When the business is running, you're tempted to leave it to the parents and go off for new experiences, take a six-month break, spend without counting. The relatives who put their effort into the business take offence, and without you things quickly fall into decline. Freedom is good on a schedule: a holiday, yes; running away, no. Agree who keeps the business going while the other rests.

items.title: Proper to the point of dull

captions.L: Fearing mistakes and avoiding risk
captions.R2: A clear plan and reliable work

items.meaning: Your correctness builds solid prosperity, if there's room left in it for life and not just rules and elders' advice.
text: Making a mistake frightens you more than earning less: Justice has taught you to weigh everything and not take risks. The Emperor turns this caution into a system: reliable work, a plan, a budget, savings pots, not a single debt. That's how you grow rich — slowly but surely. The Hierophant closes the line with rules and elders' advice that easily become shackles.

When friends took out their third loan for renovations, you finished yours — on savings, without a single loan. It took twice as long, but not one payment to the bank. A couple of years later you bought a second flat, while your friends are still paying off their renovations. **The caution people chuckled at overtook other people's daring.**

Here rules easily grow into guardianship: one of you starts dictating what the other should spend on, what's “proper” and what's “indulgence”. Relatives chip in with advice, and the budget becomes the whole family's business. Stinginess poses as care. Allow yourselves something outside the rules: personal money for each, spending without explanations, and decisions made without looking over your shoulder at the elders.

items.title: An honest system for two

captions.L: Weighing everything and changing nothing
captions.R2: Stable income and an orderly budget
captions.R: A tilt: one pulls, the other depends

items.meaning: Your honesty builds a system that feeds you — if there's room in it for balance between two people.
text: You weigh everything: Justice has taught you caution, and change comes hard. Money sits where it's safe, not where it grows. The Emperor builds a system out of this honesty: stable income, a clear budget, savings pots, rules you devised together. Prosperity comes through the system. Temperance watches the balance within it.

Your budget is like a contract: who pays for what, how much each saves, which expenses need both to agree. Friends joke that you live by a rulebook. But in seven years you've never once quarrelled over money, and the house fund filled two years ahead of schedule. **The rulebook you wrote together protects both your money and the peace at home.**

Balance can be upset unnoticed. One earns more and gradually takes on all the payments, the other gets used to it and stops taking part — and soon one pulls while the other depends. Or one starts saving everything while the other spends for show. Review your contract once a year: contributions change, and the rules must change with them.

items.title: Honest scales on wheels

captions.L: Weighing so long the train has left
captions.R2: Getting moving and running several ventures

items.meaning: Your honesty turns into money once it starts moving, and at home it rests on trust, not a strict ledger of contributions.
text: Justice stands at both ends of your money line: you're honest, neat, fond of clear rules and equal contributions. At first this slows you down: decisions are weighed so long that the opportunity passes. The Chariot between the scales demands movement — get going, start, take on several ventures at once. Two eights add up to sixteen, and the Tower trails behind as a reminder: standing still costs more than a mistake.

You worked for years as salaried bookkeepers and talked all that time about a business of your own. At last you take the step: three clients on the side, then five, then a small office. Now you have a firm with two assistants, and the two of you travel round the clients. **Your neatness became capital once you fitted it with wheels.**

The second scales stand inside the couple. It matters to you that everything is equal: income, spending, housework. When one earns more or is more tired, the tally starts being spoken aloud: “I did it, now it's your turn.” Justice turns into a claim, and a shared life into arbitration. Equal isn't always fair: agree that contribution is measured not only in money but in strength, time and care.

items.title: Rules of the road

captions.L: Waiting for perfect conditions and every permit
captions.R2: Getting behind the wheel and running it on the move
captions.R: Naive trust and spending on appearances

items.meaning: Your order is for the road, not the car park: money comes when you're moving, and goes on glitter and gullibility.
text: It matters to you to do everything properly: register, calculate, get the permits. Justice sometimes keeps the couple in the car park too long — until every certificate is in, until the perfect plan comes together. The Chariot says: time to go; rules are needed on the road, not in the car park. The Star adorns the journey, but also tempts you to turn off towards a pretty shop window.

For two years you gathered documents and studied regulations so you could drive tourists around the region. When you finally bought a second-hand minibus and set off on the first route, it all turned out simpler: people loved your stops at springs and your stories. Three seasons later you have two minibuses and routes across three counties. **Money started rolling in exactly when you pulled out of the car park.**

The Star has two leaks here. The first is the pretty picture: new vehicles before they're needed, an expensive sign, spending to look more successful. The second is naive trust: a partner given money without a contract because “he's one of us”. With your love of rules, it stings to slip up precisely here. Keep the same order in happy moments too: a contract — even with friends; an investment — only after the sums.

items.title: Bookkeeping for luck

captions.L: Counting everything, even when it's time to risk
captions.R2: Catching the turn and not missing the chance
captions.R: Holding on to luck by force

items.meaning: Your accounts keep money in order, and prosperity comes in waves — meet them together, without fighting for the wheel.
text: You honestly count every penny, and that is where your difficulty begins. Justice demands clarity: income above board, expenses recorded, decisions made after calculation. But the couple's luck moves in circles: the Wheel of Fortune brings money in waves, suddenly, off schedule. While you're double-checking the spreadsheet, the good moment passes. Strength shows where it wears thin: in the wish to hold back the wave with your bare hands.

An acquaintance offers you a share in a small business — you have a week to decide. In the past you'd have said no: no time to work it all out. Now you have something ready: a free reserve, a risk limit agreed in advance and a rule: “we say yes if we both agree within three days.” You buy in, and a year later the business brings in more than both your salaries. **Your accounting makes you money when it works for speed, not against it.**

The weak spot is a downturn. Strength doesn't like to retreat: one of you starts working for two just to keep income from dipping, and demands the same of the other. Everything is under control, every expense agreed, rest put off till better times. The quiet season comes anyway, and the tiredness and resentment stay. It is easier to get through if you agree in advance: in a downturn we save our strength rather than squeeze it out of each other.

items.title: A chance without family scores

captions.L: Over-insuring and missing the moment
captions.R2: A new opportunity and a change of scene

items.meaning: Your honest figures catch luck when they don't hold it back — and don't cost more because you proudly refuse help.
text: You're careful and honest: everything legal, everything calculated, not a single rash step. Justice protects you from mistakes, but over-insuring costs dearly — the lucky moment passes while you're checking. The Wheel of Fortune brings prosperity through change: a new offer, a move, a chance you have to catch in time. Judgement closes the line with family questions.

A developer buys up the land under your old garage, and the neighbours accept the first price offered. You don't rush: you dig out the documents, find out what the plot is really worth and negotiate three times as much. The money goes not on a car but into a business — a small warehouse you let out. **Luck you approached with documents in hand is worth three times as much.**

Judgement tests your pride. Your parents offer to invest in the warehouse or at least cover part of the repairs, and you refuse on principle: honest people manage on their own. Instead of help — an expensive loan; instead of a family venture — hurt elders who feel like strangers in your life. Accepting help is nothing to be ashamed of if it's set out honestly: take it on clear terms and in writing, and it will become a support rather than a source of grievances.

items.title: Closing an old account

captions.L: Fearing change, clinging to stability
captions.R2: Letting go of the surplus and starting anew

items.meaning: Prosperity comes after an honest parting with the old — as long as relatives don't take charge of your budget.
text: You're at ease when everything is stable: a job for the long term, income on schedule, changes only when necessary. Justice gives the couple reliability, but timidity too — it's frightening to risk what you already have. Death says it plainly: let go of the surplus. Close what has outlived itself, cut what isn't needed, dare to begin a new stage — and money starts to grow. The Hierophant, meanwhile, guards rules that can shackle you.

For years a country cottage ate your money and weekends, and you kept it because “how can you not have a cottage”. One day you honestly count what it costs you a year — and sell it. The money goes into a deposit on a flat that you let out, and your weekends are freed for extra work. **Money started arriving when you honestly closed the old account.**

Here the Hierophant speaks with your relatives' voice. “Sell the cottage? Grandma wouldn't have approved”, “why do you need new things if the old still work?” Other people's rules seep into your budget, and every decision has to be defended. Inside the couple it turns into stinginess and control: one decides that “we're not supposed to”. Listen to your elders with respect, but keep the last word on your money between the two of you.

items.title: Close honestly, start in measure

captions.L: Clinging to stability, afraid to change
captions.R2: Letting go of the outworn, a new stage
captions.R: Living with an eye on others' opinions

items.meaning: Prosperity comes when you honestly close what's outworn, and holds as long as others' opinions don't decide for you.
text: Change comes hard to you: Justice holds you to stability, an official job, clear rules. But prosperity lies on the far side of an ending: Death offers to let go of what has run its course and start again. A stage honestly closed becomes the foundation of the new. Temperance makes sure the changes don't throw you off balance.

Your first flat, bought on a mortgage fifteen years ago, had become cramped, but selling it was frightening: “what if we sell too cheap.” When you finally decided, you valued it honestly, closed the mortgage and moved to a house out of town. Now your dog hotel runs there, where owners bring their pets while they're on holiday. **A stage honestly closed became the soil for a new business.**

Moderation easily comes to depend on others' opinions. Acquaintances chuckle at the “dog hotel”, relatives ask when you'll take up something serious, and you're either shy of raising prices or spending on a sign and a car to look more respectable. Money swings between modesty and show, and your own measure gets lost. Decide about prices and spending by your own figures and goals, not by what people will say.

items.title: Break down to build honestly

captions.L: Fearing change, living strictly by the rules
captions.R2: Rebuilding life and a big shared build
captions.R: Counting who put in how much

items.meaning: Prosperity comes through bold rebuilding, and honest accounts keep it — with no “my” and “your” contribution.
text: Justice opens and closes your money line: you like everything by the rules, written down and fairly divided. Two eights make sixteen, and between them stands the Tower. Your money grows not from neatness alone but from decisive rebuilding: changing profession, selling an old home for a new one, starting a big build. Your honesty is needed to keep this upheaval from turning into chaos.

For many years you rent a flat, pay on time and save a little. One day you take the plunge: you buy a plot outside town and build a house yourselves, to a budget you track to the penny. Two years of building, a payment schedule on the fridge, arguments over every brick. But now you have a house worth twice what you put in. **Your capital grows from a big rebuild done on honest figures.**

The flip side of the second eight is bookkeeping inside the couple. Who put more into the build, whose salary went on the roof, who spent how much on themselves — the tally is kept silently but precisely, and one day presented in a quarrel. Justice easily turns into a trial where each proves their contribution. Agree that big shared things are shared without percentages, and that each has their own money that needs no reporting.

items.title: Honest building, no gilding

captions.L: Over-insuring and a habit of stability
captions.R2: Bold rebuilding and a big shared venture

items.meaning: Your honest figures withstand a big rebuild, as long as you don't spend on beauty before the building's done.
text: You prefer stability: Justice has taught you to register everything, count and not take risks. But your prosperity is born in the Tower — in rebuilding: sell the old, start the new, take on a big shared venture. Honesty is needed here to keep the upheaval from becoming chaos. The Star wants the new to be beautiful — and that comes at a high price.

When the factory where you'd each worked for ten years closed, you put your redundancy money not into a holiday but into an old warehouse on the edge of town. Two years of rebuilding to budget, without a single loan — and now it's a co-working space for craftspeople, where joiners and potters rent benches. **A rebuild done honestly and to budget paid off better than any steady salary.**

The Star loves beautiful things, and the temptation comes at the finish: a designer sign, expensive furniture for the lounge, advertising before the first profit. You want everything to look “like the picture” at once. And one of you may trust a partner with a grand project. Decorate from profit, not from the reserve, and don't take a new loan while the old one is still open.

items.title: Honesty you can see from afar

captions.L: Afraid to risk, keeping a private stash
captions.R2: Both shining, fulfilled and in view
captions.R: Work without rest and a contest of who's stronger

items.meaning: Your prosperity grows when honest work steps into the light: you're seen, trusted, and each fulfilled in your own way.
text: You are careful with money: every step weighed, risk seems unnecessary, and each keeps something of their own aside just in case. Justice makes the couple reliable but sometimes invisible too: you work honestly, but few people know it. The Sun brings you into the light — to success that's noticeable, to work where each is fulfilled. Strength warns: brightness has its price.

For years you worked as lawyers in other people's firms, where others signed off your decisions. One day you open your own practice and put your names on the door for the first time. Reputation brings the clients: people say of you, “with them everything is honest and clear”. You speak at conferences, write columns, and income grows with your profile. **The light you stepped into with your honest work brings more than years of careful work in the shadows.**

The light burns when there's too much of it. The Sun loves to blaze, and one of you stops resting, then expects the same dedication from the partner: “we're building this together, aren't we.” Or a hidden contest appears in the couple — whose name is bigger, whose contribution counts more. Money grows, while warmth drains away. Share not only income but recognition: thank each other aloud, especially in front of others.

items.title: An honest name for all the kin

captions.L: Caution and invisible work
captions.R2: Recognition and success people can see

items.meaning: Your honesty comes into the light and brings recognition — and prosperity is lost when relatives pay with your name.
text: Honestly, carefully and unseen — that's how you work: Justice dislikes risk and noise. The Sun pulls it into the light: your honesty is noticed, trusted, and becomes your name. The more you're seen, the more orders you get. And the family, represented by Judgement, wants its share of the success.

You ran your household-appliance repair shop quietly, until the local paper wrote about “repairers who don't pad the bill”. After the article the phone rang non-stop for a week, and for the first time you chose your jobs yourselves. Now you have three repairers and a second shop. **Honesty that was finally seen became your most valuable asset.**

Everyone knows your honest name now, and the relatives are happy to use it: “say it's your order and they'll skip the queue”, “vouch for us at the bank — they'll believe you”. Refusing is awkward — you're the honest ones, after all, and Judgement dislikes your own being refused. So your name starts working for other people's debts, and if something goes wrong, you'll answer for it. Lend it only where you answer yourselves, and decide on guarantor requests together and only on paper.

items.title: Cautious souls on a free wind

captions.L: Afraid to leave a secure job
captions.R2: A bold step into the unknown, your own path

items.meaning: Your honest work earns more in freedom when you dare to leave the secure and don't skimp on growth.
text: Security matters more to you than risk: Justice keeps you in official jobs with salaries on the books, and leaving is frightening. But prosperity waits beyond the threshold. The Fool calls you into the unknown: a business of your own, your own hours, a path nobody has laid. Your honesty is excellent luggage for such a path. The Hierophant closes the line with the voice of elders who disapprove of risk.

You worked at the tax office for twelve years and knew every rule by heart. When you left to advise farmers and craftspeople, to whom those rules seem a dark forest, the relatives gasped. Now you have clients across the county, and you drive out to them yourselves in a car stuffed with folders. **Honesty taken out into the open air became your best product.**

The Hierophant economises out of an old tax-office habit. You don't buy a new car until the old one breaks down in the middle of a field, you don't get accounting software — “we'll manage with spreadsheets”, you don't hire an assistant because it's an extra cost. Fear of overspending saves pennies and eats hours: you spend more time on the road to clients than at work. Budget money for growth and don't justify it to anyone, not even yourselves.

items.title: From the office to freedom

captions.L: Clinging to a salary and fearing risk
captions.R2: Freedom, a fresh start and your own hours
captions.R: Mismatched spending and one partner depending

items.meaning: Your honest work earns more once it breaks free — as long as neither of you lives at the other's expense.
text: Justice has accustomed you to the secure: a salary, a permanent contract, taxes, everything by the law. Only such security often marks time, and leaving is frightening: what if it doesn't work out? The Fool in the middle of the line says: it will, and that's exactly where. Freedom, your own hours, a business from scratch, the ease with which you find a way out of any situation — the path to prosperity runs through a bold step out of the office. Temperance at the end of the line watches the balance.

“What do we have to lose?” one of you asks the night the other is once again refused a rise. The answer is surprisingly short: nothing but a salary that never grows. A month later you're both on your own hours, and your experience as a lawyer and an HR officer turns into a small consultancy for new entrepreneurs. You work as honestly as ever, only now for yourselves. **Out in the open your carefulness is worth more than in the office.**

Temperance at the end of the line is about a measure easily lost in freedom. Income becomes uneven, and one of you starts saving every penny while the other lives as if every month were a good one. Or one earns while the other is still at a crossroads, and the balance tilts. Decide in advance how much of each fee goes into the shared reserve and how you support whoever is having a quiet season — without tallies or reproaches.

items.title: Modesty that allowed abundance

captions.L: Austerity and not knowing how to take
captions.R2: Growing home, family and shared abundance
captions.R: Spending the harvest on comfort and gifts

items.meaning: Abundance comes when your modesty allows itself to grow, and stays as long as the harvest isn't spent away.
text: Modesty is your old habit: the Hermit won't let you ask, let alone take. The Empress, standing twice further on, calls doubly loudly to abundance: grow a family, a home, a shared business, let money keep arriving. The threes add up to six, and the Lovers trail behind to suggest that abundance is something you must decide on together. The second Empress teaches you not to squander the harvest.

One of you learned bobbin lace from a grandmother and for years made it “for the soul”. One day the other photographed the doilies and posted them online. Orders came from fashion houses, and lace became your family income and pride. **Allowing yourselves abundance, you found it had long lived in your fingers.**

A harvest is easy to squander. When money has finally arrived, you want to make up for lost time: new furniture, presents for all the relatives, celebrations. Modesty gives way to generosity without measure, and the reserve melts. There's inequality too: one earns, the household rests on the other, who gradually loses their own. Spend by the season, as in a garden: some for joy, some for planting next year.

items.title: Modest souls in a blooming house

captions.L: Wanting little and not asking
captions.R2: Growing a home, a family and shared prosperity
captions.R: Sacrificing your own for the shared

items.meaning: You grow rich when you stop seeing abundance as excess — as long as the growth isn't paid for by one partner's sacrifice.
text: You don't need much: the Hermit makes do with little and is shy of asking. The Empress permits what you've denied yourselves — to grow: a shared home, a family, investments, plans for years ahead. Abundance arrives when you stop thinking of it as excess. The Hanged Man at the end of the line asks whose hands pay for this growth.

For years your vegetable plot fed only the two of you, until the neighbours started asking to buy greens and seedlings. You put a table with a price list by the gate — and within a season people were coming from neighbouring villages. Today — three greenhouses and a market stall on Saturdays. **Once you allowed yourselves to grow, you discovered how much you could grow.**

The one who pays is most often the one who isn't noticed. Often one of you carries the house and the household, giving up their own job, while the other grows in the shared business. Outwardly all is well, but a feeling builds that the sacrifice goes unseen. Let each one's contribution be named and paid for — at least with money of their own, spent without accounting.

items.title: From austerity to abundance

captions.L: Making do with little, not wanting more
captions.R2: A shared home, growth and fruitful investment
captions.R: Living for the house, not in it

items.meaning: Your modesty blossoms into abundance when you grow something shared — and withers when the house starts running you.
text: Little is enough for you: the Hermit is used to modesty and doesn't reach for wealth. The Empress says it's time to allow yourselves abundance: a garden, a house with room for guests, investment in shared goals. The World at the end of the line gathers it all into a stable whole — and watches that this whole doesn't become more important than you.

For a long time a small flat seemed enough: “we have all we need.” The decision about a big house ripened unexpectedly — when you realised you wanted a garden and room for guests. You took out a mortgage, planted trees one by one and let a room to students. Today the house is worth three times as much, and the garden feeds you in summer. **Abundance came when you stopped thinking of it as excess.**

The World turns abundance into an establishment that mustn't be touched. House, garden, lodgers, mortgage — all running smoothly, and any new expense loses out to them: the trip is postponed because the roof needs doing, study because it's the season. A few years on you live modestly again, only in a big house, and the Hermit's modesty returns disguised as order. Once a year spend money on something you can't nail to a wall: travel, learning, new people.

items.title: Quiet that needs company

captions.L: Working alone and silent about the price
captions.R2: Partnership and shared work you love
captions.R: Dropping things once you've gone off them

items.meaning: Your quiet work starts paying when you do it together and with people — and don't drop what you've started on a whim.
text: The Hermit at the way in means each of you is used to working alone: quietly, meticulously, without much talk of money. The Lovers, holding the middle and end of the line, answer simply: together. A shared business, partnership with each other, a circle of people it's a pleasure to work with — that's how prosperity reaches you. And that's how it can leave too: the second Lovers not only choose with the heart but also walk away.

For years one of you wrote software for other people's companies and the other drew illustrations for other people's books, and you hardly talked about work. One day you make a small children's game together — just for a nephew. It gets noticed, bought, and people ask for more. Now you have a studio for two and a few freelance friends around you. **Two workshops that opened their doors to each other earned more than each on its own.**

The Lovers run business with the heart, which means they also leave it with the heart. A quarrel with a freelance friend — the project dropped halfway; bored with a game — on to a new one with the old unfinished; a good client turns out dull — refused. Income comes in fits and starts, and every empty month sounds like a reproach: “not enough again”. Decide which jobs you finish in any mood, and choose only the rest for love.

items.title: Know-how that met its public

captions.L: Knowing a lot and shy about asking for money
captions.R2: Connections, choice and work you love
captions.R: The lure of quick money and the reproach “too little”

items.meaning: Your knowledge pays once it reaches people — as long as the thrill of earning doesn't become the measure of love.
text: You can both do more than you show, and you're underpaid for it. The Hermit at the way into money is a craftsman in a workshop: years of study and depth, while talking price feels awkward and advertising seems like vanity. Money comes when the Lovers walk in through the door: people, acquaintances, the choice of work you both enjoy. The Devil both lures and tests: how much are you willing to give for a big income?

For ten years you repaired old clocks “for friends”: one of you is wonderful with their hands, and money never came up. One day the other posts photos of the work in the neighbourhood chat — and the next day three people call. Six months later there's a queue, and the other's way with clients brings them back with their neighbours. One partner's craft and the other's sociability add up to a business. **Your prosperity rests on the alliance of knowledge and people: neither sells without the other.**

The dangerous turn comes once the business takes off. The Devil suggests shortcuts: take an order with something shady about it, inflate the price for someone who doesn't know better, work through the night just to beat the workshop next door. “Others earn more” is heard in the couple, and income becomes the measure of respect for each other. Name your shared goal in words — how much you need and what for — and the thrill pulls you towards it, not away from each other.

items.title: Three lanterns on one trail

captions.L: Content with little, never asking for more
captions.R2: Rare knowledge that people pay for
captions.R: Skimping on yourselves, silent about trouble

items.meaning: Your prosperity builds up quietly, through knowledge and patience — until modesty becomes a refusal to grow.
text: Your whole money line is the Hermit. Money has never been the goal for you: understanding, learning and doing things properly matter more. Hence the difficulty, the path and the leak. The difficulty: a little is enough for you, and you don't ask for more. The path: depth — knowledge others lack, work you study for years, an unhurried pace that always leaves a reserve. The leak: silence, where each is on their own.

For fifteen years you've studied old wooden houses and local history, each your own half. You did it for yourselves until restorers and museums started coming to you: who else knows how window surrounds were carved in this county? Now you consult, write expert reports and go on expeditions at others' expense. **You are paid for knowing more deeply than others, and the longer you dig, the more it's worth.**

Modesty costs you dearly. Working for half price because naming a sum feels awkward. Not spending on yourselves even what you need. Living through money worries in silence so as not to burden the other, and ending up side by side like two hermits in neighbouring cells. The couple benefits from someone outside to spur you on: an agent, a partner, a friend with ambition. And with each other — say aloud how much you really need.

items.title: Mastery in the shadows

captions.L: Working for an idea, shy about the price
captions.R2: Deep knowledge of a rare craft

items.meaning: Your rare skill pays once it leaves the shadows, while money drains into fog, unspoken things and trust in the wrong people.
text: The Hermit stands twice at the start of your money line: your difficulty and your path are one — solitary work. For a long time you work for an idea and treat money as secondary. But it's depth that leads to prosperity: you know your craft as only a handful do, and people are willing to pay for that. The Moon at the end of the line reminds you that in the shadows it's easy to lose not just time but money.

Together you tune old pianos, and for years charged a token fee for it — “for the pleasure”. Everything changes when a concert hall looks for tuners for the season and learns there are only two in town. For the first time you name a price that embarrasses you yourselves — and it's accepted without haggling. **The rarity of your skill turned out to be worth more than you thought.**

The Moon makes your figures foggy. You don't like poring over contracts, you take intermediaries at their word, and you don't always know how much you actually earned in a year. One of you may worry quietly and say nothing, while the other doesn't notice. The fog is cleared by simple things: a written contract for each job, joint accounts, and talking about money even when it's awkward.

items.title: A slow harvest

captions.L: Not asking for more, silent about the price
captions.R2: Patience and work for others
captions.R: A tilt: one grows, the other serves

items.meaning: Your slow path brings a harvest, as long as patience doesn't turn into one living for the other's growth.
text: You're modest with money: the Hermit doesn't know how to ask, and you name the price of your work apologetically. The Hanged Man says your path is patience: serve the work, don't expect quick results, give first. Prosperity comes slowly, like a harvest. The Empress decides what it will go on and whether you grow equally.

For eight years you ran a free robotics club for the neighbourhood's teenagers. Many grew up and went on to good universities, and one former pupil, having started his own company, invited you to head its training centre. Now you teach the same things, only for decent pay. **You sowed for free for a long time — and the harvest came from where you didn't expect it.**

Comfort and growth are what the Empress works for, and a tilt can appear here. One of you develops, studies, grows at work, while the other carries the whole household and gradually falls behind. Or long-awaited prosperity goes on fitting out the home so fast that there's no reserve again. Both of you grow, share housework fairly, and spend on comfort what's above the reserve.

items.title: The patience of quiet people

captions.L: Being modest and not claiming your due
captions.R2: Service, discipline and long patience
captions.R: Sacrifices, debts and a sense of injustice

items.meaning: Your prosperity comes slowly, through patient service — as long as patience doesn't turn into sacrifice and resentment.
text: You're quiet people who find it awkward to claim your due: the Hermit teaches you to make do with little. The Hanged Man stands twice further on and says what you already feel: your path is patience. Work where you serve others, discipline, payments on time, no debts. Prosperity comes slowly, but it comes. The second twelve warns: patience has its limit.

For twelve years you've kept a small shelter for stray dogs — first on your own money, then on donations. One day the city paper writes about you, and a company comes along offering to buy land for the shelter and pay you both a salary. **Years of quiet service came back to you a hundredfold.**

The second Hanged Man shows the limit. Giving more than you receive, it's easy to store up resentment: “we do so much, yet live worse than others.” Debts appear that you're too awkward to ask to be repaid, and one becomes dependent on the other when someone has left their job for the shared cause. Patience is a strength as long as it's chosen, not imposed. Name your price and learn to say “no”.

items.title: Quiet service, solid walls

captions.L: Being modest and not naming your price
captions.R2: Serving people and waiting your turn
captions.R: Clinging to a tried and tested method

items.meaning: Your quiet work for people's good pays off one day — as long as you don't then stop learning yourselves.
text: Modesty stops you naming a price: the Hermit works quietly and talks awkwardly about money. The Hanged Man carries this quiet on with patience: serve people, work conscientiously, wait without hurrying things. Prosperity catches up late — with those who didn't turn off. And the World at the end holds on to the tested — sometimes longer than it works.

A July morning, a call from a former pupil: “I got in. With a scholarship. You were right about those tricky equations.” There are nine such calls that summer, all from children you taught for years for a token fee. By September the whole town knows of you, parents come asking how much an hour costs, and for the first time you name a price without apologising. **The patience you gave to other people's children came back as recognition and prosperity.**

What you've achieved tempts you to teach as you taught ten years ago. New exams, online lessons, other textbooks seem frivolous to you: “our method is proven”. The queue is long for now, but the World at the exit doesn't notice everything around changing, and the Hermit's modesty stops you asking younger colleagues what they do differently. Once a year learn something new yourselves — then the price of your time won't go out of date either.

items.title: Modesty with big ambitions

captions.L: Austerity, awkward talking about money
captions.R2: Ambition, grip and well-paid work

items.meaning: Let yourselves want money: austerity holds you back, desire and grip bring prosperity — if it isn't spent on show.
text: The Hermit has taught you to make do with little: money seems slightly shameful, talking about it is awkward, asking for more even more so. The Devil lifts this ban. The wish to live better, ambition, hard and well-paid work, extra income, investments — all this opens up when you let yourselves want. The Lovers close the line and ask what you'll spend it on.

For ten years one of you was a quiet engineer who knew the system better than anyone and was paid less than anyone. One day the other can't stand it: “You're worth three times that.
