Go and tell them.” The money talk is agonising, but a year later the engineer has a contract with a large company, and a year after that a consultancy of their own at a high rate. **A wish spoken aloud brought you more than years of quiet modesty.**

The Lovers at the end of the line make money a matter of feelings. You want to spend the first large sums beautifully: presents, restaurants, new things that say “look how we live now”. Sometimes a present becomes a way to make amends or prove love, and dissatisfaction with the other's income a way to sting. Spend on joy, not on proofs: discuss big purchases in advance and don't measure love by a price tag.

items.title: A Hermit who got a taste for it

captions.L: Modesty and not knowing how to ask
captions.R2: Ambition, a strong grip and high stakes
captions.R: Greed and money as a leash

items.meaning: You need to want money in earnest — and not let that want turn into greed and power over each other.
text: Modesty is your starting point: the Hermit is shy of talking about money and considers it vanity. The Devil waits twice further along the line, and his message is doubly loud: want. Ambition, hard work for good money, a second income, investments — prosperity responds to an appetite you've allowed yourselves. But the second Devil warns that appetite easily grows into greed. Add two fifteens and you get three, and the Empress's generosity follows as a reminder of what it's all for.

For years you grew rare varieties of roses — for yourselves, for the soul. One day a big nursery offered to buy cuttings for a pittance. Instead of agreeing, you registered rights to the variety and showed it at a major exhibition. Now your roses sell across the country, and for the first time you haggle without embarrassment. **The appetite you allowed yourselves grew more than years of modesty did.**

The second Devil knows how to spoil prosperity. Money multiplies, and you want more: raise prices to the limit, work without days off, take on a dubious order. And at home money becomes a leash: whoever earns more keeps the other tethered — “without me you'd…” Remember the trailing three: money is there to grow a shared life, not one partner's power over the other.

items.title: A quiet business on a hunch

captions.L: No drive to earn more than you need
captions.R2: A quiet business of your own, instinct and imagination
captions.R: Each shut away in their own work

items.meaning: Your income grows in quiet — from work you sense in your gut and run yourselves, until it drives you into separate corners.
text: Two Hermits at the ends of the line make you a couple who need little. You don't chase money and don't like talking about it, so for a long time you earn less than you could. The Moon stands in the middle, and prosperity follows her road: work you guessed by instinct rather than read in a business plan — creative, family-run, a little strange to others.

Night walks and old photographs are your shared passion. One day this grows into a small publisher of postcards showing your town at dusk — no investors, no advertising, all on instinct. People find you by word of mouth and order print runs for hotels and museums. **Your money is born where you trusted a hunch and didn't ask how things are usually done.**

A quiet business easily becomes a wall between you. Each retreats into their own part of the work, in the evenings you sit in different rooms, and money worries are lived through alone, so as not to alarm the other. The Moon adds suspicion: things left unsaid grow into conjecture. Share not only the work but your doubts — one talk over tea is worth a dozen anxious nights.

items.title: A night-time craft

captions.L: Working in the shade, not thinking of money
captions.R2: Work found by intuition

items.meaning: Your quiet work found by intuition earns money, and you lose it where you won't look into the future.
text: The Hermit begins your line: you're used to working in the shade without thinking of profit. Two Moons further on add up to exactly nine — and say where this quiet leads: to instinct, imagination, work found by intuition. Strange to others, it becomes your income. But the second Moon leaves fog at the exit too.

At night one of you drew maps of invented countries — just for fun, for themselves. When a writer friend asked for a map for his book, you drew it in a week. Today authors and game developers from different countries come to you, and the queue for maps is booked six months ahead. **Work invented at night turned out to be your most reliable earnings.**

The fog at the exit is the future you don't look at. Orders are booked six months ahead, and it seems it will always be so: taxes are put off till the last day, there's no reserve, and the question “what if the clients leave” sounds like a bad omen. One sometimes worries at night but says nothing so as not to jinx it, the other is sure everything's clear anyway. Once a quarter sit down together and draw one more map — of your own money for the year ahead.

items.title: Quiet people of the wide world

captions.L: Working quietly, not looking for more
captions.R2: Distant horizons and money that works
captions.R: Growth with only one name on it

items.meaning: Quiet mastery brings you prosperity in the wide world — as long as there's room in it for both names.
text: Quiet is your element: the Hermit works without fuss and doesn't seek more. The World widens the horizon: your skill is needed far beyond your own yard, and money can grow by itself — in rental income, in ventures that work without you there. The Empress generously spends what the world brings.

For years you translated old cookbooks from French for yourselves. When you posted the translations, a foreign publisher noticed and offered a contract for a series. Now fees come in from three countries, and part of them you invest in a flat you let out. **Your quiet work found readers in three countries.**

The wide world remembers one name. The contract is signed in the name of the faster translator, invitations to book fairs and interviews go to them too, and the other, who checked every chapter, remains “the assistant” — at the publisher's and, little by little, at home. The Empress can't stand unequal growth: after it come resentment and spending to drown it out. Put both names on the contract, and share not only the fee but the trips.

items.title: Out of the study, into the world

captions.L: Keeping quiet and not asking for more
captions.R2: The wide world, abroad, passive income

items.meaning: Your quiet work brings prosperity once it goes out into the wide world and your savings stop lying as dead weight.
text: You're used to working quietly and hard without asking for reward: the Hermit is a modesty that keeps you from naming your price. The World in the middle of the line opens the horizon: your knowledge is needed far beyond your town, and money can work by itself — deposits, investments, income that doesn't need you present. The Hanged Man shows where it all gets stuck: in sacrifices and in fear of taking a step.

Years of working for a local institute — translations, bookkeeping, reports — accustomed you to modest money. One day you respond to an international project, first one of you, then the other. Now you work with clients from four countries, and part of your earnings goes into funds that bring income while you sleep. **The world turned out to be bigger than your office, and your knowledge found its price there.**

The Hanged Man at the end of the line is money left hanging. You once put part of your earnings into funds, while the rest has sat in your account for years “just in case”, quietly eaten away by rising prices. The decision is put off until “when we've worked it out”, and working it out feels awkward: you're not financiers, and asking feels awkward too. Invite someone who understands it for one evening, and together draw up a plan for where each part of your savings goes.

items.title: A hermit's window on the world

captions.L: Modesty and working in the shadows
captions.R2: The wide world and money that works
captions.R: Saving for the sake of the balance

items.meaning: Your quiet knowledge finds the wide world and brings prosperity — if money doesn't become the goal instead of the road.
text: Quiet work without fuss is your norm: the Hermit can't sell himself and long makes do with little. The World, repeated twice further down the line, throws the horizon wide open: your knowledge is sought in other towns and countries, and what you earn can grow without you. The cell gains a window on the wide world. Only the second World likes saving more than living.

You once learned Icelandic out of love for the sagas and for years told nobody. When a publisher needed a translator for a series of Scandinavian novels, you were the only ones to be found. Now you have contracts with three countries, and part of the fees works in savings accounts. **A language learned for yourselves opened a window on the wide world.**

The World at the exit loves to save. Fees go into deposits, interest grows, and the figure in the account pleases more than a trip to the country whose language you translate. You both work from home and for weeks see nobody but each other and clients in your inbox. Money has become the goal, not the road. Spend part of the interest on what you once learned the language for: the sagas, travel, people.

items.title: Chance turned into a way of life

captions.L: Money from one lucky break to the next
captions.R2: Study, tradition and the elders' experience
captions.R: Hesitating while the chance slips away

items.meaning: Your luck becomes steady income through study and settled ways — until caution lets the next chance slip.
text: From one lucky break to the next — that's how money comes to you: the Wheel of Fortune throws up chance earnings but promises nothing for long. The Hierophant offers something else: study, take on the elders' experience, enter a trade with a tradition, build a family way of life. Then chance turns into stability. The Emperor closes the line with a firm hand — sometimes too firm.

Your first wedding cake was a fluke: a friend asked. You didn't wait for the next fluke but went to learn from an old-school confectioner who for twenty years had baked for the city's best restaurants. Two years later he handed his clients over to you. **A chance order became a profession once you found a teacher.**

The Emperor decides slowly, and luck doesn't like to wait. The teacher retires and offers to sell you his bakery — you spend three months checking figures, and it goes to others; a restaurant offers a big contract — you ask for time to think until next season. Order protects you from mistakes, but a habit of measuring everything twice leaves you with what you already have. Decide in advance which opportunities you'll take at once, and keep a reserve for them.

items.title: Luck given a rulebook

captions.L: Waiting for luck instead of order
captions.R2: Knowledge, a mentor and family ways
captions.R: Clinging to work that has had its day

items.meaning: Your income stops swinging once luck gets a teacher and some order, and one partner's changes don't frighten the other.
text: At first money comes to you by chance: a side job turns up, a sale goes well, someone remembers you. The Wheel of Fortune at the way in promises a lot but holds on to nothing. The Hierophant turns chance into order: study, a mentor, a profession with rules, a shared family budget. And Death asks the main question of this line: are you ready to let go of what no longer feeds you?

For years translation was a random sideline for you: if they call, good; if not, we wait. One day you decide together: enough waiting for calls — time to sit the exam, get accredited and join the professional body. A year of evenings over textbooks, the exam, the first clients through colleagues. Now income doesn't depend on luck: you are known as specialists. **Your luck becomes prosperity once it acquires knowledge and the rules of the trade.**

The weak spot is the moment when it's time to change. Work that once supported the family has stopped paying, but leaving is frightening: that's where your years of service are, the familiar people. Or one of you dares something new, and the other meets it coldly, as if the partner's growth threatened the union. Money drains away into waiting and resentment. Put aside a reserve for the transition in advance: with a cushion, change stops frightening you both.

items.title: Luck under a master's eye

captions.L: Living from one chance to the next
captions.R2: A profession, a mentor and a joint budget

items.meaning: Your luck holds when it rests on a profession and shared ways, and flies away when it's spent carelessly.
text: Luck comes to you but doesn't stay: the Wheel of Fortune throws up a side job, then a bonus, then a good sale, with emptiness in between. The Hierophant offers support: a profession, a mentor, the rules of a trade, a joint family budget. That's how chance becomes income. The Fool calls you back to carelessness.

“You do everything right, but by guesswork,” said an old tiler you once worked for in the summer. And he took you on as an apprentice. Meanwhile the other trained as a cost estimator, to price jobs without losses. Two years later — your own crew, regular clients and a price list that scares nobody. **A mentor turned your random luck into a profession.**

The Fool dislikes reserves. It's easy to celebrate a good season so thoroughly that nothing is left by winter: trips, presents, new equipment “since things are going well”. One of you may tire of working for someone else, and then it's easy to walk off into nowhere. Carelessness is pleasant until the quiet season comes. Agree: a third of any lucky sum goes into reserve, the rest on joy without guilt.

items.title: Luck under contract

captions.L: Catching random earnings
captions.R2: Contracts, the law and an honest reputation
captions.R: Speeding up on credit and sharing blame

items.meaning: Chance turns into contracted income for you — and stays as long as you don't race ahead on borrowed money.
text: Luck at the way in is your familiar ally: work turns up by itself, money comes all at once and runs out just as fast. The Wheel of Fortune won't let you go under, but it won't let you lean on it either. Justice offers support: a contract instead of a verbal agreement, official income, a fair price and a reputation as people who do what they promise. The Chariot calls you to speed up once everything is running.

You win your second tender not on price. The client opens the file on your first project — the one you bid for “just to try” — and shows the panel the sign-off: delivered on time, on budget, without a single complaint. That's enough. Since then invitations come by themselves, and income has stopped jumping: it's set out in contracts a year ahead. **Luck secured with a signature feeds you longer than any lucky break.**

You want to speed up faster than the money allows. Take three contracts instead of two, buy equipment on credit against future payments, hire people in advance. If a client pays late, the whole acceleration lands on your budget — and the couple starts looking for someone to blame. Grow on your own money: a new contract when the old one is paid, new equipment when it's saved for.

items.title: Fortune with a receipt

captions.L: Hoping for chance instead of a plan
captions.R2: Honest work, paperwork and calculation
captions.R: Different family yardsticks, fear of the sudden

items.meaning: Luck comes to you by chance and stays by law and calculation: registered, counted and protected from the sudden.
text: Chance often bails you out: an order turns up, something sells well, an acquaintance remembers you just in time. The Wheel of Fortune teaches you to hope, and that's the difficulty: you can't build a budget on hope. Justice turns chance into a system: every income is registered, taxes paid, agreements written down. The Tower reminds you that the system needs a safety margin: changes can be abrupt.

At a fair your first painting sells by chance, a month later the second. Instead of rejoicing and waiting for the next time, you register as self-employed, draw up a price list, a contract for galleries and a sales ledger. A year later you have regular buyers and a steady income rather than a string of lucky breaks. **Chance becomes prosperity for you once it is put on a proper footing.**

The crack runs along the fear of the sudden. One of you grew up where money could vanish in a day and expects a catch even in good news; the other grew up where there was always a reserve and doesn't understand this anxiety. Arguments arise from the difference: save everything or live now. And when change comes, you look in different directions. Agree on a reserve that calms the anxious one, and a sum that can be spent without a second thought.

items.title: Holding steady between tides

captions.L: Feast, then famine — and feast again
captions.R2: Composure, and a quick reserve in fat seasons

items.meaning: Your income comes in waves; you grow rich by saving in fat seasons and keeping your heads in lean ones.
text: The Wheel of Fortune stands at both ends of your money line, and the couple's life runs in seasons. A big order comes, a bonus, a good sale — then months of quiet. Fighting the change itself is useless. Strength in the middle teaches composure: don't panic in a slump, don't lose your head on the rise, put money aside fast while it flows, and hold your course calmly while it doesn't.

You have a rule born of one hard winter: half of any unexpected money goes into reserve, no discussion. In summer, when orders are plentiful, it seems tiresome. In winter, when the phone is silent, you pay the rent from the reserve and even manage to buy a course that later brings in new clients. **Your wealth lies not in the height of the wave but in how much you carry away from its crest.**

The hole in the hull is the belief that the rise will last for ever. On the crest it's easy to borrow against future income, promise relatives big help, lend to a friend. The wave rolls back, and the obligations become crushing. Another crack is envy, when one of you is carried up and the other isn't. Greet the other's rise as a shared one: the next turn may lift the other.

items.title: Your own sun after the swings

captions.L: Income swinging from season to season
captions.R2: Hard work and quick saving
captions.R: Someone else's glare, and arguing whose win it is

items.meaning: Luck swings your income, and endurance makes it steady — until one partner's success eclipses the other.
text: Feast one year, famine the next: the Wheel of Fortune rocks your money, and it's hard to plan beyond a season. Strength in the middle is your answer to the rocking: don't chase, endure; save quickly while there's money; look for a solution when there seems to be none. The Sun at the end of the line promises success and asks how you'll share it.

Your photo studio has survived both the wedding boom and years with three orders a month. In the bad years you didn't close: you studied, shot for free for your portfolio, looked for new genres. When the market rose again, you were the only ones in town who could shoot both weddings and products for catalogues. **The slump you endured while others left is what gave you success.**

Success warms, but it can blind too. You want to show it off: expensive equipment, a status car, holidays for display. And in the couple one may end up in the spotlight and the other in the shade, and then a victory becomes a cause for argument: “it was my idea”, “and I carried everything else”. Share the glory as you share the money: both names on the sign, both voices in the decisions.

items.title: Steady amid the swings

captions.L: Income that soars and plunges
captions.R2: Measure, the middle way, living within means
captions.R: Tight control and one opinion for two

items.meaning: Income swings; you grow rich by keeping to the middle in every season — without turning order into commands.
text: Your money comes in waves: a good year gives way to a hard one, and each time it seems things will now stay that way for ever. The Wheel of Fortune doesn't ask permission. Temperance teaches you to stand in the middle: in a good year don't live large, in a bad one don't cut everything to zero, spend in line with income and always put a little aside. The Emperor wants to hold this order with an iron fist.

“The average month” — that's what you call the sum you spend, however much comes in. In a good season the difference goes into reserve; in a quiet one the reserve tops up to the average. Friends are amazed: you never have parties on your last money, or panics. A few years later the reserve covers a flat to let. **The middle you hold in any weather is your capital.**

Order can stiffen. One of you starts policing the rules more strictly than needed: every expense above the norm is a reason for a talk, every exception a violation. The other feels under command and loses interest in the joint budget. Rules that helped you ride out the swings become a cage. Review your “average month” together and leave room for joys outside the rules.

items.title: Steady through the changes

captions.L: Highs and lows with no reserve
captions.R2: Measure, the middle way and calm growth
captions.R: Clinging to a scheme that has served its time

items.meaning: Measure makes your swinging income steady — and it's lost when fear of change keeps you where it no longer feeds you.
text: A swing is the right word for your income: the Wheel of Fortune lifts and drops without warning, and there's no reserve for the fall. Temperance advises the middle way: save on the way up, don't panic on the way down, grow slowly and surely. Measure turns the swing into stability. Death waits where it's time to change and you hold on to the outlived.

For a long time you lived on seasonal orders alone. The solution came simply: one of you took a steady part-time job, the other carried on with seasonal projects. Together they give an income that doesn't swing and a reserve you never had before, and seasonal money now goes into growth, not patching holes. **Mixing the steady with the seasonal, you got money that isn't afraid of rough water.**

A scheme that saved you from the swings can outlive its use. The part-time job holds you even as it pays less and less, and the seasonal projects haven't grown for three years, but changing what once worked is frightening: what if it swings again? Death at the edge of the line reminds you that every stage ends, and it's better to meet change with a reserve and together than to wait until it comes by itself. Once a year ask each other what in your scheme it's time to let go.

items.title: Luck in measure

captions.L: Swings of good and empty months
captions.R2: The middle, a reserve and a calm pace
captions.R: Letting the other sort it out

items.meaning: Luck swings your income and measure makes it steady — until each of you hopes the other will sort it out.
text: Your income is a swing: the Wheel of Fortune throws up a good month, then an empty one. Temperance suggests holding the middle: save in good months, don't panic in empty ones, live within your means and grow without fuss. Then the swing turns into calm motion. And the Fool likes the boring bits to go to someone else.

Your boat hire lives by seasons: a queue in summer, silence in winter. In the first years winter ate everything summer brought. Then you stretched income over the whole year: in winter, on the same shore, you hire out skates, and you divide the summer money by months. **Luck stretched over the whole year became real income for you.**

The Fool likes someone else to take care of the boring things. The summer money is divided by months, but who makes sure it isn't touched early is unclear: one is sure it's the other, the other that it's the first. Taxes, boat repairs, the lease on the shore — all “later, you're better at this”. Such carelessness costs more than light spending: the holes are found when it's too late. Write down who answers for which part of the money, and check each other once a month.

items.title: Talent's lucky ticket

captions.L: Waiting for luck to drop in by itself
captions.R2: A name, talent and the public's trust

items.meaning: Luck opens the door, but prosperity comes through talent and a name — as long as chasing bigger doesn't burn your earnings.
text: Your income is uneven: a lucky break, then a long pause. The Wheel of Fortune teaches you to wait for luck. The Star answers the waiting differently: luck favours those who can be seen. Your name, your gift, your openness — that's how prosperity reaches the couple, and chance starts working for you rather than you for chance. The Chariot speeds up what you've earned — sometimes too much.

For years music fed you through tips in cafés, until one video of your performance spread online. You didn't wait for the next lucky break: you recorded an album, set up a page, began playing weddings and town festivals under your own name. Now people book you by name, not by chance. **Luck dropped in on you once and stayed because you became visible.**

The Chariot is both the engine and the leak. You want to secure success with a dash: new equipment on credit, a tour at your own expense, a move to the capital “while luck holds”. And it's easy to start a race inside the couple: whose career matters more, who gives more time to the work, who's holding whom back. Before you dash off, check whose money you're driving on and whether the other agrees with the route.

items.title: A star caught on the turn

captions.L: Waiting for a lucky break, not preparing
captions.R2: Talent, publicity and recognition
captions.R: A sharp fall after a rise

items.meaning: A lucky turn brings your talent to people and money, and a reserve is needed in case the rise ends just as sharply.
text: Chances come to you in turns: someone remembered, called, made an offer. The Wheel of Fortune brings the chance but doesn't prepare you for it. The Star shows what to do with it: go out to people with your talent, show your name, your work, your face. The more visible you are, the more often the wheel turns your way. Only your sharp rises sometimes end just as sharply — the Tower reminds you of that.

For years your duo played at friends' weddings. One day the host of a town festival didn't turn up, and you were asked to step in. You ran the evening so well that the next day you were asked to host the New Year concert, and then a festival. Now you have your own billing. **Your moment came by chance, and stayed because you were ready to shine.**

A rise that came suddenly can end just as suddenly: a season cancelled, the main client gone, fashion changed. Such a fall is worst for those who live at the peak and spend everything a good year brings. And one of you may be so frightened of a crash that you start expecting the worst even in good times. Keep a six-month cushion and live at the level of an ordinary season: then a fall will be unpleasant, but not frightening.

items.title: A wheel bound by family

captions.L: Living from one lucky break to the next
captions.R2: Family, kin and a shared business
captions.R: Borrowing on a high, and envy

items.meaning: Your luck swings until it rests on family: a shared business and budget turn chance money into an inheritance.
text: The Wheel of Fortune opens and closes your money line, so the couple's income moves in circles: lucky years, quiet years. Two tens make twenty — and in the middle stands Judgement, the energy of kin. Family turns the circles into an ascent: a shared business, support from relatives, a budget you plan together and discuss along with its risks. Prosperity often rises noticeably after you officially become a family.

One partner's father kept bees all his life, and for a long time you thought it his eccentricity. In a bad year for you both you go to help, stay for the season — and see that the honey could be sold differently: in the city, with the family's story on the label. Now the apiary feeds three generations, and odd jobs in town have become a sideline. **Your wheel stops throwing you up and down once it rests on your family.**

The cycle hits the purse too. In a lucky year you want to take out a bigger loan, invest without looking, help all the relatives at once. Then the slump comes, and the debts fall on the whole family, and with them grievances and talk of who owes whom. Envy lies in wait too: of cousins who did better. Decide on large sums together, planning for a quiet year, and don't turn relatives into creditors.

items.title: Luck that became the family's

captions.L: Lucky breaks and failures with no system
captions.R2: Kin, family and a shared business for years
captions.R: Pride in success, sharing glory in the family

items.meaning: A lucky break becomes a family business for years — if success doesn't turn into an argument over whose credit it is.
text: Lucky breaks and failures alternate for you without any system: the Wheel of Fortune lifts you, then drops you. Judgement gives support — kin, family, a shared business that can be handed on. Luck invested in the family stops being random and becomes the family's own. The Sun waits where money is tested for strength: success will come, the question is how you'll share it.

You entered your grandmother's dumplings in a town competition almost as a joke — and won a prize. Orders poured in by themselves, and you brought the whole family into the business: Mum makes them, a brother delivers, you handle the accounts and advertising. For five years now the family dumpling kitchen has run three workshops and sold in its own shops. **A lucky break you invited the whole family into became the family's business.**

When a family business thrives, you want to dazzle: expensive cars, loud parties the whole town talks about. And the question that breaks families apart appears: whose credit is it? You invented it, Mum makes them, the brother delivers — each sure they're the main one. Share profit by an agreement written on paper, and share glory equally, at a common table.

items.title: Strength under a charter

captions.L: Forcing your way through and wearing out
captions.R2: Order, a system and clear roles

items.meaning: Two strengths in a couple earn money when they submit to a shared order rather than argue over who's in charge.
text: The start and end of your money line belong to Strength: two strong characters used to getting their way by force. Money comes, but hard, and often your strength goes into fighting each other. The Emperor in the middle offers what tames you both: a system. Clear roles, a transparent budget, stable income, rules that are the same for both. Two elevens add up to twenty-two, and the Fool's lightness follows where the fighting has stopped.

After a particularly loud row over buying a car, you wrote a “constitution”: who handles the bills, who the investments, what sums each can spend without asking and which only together. Friends laughed at the sheet. But the money rows stopped, and three years later you bought that very car — without a loan. **An order accepted by two strong people turned out stronger than either of them.**

The second Strength tests your constitution with raised voices. An argument about a purchase quickly becomes an argument about who's right, and out come words you're ashamed of later: “you understand nothing about money”, “without me you'd…”. Each has their own truth and is sure it must be defended. No money is spent this way, but respect is. Add a pause rule to your constitution: contentious money matters are discussed the next day, when you've both cooled down.

items.title: Strength gathered into a system

captions.L: Pulling everything through by force
captions.R2: A system, clear roles and a reserve

items.meaning: Your strength brings steady money once it's a system, and doesn't leak while relatives hold no key to your pots.
text: Drive is your main way of earning: you work more than others, pull through on stubbornness, don't give up. Strength gives grip but wears you out. The Emperor gathers this energy into a system: clear roles, a plan, a budget, a reserve for each goal. Money stops depending on how much strength you have today. Judgement brings family matters — sometimes costly ones.

Every month used to be a feat for you: earn, close, pull through. One day you sat down and wrote everything out: who does what, how much goes into reserve, which jobs can be outsourced. A year later you were working less and saving more. **Strength gathered into a system stopped demanding feats of you.**

Judgement brings family customs into your budget, and they're expensive. An uncle's milestone birthday “done properly”, a niece's wedding where you're expected to bring a fatter envelope, a holiday with all the relatives that it's awkward to refuse — what the system saved goes in a single season. Persistence helps you earn but not to say “no”. Set up a “family” pot in your system with a fixed sum, and don't top it up from the others.

items.title: Drive on wheels

captions.L: Forcing everything head-on
captions.R2: Work on the move and projects away from home
captions.R: Living by others' rules of “what's proper”

items.meaning: Your drive earns money on the move, and it leaks when family rules start deciding what you're allowed.
text: You're used to forcing money through: with drive, stubbornness, the ability not to back down. Strength gives character but also a habit of charging head-on where you could go round. The Chariot turns that drive into movement: projects on the road, travel, several ventures, a speed at which persistence finally pays. The Hierophant closes the line and brings rules that can feel confining.

Your children's swimming club ran on sheer stubbornness: a small pool, a constant shortage of money. The solution came one summer: you take the pupils to training camps by the sea — first one group, then three. Now the camps feed you all year round, and the pool has become the place where you recruit beginners. **Your stubbornness goes out on the road — and only there does it start to pay.**

Relatives feel that “normal people don't go gadding about running camps”, and every holiday turns into a report. And within the couple one takes it on themselves to decide for both what it's “proper” to spend on and what not. Respect your elders but don't report to them, and inside the couple agree on rules rather than inheriting them.

items.title: Engine, wheel and brake

captions.L: Working flat out, sparing yourself nothing
captions.R2: Your own business, projects and the road

items.meaning: Your strength speeds up income, and agreement keeps it: what pace to live at and how much of what you earn to spend.
text: You earn money through persistence. Strength at the way in is the ability to endure what others flee from: a hard project, a long start, work without days off. The flip side is a habit of taking everything by force, even what could be taken by wit. The Chariot turns force into movement: a business of your own, several lines of work, travel, growth. And Temperance decides whether what you earn stays in the house.

You open a small car repair shop. For the first six months one of you practically lives in the garage, the other handles orders and purchasing. In the second year you have two lifts and a hired mechanic, in the third a second site on the other side of town, and you shuttle between them like dispatchers. **Your income grows where persistence gets a steering wheel and a road.**

What you'll argue about is the pace of spending. One of you puts aside every spare note, the other thinks that if you're working this hard you might as well live: a better car, a pricier holiday, a restaurant on Fridays. Both are right, and the argument goes round in circles. It's worse when prosperity starts being shown off — to others and to each other. Agree on a ratio: so much into reserve, so much for living, and the rest each spends without accounting for it.

items.title: Stop pushing the wheel

captions.L: Taking income by force alone
captions.R2: A lucky chance, a change, a new wave

items.meaning: Money comes when persistence stops pushing luck and catches its turn instead — and agreements get written down.
text: You're used to winning money by force: overworking, pushing through, squeezing. Strength gives persistence, but with money it often hits a wall. The Wheel of Fortune suggests another way: luck isn't pushed, it's caught. A change of job, a chance meeting, a trip, a move — prosperity comes to you in a wave, and what matters is catching it in time. Justice makes sure luck is secured honestly — and on paper.

For three years you tried to pull a loss-making shop through, working without days off. One day on holiday the people at the next table mention they're looking for staff for their chain. You take the plunge: sell the shop, join them — and eighteen months later you're earning more than in three years of struggle. **The wheel turned as soon as you unclenched your hands and stopped pushing it.**

Justice judges others by itself. You're honest and expect the same of everyone: you agree with new partners verbally, discuss your share in the chain over dinner without paperwork, take the bonus terms on trust — they're good people, they invited you, after all. The wheel can turn back, and then it emerges that everyone remembers the deal differently. Write down everything you agree on, even with those you trust: honesty on paper offends no one.

items.title: Luck for the stubborn

captions.L: Wresting income with your bare hands
captions.R2: A turn, a move, a sudden offer

items.meaning: Luck turns to you when persistence gives it a chance, and fails you when the good life is paid for with future income.
text: Strength is your ability not to give up. You're ready to work harder than others, and for a long time this seems the only way to get money. The Wheel of Fortune shows a second way: hold on until it turns. Your best money comes unexpectedly — with a move, a new circle of acquaintances, an offer you didn't expect. Persistence is needed to meet the turn in good shape. The Star closes the line with the temptation of a beautiful life.

For five years one of you has worked as an interpreter at a factory, the other as a foreman on the shop floor. When a foreign delegation arrives, it's the two of you who are asked to show them round. Six months later you're offered posts at that company's local office — with a different salary and business trips. **Luck found you where for years you'd held on better than others.**

The Star at the end of the line likes things to be beautiful. Once you've risen, you want to live up to it: a new flat on instalments, holidays worth talking about, things “for status”. Having paid off one debt, you easily take on the next, since everything ahead looks good. And when one of you starts to pride themselves on their position over the other, the crack runs through the relationship itself. Live a step below your means — the difference will become your reserve.

items.title: The strength to let go

captions.L: Holding on to the last to what isn't working
captions.R2: Ending on time, starting with a clean slate

items.meaning: Your strength earns money when it can not only hold on but let go: end at the right moment and begin again.
text: Two Strengths at the edges of your money line: you're a couple who know how to hold on. Hold a business, hold out against a blow, hold the bar high. Only you also hold on to what should long since have been let go: a loss-making business, a job with no growth, an investment that will never pay off. Death in the middle teaches another strength — ending in time. It's precisely where you dare to end something that growth begins.

For five years you've dragged along a café that barely breaks even, saying every month: “A bit longer and it'll take off.” One evening one of you puts two sheets on the table: how much you've put in over five years and how much you've got out. Selling the equipment, closing, a hard week — and three months later you're managing someone else's restaurant on twice your old profit. **Your most profitable step turned out to be a step back, taken in time.**

The second Strength looks for something else to hold on to, and often finds the purse. One of you becomes the head of money: allocating, checking, handing out. It looks like responsibility until the other starts to feel watched. Another crack is working without rest once the new venture takes off. Share the management of money, and don't turn endurance into a contest of who can bear more.

items.title: The resolve to end in time

captions.L: Holding on to the last out of stubbornness
captions.R2: The resolve to draw a line
captions.R: Family claims and disputes over shares

items.meaning: The resolve to draw a line in time earns you money — if family claims don't pull you back.
text: You have stubbornness enough for two: Strength holds on to a business to the last, even when it stopped paying long ago. Death teaches another strength — drawing a line. Sell, close, leave in time — and free space for something new that grows faster. Judgement, though, holds family matters that don't always let go so easily.

A tool-hire shop opened with your last money barely made ends meet for five years. You held on out of principle. When you finally decided to sell it to a competitor, the proceeds were enough for a share in friends' building firm. Now you're partners with an income the hire shop never dreamed of. **A line drawn in time became the start of your most profitable chapter.**

Once a business is sold or closed, relatives turn up sure of their right to it: a relative who once put in a small sum, heirs you hadn't thought of. Disputes over shares take strength and money. Put all family investments on paper from the very start, and closing things will be easier.

items.title: Strength recast by a crisis

captions.L: Pushing on stubbornly until it breaks
captions.R2: Rebuilding life after a shake-up

items.meaning: Your prosperity grows from a shake-up that breaks the old order, and leaks when a new venture waits for perfection.
text: You hold on stubbornly for a long time: carrying a job you don't like, a business that doesn't grow — giving up isn't in your nature. Strength gives stamina but makes it hard to admit it's time to change. The Tower does it for you: a shake-up, a break, an unexpected turn. Prosperity comes through it — on the site of what collapsed you build something better. The Hierophant guards what you earn — and demands that everything new be flawless.

Your family restaurant closed within one season, and for a long time neither of you could believe it. Then you sat down and worked out what went wrong — and instead of a new restaurant you opened a cookery school where you teach. Lower rent, lower risk, and a two-month waiting list for classes. **The collapse of the old business gave you material for a new one — sturdier than before.**

After a collapse the Hierophant becomes a perfectionist. You didn't open the school until every recipe was perfected, you don't launch a second course because not everything is ideal yet, and you discuss every development expense as if at an academic board. The old business fell, and now you're afraid to get even a detail wrong. Money stands still while you polish. Allow yourselves “good enough”: launch when it's eight out of ten ready, and finish the rest on the move.

items.title: Saved by a demolition

captions.L: Dragging on what isn't working to the end
captions.R2: Rebuilding, renovation and a fresh start

items.meaning: A collapse breaks your stubbornness and opens the way to prosperity; measure, not comparison, keeps it.
text: You don't know how to give up: Strength pulls the couple through difficulties even when the business stopped paying long ago. The Tower does what you won't dare: it breaks things. And prosperity grows where the broken thing stood — rebuilding, a new place, a big shared venture started from scratch. Temperance warns: measure lost in the struggle is even easier to lose once you're back on your feet.

You kept a failing car-repair shop going for seven years, until it was demolished for a new road. The compensation was enough for a plot by the motorway, and you built a tyre centre there with a café for lorry drivers. You work less and earn three times as much, and the road brings the customers by itself. **The demolition you feared cleared the ground for your real business.**

Measure is lost through comparison. Business has picked up, but there are always those nearby who never fell: acquaintances have a second home, former colleagues a chain of garages, and your honest prosperity starts to seem modest. Envy pushes you to catch up: a second site on credit, a better car, a renovation for show. Your road is different, and it has its own measure. Compare yourselves only with yourselves before the demolition — then you can see how much you've really built.

items.title: Strength out in the sun

captions.L: Working yourselves ragged for results
captions.R2: Success that is seen and recognised
captions.R: Unequal contributions and a tally of grievances

items.meaning: Your persistence becomes recognised success if each of you shines in their own work and contributions aren't weighed.
text: You don't lack persistence: Strength gives stamina and character, but at first it all goes into fighting — with bosses, with circumstances, with each other. The Sun shows where to direct this fire: into your own fulfilment, into work that is visible, where your name counts for something. Justice weighs contributions and makes sure nobody pulls alone.

One of you opens a pottery studio, and the other takes on everything around it: the rent, the accounts, the online page, the exhibitions. Three years later your workshops are booked a month ahead, the city magazine writes about the studio, and the potter is invited to teach courses in another city. **Your success shines brighter when it shows two people: the one at the wheel and the one holding the house together.**

The balance of contributions is your weakest point. The one in view gets the praise, while the one keeping the household and the accounts stays in the shadow — and starts counting. Or the reverse: one slogs away, while the other is in no hurry to find work because “we have enough anyway”. Justice can't stand a tilt, and it surfaces as resentment. Talk about each one's contribution aloud, and share both money and recognition so that it feels fair to you both.

items.title: Persistence in the spotlight

captions.L: Pushing through without rest
captions.R2: Recognition, success, both fulfilled

items.meaning: Your persistence brings you to recognition and money — and it matters not to spend it on looking rather than being.
text: Persistence is your main capital: Strength gives you stamina, and you get your way where others give up. The Sun directs this drive towards recognition: visible success, fulfilment for both, work to be proud of. Money comes along with the light. The Star adorns that light — sometimes on credit.

For three years your dance studio worked out of a basement, and you mopped the floors yourselves. In those years you didn't cancel a single class — and one day your students took first place at a big competition. Every local paper wrote about the studio, and enrolment closed within a week. Now you rent a bright hall in the centre. **Persistence nobody saw for three years stepped into the light and began to pay.**

The Star and the Sun demand a certain look. With the move to the bright hall comes a rule: in public you must be flawless — new costumes for every performance, photo shoots, expensive haircuts — and you start making these demands of each other: “you're wearing that?”, “you need to tone up.” Money goes on the picture, and home grows cramped with judgements. Remember what your students loved you for: persistence in the basement, not glitter in the centre.

items.title: Strength allowed to play

captions.L: Achieving everything by force
captions.R2: Freedom, lightness and a bold start

items.meaning: Money comes to you when strength allows itself lightness — and goes on gear better than last year's.
text: Strength holds your money line twice — at the start and at the end: you're used to winning money by persistence and keeping it by persistence too. Two elevens add up to twenty-two — and the Fool in the middle suggests the unexpected: prosperity comes when force lets go of itself. A flexible schedule, a bold start from scratch, work that feels like play. Where strength unclenches its fist, money appears.

For years you both worked for employers to the point of exhaustion, and one day, after yet another refused promotion, you go off to the mountains for a season as instructors, with no plan and almost no money. Three years later you have your own hiking school, the groups are booked to the end of the year, and you work less than before. **Money started coming the minute you stopped wringing it out.**

Strength spares no money on what it loves. New tents while the old ones still serve, the best boots, the best rope, a training trip to the Alps — all justified: “it's for the business”. The business really does grow, but so does the store of gear, and there's no reserve for a quiet winter. A passion turned into work easily eats its own earnings. Set an annual budget for gear and buy new only when the old has served its time.

items.title: Strength gone freelance

captions.L: Working yourselves to exhaustion
captions.R2: Freedom and a bold start from scratch

items.meaning: The freedom you released your strength into feeds you — and income is lost to family claims and disputes.
text: Pulling hard is your habit: Strength keeps the couple working to exhaustion, where everything is won by persistence. The Fool suggests letting go: going freelance, starting from scratch, making work feel like play. Strange as it seems, freedom is what feeds you. Judgement presents its own bill: family and kin lay claim to their rights.

You left your corporate posts almost at the same time, and the relatives decided you'd lost your minds. You converted an old minibus into a mobile workshop for sharpening and repairing tools, and now you tour the villages. There are orders to spare, and less work than there was in the office. **The strength you set free the world valued more highly than the office did.**

Family expectations grow along with your freedom. The relatives reckon that since you have “flexible hours”, you can help everyone — with money and time. Disputes arise over inheritance, over who looks after the elders, who got more. Family affairs eat up weekends and savings. Decide together how much you give the family, and say so plainly.

items.title: Growth after a long winter

captions.L: Stagnation, waiting and dependence
captions.R2: Growing what's shared, allowing abundance

items.meaning: Your long winter gives way to growth when you allow yourselves abundance — if stinginess doesn't become a habit.
text: Winter is the right word for your money at the start: waiting, stagnation, dependence on others' decisions. The Hanged Man teaches endurance. The Empress brings spring — growth: a shared business, a home, savings, fulfilment for both. Abundance arrives as soon as you allow it to yourselves. The Hermit closes the line with a habit of economising that stays even after winter.

While one of you was waiting for a promotion, the other quietly learned to make soap and gave it to friends and family. One day the waiting simply ended: you opened a small soap workshop. Three years later it feeds you both, and the promotion is no longer needed. **Spring came when you stopped waiting for it from others and started growing your own.**

After a long winter it's hard to believe in spring. Even when prosperity has come, you keep tightening your belts: on holidays, clothes, celebrations. Each keeps their own and stays silent about plans. Abundance that isn't used stops growing. Spend together on what makes you happier, and talk about your plans.

items.title: A pause, then everything bloomed

captions.L: Living in waiting, dependent on others
captions.R2: Growing what's shared, investing in the future
captions.R: Not knowing where the money comes from

items.meaning: Your long pause turns into growth once you grow something shared; abundance leaks where one stops knowing the figures.
text: Long waiting is a familiar state for you: one of you depends on the other or on parents, change doesn't come, decisions aren't made. The Hanged Man suspends. The Empress cancels the pause with growth: shared goals, investment in the home and the future, fulfilment for both. Abundance begins as soon as you stop waiting and start growing. And the Moon leaves shadows where money disappears.

Waiting for “better times” lasted some five years for you — until you decided to grow something of your own right now: a small children's club in the flat next door, where one runs the classes and the other the housekeeping and accounts. The club grew to three groups, and then to premises of its own. **Once you stopped waiting and started growing, you saw that money grows too.**

A shadow falls where one stops knowing. The accounts for the club and the home have long been kept by the one who “understands it better”, and the other doesn't ask about money: why, if everything's growing. Convenient — until it turns out the rent has gone up, the loan for new premises was taken earlier than planned, and the reserve went on repairs. The Hanged Man makes one dependent again, only now through not knowing. Once a month look at the figures together, even if they're dull.

items.title: A choice that ended the pause

captions.L: Living in waiting and sacrificing yourselves
captions.R2: Deciding, choosing together, going out to people

items.meaning: Income moves once you choose together — and holds as long as you don't compete over whose work counts more.
text: For long stretches your money seems to be waiting: there's work but no movement, and one of you sacrifices their own for the other. The Hanged Man teaches you to see differently, and the Lovers suggest what exactly: it's time to choose. Decide on work you love, a partnership, people you feel good with. The Empress will decide where the earnings go.

For years one of you put up with a job they disliked for the sake of stability, while the other waited for the “right moment” for a business of their own. The moment never came. One day you decided together: we're leaving. You opened a small interior textiles studio where one sews and the other talks to clients. **Deciding to leave together ended your long pause.**

The Empress measures contribution by what you can touch. One sews the curtains and bedspreads, and it seems they bring the money into the studio, while the other's client talks, estimates and fittings are “just help”. One day this is said aloud, and the one called a helper starts spending out of spite — on fabrics, presents for relatives, anything that proves their right to decide. Write down each one's contribution to the shared business and split the profit equally: without the other, not a single curtain would have been sold.

items.title: A choice in place of sacrifice

captions.L: Waiting and sacrificing your own
captions.R2: Choosing yourselves and work you love
captions.R: Giving everything away again, left with nothing

items.meaning: Your income is freed when you choose work you love over sacrifice — and lost again if you give everything away.
text: The Hanged Man meets you twice on the money line: patience, waiting, self-sacrifice are familiar states to you. For a long time you give, wait and don't ask. Add two twelves and you get six, and the Lovers in the middle of the line offer the main thing: choose. Work you like, people you feel good with, yourselves — on a par with others. Prosperity comes after that choice.

For years you worked in a relative's business for token pay, because “it would be awkward to leave”. Deciding to leave and open your own small language school came with guilt. The relatives took offence, but six months later sent you their own children. **By choosing yourselves you didn't betray your family — you started earning for the first time.**

Sacrifice knows how to come back. A new business can also be turned into unpaid service: discounts for everyone, free hours, loans to anyone who asks. Or one of you again puts their interests below the other's. Set an honest price, keep track of what you give away, and ask yourselves: is this a choice or a habit of sacrifice?

items.title: A choice that opened the world

captions.L: Waiting and living by others' decisions
captions.R2: Making your own choice together
captions.R: Groundhog Day in a business that works

items.meaning: Your pause ends with a choice made together — and money freezes when a successful business turns into Groundhog Day.
text: For long stretches you live by other people's decisions: the Hanged Man puts the couple in a state of waiting — for work, a promotion, a convenient chance. The Lovers say: choose for yourselves. Work you love, people you feel good with, a decision taken together — that's what gets money moving. The World then gathers it all into a stable life and tests whether it will become a cage.

You waited so long for a promotion that you stopped talking about it. The decision to leave you took together, in one night of talking: open a small gardening school for town-dwellers — what one of you had long dreamed of. Students came through acquaintances, then through happy graduates, and in spring the groups fill within a week. **Your shared choice moved what had stood still for years.**

The World turns luck into a timetable. The school runs like clockwork, the groups fill by themselves, and life curls into the same circle: the same courses, the same prices, the same season. Income hasn't grown for three years, but changing anything seems ungrateful to fate. One already misses the new but doesn't dare say so — everything's fine, after all. Your prosperity began with a bold choice, so give yourselves the right to the next one at least every couple of years.

items.title: A pause spent learning

captions.L: Stuck, waiting for change from outside
captions.R2: Deep knowledge found in a pause
captions.R: One stints, the other wants a party

items.meaning: An enforced pause turns into prosperity when you spend it on knowledge — as long as joy doesn't become an argument.
text: Sometimes the couple's money freezes: work doesn't grow, nothing changes, and it feels as if you're waiting for something that never comes. The Hanged Man suspends, but also gives time to look differently. The Hermit suggests what to spend the pause on: study, go deep, become experts. Prosperity grows out of this quiet time. The Lovers show how easy it is to squander.

The year one of you was out of work you now remember as the best. Instead of waiting for calls, you turned it into study: courses, books, practice with a craftsman you knew. Today people seek you out as furniture restorers, and that year has paid for itself many times over. **The pause you didn't waste on waiting became your most profitable investment.**

The Lovers at the exit pull you in different directions. After a year without work, one is afraid to spend even on joy: every purchase seems a step back into that void. The other, on the contrary, wants to finally live — travel, treat, celebrate. One stints, the other takes offence, and money becomes an argument about whether you're allowed to be happy. Decide together what share goes on joy — and spend it without guilt, leaving the rest alone.

items.title: Tested by profit

captions.L: Stagnation and fear of taking a step
captions.R2: Studying your trade in depth
captions.R: The lure of profit at any price

items.meaning: Your pause turns into mastery and money — until profit starts dictating whom you work with and how.
text: The couple's money stands still for a long time: waiting, doubts, fear that any move will make things worse. The Hanged Man suspends you, and in this suspended time the Hermit offers an occupation — study. Go deep into your trade until you become the people others seek out. That's how your future prosperity builds up. The Devil tests it with temptations.

You used two years without promotion in your own way: in the evenings you worked through land law, at weekends you went out surveying with an experienced land surveyor. Now you have your own office, and people bring you the most tangled plots that others won't touch. **Time that could have gone on waiting turned into a rare speciality.**

The Devil knows experts are valuable and slips you lucrative but murky offers: “turn a blind eye to one detail”, “we'll register it differently”. Working without rest for a big windfall is in his arsenal too. Value your reputation above any deal — for a master, it is the capital.

items.title: Double patience

captions.L: Waiting for change, living in limbo
captions.R2: Service, discipline and a long road

items.meaning: Your prosperity comes through long patience and service — if patience doesn't turn into austerity and silence.
text: The first two points of your line are the Hanged Man, so patience shapes both the way in and the road to money. At first it's a burden: money seems suspended, change doesn't come, you wait. Then it becomes a strength: a way of seeing value where others walk past, discipline, bills honestly paid, no loans. Money arrives slowly but surely. The Hermit waits at the very end with a habit of skimping on yourselves.

For years you bought old flats everyone avoided for a song and slowly put them right — one every few years, with your own hands. Friends tapped their temples. Today you have five flats to let and an income not tied to a salary. **Where others saw junk, your patience saw capital.**

The Hermit turns patience into austerity. Used to waiting and making do, you keep economising even when there's money: on holidays, on yourselves, on joys. Each withdraws into their own worries, and you keep quiet about money so as not to worry each other. Patience deserves a reward: give yourselves a celebration with each goal you complete, and don't be shy about discussing money.

items.title: Patience and shadows

captions.L: Waiting and living on pause
captions.R2: Service and long patience

items.meaning: Your prosperity ripens slowly, through patience and service — and is lost in things unsaid and naive trust.
text: The Hanged Man starts your line twice: first a pause when nothing moves, then a path — patient service to work and people. Money comes slowly, like a harvest on hard ground, but it comes to those who didn't give up. The Lovers sound as a trail — two twelves make six — and remind you of choice. The Moon leaves things unsaid at the end, where money can vanish.

The call comes in the depths of winter, when there's a month's hay left and a week's money. The head of a riding school asks whether it's true you keep calm old horses a child could safely ride. You stand in the cold stable with the phone and can't believe it: what you've done at a loss for years is needed by someone. From spring you run lessons for children, and the horses earn their own hay. **The patient care you gave without calculation one day began to feed you too.**

Shadow enters money without knocking. One of you hides a debt or a purchase, ashamed to admit it, and the other guesses and stays silent. Naivety is close by too: money is lent on a word of honour to people who promise to pay back “soon”. Patient people find it hard to ask for what's theirs. Talk about money directly, even when it's awkward, and put loans in writing.

items.title: From patience to grip

captions.L: Working for thanks and waiting
captions.R2: The wish to earn big and boldly
captions.R: A generous life that eats your earnings

items.meaning: Your patience turns into money when you allow yourselves grip, and doesn't leak away unless generosity eats the earnings.
text: Working for thanks comes naturally to you: the Hanged Man teaches you to wait, to give and not to remind people of yourselves. The Devil turns this habit upside down: to want in earnest, to set a price, to take on what pays well, to take a risk. The ambition you were shy of starts to feed you. The Empress then calls you to spend your earnings generously — sometimes more generously than you can.

The turning-point evening looks ordinary: you're sitting on the floor of someone else's new flat among the boxes, the third time this month, and the friend you helped move holds out an envelope “for petrol at least”. You refuse — and on the way home, for the first time, you add it up aloud: twelve Saturday moves in a year, not one weekend of your own. A week later an advert for “Full-service removals” is online, and the first to call are friends of those you moved for free. **Free help became income the moment you allowed yourselves grip.**

Having earned, you finally want to live a little: redo the flat, give presents, eat out, help family. Money won with a thrill goes out just as fast. An unequal load is dangerous too: one carries the business, the other in time becomes dependent and quietly resentful. Put a cap on comfort, and keep a field of your own for each.

items.title: From waiting to ambition

captions.L: Enduring and waiting to be noticed
captions.R2: Ambition and the nerve to claim your due
captions.R: Giving away earnings and living in debt

items.meaning: Your patience turns into money when you allow yourselves ambition, and melts again when earnings are given away.
text: The Hanged Man both opens and closes your line: patience, waiting, a habit of giving more than you get. Money hangs for a long time, and you hope to be noticed. The Devil in the middle breaks this pose: want in earnest, claim your due, take on work that pays well, start a second income, invest. The desire you hid for so long becomes the engine.

For years you helped everyone for free: fixing the neighbours' computers, setting up relatives' gadgets. One day you added up how many hours a month this took and put up a notice with prices. The neighbours didn't take offence — they started paying and bringing friends. A year later — a repair workshop with two assistants. **By putting a price on your time, you saw for the first time what it's worth.**

The old habit of giving comes back with the first money: loans to relatives, help for friends, discounts “for our own”. Or one again gives up their own for the other and ends up dependent. The Devil in the middle can also turn into greed — as an answer to years without money. Keep to the middle: an honest price, and help only of the kind you've both agreed on in advance.

items.title: A wish that woke the quiet one

captions.L: Enduring and not asking for your due
captions.R2: Ambition and the nerve to earn

items.meaning: Your long patience wakes up as ambition and brings money — and prosperity freezes when every hour starts being sold.
text: You're better at enduring than asking: the Hanged Man leaves the couple waiting to be noticed and valued. The Devil wakes a wish in you — to set a price, ask for a rise, take on well-paid work, take a risk. It's precisely the ambition you were shy of for so long that brings income. The World, waiting at the end, then wants to lock it all away.

You helped colleagues out without counting: covering for them, writing their reports, working extra hours for free. One day you added up how many hours you'd given away, and proposed a paid programme for gifted children to the school. The head agreed, parents queued up, and your hours are finally paid. **The patience you finally put a price on proved a valuable commodity.**

The world you've finally set up, you want to fence in. Everyone who asks for help seems to be after your time, colleagues look like rivals, old friends like debtors. Years of unpaid work swing to the other extreme: not an hour without payment, not a penny without a receipt. Patience that became a commodity shouldn't become meanness: keep a couple of hours a month that you give away for nothing — that's the kind of help your programme once began with.

items.title: A dream that became a business

captions.L: Freezing while waiting for better
captions.R2: Fantasy and work born at night
captions.R: Spending on emotions, making up with purchases

items.meaning: Your long pause ends when you trust your imagination — and money doesn't leak as long as it isn't spent on emotions.
text: The pause drags on: work brings no joy, change doesn't come, and taking a step is frightening. The Hanged Man teaches you to wait — and to look differently. The Moon suggests where to look: fantasy, dreams, quiet creative work, something born of intuition. Money appears when you trust your imagination. And the Lovers, closing the line, pay for feelings.

The bedtime stories one of you made up for nephews and nieces were once recorded on a phone and posted just for fun. A year later the audio stories have tens of thousands of listeners, and a publisher offers to bring out a book. The other draws the pictures for it. **The night-time inventions you long thought nothing of became your income.**

Feelings easily become an item of expenditure for you. After a quarrel — an expensive present; after a hard week — a purchase “to cheer ourselves up”; after a success — a party on all the fees. Sometimes dissatisfaction with income is voiced, and it hurts more than it seems. Let joy be a separate line in the budget, and reconciliation a conversation, not a receipt.

items.title: Imagination kept in check

captions.L: Waiting and a habit of enduring
captions.R2: Imagination and a venture born of fantasy
captions.R: The lure of easy money and murky deals

items.meaning: Your long pause turns into a venture born of fantasy — and money leaks away when success lures you into murky deals.
text: Waiting is familiar to you: the Hanged Man keeps the couple on pause, when nothing changes and deciding is frightening. The Moon suggests a way out — imagination: dreams, fantasies, quiet creativity, a venture invented on instinct. That's where income comes from. The Devil at the exit offers to multiply it by quick and not entirely clean means.

The dark stories you made up for friends round the campfire one day turned into an escape room: you rented a basement, made it into an “abandoned laboratory” and let in the first players. Now there are three rooms, and the scripts are still born at night. **The fantasy you finally gave room to became your income.**

The Devil loves those on a roll. Offers of a “lucrative partnership” with opaque money, the temptation to cut corners on safety, a fourth room on credit before the third has paid for itself. And at home the takings start deciding whose idea mattered most. Keep the business transparent: in your field, the trust of your guests is your capital.

items.title: Turning your view of the world

captions.L: Waiting, and fearing your own growth
captions.R2: Going out into the world and thinking bigger
captions.R: Stinginess, each in their own cell

items.meaning: Your income stops hanging once you look at the world beyond your own yard — and don't hide your earnings from each other.
text: Being stuck in limbo is the main feeling of your money: there's work but no growth, and taking a step is frightening — what if it gets worse? The Hanged Man teaches you to look differently, and the answer he suggests is the World. Turn your view around and see that your work is needed beyond your own yard, that money can work for you, that the rules of life can be written anew, together. The Hermit waits at the end of the line with a question: will you retreat into separate corners?

For eight years you've worked at the local library and the music school, and no other future is in sight. One day an acquaintance abroad asks you to run online lessons for emigrants' children. A year later — pupils in six countries, and the modest salaries have become a sideline. **You only had to turn your view around for your small world to turn out huge.**

The Hermit leaves the couple alone with itself. Once you've earned, you start saving too hard: the new coat waits for one more winter, the holiday is postponed, and each keeps their plans to themselves. You live side by side but in separate cells, and the money lies in separate cells too. Once a month open your purses and plans to each other: prosperity with no one to share it stops bringing joy.

items.title: A pause that opened the world

captions.L: Being in limbo and fearing growth
captions.R2: The wide world and work without borders
captions.R: Tax questions put off for later

items.meaning: Your pause ends with a step into the wide world — and money is lost where paperwork is put off for later.
text: Long periods in limbo are familiar to you: there's a post, but no movement, and a step forward is frightening. The Hanged Man suggests looking differently, and the World shows where: a horizon wider than your town. Clients in other countries, work not tied to a place, investments that grow by themselves — that's how the pause turns into prosperity. The Moon leaves a fog at the end, where it's easy to make mistakes at a distance.

For years one partner's fine voice was heard only at council meetings. In a long year without promotion you tried narrating audiobooks for an overseas service — first as a trial, then for a fee. Today you have a home studio and orders from six countries. **The pause in which you looked beyond the horizon turned into work without borders.**

Distance breeds fog in your own paperwork too. Fees arrive in different currencies to different accounts, some through an intermediary, and how to pay tax on them you mean to work out “when there's time”. The time hasn't come for three years. The Moon pretends that if nobody asks, there's no question, and the Hanged Man helps you put it off. Find an accountant who understands foreign income and sort it out now, while it costs less than it will later.

items.title: A new chapter with a textbook

captions.L: Clinging to the outworn, afraid to begin
captions.R2: Study, a mentor, a profession with rules
captions.R: A budget kept only for show

items.meaning: You close an old chapter and learn anew — and prosperity comes, as long as your budget is more than a spreadsheet.
text: Your money often starts with the end of something: an old job has run its course, the city feels cramped, the old way of earning no longer feeds you. Death demands that you let go, and letting go is frightening, so the couple lives for a long time on the ruins of the familiar. The Hierophant offers a way out: learn something new, find a mentor, enter a profession with clear rules. The Wheel of Fortune tests whether you're relying on chance.

When one partner's long years of service ended in redundancy, for the first time you went to study together — a cost estimator course at a building college. The tutor took you on his crew for practice, then recommended you to clients. Now you have a shared business where one does the figures and the other checks them. **Your new chapter began with a textbook, not a lottery ticket.**

The Wheel teaches you to treat money as a formality. You do have a budget: a spreadsheet, columns, a savings plan — but you live past it and check it twice a year, when something has already happened. One is sure the other is keeping track, the other that it's all in the spreadsheet anyway. You count other people's estimates to the penny but leave your own to chance. Look at your own figures as strictly as at your clients': once a month, together, by the facts rather than the plan.

items.title: After the end, apprentices

captions.L: The emptiness after a stage ends
captions.R2: Learning, tradition and sound rules
captions.R: Pride in success and dividing credit

items.meaning: A new stage begins for you by learning from masters, and prosperity holds as long as success doesn't breed pride.
text: The end of the old is a frequent turn in your money story: a job closed, an old path exhausted. Death leaves an emptiness. The Hierophant fills it with learning: find a master, take up a profession with a tradition, enter a circle where knowledge and rules are valued. That's how new income begins. The Sun promises success and tests you with pride.

After closing your shop, you both became apprentices to an old stained-glass master who had no successors. Three years of work for modest money — and the master handed you the workshop and his clients: churches, museums, private houses. **Learning after a loss gave you back more than the loss itself took.**

Recognition is a test no easier than loss. You want to show what you've achieved: an expensive car, loud interviews, fame as “the best in town”. And between you it's easy to start tallying credit: who brought the clients, who works better. Pride drives away both students and clients. Remember that the craft was passed on to you — and pass it on in turn, sharing the glory equally.

items.title: Honest tally, new charter

captions.L: Closing the old, not knowing what's next
captions.R2: An honest tally and clear agreements
captions.R: A plan that shuts out luck

items.meaning: Your new stage earns money when it starts with an honest tally, and fails you when the plan matters more than opportunity.
text: A new money cycle opens for you with the ending of the old one: a business closed, a job left, a move. Death leaves you on the threshold without a plan. Justice suggests the first step: take an honest tally — what you have, what you owe, what you can do — and build on agreements rather than hope. The Emperor brings order, but risks bringing it too strictly.

When you closed your sign-making workshop, the first thing you did was sit down and make an honest list: debts to suppliers, leftover stock, clients ready to stay. You paid off the debts within six months and took the clients with you into a new business — shop-window design. Not a single supplier was left aggrieved, and two of them now work with you again. **An honest tally of the old business became the foundation of new income.**

The Emperor builds a new charter and holds on to it so tightly that he stops seeing opportunities. An old client asks you to dress a whole shopping centre — you refuse, because “it's not in the plan”; a supplier offers a good batch — “the quarter's budget is already approved”. Order protected you after the old business ended, but rigidity makes your income as narrow as a shop window. Give your plan a line for “unexpected good things” and the right to revise it together in one evening.

items.title: An honest count at each crossing

captions.L: Closing stage after stage without a tally
captions.R2: An honest count and clean agreements
captions.R: Dragging debts from the past into the future

items.meaning: Your life goes in stages, and prosperity comes when each is closed with honest accounts, not carried as debt into the next.
text: Death meets you at the threshold of the money line and waits at the exit: the couple's life goes in stages — a job, a city, a business — and each one ends.
