Since you're building for ever — dearer windows, better timber, a staircase to a craftsman's design — and each such detail is honest in itself, but together they eat the reserve. Debts for materials grow on the promise of “we'll pay when the studios are let”. A dream built on credit becomes a burden. Agree the budget together, and discuss any expense beyond it separately, as a new purchase.

items.title: Stars over a building site

captions.L: Talent waiting for a miracle
captions.R2: An upheaval that opens the road

items.meaning: Your talent starts paying after an upheaval breaks the familiar — as long as the new isn't decorated on credit.
text: The Star shines at the first and last points of your money line: talent, dreams, a taste for the beautiful — you have everything except resolve. The Tower decides for you: an upheaval, losing the familiar, a forced move — and on the ruins of the old your gift finds a use. Two seventeens make seven, and the Chariot trailing behind urges you on: get moving. The second Star tempts you to decorate the new life before it's built.

When the landlord suddenly evicted your small art school, you had a month to find a new place. All you found was a derelict workshop on the edge of town. You rebuilt it yourselves together with your students — and got a space three times bigger, which now hosts exhibitions, talks and fairs. **The eviction that seemed like the end built you a big venture.**

The second Star loves beauty without delay. The workshop walls haven't dried yet, and you already want designer lighting, expensive chairs for the talks, a sign visible from the main road — the best people in town must come to the opening. One debt pulls another after it, for “the finishing touch”, and the school your students built by hand starts living on a bank loan. Build first, decorate later — and only from what's already been earned.

items.title: A star that became a sun

captions.L: Shining for friends, shy of the public
captions.R2: Recognition, success and each fulfilled
captions.R: Overwork and arguing who's in charge

items.meaning: Your talent turns into income when it reaches a wide public, and doesn't burn out in overwork and a fight for first place.
text: Your light is gentle at first: the Star gives talents, but you show them only to your own and are shy of a big audience. The Sun asks for more: step into the light, accept recognition, become visible. Each one's fulfilment is the road to prosperity. And Strength tests whether you'll bear this light and not start fighting each other for it.

For years your photos of the old town were seen only by a couple of hundred friends online. When a museum offered an exhibition, you refused for a long time. Thirty thousand people came, and afterwards came commissions from publishers and travel companies. **Once it reached a big audience, your talent got its real price for the first time.**

Light takes strength. One of you forgets about weekends, keeping everything in their own hands, the other feels superfluous. Or you both compete for the credit: whose name is bigger, who comes first in the shared business. Money grows while the relationship gets spent. Divide the stage: each has their own role, and rest is as much part of the work as the shoots.

items.title: A star the family saw

captions.L: Hiding talent and waiting for recognition
captions.R2: Stepping onto the big stage

items.meaning: Your hidden talent reaches the big stage and brings money — and it leaks away into family accounts and inheritance disputes.
text: Your talent lives in the shadows for a long time: the Star burns at half strength, and you wait for recognition without daring to step out. The Sun brings you onto the big stage: recognition, fees, a shared business you're not ashamed to show. The brighter the light, the fuller the till. Judgement reminds you that relatives flock to the light too — with inheritance, debts and old scores.

For years one partner's metal sculptures stood in the garage, and only the neighbours saw them. The other persuaded them to take the work to a town exhibition. There the council bought them for the new riverside promenade, and orders from parks and hotels came pouring in. **Out of the garage and into the light, your talent found its true price.**

Relatives flock to the light. They remember your share of Gran's flat, ask for money for the nephews' education, take offence that you've “got above yourselves”. Old family debts surface too. Money and time go on scores that have nothing to do with your talent. Agree how much you're prepared to give the family, and settle inheritance matters through a lawyer.

items.title: Talent on a free wind

captions.L: Hoping for recognition without risk
captions.R2: Freedom, a bold step and your own path
captions.R: Relatives' advice and stinginess “just in case”

items.meaning: Your talent earns in freedom when you risk showing it to the world — not when relatives decide how you should live.
text: You have a gift, but for a long time you wait for it to be noticed: the Star shines, yet little money comes of the light. The Fool says: don't wait, jump. Your own schedule, a bold first step, work nobody approved in advance — that's how your talent starts to pay. The Hierophant at the end of the line brings back the elders' voice: “where's the stability?”

One of you has always had a good voice, but it was only heard at the festive table. One day you buy tickets to a town hosting a street festival and perform right in the square — no posters, just one guitar. A year later you're booked for weddings and parties across three counties. **Talent began earning the moment you stopped waiting to be invited.**

Rules arrive along with relatives: you're asked when you'll find a “proper job”, and every performance has to be justified. Within the couple a stinginess “just in case” may appear: any spending on instruments and trips is discussed like a crime. Or one starts deciding how much the other may spend on the dream. Agree what share of income goes to your work — no discussions, no excuses.

items.title: Abundance grown out of fog

captions.L: Not seeing the future, living by feel
captions.R2: Shared goals, a home and investing in growth

items.meaning: Your fog lifts when you start growing something shared — and abundance holds as long as it doesn't go on extravagance.
text: For a long time you don't look beyond a month: the Moon keeps money in fog, and it arrives at random. The Empress meets you twice further on and speaks loudly: grow. Shared plans, a home of your own, investments that increase every year, each one's fulfilment — abundance begins with the first shared plan. The second Empress reminds you how easily it can be squandered.

Your first investment was saplings: you planted sea buckthorn on an empty plot inherited from a grandfather, though everyone said it was a waste. Five years later the bushes give a crop you sell to farm shops, and the juices and fruit leather made from your berries fly off the stalls at fairs. **Your first shared investment grew into an abundance you didn't expect yourselves.**

The second Empress can turn into extravagance. Once money starts coming, you're tempted to spend it all at once: new furniture, presents for relatives, purchases put off for years. Not enough — another call to the parents. Unequal growth is dangerous too: the one growing in the business quietly becomes the main one, and the other dependent. Spend the harvest from a list drawn up in advance, and make sure each has work of their own.

items.title: A harvest after a long night

captions.L: Not seeing the future, living on help
captions.R2: Growing a shared home, reserve and plans

items.meaning: Your prosperity grows when you stop living at random and grow something shared — if it isn't only one who pays for it.
text: For a long time the future seems foggy: money arrives in mysterious ways, plans don't take shape, and in hard moments parents bail you out. The Moon keeps you from seeing beyond a month. The Empress teaches you to grow: shared goals, a home, a reserve, investments that increase every year. Once you start thinking like gardeners, the fog lifts. The Hanged Man shows where the growing starts to rest on one pair of hands.

In the early years you lived any old how and borrowed from your parents. The turning point came with your first shared plan, written on the back of a bill: in three years, a flat of your own. You opened a savings account, both got promoted and each month watched the sum grow. You bought the flat after four years — with a room you use as a study for now. **Your first shared plan, written on the back of a bill, grew into a whole home.**

The Hanged Man shows who pays for this growth. Often one puts work, study, their own money on hold for the shared home, and gradually the other decides everything. From outside it looks harmonious, but inside resentment builds: “I gave everything, and I have nothing.” Both need their own fulfilment and their own money: a garden grows better when two equals tend it.

items.title: From fog to a clear choice

captions.L: Money in a fog, spending by feel
captions.R2: Choosing together and openly
captions.R: Spending on emotion, giving with a motive

items.meaning: Your income comes out of the fog when you decide about money together and out loud, not on impulse or in secret.
text: The Moon wraps your money in fog: it's unclear where it comes from and where it goes, and looking to the future is unsettling. The Lovers stand twice further along the line, and their lesson is a choice made together and in daylight. Prosperity comes when you stop guessing and start agreeing: what work to choose, whom to do business with, what to spend on.

For a long time you lived “somehow”: there was money but no plans. The turning point comes when the two of you choose a shared business — wedding floristry, where one has a feel for colour and the other knows how to talk to brides and their mothers. Orders come through acquaintances, happy clients, friends' weddings. **The fog lifts as soon as you choose your money together.**

The doubled Lovers rock your spending too. A purchase for the mood, a present to smooth over a quarrel, something new because “other couples look better”. One partner's impulse becomes the other's grievance, and dissatisfaction with income sounds like a reproach. The Moon makes all this secretive: purchases are hidden, receipts thrown away. Give each of you a sum for impulses, and anything bigger only after a conversation.

items.title: Clarity against temptation

captions.L: Not seeing where the money leaks
captions.R2: Choosing work and people openly
captions.R: The lure of murky schemes and power through money

items.meaning: Your fog clears through honest choice — of work, people, spending — and thickens when money starts buying influence.
text: Your money sits in half-light for a long time: it's unclear how much there is or where it went, and you'd rather not look ahead. The Moon confuses things, and decisions are made at random. The Lovers bring clarity through choice: what work to take, whom to trust, what to invest in. Prosperity comes when the choice is made openly and together. The Devil tempts you to settle everything quickly and not quite cleanly.

The decision ripened after a night-long talk, when for the first time you wrote down all your income and debts on a sheet. The sheet showed that half your money came from work you both dislike. You choose different work — it pays less, but you believe in the work and the people you do it with. Two years later it's what brings in the most. **A choice made in daylight led you to money more directly than any back road.**

The Devil thrives in half-light. Once money appears, there's always a lucrative offer nearby that it's better not to ask too much about. And inside the couple money becomes power: whoever earns more decides, and the other is left with “thank you”. Reproaches over earnings are dangerous too. Keep deals transparent and the joint budget open to both: the shadows love secrets, and secrets cost you dearly.

items.title: A lantern in the money fog

captions.L: Not knowing where the money comes from
captions.R2: Digging deep and becoming an expert

items.meaning: Knowledge clears the fog around your money: the better you understand where income comes from, the calmer it grows.
text: For a long time money remains a fog for you: it comes from somewhere and goes somewhere, and asking how much you actually have is a little frightening. The Moon muddles the tracks and breeds an anxiety easier to hide than to name. Further along the line the Hermit stands twice, and two nines add up to exactly eighteen: the answer to fog is a lantern. Look into it, learn, understand more deeply than usual — that is how both income and calm come to you.

For years you didn't open your bank statements, until one weekend you sat down with them together. It turned out a third of the money was going on subscriptions and interest. One of you gets hooked: reads up on taxes and savings, picks apart contracts — and a couple of years later friends come for advice, and then paying clients. **Knowledge about money became money for you: a lantern lit for yourselves now lights the way for others too.**

The second Hermit at the end of the line shows the other side of silence. Each of you may retreat into your own cell: worrying silently, keeping savings “just in case”, saying nothing about a debt until it grows. You think you're protecting each other, but in fact the fog returns — now between you. Set aside an evening a month for an honest talk about money: how much there is, what frightens you, what you want.

items.title: Clarity between two nights

captions.L: Money with no clarity and no plans
captions.R2: The light of knowledge, unhurried digging
captions.R: A secret stash born of anxiety

items.meaning: Between two fogs knowledge holds you: the more clearly you understand your money, the fewer secrets and fears it holds.
text: The Moon surrounds your money on both sides: fog at the way in, fog at the way out. Where income comes from, where it goes, what will happen in a year — all this stays unclear for a long time, and anxiety grows in the dark. Add two eighteens and you get nine, and the Hermit in the middle holds the lantern. Your path to prosperity is knowledge: get to the bottom of things, master what others can't be bothered with, see deeper.

Archives were your quiet passion: old maps, registers, letters. One day an acquaintance asks you to trace her great-grandmother — and you do. Now you compile family trees to order, people come to you by recommendation from other cities, and you unravel the most tangled stories together. **The light you learned to find in other people's archives became your income.**

The second Moon brings anxiety back, only now it hides behind caution. One of you saves “for a rainy day” behind the other's back, the other turns down a lucrative order in case it doesn't work out, and you still don't look beyond next month. You know how to untangle other families' secrets, yet keep your own money secrets in separate drawers. Lay them out on one table: what each has, who owes whom, and how you'd get through a year with no orders.

items.title: Fog you wait out

captions.L: Uncertainty and fear of looking ahead
captions.R2: Waiting it out and seeing differently
captions.R: Parents' money out of old habit

items.meaning: Anxiety about the future fades when you wait it out and look differently — unless you go to your parents for what's missing.
text: Looking ahead with money is frightening: the Moon puts out the landmarks, and the couple lives by feel. The Hanged Man advises not to rush about but to wait — and look at the situation upside down: what seemed a dead end can be a door. Patience pays off here. The Empress at the end calls you to spend on comfort and beauty — sometimes before there's money for it.

The year with your parents after a failed rental became a time of observation for you, not complaint: you noticed there wasn't a single place in their neighbourhood to leave a child for an hour. Your “playroom by the hour” opened six months later and paid for itself within a year. **A year with your parents, lived with open eyes, suggested your business.**

The year with your parents left a habit: if you're short, you can ask. The Empress pulls you towards comfort and generosity, spending on the home and celebrations outruns income, and what's missing is borrowed from the parents again — and along with the money come their tips on running your “playroom by the hour”, and the anxiety you once moved away from. Spend on comfort only above your reserve, and take advice from your parents, not money.

items.title: Patience at dusk

captions.L: Anxiety and murkiness with money
captions.R2: Patient service and another view
captions.R: Giving without measure, losing your own

items.meaning: Murkiness in money passes through patience and seeing differently — if patience doesn't become endless sacrifice.
text: Anxiety about money is familiar to you: the Moon hides what you can rely on. The Hanged Man waits twice further on, and his lesson is patience. Don't rush about, but wait things out, look differently, serve work that people need. Prosperity ripens slowly but surely. The second Hanged Man warns: patience without measure becomes sacrifice. Two twelves add up to six, and the trailing Lovers remind you to choose yourselves.

Years of night shifts as dispatchers for the city's emergency repair service seemed temporary to you. You endured, learned, took the hardest calls. When the service was reorganised, it was you who were appointed to run the night centre, and your experience came in useful in consulting for neighbouring towns. **The night shifts you patiently saw out one day became your standing.**

The second Hanged Man pulls towards sacrifice: working for two without a rise, lending without a receipt, living for others' needs — and storing up quiet resentment. Sometimes one of you gives up their own for the partner and loses their footing. Patience is a strength as long as it can be stopped: set a limit and keep to it.

items.title: Waiting that became clarity

captions.L: Anxiety and fog around money
captions.R2: Patience and a view from the other side
captions.R: Guarding calm at the cost of gain

items.meaning: Patience and a view from the other side lift your money anxiety — and prosperity freezes when calm matters more than gain.
text: Money makes you anxious: the Moon hides clarity, and the future seems shaky. The Hanged Man teaches you not to run from this uncertainty but to wait it out and look from the other side: what frightened you may turn out to be an opportunity, and the waiting a preparation. Prosperity comes slowly, through patience and service. The World, though, tends to lock up what you've saved.

Renting was your anxiety for five years: it seemed you'd never buy a place of your own. One day you stopped chasing a mortgage in the capital and looked at it differently: you moved to a small town where a flat costs what a year's rent in the capital does, and switched to remote work. The waiting ended within six months. **A problem turned the right way up cleared the fog over your money.**

The World dislikes change, and for those who lived long in anxiety, calm becomes sacred. You're invited back to the capital for good money — you refuse before hearing it out; the flat has long been cramped, but moving is frightening; any spending beyond the usual is discussed for weeks. The waiting you once beat comes back disguised as caution. Once a year ask each other what you turned down only out of fear.

items.title: From fog to clear ambition

captions.L: Murkiness and fear of looking ahead
captions.R2: Strong desire and well-paid work

items.meaning: Your murkiness gives way to clear ambition, which earns money — until it's spent on rewarding yourselves for tiredness.
text: Fog around money is familiar to you: unclear how much there is, where it goes, what comes next. The Moon makes the couple indecisive. The Devil blows the fog away with strong desire: understand what you want and work for it in earnest — hard, a lot, for good money, with extra income streams and investments. The last word on the line belongs to the Lovers, and they spend on feelings.

For years your money flowed without direction, until one day you wrote a single goal on a sheet: a house of your own, deadline five years. The goal fired you both. One moved to a job with commission on sales, the other took on extra work and learned to invest. There was twice as much work, but for the first time you both knew what for. You got the keys sooner than you'd reckoned. **As soon as your desire had a price and a deadline, the fog lifted.**

Money earned hard begs to be spent beautifully: expensive surprises, dinners, purchases “because we've earned it”. After every big order — equipment you never use, after every hard week — a thing as a reward, and the reward becomes a habit. The house you worked for starts filling up with purchases. Agree on big spending before, not after, and reward yourselves with what brings the shared goal closer.

items.title: Double grip, no shadow

captions.L: Uncertainty and fear of money
captions.R2: Clear ambition and hard, well-paid work
captions.R: Greed and money as a leash

items.meaning: Your uncertainty clears with a clear wish and hard, well-paid work — until the second Devil turns money into a leash.
text: For a long time money frightens you with its murkiness: the Moon hides both the figures and the future. The two Devils further down the line answer fear with desire: name your goal and go at it with grip — hard work, good pay, a second income, investments. But grip repeated twice easily becomes a leash. Two fifteens make three, and the Empress trailing behind reminds you what you're working for.

You got fed up with uncertainty one autumn evening and decided to earn big. One of you got behind the wheel of a lorry on long-haul runs, the other took on finding profitable loads and doing the sums. Four years later you have your own lorry and a small haulage company. **A clear goal turned your grip into a company of your own.**

The leash appears unnoticed. The one who brings in more starts deciding, and the other starts hearing that without them they're worth nothing. The temptation of a profitable but dubious load is close by too. Runs without rest for a little extra eat up everything you started for. Keep the shared goal in view, and don't let money speak for you.

items.title: Work found at dusk

captions.L: Anxiety and murkiness with money
captions.R2: Intuition and unusual work

items.meaning: Your anxiety becomes a resource when you trust instinct and build unusual work together — if both have a voice in it.
text: The start of your money line belongs twice to the Moon: murkiness, anxiety, money that's hard to understand — and at the same time instinct, imagination, a pull towards the unusual. The same fog that frightens leads to prosperity once you trust it: work guessed by intuition, creative, quiet, unlike any other. Two eighteens add up to nine — to the Hermit, the last card of the line.

Night shifts were once your misfortune. Now the night is your business: you host a late-night radio show and a podcast for people who can't sleep — stories, music, quiet conversations. Advertisers found you themselves, and listeners send letters from different cities. **The darkness you once feared turned out to be your stage.**

The Hermit makes one of you the voice of the show and the other its shadow. The one on air decides everything: which stories, which ads, what an episode costs; the other writes the scripts and keeps quiet about their own idea — a night show of their own — because “two voices isn't the same”. Money comes in, but one dream in the house quietly fades, and half your strength with it. Give the second idea at least a pilot episode: your instinct is shared, and it pays better heard in two voices.

items.title: Three moons over one trade

captions.L: Fog, anxiety and murky money
captions.R2: Intuition and work born of imagination

items.meaning: Your money lives at dusk: the fog frightens, instinct feeds, secrets take away, and all depends on what you choose.
text: The Moon takes all three positions on your money line. Fog at the entrance: it's unclear where money comes from and where it goes, and anxiety multiplies in the dark. Dusk in the middle: it's precisely instinct, imagination, a night-time craft others don't understand that brings you income. And shadow at the exit: secrets, fears, naive trust. Three eighteens add up to nine, and the Hermit trails behind to suggest that here you must light the lamp yourselves.

You wrote your dreams down in a notebook and then painted them — strange, misty, like nothing else. One day the owner of a late-night café asked you to paint such dreams on the walls. Today you paint cafés, nurseries and bedrooms, and clients wait their turn to get “their own dream”. **The dusk you lived in became your palette and your income.**

The third Moon hides things. Stashes “just in case”, a debt it's awkward to admit, money given to someone who talked a good game — in the fog all this is lost quietly. Fear is expensive too: because of it you don't spend even on what's needed and don't dare do good things. Light the lamp yourselves: an open talk about money every week, and paper for every deal.

items.title: From fog into the wide world

captions.L: Money with no clarity or plans
captions.R2: The wide world, rules for two and savings
captions.R: Abundance that melts into home comforts

items.meaning: The murk lifts when you go out into the wide world and write shared rules; abundance holds while it isn't squandered.
text: Murkiness accompanies your money for a long time: the Moon hides the answers to simple questions — how much there is and what it will cover. The World brings a clear picture and a wide horizon: budget rules drawn up together, work not tied to one place, investments growing without your involvement. The third card of the line is the Empress, and her generosity can squander what's been gathered.

A map of all your income and spending, laid out on the table one day, ended your anxiety. It turned out remote work for foreign clients brought in more than you thought, and it was all going on trifles. You drew up rules, opened a savings account in another currency, and two years later bought a flat by the sea. **A clear map and the wide world together led you out of the fog.**

The flat by the sea keeps asking for more: furniture, repairs, guests all summer — and money that came from far away goes very close to home. The map that once led you out of the fog lies in a drawer, and spending is by feel again, only the sums are bigger. The Empress is generous, the Moon dislikes recounting. Get the map out once a quarter: the rules you drew up together only work while you check against them.

items.title: A clear world, a quiet sacrifice

captions.L: Anxious uncertainty with money
captions.R2: A wide horizon and order for two

items.meaning: Your anxiety yields to the clarity of the wide world and shared order — and money goes to those whose name is on your work.
text: Anxious uncertainty is your starting point: the Moon hides how much there is and what's to come. The World gives clarity and space: shared rules, a clear picture of money, work and investments beyond the familiar. There anxiety gives way to confidence. The Hanged Man at the end pulls you back to giving and waiting.

For several years you volunteered on international projects — for food and a roof over your heads. The experience, languages and contacts you brought back turned out to be capital: today you organise placements abroad for students, and the programmes are booked two years ahead. **The world you served for free began paying you for your experience.**

The Hanged Man makes you invisible in your own business. You devise the programmes, you deal with the host families, yet on the partner university's website these are “its international placements”, and most of the fee stays there too. Talking about money is awkward: after all, you started as volunteers. Put a price on your experience, write into the contract whose name is on the programme, and don't be shy of holding to that price.

items.title: A world that came out of the fog

captions.L: Anxiety and fog around income
captions.R2: Clear order and a wide horizon
captions.R: Suspicion and life behind a wall

items.meaning: Your fog clears in a wide and orderly world — and money freezes when that world becomes a wall.
text: Anxiety about the future is your constant companion: the Moon shows no road beyond the next month. The World, standing twice after it, answers anxiety with order and space: clear rules, work without borders, investments that grow by themselves. Where anxiety gives way to a map, prosperity appears. The second World makes sure order doesn't become a fortress wall.

Moving to another country seemed madness to you, until one of you was offered a contract. You went for a year “to see” and stayed: work, a new language, rules that turned out clearer than the familiar ones. Now you help other families move and charge more for consultations than that contract paid. **The world you were afraid of turned out to be your clearest income.**

The second World builds walls. When everything is running, you want to protect what you've achieved from any change: “the old is better”, suspicion of new people and offers, an account for every expense. Suspicion infects the couple too: you check up on each other and hide small things. A world walled off from the world stops growing. Leave the doors open — to new people, ideas and trust in each other.

items.title: A sun in tradition's service

captions.L: Spending on glitter and status
captions.R2: A profession, tradition and people's respect

items.meaning: Your brightness earns money when it serves tradition and the work, and fails you when rules go unrevised for years.
text: Beautiful things, status, a life worth boasting about — the Sun draws you to glitter. But glitter without foundation is costly. The Hierophant gives the foundation: a profession with a tradition, colleagues' respect, knowledge passed down the generations. Your light becomes income when it serves the work, not the shop window. The Emperor brings order, sometimes too strict.

For a long time you built your events-hosting agency on your own charm, until you understood charm doesn't sell without schooling. You went to learn from the city's most senior master of ceremonies, took on the rituals, traditions, rules. Now you're invited where things must be done “properly”, and paid twice as much. **Charm grounded in tradition came to be valued twice as highly.**

The Emperor and the Hierophant like everything “as established”, and that includes prices. You haven't raised your rates in five years because your teacher charged the same; you host celebrations to the old script though clients ask for something new; you don't take on an assistant because “the host must do everything”. The order that earned you respect starts holding your income still. Once a year review prices and rules together, and ask yourselves what you do only out of habit.

items.title: A sun that teaches

captions.L: Chasing status before substance
captions.R2: Knowledge, teaching and family values
captions.R: Clinging to a role and fearing change

items.meaning: Your light earns money when it serves knowledge and family rather than status — and when roles in the couple can change.
text: You like being in view: the Sun pulls the couple towards status, success, a life to be proud of. Only sometimes you want the status before the substance. The Hierophant directs this light: teach, pass on knowledge, build a way of life with room for family and rules. That's how prosperity comes. Death reminds you that every role ends one day.

The stage was once your life, and now forty children learn to sing in your studio. Parents bring younger brothers and sisters, graduates come back to teach. The town knows you not as former performers but as teachers, and enrolment for the new year closes in August. **Your light became income when you started passing it on to others.**

Attachment to a role is dangerous. The one used to being in charge and in view takes it hard when the other starts to grow and step forward. Or it's time to close a line of work that has stopped paying, but it's a pity: so much has gone into it. Change comes anyway — the only question is whether you meet it together. Be glad when the light passes to your partner: in your couple there's enough for two.

items.title: Shine that found a teacher

captions.L: Wanting to dazzle at any cost
captions.R2: Study, rules and respect for tradition
captions.R: Careless spending and running off “to be free”

items.meaning: Your wish to shine earns money when it rests on knowledge and order, and leaks if freedom is mistaken for carelessness.
text: You want to shine — at work, at home, in life. The Sun gives brightness, but impatience too: status is wanted before it's earned. The Hierophant gives direction: learn from masters, get a real profession, live by rules people respect. Shine built that way holds. The Fool, closing the line, calls you to drop everything for freedom — sometimes at the worst possible moment.

The mentor under whom one of you spent three years learning jewellery-making says one day: “Now put on your own hallmark.” The first piece with your mark sells within a week, the second within a day. You know the value of every stone and every hour of work, and that's exactly what clients pay for. **The shine became real once there was mastery behind it.**

The Fool creeps up with a cheerful “why not?”. Drop a tiresome order, go away for a month, buy what you fancy without thinking about bills. Freedom is good, but carelessness costs dearly: debts, missed deadlines, a melting reserve. Give your freedom a budget: a sum for the spontaneous you can spend without guilt, and a rule not to drop what you've started halfway.

items.title: Honest light, no gilding

captions.L: Spending on status beyond your means
captions.R2: Honest work, the law and precise figures
captions.R: Risky dashes and loans for speed

items.meaning: You want to live brightly, and prosperity comes from honest, costed work — without borrowing for a quick shine.
text: The Sun draws you to brightness: good things, status, a life to be proud of. The catch is that you want the brightness before it's earned, and money goes on the look of success. Justice shows the real path: honest income, official contracts, precise figures, a plan B. The Chariot closes the line, and it has its own temptation — to dash ahead without counting.

For a long time you lived large and on credit, until you decided to recount everything. The spreadsheet was unpleasant but honest. For a year you paid off debts and learned to live within a budget, then opened your own party-planning agency — with contracts, deposits and clear estimates for clients. Now clients choose you for your transparency. **The light you're proud of today has been paid for by honest figures.**

The danger point is a dash. When things are going well, the Chariot eggs you on to expand fast: a second hall rented on borrowed money, staff hired “to grow into”, a car for status. If the dash fails, blame-shifting starts in the couple: who insisted, who should have stopped it. Before you accelerate, check the figures as strictly as you did at the start, and share responsibility equally.

items.title: Brightness with a safety margin

captions.L: Living at a level you haven't reached
captions.R2: Honest sums and declared income
captions.R: A sudden fall in your standard of living

items.meaning: Your light rests on honest figures, not credit — and then even a sudden collapse doesn't put it out.
text: You want to live beautifully: the Sun calls you to a bright life, and the couple often lives at a level it hasn't yet earned. Justice brings you back to honest figures: declared income, contracts, spending within your means, a backup plan. That's how prosperity comes — solid, without gilding. And the Tower asks whether your standard of living has a safety margin.

Your house-warming in your first shared flat was the grandest among your friends and the most expensive: you paid off the loan for it for two years. After that you agreed: not a single purchase on credit. A holiday when it's saved for, a car when you have the full sum, a renovation by estimate. Your life is no less bright now, but every detail of it is paid for. **Shine you don't have to pay for later glows brighter for you than before.**

Here the sudden strikes at your standard of living. A job lost, a crisis in the industry — and everything you're used to becomes unaffordable. It's hardest for the one used to the shine: a “step down” stings, and you want to hide it from acquaintances. And each of you brought your own money habits from childhood, which clash in trouble. Keep a cushion, and don't build a life that one salary can't sustain.

items.title: A sun you have to earn

captions.L: Wanting the shine before there's a footing
captions.R2: Persistence and an unconventional solution

items.meaning: Your light starts earning when hard work stands behind it — and doesn't go out in complaints about bad luck.
text: You both want to live brightly: a good neighbourhood, beautiful holidays, work that's pleasant to talk about. The Sun pulls towards success, but sometimes towards its appearance before the thing itself. Prosperity comes through Strength: persistence, endurance and the ability to solve a problem in a way others didn't think of. The Wheel of Fortune shuffles luck around and tests how you cope with downturns.

You're offered a lucrative but almost impossible project: two weeks for a tender where rivals have twice as many people. You take it. At night you work on an idea that gets round the budget limits, and you win. The next orders come in by name. **Your shine is persistence visible from outside, and that is exactly what you're paid for.**

The wheel turns, and after a loud victory comes a quiet year. There are fewer orders, and instead of looking at what has changed, you start blaming fate, the market and then each other: “if only you'd agreed back then”, “you were the one who turned that client down”. Complaints eat the strength that used to go into unconventional solutions. A downturn isn't a sentence but a problem: take it apart together as you took apart that tender, and find the move nobody else thought of.

items.title: Two suns, one staying power

captions.L: Wanting to shine at once and brightly
captions.R2: Persistence and endurance without show
captions.R: Rivalry for glory and spending on status

items.meaning: Two bright people earn when shared persistence stands behind the shine, and lose when they start competing for the light.
text: Two Suns on your money line: you're both bright, both want success and recognition. Two nineteens add up to eleven, and Strength in the middle explains how this turns into money: through persistence. Not glitter but endurance — years of work, enduring the invisible stages, keeping your nerve. The light comes later and stays for a long time.

For five years your patisserie stayed small, though you dreamed of fame. You patiently perfected recipes, didn't chase fashion and didn't cut prices. When a well-known restaurant critic finally wrote about you, it turned out you were ready: recipes perfected, processes running, the queue didn't scare you. **The light came when years of persistence already stood behind it.**

Two suns side by side can start competing. Whose name is on the sign, whom the customers praise, who invested more — victories are split into “mine” and “yours”. You want to show off success too: a status car, an expensive holiday. Glory that's divided quickly cheapens. Speak of victories as “we”, and spend on what's shared, not on show.

items.title: Brightness in measure

captions.L: Splashing out or cutting back hard
captions.R2: The golden mean and patient growth

items.meaning: Your love of a bright life brings prosperity when it finds measure — as long as measure doesn't put out the joy.
text: Money throws you to extremes: the Sun wants to splash out, and after the party comes hard economising. Temperance teaches the middle: live brightly but within your means, grow without fuss, spend with joy and save without strain. The middle becomes your prosperity. The Emperor strives to fix the order — sometimes too imperiously.

You used to throw parties on your last money and then live on porridge for a month. One day you agreed on something simple: a fixed sum for joy every month, no more and no less. The parties stayed, the debts disappeared, and by the end of the year there was a reserve for a trip that used to seem a luxury. **A bright life in measure turned out richer than a bright life on credit.**

The Emperor makes the middle too serious. The sum for joy is approved, but spending it becomes ever duller: a party to budget, a present from a list, a trip costed down to the last cup of coffee. The money is in order, but there's less sunshine in the house, and talking about what you want now feels awkward — everything seems right. Order is there so you can live brightly without debt, not so you stop enjoying yourselves: once a year allow yourselves one purchase without calculation.

items.title: Light kept to measure

captions.L: A glamorous life income can't cover
captions.R2: Living brightly but within your means

items.meaning: A bright life within your means is how you grow rich — and prosperity leaks into what once shone but no longer pays.
text: You want glamour — and right away: the Sun pulls you towards a bright life your income can't yet cover. Temperance suggests not putting out the light but rationing it: live beautifully but within your means, spend with joy but not everything, grow without leaps. Then brightness becomes lasting. Death at the end reminds you that any glitter changes shape one day.

You opened your lakeside glamping site in grand style: tents, fairy lights, music — and debts. The second season you did differently: kept the best, cut the extras, raised weekend prices and lowered weekday ones. Now the tents are full all summer and the debts are paid off. **Glitter kept within your means proved more profitable than glitter without measure.**

Death comes with changes that can't be avoided. The fashion for lakeside tents will pass, guests will want something else, and one of you will be drawn to a new venture before the other. Clinging to past success is expensive: buying more tents and lights for a place where they no longer pay, only because it once shone. Let go in time, and choose together what to invest in next.

items.title: Light without a binge

captions.L: Celebrations on your last money
captions.R2: The middle way and a calm rhythm
captions.R: Working when you feel like it

items.meaning: Celebration brings you money when it has a rhythm — and stops when discipline gives way to mood.
text: Celebrations happen often for you, and on your last money: the Sun adores brightness and generosity. Temperance offers a rhythm: shine steadily, live within your means, rejoice without strain and save a little at a time. Brightness with a rhythm brings steady money. The Fool lies in wait at the end of the road and suggests breaking loose — in high spirits and without a backward glance.

The winter fairs you used to hold in the courtyard for the neighbours one day grew into a town fair. In the first year you put in everything and nearly went under. From the second you've kept a rhythm: one big fair a season, a clear budget, a reserve for bad weather. Now the town itself offers you the square. **Celebration that found a rhythm began to bring in money.**

The Fool dislikes discipline. The rhythm that saved you holds while it's fun, and then replies to stallholders get put off “till tomorrow”, the contract for the square is signed on the last day, and in summer you don't think about the winter fair until October. Each time a festive miracle comes to the rescue, and one day it won't. Celebrate as much as you like, but keep the preparation calendar as firmly as the budget.

items.title: A sun that found its star

captions.L: Chasing glitter, not meaning
captions.R2: Talent, creativity and inspiration
captions.R: A race for growth and loans for a dash

items.meaning: Shine feeds you when talent, not status, stands behind it — and doesn't burn out in a race for fast growth.
text: Brightness attracts you: the Sun wants success, recognition, a life on display. Sometimes the shine matters more than the substance, and earnings are spent on the shop window. The Star shows what real success is built on: talent, inspiration, creative work that finds a response. The Chariot speeds you up — and can speed you up too much.

For years you made other people's brands famous — beautifully, loudly and without soul. One day you decide to make a small film about your town, just for yourselves. It's shown at a festival, and you're invited to make documentaries for museums and foundations. Today three more people work in your studio. **The light truly began to shine when you turned it on what you love.**

The Chariot is in a hurry to lock in success: make the second film at once, rent a bigger studio, buy equipment on credit. Each pulls their own way: one towards advertising, where money comes faster, the other towards film, where it's more interesting. After a failure it's easy to start shifting blame. Grow at the speed of your income, and agree where you're going before you put your foot down.

items.title: Star success with a cushion

captions.L: Living brightly on your last penny
captions.R2: Talent, inspiration and renown
captions.R: Success cut off with no reserve

items.meaning: Your talent brings visible success, and it lasts if a reserve is set aside for a sudden cliff edge.
text: You want to live brightly right away, even on your last penny: the Sun loves the beautiful and the visible. The Star points to the foundation of real brilliance — talent, inspiration, a name people recognise. When you shine with your work rather than your things, money comes. The Tower punishes those who settle at the very peak without a safety net.

The cookery videos you filmed in your kitchen as a joke one day got a million views. You spent the first advertising money not on a new flat but on a studio, training and a recipe book. Today you have your own TV show and a book in every shop. **Brilliance built on talent shines longer than brilliance bought on credit.**

The cliff edge comes suddenly: the platform changed its rules, the main advertiser left, fashion turned. Those used to the heights fall hardest: expensive habits and no reserve. Sometimes one of you panics while the other pretends nothing has happened. Set aside at least a year's expenses while the light shines, and agree in advance how you'll live if it goes out.

items.title: Sun over the family house

captions.L: Wanting glitter and spending on status
captions.R2: Family support and a shared family business

items.meaning: Your brightness becomes income in the family business — and fades when the business closes in on its own people.
text: Living brightly is your weakness: the Sun pulls towards status, beautiful things, success people talk about. While the light shines only on the two of you, there's little money. Judgement turns it towards the family: a family business, relatives' support, a shared future, an inheritance you not only receive but create. The turn towards prosperity often coincides with a wedding or the birth of a shared venture. The Wheel of Fortune rocks it, testing its strength.

The restaurant one partner's family ran was a place for regulars. You brought to it what you know: brightness, celebrations, an open kitchen, photos online. Two years later guests come from other parts of town, and the parents can finally rest — and are proud. **The family business became the best stage for your shine.**

The wheel turns, and everything with you stays within the family: suppliers are relatives' acquaintances, the cook a cousin, advice only from the elders, and new people aren't let into the business. While the wheel is at the top, it's cosy, but when the season dips, it turns out nobody can help except those who are struggling themselves. You want to lock in good years broadly — a new dining room on credit — and then the whole family pays. Widen the circle before the budget: new people in the business are safer than new debt.

items.title: Two suns of one family

captions.L: Wanting to outshine everyone in the family
captions.R2: A shared business with family and a legacy
captions.R: Pride and disputes over who's in charge

items.meaning: Two bright people earn in a family business — if success doesn't become a contest for first place in the family.
text: Brightness went to you both: the Sun stands at the first and last points of your line, and being noticed matters to you. Judgement in the middle says where that light brings money: in the family. A shared business with relatives, a legacy you multiply, the support of kin — here your brightness works for everyone. Two nineteens make eleven, and Strength trails behind to remind you of self-control.

The circus dynasty of one partner's parents was living out its days at small fairs. You brought light, music and modern direction to the old acts — and for the first time in twenty years the family circus filled a hall in the regional capital. Now you're booked on tour a year ahead. **The light you brought restored the shine to a family business that had almost gone out.**

The second Sun dislikes sharing the stage. When the business is thriving again, the dispute begins: whose credit is it, who's in charge — you, the elders, one of you two. Pride eats away a family business faster than any debt. And you want to show off success widely too. Agree on roles and on the bill: whose name goes where — and thank aloud everyone who kept the business going before you.

items.title: Building a fortress of your own

captions.L: Instability and quarrels over family property
captions.R2: A system, savings pots and clear duties
captions.R: A struggle over who runs the budget

items.meaning: Your prosperity is built like a fortress — a system, pots for goals, clear roles — until the budget becomes a battlefield.
text: Family history enters your money with Judgement: an inheritance divided for years, help from parents, an instability familiar since childhood. Because of this the couple's financial life depends on others' decisions for a long time. The Emperor builds a fortress of your own: stable income, a savings pot for each goal, an order in which everything is decided in advance. Strength at the end of the line tests who is in charge of that fortress.

Once a year, on the first weekend of January, you sit down with a notebook and divide the money into pots: cushion, renovation, holiday, studies, a big purchase. Each gets its own monthly sum, and nobody moves money from one to another without a conversation. Five years later you don't have a single loan, and the inheritance your relatives argued over so much you no longer need. **The fortress you build yourselves is more reliable than any ancestral home.**

From inside, the fortress is tested by quarrels over who's in charge. Order needs a commandant, and one of you easily becomes one: allocating, permitting, “I know better”. The other gives way but stores up disagreement. Working for the pots can eat up your rest too. Share the power: each has their own pot they answer for, and one shared pot you decide on together.

items.title: Order between two families

captions.L: Family expectations, inheritance with strings
captions.R2: A system of your own and clear rules

items.meaning: Family surrounds your money on both sides, and prosperity rests on a system of your own, not on family arrangements.
text: Judgement holds both sides of your money line: family, kin, inheritance and the expectations tied to them. For a long time the couple's money isn't only yours. Two twenties add up to four, and the Emperor in the middle offers a way out: a system of your own. Your own budget, your own pots, your own rules both understand, and a stable income independent of the family council.

When the elders suggested you live “temporarily” in a grandmother's flat in exchange for looking after the country cottage and helping all the relatives, you politely declined. You rented a place of your own, set up a budget with three pots, and five years later bought a flat without anyone's help. The relatives sulked for a year, then started coming for advice. **Your own system proved more reliable than any family arrangement.**

The second Judgement brings family matters back at the end of the road. Dividing an inheritance, a dispute over a share in the cottage, grievances over who was helped more can drag on for years and eat up savings. In the couple there's a temptation to keep “family” money separate and not show it to the other. Put family matters in order with a solicitor, and keep the joint budget open between yourselves.

items.title: Out of the family nest

captions.L: Waiting for relatives to help and decide
captions.R2: Your own business, travel and a bold start

items.meaning: Your income starts growing when you leave your relatives' wing for your own road and take no money with strings.
text: Your money is tied to family: inheritance, parents' help, family expectations, old disputes over who is owed what. The difficulty is dependence: as long as decisions are made at a family council, your income isn't yours. The Chariot leads you out of the nest: your own business, a move, several projects, the speed with which you build your own. And the Hierophant at the very end brings the family theme back — this time as a risk.

Every Sunday you used to visit your parents and hear how to live properly. At some point you stop going to report and start going as guests. Between those Sundays fits your first project of your own — turnkey flat renovations — and then a second. The parents grumble at first, then boast to the neighbours. **For you, the road to money starts beyond the gates of the family nest.**

The Hierophant brings relatives back into the budget through help. The parents offer money for a new van, and along with the money their voice enters the business: which clients to take, how much to save, why you're working on a Saturday again. Refusing is awkward; accepting means going back to Sunday reports. Take help from relatives only as you would from a bank: with a sum, a term and no say in your decisions.

items.title: An inheritance put to work

captions.L: Keeping family property as dead weight
captions.R2: Moving, risking and building your own
captions.R: One always giving way on money

items.meaning: Your family property earns once it's set in motion, and leaks when the same one always gives way on money.
text: Much in your money is decided with an eye on the family: something was inherited, something is expected. Judgement makes family property both a support and a burden: selling seems a pity, investing frightening, and it lies idle for years. The Chariot sets it on the road: turn the inheritance into a business, travel, take a risk, build your own. Temperance at the end of the road keeps measure — or loses it.

From a grandfather you inherited an old motor boat that sat at its moorings for ten years. The family expected you to sell it. Instead you put it in order and start taking tourists up the river, and by the third season you have two boats and a jetty of your own. **Family property became capital once you let it sail.**

Temperance keeps the peace, but sometimes at one person's expense. The boats and the jetty are registered to the one whose grandfather it was, and somehow all money decisions became theirs too: where to invest, when to rest, how much to pay yourselves. The other gives way so as not to disturb the calm and stores up what goes unsaid. From outside — an even life; inside — a tilt that will one day surface. Make the other a full owner of at least one part, and decide big things together.

items.title: Family script, your own chance

captions.L: Living by your relatives' money scripts
captions.R2: Catching your own chance, changing scene
captions.R: Debts, arrears and a tally of grievances

items.meaning: You leave family money scripts behind by catching your own chance, and keep it by honest reckoning, free of debts.
text: Relatives stand at the source of your money: what was customary in your families, who helped whom, what was inherited and what was taken away. Judgement brings family scripts — “we've never had money” or “we decide everything as a family”. The Wheel of Fortune pulls you out of the circle: a change, a move, an unexpected chance of your own, not the family's. Justice demands clear accounts with everyone — relatives, the bank, each other.

One partner's parents expected you to stay in their town and help in the family shop. You're offered work at the other end of the country — and after long talks you leave. Two years on you have your own income, and you help the parents not with your time but with money, of your own free will. **Your chance comes when you let the wheel carry you out of the family circle.**

Money leaks through debts and grievances. Borrowing from relatives and dragging out repayment, borrowing till payday and forgetting, promising and not managing — Justice doesn't forgive such loose ends. Inside the couple it keeps a tally too: whose relatives got more help, who put more into the shared pot. Agree on rules: lend to relatives only what you're ready to part with, and meet your own obligations on time, even the small ones.

items.title: Family luck and stardust

captions.L: Depending on the family and its decisions
captions.R2: A lucky turn and a change of scene

items.meaning: Luck leads you out from under the family's wing, and stays as long as you don't measure it by others' successes.
text: For a long time your couple's money depends on family: parents' help, shared property, decisions made by the older generation. Judgement keeps you within the family. The Wheel of Fortune leads you onto your own road: change, a move, a chance you catch yourselves. The Star adorns the new life — sometimes too expensively.

The offer came out of the blue: an acquaintance was moving abroad and looking for someone to take over a small hotel by a lake. Your parents tried to talk you out of it — “risky, not your thing”. You took it on, and within three seasons the hotel was more profitable than under its previous owner. For the first time you're earning what nobody allotted you. **A chance caught despite family doubts became a business of your own.**

The Star likes comparisons. The hotel is more profitable than under the previous owner, but acquaintances on the far shore have a pool and a sauna, cousins a flat in the capital, and your success suddenly seems small. Comparisons push you to spend not on the business but on keeping up: a new wing on credit, a renovation “like theirs”. The parents who tried to dissuade you watch in silence. Measure the hotel by its own figures, and adorn it from profit, not from comparisons.

items.title: Leaving the family shop

captions.L: Clinging to family property, waiting for help
captions.R2: A decisive break with the outworn
captions.R: Disorder in the new business's money

items.meaning: Your prosperity begins by leaving the family script and holds as long as there's order in the new business.
text: Your money stays tied to the family for a long time: a family home, inheritance, the elders' shared business, their decisions and expectations. Judgement holds on tight. Death shows the way out: decisively finish what belongs to the past — and start your own. The freed space fills quickly. Strength tests how you'll use your freedom.

The family shop where you worked “for the parents” for ten years brought you nothing but a salary and reproaches. Deciding to leave was hard, and the relatives took offence. A year later — your own farm-produce delivery service, you earn three times as much, and with your parents you finally talk about something other than work. **By letting go of the family business, you got something of your own for the first time.**

Strength pulls forward, paperwork later. Orders come in, the delivery service grows, but receipts lie in a shoebox, contracts with farmers in message threads, and who owes whom what is remembered only by whoever's driving. While luck holds, the disorder seems the price of speed. The first audit or row with a supplier will show what it costs. Once a week sit down together and put the money in order, even when you're tired.

items.title: Breaking the family script

captions.L: Family expectations and an inheritance with strings
captions.R2: Decisive rebuilding and a new start

items.meaning: Prosperity begins where you break the family script, and melts away in lawsuits with relatives over what was sold.
text: Family is present in your money from the very start: what was inherited, what was promised, what's expected of you. Judgement brings an inheritance with strings and a script written before you. The Tower breaks it — and prosperity comes through that break: decisive rebuilding, selling what held you back, a big shared venture in a new place. Last stands the Hierophant with the old rules.

A grandmother's flat, which the relatives regarded as a family shrine, stood empty for five years. You took the plunge: sold it despite the hurt feelings and put the money into a plot where you're now building a house with a workshop. Half the family still grumbles; the other half asks to visit. **The broken script made room for a home of your own.**

The Hierophant doesn't forgive broken rules. A cousin decides the grandmother's flat was shared property and contests the sale, an aunt backs him, and instead of building you spend two years going to hearings. Money goes on lawyers, strength on explanations, and the house with the workshop waits. Money disputes with relatives are won by paperwork, not grievances: put everything in order as if you'll be audited tomorrow, and decide together where giving way costs less than going to court.

items.title: The break the family awaited

captions.L: An inheritance that holds you in place
captions.R2: Boldly rebuilding the family way of life

items.meaning: Your prosperity grows from boldly rebuilding a family legacy — and lasts as long as you keep measure after the changes.
text: An inheritance can be not only a gift but an anchor: the family house, the old business, obligations to kin that hold you in place. Judgement ties your hands. The Tower frees them — by decisive rebuilding: sell, demolish, remake, move. Your money grows right where the old was broken. Temperance makes sure you don't lose measure after the storm.

The old family house on the edge of the village was falling apart, and the relatives had argued for ten years about what to do with it. You took the decision on yourselves: dismantled it, built a new house with a workshop from the sound logs, and sold the rare old timber to designers for interiors. **The nerve to break up the family nest gave your family a new home and an income.**

After big changes it's easy to lose balance: one can't wait to live on their own money, the other is afraid and hides every penny. You're tempted to show prosperity off to relatives who already resent the changes. And if one carries the new business, the other ends up dependent. Find a new middle: rules for spending and reserves made for the new life, not carried over from the old.

items.title: Heirs who shine on their own

captions.L: The shadow of family and its expectations
captions.R2: Your own success and a shared business

items.meaning: You step out of the shadow of family expectations through your own success, which lasts while you split shares honestly.
text: Judgement ties your money to family: parents' expectations, inheritance, comparisons with brothers and sisters. The difficulty is the shadow the family casts: it seems everything important was decided before you. The Sun leads you out of that shadow — to success of your own, work that's yours, recognition you earned yourselves. Justice demands honest accounts with everyone.

You were expected to take the top chair at the family firm. You declined and opened your own agency — small, but yours. The first year was frightening: no family connections, no safety net, only your names on the door. Five years later the agency had outgrown the family firm, and the head of the family asked your advice for the first time. **Your own light turned out brighter than the inheritance you were destined for.**

Justice keeps a tally, and family money dislikes it. A share in an inheritance, a contribution to the parents' house, a debt to a brother — all this can turn into lawsuits and grievances. And the couple acquires its own tally: who invested more in the shared business, whose success counts for more. Put family agreements on paper, and between yourselves share not only money but credit.

items.title: Bright children, modest kin

captions.L: Others' expectations and the family script
captions.R2: Your own recognition and shared success
captions.R: Showing the family you've broken free

items.meaning: You step out of the family script into your own success — and keep it, as long as you don't spend it proving yourselves.
text: In your family it's the custom to live modestly and “like everyone else”, and Judgement holds you in that script for a long time. The Sun calls you out into the light: your own success, recognition, work you're both proud of. Your brightness brings money when you stop apologising to the family for it. The Star tempts you to live straight away like the picture.

You carved your first ice sculpture for a bet at a family New Year's party, and the relatives laughed at the “nonsense”. Three years later your sculptures stand at town festivals, and wedding planners across the region know your name. **The nonsense the family laughed at became your name and your income.**

The Star wants the relatives who laughed at the “nonsense” to see how you've broken free. The car at the family gathering is the showiest, the presents the dearest, the stories about orders come with figures. Spending is done not for life but for the audience at the family table, and half of it on credit. You have nothing left to prove: your name is known across the region. Spend on what you and the business need, and give the family time, not glitter.

items.title: Breaking out of the family plan

captions.L: Living by a plan the family drew up
captions.R2: Freedom, lightness and unusual work of your own
captions.R: Overwork and power over the purse

items.meaning: Income comes when you free yourselves from the family plan, and holds while one's strength doesn't become power.
text: The family mapped out your path long ago: study, work, housing near the parents. Judgement keeps the couple in that plan, where money is predictable and small. The Fool suggests turning off: do what nobody approved, start without anyone's prompting, live more freely. That's where money increases. Strength tests whether freedom will turn into a new harness.

The family expected you to continue a dynasty of lawyers. Instead you went into organising holidays for people with dogs — all the relatives laughed. Three years later your little travel club is known across the country, and those who laughed ask whether they can come at a discount. The law degree came in handy too: you draw up the contracts with hotels yourselves. **The freedom your relatives laughed at became your income.**

Strength lies in wait for success. A business started for the sake of freedom pulls you in, and one of you works without days off and then takes all the money under control: “leave it to me.” Freedom turns into a new harness. Rest as seriously as you work, and decide about money together.

items.title: Free between two families

captions.L: Family expectations at the start
captions.R2: Freedom and your own unusual path

items.meaning: Family flanks you on both sides, and prosperity comes through freedom — unless relatives divide what you built yourselves.
text: Judgement stands at the entrance and the exit of your money line: kin and family with their expectations and rights. First they decide who you should be, then how much of your success they're owed. The Fool in the middle sets you free: to do your own thing, unusual, approved by nobody, to start from scratch without looking back. Add the two twenties and you get four, and the Emperor's trail reminds you that freedom needs order.

By the family plan you were meant to stay in your father's building firm. You chose something else — a surf school on a northern sea where, as everyone said, “nobody surfs”. Three years later people come from all over the country, and the father's firm has a new order — to build your guest cabins. **Choosing freedom against the family plan, you came back to the family as partners.**

The second Judgement comes when you've succeeded. The relatives recall who helped at the start, who has a right to a share, who “could also” work for you. Grievances and claims take both nerves and money. Put everything with relatives in writing — loans, shares, agreements — and don't confuse gratitude with debt.

items.title: A garden planted by two

captions.L: Clinging to the old and fearing change
captions.R2: Shared goals, growth and investing in the home
captions.R: Skimping on joy and living apart

items.meaning: Your prosperity grows like a garden, from shared goals and investment in the home — until stinginess leaves it unwatered.
text: You value the tried and tested over the new: things last a long time, rules were set long ago, change seems an unnecessary risk. The World at the start of the line guards what has been gathered. Hence the difficulty — income doesn't grow for years, because growth is frightening. The Empress shows another kind of growth — living, like a garden's: shared goals, investment in the home and in each other, prosperity that increases every season. The Hermit makes sure the garden isn't overgrown with silence.

You were in no hurry to become a family officially — “things are fine as they are”. When you finally married, a lot suddenly fell into place: a joint mortgage on a house with a garden, tax allowances, your first joint savings account. You plant apple trees and laugh that everything grows for you now. **Your money grows like a garden — from shared investment and patient care.**

The garden withers from stinginess and estrangement. You start economising on joy — presents, holidays, seeing friends — and the garden becomes a vegetable patch where everything is for stockpiling. Each withdraws into their own worries, and money is rarely discussed. Find time together and spend part of the harvest on yourselves: money you don't allow yourselves to spend joyfully stops growing.

items.title: A familiar world and new faces

captions.L: A closed circle and distrust of outsiders
captions.R2: Partnership and choosing by heart

items.meaning: Income grows when new people and shared decisions enter your world — and melts when generosity outruns earnings.
text: Your world is secure and closed: your own people, old connections, caution towards the unfamiliar. The World protects but keeps income at one level. The Lovers open the doors to new people and shared decisions: partners, acquaintances, work both of you love. The Empress hands out what you earn generously — sometimes too generously.

For many years the two of you kept your forge to yourselves, letting nobody in. One day you let in a young couple of designers — at first temporarily, then as partners. They bring new ideas and new clients, you bring craftsmanship. Two years later you have twice as many orders, and your wrought-iron gates stand at new houses across the county. **New people in an old circle turned out to be your best investment.**

The Empress's generosity now goes to the new people too. You give the young partners the best orders “to grow into”, pay for their ideas from the shared till, lay a table for everyone at every celebration in the workshop — and by the end of the year it turns out the forge feeds everyone except the two of you. Out of old habit you help relatives without counting too. Be generous within what you earn: your share first, then the presents.

items.title: Opening the doors to people

captions.L: Being closed and wary of the new
captions.R2: People, connections and choosing by heart
captions.R: Giving everything and depending on the other

items.meaning: Your income grows when you open your doors to people and choose work by heart — without sacrifices you later regret.
text: You keep to your own circle: trusted people, familiar work, distrust of everything new. The World shuts the couple inside its own universe, where everything is clear but income doesn't grow. The Lovers open the doors: acquaintances, partnerships, choosing an occupation you love, socialising that grows into orders. The Hanged Man shows that in all this socialising it's easy to give too much.

For years you knew your neighbours in the building only by sight. One day you organise a sale of household things in the courtyard — just to get rid of clutter — and meet half the building at once. A year later the sale is monthly, you charge for pitches, and three more neighbourhoods have come asking. **The doors you opened to people turned out to be the entrance to your income.**

The Hanged Man turns generosity into sacrifice. You bail out everyone who asks, lend, work for free “as a favour”. Sometimes the shared business rests on one, and the other, having given them everything, is left with nothing of their own. Kindness without limits turns into debts and resentment. Decide how much you can give without harming yourselves, and learn to say no to those who are used to only asking.

items.title: Two worlds joined by a choice

captions.L: Insularity and a habit of the old
captions.R2: People, connections and a choice made together
captions.R: Pulling the shared business your way

items.meaning: Money grows when two settled worlds open to each other and to people, and dries up when each grabs the business.
text: The World frames your money line on both sides: you like life to be settled and secure, and you let the new in reluctantly. Two twenty-ones add up to six, and the Lovers in the middle explain how to open this circle: through people, choice, contact, your union with each other. Prosperity comes when two worlds open up to each other and to the world around.

For a long time you ran your businesses separately: one kept the books for three shops, the other had a small warehouse. One day you decide to join forces and offer the shops both accounts and storage. The clients are pleased: one team, one contract, one point of responsibility. A year later you have twice as many clients. **By joining your two worlds into one, you doubled both clients and income.**

The second World reminds you that you came from two different worlds. Once the shared business has grown, each starts claiming the credit: the accounts side thinks the warehouse would be worth nothing without it, the warehouse that clients stay for its sake, and one day the “whose business is it” argument breaks out in front of a client. Money goes on doubled costs: each has their own contractors, their own till, their own rules. Write down the rules of the joint budget together and review them yearly, like a contract with your most important client.

items.title: The whole world in one workshop

captions.L: Fearing the new and demanding accounts
captions.R2: Narrow mastery and unhurried growth
captions.R: Impulsive spending as a token of love

items.meaning: Your world widens as you go deeper into one craft, and money leaks where it's spent to prove your feelings.
text: You're calmer when life is settled and secure: things last for years, the budget rules were set long ago, and the new is met with suspicion — “the old is better”. That's how the World holds the way into your money. Hence the difficulty: change is feared, income stands still for years, and every expense invites checking. The Hermit offers a path that doesn't frighten: not to expand but to go deeper and become the best at what you do. The Lovers close the line with spending from the heart.

The turning point comes on an ordinary Tuesday, when one of you gets a letter from abroad: “We found your article on old textiles. Could you advise our museum?” Twenty years of painstaking study of one subject suddenly turn out to be needed by people on the other side of the world. You reply together: one writes, the other draws up the estimate. **The world came to you of its own accord once you'd gone so deep into your craft that you became irreplaceable.**

Spending for love is a separate line in your budget. A present dearer than you can afford, a dinner to make up after a row, something new to cheer the other up — and the other's checking glance: “why?” One spends to show feelings, the other demands an account, and both take offence. Agree on a sum for presents and treats that needs no explaining — then love doesn't turn into bookkeeping.

items.title: Quiet craftsman, loud temptation

captions.L: Shutting yourselves in your familiar world
captions.R2: Expertise people seek from afar
captions.R: Hunger for more and dubious offers

items.meaning: Your knowledge earns money when it goes beyond your familiar world, and lets you down when it draws you into murky deals.
text: Your world is settled and closed: a familiar circle, trusted work, distrust of the new. The World at the start gives stability, but also narrows income to what you already have. The Hermit leads to prosperity through depth: become the people others turn to for rare knowledge, whom they seek from far away. The Devil offers to trade that knowledge for quick money — and not always honestly.

“You're the only ones who still remember how to fix this,” says a client who has brought an old machine tool four hundred kilometres. For years you tinkered with old machinery for pleasure, and now you have a waiting list and a workshop people come to from three counties. **Knowledge nobody else kept became your capital.**

The Devil knows the price of your rarity and throws temptations your way. Taking an order whose details you'd rather not look into; raising the price for someone who has no choice; working non-stop because “while they're calling”. Keep the price honest and the work within limits that leave room for life.

items.title: The old world, seen anew

captions.L: Living in a familiar world and fearing the new
captions.R2: Seeing differently and waiting for your own

items.meaning: Your settled world starts earning more when you look at it differently — if you don't skimp on what feeds you.
text: The familiar is dear to you: the World holds you steady, and also makes you wary of everything new. The Hanged Man suggests not breaking the familiar but looking at it from the reverse side.
