What you thought a burden may turn out a treasure; what seemed empty waiting, preparation. Prosperity goes to those who can wait and see differently. And the Hermit is in no hurry — even where delay is costly.

For many years you thought of your parents' old country cottage by the woods as a burden: you paid the fees and went to paint the fence. One day you looked at it differently: quiet, woods, a stream, and only two hours from town. You turned the cottage into a place for quiet breaks without internet, and bookings are full a season ahead. **The burden you looked at in a new way became your income.**

The Hermit doesn't hurry, even when he should. The guest house roof has leaked for a second season — “we'll see in spring”, the sauna needs a new stove, and you put it off though there's money in the account. Guests start writing in reviews that the quiet is the same but the cosiness isn't. Stinginess disguises itself as an unhurried pace, and the place that feeds you gradually runs down. Decide together which business expenses are never debated for more than a week, and make them at once.

items.title: Patience with nothing hidden

captions.L: Clinging to the settled and checking everything
captions.R2: Patience and work that helps people

items.meaning: Your prosperity ripens slowly, through patience and serving people — as long as friendship and money don't get mixed up.
text: Settled order is your main value: the World has taught you to hold on to what's been gathered and to look at change with suspicion. Because of this income doesn't grow for years. The Hanged Man doesn't hurry you but turns your view around: prosperity will come through patience, through work that's useful to people, through a discipline where bills are paid on time and there are no debts. And the Moon hides at the end of the line what's awkward to say aloud.

You've run a small reading room at the community centre for a long time, and money was always just enough. You didn't leave: children who grew up among your shelves now bring their own children. When the town announced a competition for an education centre, it was you who were chosen to run it — with a budget and salary you'd never dreamed of. **Your patience turned out to be an investment that came back with interest.**

The shadow comes through your own people. You can't refuse long-standing readers a loan till payday, craftsmen you know are paid “as neighbours”, without paperwork, and who owes whom what is remembered only by word of mouth — each remembering differently. When the whole neighbourhood can see you, any murkiness in money quickly becomes a rumour, and the Moon is happy to colour it in. Keep the centre's money separate from your own, loans on paper, and friendship separate from both.

items.title: A desire that feeds the home

captions.L: Making do with what you have
captions.R2: Zest, ambition and well-paid work
captions.R: Spending on comfort faster than it comes

items.meaning: Your calm world grows richer when strong desire wakes, and stays so while abundance doesn't melt in spending.
text: What you have is enough for you: the World keeps you in a settled life where everything is familiar and secure. Only income doesn't grow in it. The Devil wakes desire — to live better, work where the pay is good, take a risk, invest, take more. The zest you used to be shy of becomes an engine. And money leaks where the generous Empress stands.

“Why not?” said one of you when an acquaintance suggested renting an empty workshop to make furniture to order. You'd both been salaried all your lives and weren't used to risk. The first year was hard, the second profitable, the third so good that you bought the workshop outright. **One bold “why not?” outweighed years of the familiar “we have enough”.**

The Empress's generosity pulls money towards the home. As soon as the workshop was bought outright, you wanted a new kitchen, furniture from your own workshop “at cost” that somehow comes out dearer than ordered pieces, presents for relatives at every holiday. The shortfall is covered by the credit card again. Furnish gradually: one big purchase a year, and only from profit, not from the workshop's working capital.

items.title: Appetite that broke the shell

captions.L: Content with a settled world
captions.R2: Strong desire and bold stakes

items.meaning: Strong desire leads you out of your shell to money — as long as fear doesn't then hold you back from the next step.
text: You're comfortable in a settled world: your own people, familiar work, “a bird in the hand”. The World keeps the couple in a shell. The Devil breaks it with strong desire — not just to feed your own, but to earn from what you do better than others, and as much as it's really worth. The appetite you were shy of turns out to be an engine. The Hanged Man shows where that engine stalls.

For twenty years you ran a modest factory canteen, and it seemed you needed nothing more. One day you saw how much people paid for office lunch deliveries at the business park next door — and caught fire. A year later your lunches are delivered all over the area, and profit has grown fivefold. **The desire you allowed yourselves broke the familiar shell.**

The Hanged Man brakes at the moment of take-off. The lunches have spread across the area, it's time to open a second kitchen, but it's frightening: what if it was luck, what if you can't cope, what if it all collapses. You're more afraid of your own ideas than of other people's: the offer from the business park next door has gone unanswered for three months, and the money for expanding sits in an account earning nothing. Decide together at what figures you take the next step, and take it when the figures add up.

items.title: A thrill between two walls

captions.L: A closed, familiar world
captions.R2: Strong desire and bold deals

items.meaning: Your settled world grows rich through bold desire — until what you've earned is hidden behind a wall of greed.
text: A settled life, a familiar circle, walls behind which it's calm — the World holds both end points of your money. The Devil in the middle breaks through these walls with desire — to earn a lot, to take risks, to take on big deals and hard work. The thrill brings money the quiet world never knew. The second World wants to close the gates again — this time to guard the spoils. The six trailing behind, the Lovers, reminds you of choice.

For years you ran a small fish stall at the market, content with your own circle of customers. One day you took a risk: a loan for a refrigerated van and a direct contract with a fishing cooperative up north. Today your fish is sold in twenty restaurants. **The risk you dared to take led you beyond the walls of the familiar world.**

The wall around your earnings grows by itself. A second refrigerated van is “too soon”, you don't ship to new restaurants without a month's prepayment, you don't trust a southern cooperative in advance, and at home every purchase goes through “do we really need this?”. The thrill that led you beyond the walls now guards them. Keep the gates open: earnings should serve life, not guard duty.

items.title: Settled world, secret path

captions.L: Living in a rut and not letting the new in
captions.R2: Trusting instinct and an unusual venture

items.meaning: Your stable world earns more when you trust instinct, and loses no money as long as there's order in it.
text: A well-worn rut is familiar to you: the World gives stability, things last a long time, the order has long been known, and everything new is met with doubt. The Moon offers a path off the beaten track: trust instinct, take up something unusual, creative, not fully understood by others. That's exactly where money increases. Last stand the Lovers, and they don't like counting.

Your hobby — unravelling old city legends and taking friends round the sites after dark — was considered an oddity by the family. One day you turn it into a paid tour, and a year later you're running four routes — with assistant guides and tickets that sell out in a week. **The strange path you turned onto on a hunch led to money.**

The Lovers don't like order in money. The takings from the tours sit as cash in a book on the shelf, part comes into one partner's account, part into the other's, the guides are paid “from whatever's to hand”, and nobody knows how much you actually have. The chaos feels like lightness until the tax bill comes or it turns out one has already spent what the other set aside. Set up one shared till for the business and check it together once a month.

items.title: A night path and a daytime lure

captions.L: Holding to the familiar order
captions.R2: Intuition and work not everyone understands

items.meaning: Your stable world grows with work found by intuition — and loses when success pulls you towards greed and murky deals.
text: The familiar order is dear to you: the World guards stability and dislikes the unknown. The Moon calls you off the beaten track — trust instinct, take on something strange, nocturnal, something others won't understand at once. That's where income appears. The Devil lies in wait where it starts flowing freely, with offers best not examined up close.

One clear night decides everything. Neighbours' children are queuing at your telescope at the country cottage, and one of the adults asks whether they could bring nephews from town here — and offers to pay. You exchange glances: the oddity people chuckled at turns out to be something people will drive a hundred kilometres for. A year later a small dome stands at the edge of the village, and a sign by the gate shows the price of a night at the telescope. **The night-time oddity you trusted became your brightest income.**

When things are going well, there's always someone nearby offering more: “let's keep it simple on paper”, “why pay taxes”, “there's one lucrative option”. The Devil tempts precisely those who've started to succeed. Visitors pay in cash, and the temptation not to ring it up comes every clear night. Keep the business clean and the joint budget joint.

items.title: A world grown wider

captions.L: Clinging to the familiar circle and order
captions.R2: Scale, distant markets and money at work

items.meaning: Your world brings prosperity when it widens beyond its usual borders, and shrinks when study replaces selling.
text: The World meets you twice on the money line: first as a familiar circle where everything is clear and secure, then as the wide world where your money can grow. Moving from the first to the second isn't easy: “the old is better”, the new frightens, and income stays where it was. Prosperity increases when you widen the scale: distant markets, savings, work without geography. The Hermit closes the line with silence.

For twenty years your dressmaking studio sewed for the people of one neighbourhood. One day you post photos of linen dresses online — and orders come in from other countries. Now you have a separate stockroom for shipping, and part of your income sits in savings that grow without your involvement. **The world beyond your neighbourhood turned out ready to pay for what you'd always known how to do.**

The Hermit at the exit likes studying more than selling. One more pattern-cutting course abroad, a rare book on the history of costume, six months spent “perfecting the collection” — money and time go into depth, while orders from abroad wait weeks for a reply. It seems your mastery is growing, but in fact it's the pause that grows. Study out of profit and to a plan, and show buyers the new at once, not a year later.

items.title: A big world without shadows

captions.L: Holding to your circle and familiar ways
captions.R2: Widening the horizon, working without borders
captions.R: Murky deals and fog in the figures

items.meaning: Your world brings prosperity when it widens beyond familiar borders — and loses it in the fog of murky deals.
text: You have two worlds: first your own circle, familiar ways and caution towards the new, then the whole wide world, where your income can grow. The path to prosperity is the move from one to the other: work without geography, distant partners, money invested wisely. The Moon, though, thickens the fog: the wider the world, the easier it is to get lost in it.

For years your small online shop selling seeds of rare tomatoes sold to neighbouring allotment holders. One day you translated the site into English — and parcels went to twenty countries. You had to learn customs, foreign-currency accounts, international shipping, and three years on the shop earns more than both your old salaries. **What was yours, taken out into the wide world, turned out to be needed by many.**

The fog thickens at great distances. A partner in another country you've never met; a payment that's been “delayed”; a contract in a foreign language signed unread. The Moon makes you trusting, the World over-confident. Check, translate and formalise every deal, even if the partner seems reliable, and keep the shared accounts transparent to both.

items.title: First the leap, then the guild

captions.L: Starting from scratch with no safety net
captions.R2: Entering a circle of insiders
captions.R: A crest of income, then the shallows

items.meaning: Courage earns you money once it finds a channel: a circle that has accepted you as its own.
text: Your money begins with a step others won't take. The Fool leaves a secure place easily and starts from scratch, but for a long time such a step has no product: plenty of energy, little income. The Hierophant gives it a channel — a circle where you've been accepted as insiders, and its rules: how prices are set here, who is trusted first, what it isn't done to ask more than. Money flows along this channel, and the water level is changed by the Wheel of Fortune without consulting you.

The turning point usually fits in one sentence, spoken by someone inside the circle: “You were recommended; someone vouched for you.” Not a job site, not an advert — your own people. From that minute you no longer need to justify your price: the guild knows it, and the rules by which people take and pay here become yours. **Prosperity comes to you for the name you've earned among your own.**

Leaks open on the crest. When things are going up, it seems they always will, and courage pushes you to a new leap before the last one has paid off: to drop what feeds you and start something else. The water drops suddenly, recommendations thin out, and the new venture meets an ebb tide before it's on its feet. A leak in a boat isn't visible while the water is high — it's found in the shallows.

items.title: A free wind in the classroom

captions.L: Living for today
captions.R2: Knowledge, a profession and family ways

items.meaning: Your lightness becomes prosperity when it accepts rules and learns — and isn't spent on spoiling yourselves.
text: You live for today: the Fool drops things easily, starts easily and dislikes frames. Money appears and disappears, and there's no reserve. The Hierophant offers what you used to run from: study, enter a profession, accept rules, set up a joint family budget. That's exactly how prosperity comes. The Sun promises success and watches what you'll do with it.

For years you worked as party entertainers — fun, but with no future. One day you decide to train as teachers, and three years later you open a private nursery. Rules, licences and reports turned out to be less frightening than you thought, and parents book places a year ahead. **The rules you used to run from turned out to be your road to prosperity.**

The Sun gets you used to the best. The nursery is booked a year ahead, and habits quietly grow more expensive: holidays only in good hotels, food only by delivery, a new phone every year, because “we've earned it”. Each expense is small, but together they eat up everything a good year brings, and the reserve for a quiet season never appears. Enjoy success, but keep everyday life at the level of an ordinary year, and save the celebrations for celebrations.

items.title: Freedom in a frame

captions.L: Living lightly and not counting
captions.R2: Honest accounts, a contract and promises kept

items.meaning: Freedom feeds you when it comes with an estimate and a signature — and stops when order becomes surveillance.
text: You're not used to worrying about money: the Fool lives lightly, spends generously, starts again without regret. Justice brings honesty into this lightness: an estimate, a signature, a word that's kept, a price you're not ashamed to name. Freedom in a frame of honesty brings steady income. The Emperor, though, wants to make the frame tighter.

You ran your cheerful workshop of party decorations “on a handshake” — no contracts, no estimates. One day a big client didn't pay, and for the first time you sat down to the paperwork. Now every order has an estimate and a contract, and you have a reputation as reliable people who are fun and easy to deal with. **Order didn't kill your lightness — it made it profitable.**

A treasurer easily becomes a warden. One of you takes over all the payments: only with their knowledge, spending to be accounted for, no spontaneity. The other suffocates, and the lightness the business ran on drains away. Leave room for freedom: the rules are shared, but each has a sum they spend without asking.

items.title: A Fool with a calculator

captions.L: Living lightly with no reserve
captions.R2: Honest accounts and promises kept

items.meaning: Your merry life starts earning when it learns to count — as long as old debts don't move into each new stage.
text: Lightness is your strength and your trouble: the Fool isn't afraid to start from scratch, but can't save either, and debts seem to appear by themselves. Justice gives what's missing: accounts, contracts, promises kept, a plan in case of failure. Prosperity for you is lightness trained to order. Death at the end of the line demands that stages be closed honestly.

You started your first spending spreadsheet on a bet: a friend said you wouldn't last a month. You lasted three years. It turned out a merry life costs half as much if you know where the money goes, and contracts with clients spare you half the quarrels. Now you keep accounts even on holiday — and laugh at yourselves for it. **A Fool who learned to count turned out to be twice as rich.**

What leaves you most exposed is how you finish things. You close a business, and its debts quietly move over to the one who stays. You leave a job without looking for a new one, because “something will turn up”. Or one is afraid to change jobs, though the old one stopped paying long ago. Finish honestly: every closed business with its accounts settled, every transition with a reserve for the first months.

items.title: Two Fools and one pair of scales

captions.L: Starting from scratch again and again
captions.R2: Honest accounts and a word that's kept

items.meaning: Your lightness earns money when it keeps its word and its accounts — otherwise freedom turns into debts.
text: The Fool stands at the way into money and waits again at the way out: you're both light, free, not attached to money. Two twenty-twos add up to eight — and Justice in the middle becomes your centre of gravity. Honest accounts, a word kept, a contract delivered on time — that's what makes free spirits into reliable partners. And that's how money comes to you.

You've always been freelancers and long lived from job to job, losing clients over missed deadlines. The turning point was one big job you delivered on the day, with a report and not a single correction needed. The client told colleagues about you. Now you have a reputation as “the ones who never let you down” and a queue of clients. **A word kept turned out to be your most profitable product.**

The second Fool travels light again. A debt to a friend “till Monday”, a forgotten payment, a tax remembered too late — small things pile up unnoticed until they become a problem. And you might drop a good job simply because it got boring. Let Justice be your shared rule: debts first, freedom with a reserve.

items.title: Easy start, long haul

captions.L: Carelessness and living with no reserve
captions.R2: Persistence that sees things through
captions.R: Hauling the till while the other dreams

items.meaning: Starting from scratch is easy; you grow rich by holding on to what you begin, not racing at the other's expense.
text: The Fool makes you quick to get going: starting from scratch isn't frightening, losing isn't a tragedy, money comes and goes without drama. The trouble is that there's no reserve, and debts pile up unnoticed. Strength in the middle is the opposite of carelessness: persistence, endurance, the ability to keep hold of what's in your hands. The Chariot at the end of the line pulls you back into the race.

Many times you've started something new: a workshop, a food stall, an online course. Each time the spark lasted a couple of months. One day you decide to keep one business going even when it gets boring — and you do: your pancake house has been on the same street for five years now, with regulars and a queue at weekends. **You grew rich not on a bold start but on staying put for the first time.**

The Chariot divides the road unequally. The pancake house rests on the one who gets up at five, while the other catches fire again with something new — a food truck, delivery, a franchise — and thinks “standing at the stove is boring, that's your thing”. Responsibility for the takings quietly shifts onto one, the ideas and the spending on them onto the other, and in the first empty month comes “I told you so”. Decide who answers for what in money, and let new schemes wait until the till can pay for them itself.

items.title: Light hearts, strong hands

captions.L: Carelessness and life without a cushion
captions.R2: Persistence and taking a blow
captions.R: A sudden collapse with no reserve

items.meaning: Your lightness earns money when persistence joins it — and withstands a blow if a cushion has been put aside.
text: You're light people: the Fool starts from scratch without fear and spends without regret. There's no cushion, and debts don't frighten you. Strength in the middle teaches you to hold on: work persistently, tame your impulses, endure a hard stretch. Prosperity comes when lightness joins with stamina. The Tower reminds you that a blow can come when you least expect it.

You've moved for work some five times — lightly, without regret. Everything changed when you bought an abandoned cheese dairy in a small town and for the first time decided to stay. For the first two years you got up at four, learned, made mistakes, didn't give up. Today the whole area knows your cheese, and restaurants order it a month ahead. **Lightness that finally decided to stay began to earn money.**

The Tower strikes those with no reserve. Equipment breaks, the main buyer leaves, an unexpected bill arrives — and a whole year's income vanishes in a week. The Fool in you will say “we'll get through”, but getting through without a cushion is hard. Put aside at least three months' expenses for the unexpected: then a blow stays a blow, not a catastrophe.

items.title: Lightness that found its measure

captions.L: Spending lightly, not thinking of tomorrow
captions.R2: Measure, patience and an even pace
captions.R: Letting things drift and trusting to luck

items.meaning: Your lightness becomes prosperity when it finds a measure — and leaves when you hand money back to chance.
text: Money doesn't stay with you long: the Fool spends easily, gives generously and doesn't think about tomorrow. Starting over is easy for you, but saving doesn't happen. Temperance suggests not giving up lightness but diluting it with measure: live within your means, put a little aside, grow without fuss. The Wheel of Fortune tempts you to rely on luck.

You invented the “one-tenth” rule as a joke: from every sum, however small, a tenth goes into a jar on the shelf. A year later the jar held enough for a holiday without debts — for the first time in your lives. Now there are three jars, and you still joke about them. **A small measure you keep seriously has made you calmer and richer.**

The Wheel throws up a temptation: “we'll be lucky.” Let go of the reins, take a loan in a good spell, don't think about the bad season. The Fool's lightness easily conspires with the Wheel's luck, and together they blow your savings in a couple of months. Let a tenth go into reserve in lucky months too — then the wheel won't catch you off guard.

items.title: Free spirits with a reserve

captions.L: Spending easily and living with no cushion
captions.R2: The middle way between freedom and saving
captions.R: Working without days off for success

items.meaning: Your freedom brings prosperity when it finds measure — and keeps it as long as success doesn't eat your days off.
text: Money doesn't hold you: the Fool spends easily, starts again without fear and lives without a cushion. Temperance suggests a middle way between freedom and saving — keep your lightness, but give it a steady step: save a little, work at a calm pace, don't abandon what you've started. That's how freedom becomes income. The Sun at the end promises success — and asks for all your weekends in return.

You came up with your bubble show for a laugh at friends' birthday party. At first you performed whenever it came up and spent the fees the same evening. Then you set up a season's schedule and an account that takes every fifth fee. Three years on — two teams and your own stage in the park. **Freedom you gave a rhythm began to bring in steady money.**

The Sun asks you to shine every day. Two teams, a stage in the park, bookings for every summer weekend — and you perform yourselves, though you could long since have let the young ones take over. Work begun for a laugh turns into a schedule with no days off, and money earned at such a price you want to spend lavishly, to feel it was worth it. The freedom you gave a rhythm needs rest too: one show-free day a week for you both is as much a part of the business as the schedule.

items.title: Talent set free

captions.L: Carelessness and life without a plan
captions.R2: Talent, creativity and renown

items.meaning: Your freedom earns money through talent and renown, and money leaks when all the decisions are handed to one.
text: Freedom is air to you: the Fool gives work by mood, life without a plan, money easily found and just as easily lost. The Star shows how to turn freedom into income: talent, creativity, a name people recognise. The bolder you show yourselves, the more you're paid. The Emperor wants to bring order — and can overdo it.

For many years you were street musicians — no schedule, no plans. One video of your song in the underground got a million views, and you were offered an album. You agreed without betraying yourselves: the same songs, the same freedom, only now on big stages. **The songs you refused to change for money are what brought the money.**

The Emperor makes one of you the treasurer, and the other hands over everything with relief: contracts, fees, decisions. It's convenient — until it turns out the songwriter doesn't know how much money you have, what the label contract commits you to, or why the tour costs more than it brings in. The Fool's lightness turns into helplessness, and the treasurer tires of pulling for two. Let order be shared: both read the contracts, and each has their own part of the business to answer for.

items.title: A free gift, a change of scene

captions.L: Carelessness and life without calculation
captions.R2: Talent, a name and an audience
captions.R: Clinging to a role and splitting debts on leaving

items.meaning: Your freedom brings money through talent and a name, and you lose it when a stage ends and the debts fall on one of you.
text: Travelling light is how you live: the Fool doesn't plan, doesn't save and easily starts everything over. The Star finds a use for that lightness — a gift people can see, a name by which you're found, a stage where freedom gets paid for. Money arrives when you don't hide. Death, though, reminds you: any rise ends one day, and the only question is how you end it.

You drew caricatures on the seafront in summer for fun and coins in a hat. One day a festival organiser invited you to draw the guests — for a fee. Now you're asked to celebrations all over the country, and your caricatures have become the signature of lavish parties. **The freedom with which you drew for yourselves became your price on the market.**

Fashions change, festivals close, one of you wants to try something else — and it turns out that shared debts and obligations are easy to leave with one partner. There's jealousy too: one has grown, the other stayed the same. End stages honestly — with a reckoning of who takes what — and don't envy each other's success.

items.title: A star between two winds

captions.L: Lightness with no plan and no reserve
captions.R2: Talent, the stage and recognition

items.meaning: Your lightness brings money through talent and an audience — if in the quiet season you don't run away from problems.
text: The wind of freedom blows on you from both sides: the Fool at the start won't let you make plans, the Fool at the finish tends to spend everything luck has brought. And in the middle stands the Star: talent, a stage, a name people pay for. Two twenty-twos add up to eight, and Justice trails behind to suggest that a star needs honest accounting.

You put on fire shows for friends at their country cottages just for fun. One day you were invited to a town festival — and within a year you were performing at festivals all over the country. Fees are growing, and for the first time you've taken on an accountant who makes sure freedom doesn't eat up the earnings. **Once you stepped before the public, your fire began to bring in money.**

The second Fool runs off when things get hard. The season is empty, festivals are cancelled, the accountant sends unpleasant figures — and one of you goes off “to clear their head” for a month, leaving the other to deal with the bills, then on returning reproaches them: “but you wanted to live like this too.” Freedom turns into flight, and lightness into reproaches. Let the star have an account nobody touches, and a rule: you live through the hard season together, and the holiday comes after.

items.title: Prodigals of the family business

captions.L: Freedom without roots or reserve
captions.R2: Returning to kin and the family business
captions.R: A dash on credit and a fight for the lead

items.meaning: Your freedom finds support in family: the kin's shared business feeds you — until you push it on credit.
text: For a long time the Fool leads you without roots: moves, odd jobs, life without reserve or plans. Freedom is a joy but adds no money. Judgement brings you back to your roots: a family business, relatives' help, an inheritance that turns out to be a business rather than just property. Prosperity comes through the family. The Chariot hurries to multiply it.

Where haven't you worked: on the coast, in the mountains, in strange cities. When one partner's grandfather decided to retire, he invited you to run the family sawmill. You came “for the summer” and stayed: you added garden furniture for weekenders to the timber, and a business that had been ageing along with the grandfather came back to life. **The roots you kept leaving turned out to be your best business.**

The Chariot wants to grow fast: a second workshop, a new lorry, expanding into neighbouring counties — all on credit. A family business can't bear every speed, and the debts fall on everyone. There's also the argument over who's in charge: you, back with new ideas, or the elders who kept the business going for years. Grow on what you earn, and agree on roles openly.

items.title: Wanderers who found their roots

captions.L: A free life without support
captions.R2: Kin, family and a shared heritage
captions.R: Work and home under one roof

items.meaning: A free life finds support in your family line — as long as the house you live and work in isn't your only support.
text: You lived light for a long time: moves, odd jobs, a life without support or plans — that's how the Fool leads. Judgement calls you home: parents, the family house, the family craft, support that has been waiting all along. That's exactly where prosperity awaits. The Tower warns that without a reserve any blow becomes a disaster.

You thought of a grandmother's house in the village as a place for summer holidays, until after yet another move you had nowhere to live. You stayed — and unexpectedly took up what a great-grandfather used to do: weaving baskets from the willow that grew along the river. Baskets made to the old patterns sold out at the very first fair, and now garden shops order them. **The roots you searched the world for turned out to be behind a grandmother's fence.**

The roots you came back to are a roof over your head, a workshop and a store all at once: everything in one grandmother's house. The Tower hits such places hardest. The roof leaks, the river floods in spring, relatives suddenly decide to sell the house — and you lose both home and work in a single week. The Fool in you is used to wriggling out, but here you need insurance: save separately for repairs to the house, agree your rights to it with the relatives in writing, and keep part of the reserve outside its walls.

items.title: Quiet abundance

captions.R1: Home and garden as a shared venture

items.meaning: A full cellar, apples picked, orders finished — and an evening on the veranda where ten words are enough.
text: The Empress appears for you both at work and between you. At work she gives prosperity, growth, a knack for multiplying. Between you she becomes home and garden — a shared venture that feeds and delights. And you know how to rest quietly, as the Hermit does: in the contented quiet of evening, without guests or conversation.

The end of August. The cellar is full of jars, the apples are picked, and both of you have finished your orders until September. In the evening you sit on the veranda, each with a book, and in two hours you don't say ten words. Only when it gets dark does one look up: “It's been a good year.” The other nods. **Your abundance is quiet: a full house, a full garden and an evening when you can simply be silent together.**

Contented quiet imperceptibly turns into stagnation. If you have everything and need nothing, talk of the new never begins, and a rivalry over who has put more into the home smoulders without words. The one who puts in less starts to feel like a guest. The jars in the cellar stand in neat rows, and every year there are exactly as many.

items.title: Care without asking
items.meaning: Care needn't be asked for in your couple: the other senses what's wanted before the request is made.
text: The Empress repeats in your couple: at work she gives abundance and growth, between you a warm nest where everything is arranged for two. And you show care in the Moon's language: without asking, guessing, sensing what the other wants from little things others wouldn't notice.

One of you comes home and in the hall already smells their favourite soup. On the sofa lies a blanket, in the bathroom a hot bath is run, on the table lies a book they mentioned in passing a week ago. Not a word about the hard day, not a single question. They simply sit down and realise this is exactly what they wanted all day. **You don't need to ask for warmth: in a home with two caring people, it's guessed from the footsteps in the hall.**

You can guess for the other for too long. If everything is guessed, there's no reason to talk, and sooner or later the other guesses wrong and it's awkward to say so. Care turns into fussing, and the Moon into anxiety: what if I guess wrong? The soup is right every evening, and what's really needed you've never asked.

items.title: A flower on the windowsill

captions.R1: A love chosen by the heart

items.meaning: Your love speaks through care and gifts for no reason, and it matters that hard conversations don't hide behind them.
text: The Empress stands at two of your points: at work she gives work that feeds you and grows, in conversation a language of care, gifts, warmth. Between them stand the Lovers, a love chosen by the heart. Together they make a couple whose feeling shows not in words but in little things.

Tuesday, nothing special. One of you comes home and finds a new potted plant on the windowsill — a violet of the very shade they mentioned in spring. No note, no occasion either. Over dinner they ask nothing, only smile, and in the morning the other finds a chocolate bar in their jacket pocket with “because” written on it in marker. **Love shows in little things in your couple: a gift for no reason, a warm dinner, a flower on the windowsill.**

Gifts are handy because they spare you talking. If love is expressed only in things, conversations about the hard stuff get put off, and generosity becomes a way of smoothing things over. Whoever earns more gives more expensive gifts, and presents turn into a contest. There's a whole greenhouse of flowers on the windowsill, and there's been no talk about what's worrying you since winter.

items.title: Who needs it more now

captions.M: Giving way to whoever needs it more

items.meaning: You spend your growing money not by right of the stronger, but by right of whoever needs it more just now.
text: Your income keeps growing: the Empress at work gives fertility, development, prosperity that arrives year after year. You're used to deciding together where it goes, since the Lovers bind you through love and shared decisions even in small things. And the Hanged Man settles your arguments about money: whoever needs it less right now gives way.

The year's profit is bigger than expected. One wants to invest it in expanding the workshop, the other in a long trip together they've dreamed of for ages. In the evening you argue, then try to see through each other's eyes. It turns out the workshop can wait six months, but the other's exhaustion can't. You go on the trip. **Your arguments about money are settled not by whoever is louder but by whoever needs it more right now.**

“Whoever needs it more” turns out with suspicious regularity to be the same person. The workshop never expands, and the resentment of the one who gives way quietly grows. The Lovers expect gratitude, the Hanged Man stays silent. There have been three trips already, the workshop is as cramped as ever, and its owner says nothing about it.

items.title: Reshuffling the chores
items.meaning: One partner's work grows, yet at home everything is still half and half: you update the deal as life changes.
text: Love is your main choice, and the Lovers unite you through exactly that: a decision to be together, confirmed every day. It has to be confirmed in changing conditions: the Empress at work brings growth — the business expands, income rises, demands multiply. The World sets the rule by which you cope: everything half and half, and the agreement is revised when life changes.

One partner's business has tripled in a year, and the old schedule no longer works: who cooks, who collects the parcels, who pays the bills. One evening you sit down with two cups of tea and a list of chores and reshuffle the duties — so that both still have free evenings. At the end one says: “I love you on the old schedule and the new one.” **One partner's growth doesn't break equality: you reshuffle the duties together, afresh each time.**

An agreement can fall behind life. The business grows, but duties are split by old habit, and whoever has less work quietly takes on everything else. Jealousy of success hides behind words about equality. On paper everything is half and half, but in life one has long been pulling for two.

items.title: A strategy for two

captions.M: Deciding with the heart, and together

items.meaning: Prosperity and growth are shared between you, and the wisdom you share keeps them from becoming a race.
text: In your couple you both grow: the Empress in success gives prosperity, development, work that bears fruit, and each has their own fulfilment. The Hermit sets the direction of growth, bringing you close through depth: you learn from each other, see the world similarly and know how to think together. And you make decisions in the Lovers' language — with the heart, aloud, and only together.

Every January you go away for two days to a cabin with no signal — for a “strategy for two”. There each has a sheet of paper: what I want to grow this year — in my work, in myself, at home. Then you swap sheets and talk at length about where your plans help each other and where they get in the way. You come home with one sheet for two. **You both grow, and where — you decide in a long conversation, far from the bustle.**

When one partner's growth outpaces the other's, prosperity becomes the measure of love, and talks for two become awkward: one tells of successes, the other keeps quiet about theirs. Envy of the other's achievements hides behind a wise silence. In the shared garden one bed has run wild, and it shades all the rest.

items.title: No excuses
items.meaning: You earn and grow, and don't interrogate each other's weaknesses — you admit them aloud and sometimes indulge them.
text: Prosperity keeps arriving: the Empress at work gives growth, fertility, a knack for multiplying. You know how to spend it honestly — the Devil lets you own up to weaknesses and pleasures without excuses. And the Hermit keeps you from extremes, binding you through a wise quiet: in the evenings, just the two of you, you calmly discuss what you want and why.

The end of a good quarter. One of you sighs: “I want that expensive coffee machine. I don't need it. I just want it.” The other laughs: “And I want a week of doing nothing in a cabin by the lake.” You sit in the kitchen in silence for a long time, then decide: the coffee machine now, the lake in May. Nobody makes excuses. **Pleasures aren't hidden behind excuses in your couple: if you want something, you say so and allow it.**

You can allow yourselves too much. If every “I want” is granted, generosity becomes extravagance, and owning up to weaknesses a licence for everything. The quiet in which you used to discuss everything becomes a quiet in which debts go unmentioned. You now have two coffee machines, and you never did get to the lake.

items.title: Someone else's flowers

captions.R1: Understanding and giving way without reproach

items.meaning: One partner's work grows, the other gives it time without reproach, and you go off together into quiet to rest.
text: The Empress stands in your success: work grows, clients multiply, prosperity increases year by year. Growth takes strength and time, and between you is the Hanged Man — the ability to understand, wait and give way without reproach when the other needs it more. And you rest like the Hermit: far from people, in a quiet where you needn't say a word.

One of you has so many clients that weekends have vanished from the calendar. The other doesn't take offence or demand attention — simply loads a tent into the car on Friday evening and waits outside. Two days at a lake with no signal: not one business conversation, just a campfire and quiet. On Monday you both come back rested. **One partner's growth doesn't smother the other, as long as the house keeps evenings when nothing grows and nothing is due.**

One partner's growth casts a shadow over the other. The one who gives way gets used to living someone else's work, gives up their own and doesn't mention it, while the one whose work grows takes it for granted. The quiet you rested in becomes a quiet in which nobody complains. The other waters someone else's flowers and no longer remembers once planting their own.

items.title: The farm beyond the woods

captions.R1: Patience and care for the weak

items.meaning: Your prosperity grows in quiet and on the land, and you sense each other's care without words.
text: You grow prosperity on the land: the Empress gives you a smallholding, a garden, a farm, everything that grows and feeds. You feel calmer away from people, and the Hanged Man binds you through patience, care for the weak and the ability to wait until something ripens. You understand each other as the Moon bids: without words, from gestures, from the way the other holds their shoulders at the end of the day.

A small farm beyond the woods: goats, a cheese dairy, a vegetable plot. The morning starts at five, and until almost lunchtime you don't say a word to each other — each busy with their own. But when one stays by the pen longer than usual, the other already knows: a goat has gone lame and the vet must be called, and the owner needs hot tea and a minute's quiet. **Your prosperity grows where it's quiet, and you both sense when the land and each other need rest.**

A quiet life far away can become isolation. If people are distant and words unnecessary, tiredness and grievances pile up unnoticed; one works for two and endures, the other guesses, but not everything. The Moon fills in, the Hanged Man stays silent. The farm prospers, the cheese sells, and for months now you've had no time for a real talk.

items.title: A garden grown on passion

captions.R: Growing your work like a garden
captions.M: Generosity and care in every gesture

items.meaning: Your work grows from passion and generosity, and you grow it like a garden — together and with zest.
text: The Empress stands at two of your points. In success she grows your work like a garden: from a small beginning come several branches, and prosperity increases year by year. In the common language she sounds as care and generosity: presents, good food, a home where there's plenty of everything. Between them stands the Devil, and he connects you through passion: attraction to each other and a shared zest with which you grow both work and home.

One partner's small business grows into three outlets in two years. In the evening you count the takings in the kitchen, and the other, looking at the figures, laughs: “It's catching. Now I can't stop either.” You've both long been working on shared zest, and on Sundays you throw a dinner for the whole team — with pies and a present for everyone. **Abundance grows for you from passion — for the work and for each other.**

Whose business grows faster, who brings in more, who has “fallen behind” — abundance easily turns into rivalry. In such a race the Empress becomes jealous, and the Devil prompts you to hold the other with money and dependence, and presents become a way of showing who's in charge. There's plenty of everything in the house except equality.

items.title: Accepting the dark side
items.meaning: Your business multiplies and your attraction holds fast — the other meets even one partner's outbursts with a question.
text: Your business grows: the Empress gives fertility, prosperity, a knack for multiplying. But that isn't the main thing in your couple. The Devil binds you through an attraction that accepts the whole person, dark sides, outbursts and weaknesses included. And you talk about them as the Hanged Man does: trying to understand, not to remake, and seeing the outburst through the eyes of the one who flared up.

One of you can flare up so that the windows rattle — then cools down and is ashamed. After yet another outburst over a botched delivery, the other doesn't retreat into hurt. They wait for the storm to pass and ask: “What frightened you so much?” It turns out it wasn't the delivery but the fear of letting down the people who work for you. **You neither hide nor remake each other's dark sides: you see them through the other's eyes and accept them.**

You can accept the dark only until it starts ordering you about. If one partner's outbursts become the norm, the other's understanding turns into patience, and patience into an unspoken sacrifice. The attraction holds tighter than you'd like. The windows rattle more and more often, and “what frightened you?” is asked ever more quietly.

items.title: Passion without ownership
items.meaning: Nobody belongs to anybody, and yet you're drawn to each other just as at the start.
text: Passion holds you: the Devil gives an attraction that doesn't fade and a shared zest for life. But you don't consider yourselves each other's property — the World sets the rule “nobody belongs to anybody”, and each has their own space. At work the Empress brings growth: whatever you touch blossoms and brings prosperity.

Each of you has their own business: one a pottery studio, the other a small agency. You don't meddle in each other's businesses or divide income into “mine” and “yours” in arguments — only in the accounts. But on Fridays you have a shared evening for boasting about successes, grumbling about clients and forgetting work until morning. **What holds you is passion, not ownership: each grows their own, and the home is only richer for it.**

Abundance gives leverage to whoever has more of it. When one business grows faster, its owner starts deciding more, and passion turns into a wish to possess: where were you, with whom, how much did you spend. Freedom stays in words. Each grows their own, but in arguments you hear more and more who brought how much into the home.

items.title: A world invented by two
items.meaning: A business grows out of your shared world of fantasy, and you speak plainly about feelings so as not to get lost in it.
text: The Empress in success brings growth: work that blossoms, prosperity that increases. In your case it grows from an unusual root. The Moon connects you through shared fantasies and intuition: you understand each other at a hint and invent things nobody else has. And to avoid getting lost in that shifting world, you need the Lovers' plain language — you speak clearly about feelings.

You invented a board game for yourselves, for long winter evenings. Friends asked for a copy to be printed, then their friends, and now one of you has a small publishing house and a queue of orders. In the evenings you still play together — a new version nobody has seen yet. **What began as your shared fantasy grows and feeds you, as long as it stays yours.**

A game invented for two one day stops being yours. The business grows, and the world you invented together now belongs to buyers, partners, the market; one dives in headfirst, the other feels superfluous and says nothing. The Moon throws up guesses, the Lovers grievances. The shared world dreamed up by two is now known to thousands, and the two of you no longer play in it.

items.title: An evening for one fantasy
items.meaning: You don't just know each other's fantasies, you make them real from time to time — generously and with laughter.
text: Your prosperity grows: the Empress at work gives fruit, development, a generosity you can afford. The Moon binds you — a shared world of fantasies, games and secrets only the two of you understand. And you're not shy of talking about them: the Devil makes your desires bold and spoken aloud, not tucked away in a far corner.

Once a month you have an evening for one fantasy: you take turns naming something you've long dreamed of, and the other arranges it. This time it's a candlelit dinner on a rooftop, like in an old film, with a musician playing just for the two of you. You laugh that it's silly and expensive, and dance until midnight. **Fantasies don't stay in your heads: they're named aloud and sometimes made real.**

Fantasies without measure start demanding more and more. Each next evening must outshine the last, generosity turns into extravagance, and passion into a dependence on new sensations. The Moon paints what doesn't exist, and ordinary life starts to seem dull. The fantasy evenings get ever more expensive, and ordinary evenings ever more silent.

items.title: Open space instead of things

captions.R1: A shared love of open space

items.meaning: You spend money not on things but on distant roads and evenings by the fire where you talk about what matters.
text: Your work grows: the Empress gives prosperity, development, fruit that increases year by year. But you don't spend it on things. The World gives you a shared love of open space — roads, new countries, a broad view of life. And in this open space you look for quiet: the Hermit reminds you that real conversation happens far from the bustle.

Every year you go where nobody speaks your language — mountains, islands, open plains. The first days go on breaking the habit of checking email. And then, on the third evening, sitting by the fire, you start talking about what didn't fit into ordinary days: where you're heading, what you want, what it's time to let go. **Prosperity turns into open space for you, and open space into a quiet where you can hear each other again.**

Abundance can become a flight from conversations. If everything hard is put off until the next trip, trips become a way of not facing the problem at home. One grows and earns, the other comes along, and the talk by the fire gets shorter. The countries change, but the silence at dinner is the same.

items.title: Growing by instinct

captions.R1: A love of the wide world

items.meaning: Your business crosses borders easily, because you choose the direction of growth by shared instinct.
text: Your business likes to grow: the Empress at work gives fertility, development, prosperity that keeps arriving. It grows where the Moon suggests — the shared instinct you're both used to relying on. And the world doesn't seem big for this growth, since the World binds you through a love of open space and a conviction that a border is no obstacle.

One partner's small cheese dairy is ready to expand, and the logical step is a shop in the neighbouring town. But the other says: “I have a strange feeling we should try selling to Italy.” You laugh, then try — sending samples to a trade fair. Now a third of the cheese goes abroad, and there's still no shop in the neighbouring town. **Your business grows where shared instinct suggests, and the world isn't too big for that growth.**

With money, instinct lets you down more often than with people. If decisions are made on instinct without calculation, growth sooner or later gives way to failure, and on an anxious day the Moon starts whispering fears. The one growing the business gives themselves to it completely; the other feels superfluous. The cheese sells in three countries, and at home nobody has talked about the business since last spring.

items.title: Comparing notes like a board
items.meaning: Your home is solidly built: shared rules, weighed decisions, and a quiet that's working quiet.
text: The Emperor appears both at work and between you. At work he gives posts, responsibility, a habit of deciding for many. Between you he becomes order and backup: each knows the other will cover for them, and the house rules were devised together. And you talk little — the Hermit teaches you to think first and then speak, and speak to the point.

The decision to buy a house ripens for a month. Each studies the question alone: one works out the mortgage, the other goes to look at neighbourhoods. You tell each other almost nothing until you're ready. On Sunday you sit down at the table as if at a meeting, and it turns out you've chosen the same house for different reasons. You sign on Monday. **Two leaders in one home don't wage war: each thinks it through alone first, then you compare conclusions.**

Two orders side by side easily turn into two rulebooks. Each is sure their rules are more sensible, the struggle for leadership runs without words, and feelings hide behind businesslike manners — you can't tell whether it's joy or irritation. The Hermit won't let you ask directly. The home runs like a good company, only it's as warm as a meeting room.

items.title: Tenderness under the suit

captions.R: Keeping order and people in line

items.meaning: Outside you're strict and composed, at home you read each other's looks and guard what isn't usually shown.
text: A double Emperor means order both outside and inside: at work he makes you both people of order and responsibility, between you protectors who'll always back each other up. Outside you're strict and composed. And under the suits hides what only you can see: the Moon makes you sensitive to what isn't said, and able to understand each other from a look.

One partner's board meeting went badly, and in the evening they talk about it in an even, businesslike voice. The other listens, nods, asks practical questions. And then, without any transition, lays a palm on the back of their neck: “You were scared in there, weren't you?” The even voice breaks, and at last out comes what had been held in all day. **Under your two strict suits hides a tenderness only you can see.**

Strictness outside and things unsaid inside make a dangerous mix. If showing feelings isn't done, the Moon starts filling in: silence seems like coldness, a businesslike tone like resentment. Two orders argue over who's in charge, and worries hide deeper. You understand each other from a look, but look each other in the eye less and less.

items.title: After the week, the road
items.meaning: Hard weeks end with the road in your couple, and the road ends with a laid table and warmth.
text: Hard weeks are no rarity for you: the Emperor at work gives responsibility, posts, the need to keep everything under control. You recover in motion — the Chariot binds you through the road, hikes, sport, anything where you can be side by side and moving. And you come back to where the Empress rules: a warm home, a laid table, care without conditions.

Friday, seven in the evening. The one who has spent all week sorting out breakdowns at the plant gets into the car. The other is already at the wheel, rucksacks in the boot. Saturday — twenty kilometres through the mountains, a night in a tent. On Sunday at home a dinner awaits you that the other put in the oven before you left. **One partner's responsibility is balanced by movement and care: after a hard week, the road; after the road, a laid table.**

Roles can divide too neatly. One answers for things, the other drives and feeds; one gets tired at work, the other from constantly restoring the first. A rivalry over whose tiredness matters more runs without words. One is always at the wheel, the other always with the basket, and nobody suggests swapping.

items.title: The wheel is passed, not seized

captions.M: Giving up the wheel when needed

items.meaning: Two people used to leading don't argue over who comes first: on each question, the stronger one in it leads.
text: In your couple the wheel is passed, not seized, and that's the main thing to know about you. The Emperor at work makes you both people used to leading and answering for it. The Chariot binds you through moving forward, shared momentum, resolve. And so that two leaders don't pull the wheel in different directions, there's the Hanged Man: the ability to give way when the other knows this question better.

You run a shared business and argue over almost every decision. The rule was born by itself: whoever knows more about the question decides. Figures — one of you; people — the other. When talk turns to a new office, the first has already opened their mouth but catches themselves: “That's your area. You decide.” **In your couple the wheel is passed, not seized: whoever knows less right now gives way.**

Giving way doesn't become a habit in equal measure. If the rule “whoever knows more decides” always works in one direction, the other stops having areas of their own, and only one leader sets the couple's pace. Resentment stays silent until it bursts out. Your shared business has one captain, and the other has long been sitting in the passenger seat.

items.title: Two captains
items.meaning: You build a shared business across several countries, and each of you has your own line in it.
text: You build your business on a grand scale. The Emperor gives order, a system, responsibility for people and results; the Chariot between you gives forward motion, shared momentum and each one's readiness to lead their own line. And you think big: the World teaches you to agree without borders — on markets in other countries, plans for a decade, the freedom each keeps.

Your company is opening an office in a third country. One answers for order: lawyers, accounts, hiring. The other goes to the negotiations and brings back the first clients. In the evening on a video call you compare two lists and see that each covered what the other didn't see. **You build on a grand scale: one keeps order, the other leads the way, and you agree on the whole world together.**

Two captains on one ship start arguing about the course. One partner's order and the other's momentum collide, the fight for the last word runs through every decision, and broad agreements turn into imposing one's own plan. Work stops staying at work. Your meetings at home now run longer than the ones at the office.

items.title: Room for chance
items.meaning: Your plan is solid, but with room for a lucky chance — something you agreed on in advance.
text: You build your careers solidly: the Emperor in success gives a plan, responsibility and posts earned through endurance. But life loves surprises, and between you is the Wheel of Fortune — lucky chances that come to the couple and change the route. How to combine plan and chance is decided by the Lovers: you agree not by the rulebook but out of love, asking what you both want.

A five-year plan is laid out year by year: a promotion, a mortgage, a renovation, a dog — whichever comes first. Then an acquaintance invites one of you onto a new project across the ocean. The one who kept the plan frowns, the other lights up. That evening you sit down and recalculate: what we'd gain, what we'd postpone, whether we want it. You decide to go — together. **Your plan is good as long as it leaves room for a chance you agreed on together.**

Order and chance can quarrel. The builder starts defending the plan from any surprises and deciding for two, while the one who believes in chance takes risks out of spite. In such a quarrel the Lovers speak sharply and hurtfully. The diary is filled a year ahead, and there's not a single free line left in it — neither for luck nor for the other.

items.title: Owning up to ambition
items.meaning: Ambition for power is voiced and works for the business — as long as the habit of leading stays out of home.
text: You're not shy of ambition: the Devil at the point of common language lets you talk plainly about wanting power, money, influence. Your desire is a businesslike one, since the Emperor at work leads to posts, leadership, responsibility for big things. And luck often opens the doors to them: the Wheel of Fortune has taught you that you're lucky as two and must be ready when luck comes.

Over dinner comes something unexpected: “I want to be director. Not deputy, not head of department — director.” The other neither laughs nor takes fright: “Then let's prepare.” Six months go on courses and connections. When the old director suddenly leaves, the candidate is ready, and the post goes to them. **A hunger for power and money isn't hidden in your couple — it's discussed and directed, and luck finds you ready.**

Power that's loved wants to come home too. The habit of leading brings orders into the couple, the wish to influence turns into control of the other, and luck starts to seem one partner's merit. Talking honestly about power is easy when it's shared. A board of directors appears at home too, and it has only one vote.

items.title: Handing over the office keys

captions.R: Building and answering for your own

items.meaning: You build solidly, and what holds you is the ability to let go of what you've built in good time — quietly and together.
text: At work you are builders: the Emperor in success gives responsibility, order, management posts and work that lasts for years. It's hard for a builder to let go of what's been built, and here Death helps: it connects you through the ability to close chapters and not cling to the past. And you decide quietly, like the Hermit: without meetings or declarations, after long thought alone.

For ten years one of you headed a department they built themselves. Now they want something else, but leaving is frightening: what if it all falls apart? The other doesn't try to persuade. Just one evening asks: “Do you still want this, or not any more?” The answer comes a week later. The office keys are handed over, a successor chosen, and at home it's calm for the first time in years. **What helps you leave a post you built yourselves is not an order but the other's quiet agreement.**

Order can defend itself against change to the last. The one used to running things brings orders home and decides for two, and meets the other's changes with hostility. Resentment builds silently, without a single quarrel, until living side by side becomes cold. The office has long been unnecessary, yet its door is still locked.

items.title: Sensing when it's time

captions.R1: Letting go of what you built

items.meaning: Order and instinct work together for you: one keeps the business going, the other is first to notice it has run its course.
text: You know how to build solidly and for the long term: the Emperor at work gives a system, responsibility, work that lasts for years. But what you build doesn't hold you captive, because Death has taught you both to let go when the time comes. And when it comes, the Moon tells you: your premonitions are shared, and you often sense a change before the figures show it.

Things at one partner's company are going well, the reports are green, but over morning coffee they say: “I don't know why, but I feel it's time to leave.” The other answers: “I've felt it for a month too.” You don't rush, but you prepare: a cushion, connections, a plan. When the company is sold and half the staff are cut, you already have a new venture. **You sense when it's time to let go of what you built, before the figures say so.**

A premonition of change easily turns into anxiety. If you trust every vague feeling, what you've built starts to seem fragile, order a cage, and change an escape from a threat that doesn't exist. The one who builds argues with the one who senses. Every morning begins with the question of whether it's time to drop everything, and it's been that way for three years.

items.title: The foreman and soup for all
items.meaning: You've come through more than one storm together and build solidly: one keeps the plan, the other the warmth at home.
text: Answering for things and leading come naturally to you: the Emperor in success gives posts, responsibility and the ability to keep order. But what binds you most firmly is the Tower — trials passed shoulder to shoulder, and shared work done with your hands: building, renovating, moving. And the Empress makes care your common language: you feather your nest, and every corner of it is made for two.

A downpour washes away the formwork the day before the foundation of your house is to be poured. One of you, used to being in charge, has a new schedule by morning and rings round the crew. The other cooks soup for everyone and brings it to the site in a huge pot. By evening the formwork is up again, and the builders say they've never had such soup on a site. **You build a house and a union the same way: to plan, through trials, and with care for every brick.**

When the building drags on, it turns into a war. The one in charge brings an orders-only tone into the relationship, trials make both irritable, and soup for everyone becomes a duty: feed people and keep out of the way. Every breakdown is a reason to find out who's to blame. The house is finished, and you still talk to each other like foreman and contractor.

items.title: Accepting help
items.meaning: Even the most responsible of you knows: in trouble you can hand the phone to the other and get some sleep.
text: At work you answer for many: the Emperor gives leadership, responsibility, a habit of carrying everything yourself. You've had troubles too, and the Tower binds you through them — trials after which you grew closer. And the Hanged Man teaches you the main thing in trouble: to let yourself give way and accept help rather than carrying it all alone.

One partner's workshop catches fire at night, and by morning only the walls are left. The boss has been on site since dawn: calls, the insurers, the workers. By evening they can't speak. The other arrives, takes the phone from them and says: “Today I'm making the calls. You're going home to sleep.” They try to argue, then for the first time in many years simply agree. **The one used to carrying everything alone knows how to accept the other's help in trouble.**

A habit of carrying everything can turn into silent sacrifice. If the boss never gives way, the other is left on the sidelines feeling unneeded, while the boss burns out without admitting it. Irritation after trouble lands on loved ones. The workshop has been rebuilt, and you never asked for help again.

items.title: Headquarters and horizon
items.meaning: Crises lived through together have made you a team no emergency can scare — as long as home doesn't become HQ.
text: In hard times you don't scatter, you pull together: the Tower has bound you through crises lived through, each of which you came out of together. It also helps that at work you're people of order — the Emperor makes you managers the work rests on when everything falls apart. And so that order doesn't narrow your view to a single point, there's the World: in your conversations you keep the horizon in sight and remember that life is bigger than any emergency.

Night: one partner's office has flooded, the server is dead, clients are calling. The one in charge has been handing out instructions for three hours. At two in the morning the other calls, not with advice but with one sentence: “Listen. We've got out of worse than this. Soon you'll be telling it as a funny story.” The manager breathes out and sits down for the first time that night. **In a crisis one holds the order and the other the wide view, and together you lose neither your heads nor the horizon.**

A habit of emergencies turns home into headquarters. The one who keeps order starts giving commands at home too, every mishap is declared a crisis, and broad talks about life give way to evacuation plans. Irritation after a hard day lands on the other. Even on holiday you carry a map of the emergency exits in your head.

items.title: The boss stays at the office

captions.R: Answering for people and the work
captions.M: Tenderness without a chain of command

items.meaning: At work you answer for a lot, and at home there's sunshine between you, with nobody to give orders to.
text: You carry a lot of responsibility at work: the Emperor in success puts you in charge, answering for people, keeping order and deciding for others. All of it stays at the threshold, because at home the Sun greets you — warmth, guests, trips, a party for no reason. And you speak to each other in the Lovers' language: tenderly, directly and as equals, with no chain of command.

End of the quarter. The one in charge comes home on Friday with a stony face and a habit of talking in orders. The other silently puts the car keys on the table: “We're going to the lake, our friends are already there.” By evening at the campfire the boss is laughing loudest, and on the drive home says quietly: “Thank you for that lake.” **Strictness stays at work: at home you have sunshine, and it shines on both equally.**

It's hard to leave the boss at the office. The habit of deciding for everyone moves home, celebrations start being planned like projects, and warm words start sounding like a performance review. In such a couple the Sun shines on one: their success, their guests, their mood set the weather. At a family celebration the toasts follow a schedule, and the other feels like a subordinate.

items.title: An anniversary wish list
items.meaning: By day you're strict managers, at home warm, bold people who aren't shy of their desires.
text: By day you're people of order and power: the Emperor at work gives leadership, responsibility, the ability to keep everything under control. At home the Sun binds you — warmth, joy, a light in which you needn't keep up appearances. And you talk boldly: the Devil lets you confess your hottest desires to each other without a trace of shame.

Every anniversary you have a ritual: each writes a list of ten wishes for the coming year, and you swap sheets. This year one list has “learn the tango” and “a week without phones”, and the other has things people write in a whisper. You read each other's, laugh, blush and circle the items you'll fulfil together. **Desires are spoken of openly in your couple, even the hottest, and that fills the home with light, not shame.**

Power and passion side by side can become a game where one writes the rules. If the one used to leading carries control into the most intimate, the other's wishes start adjusting, and the Sun shines only for its master. The lists get shorter, and the items more cautious. The sheets are still written every year, only with fewer and fewer circles.

items.title: Trust instead of control
items.meaning: Responsibility for everything stays at work, while at home you allow yourselves lightness and don't keep tabs on each other.
text: At home trust matters more than control for you: the Fool binds you through freedom, lightness and the certainty that you needn't watch the other. That's especially valuable, because at work the Emperor makes you people who answer for everything — order, people, results. And the Hermit helps you understand each other: without questions, without reports, by quiet signs.

The one who runs a huge department at work and checks every figure checks nothing at home. The other is planning a two-week solo hike — the first only asks which torch to take. No “will you call?” or “who'll you be with?”. When they come back, the other tells everything of their own accord. **The one who answers for everything at work knows how to answer for nothing at home: trust matters more to you than control.**

Freedom at home can turn into irresponsibility. If nothing is agreed, household matters hang, promises are forgotten, and the one used to keeping order at work silently carries the home too. Talking about it is awkward — they chose trust, after all. The boss at work turns at home into the one quietly tidying up after everyone.

items.title: Play after meetings
items.meaning: By day you're strict and composed, in the evening you fool around, and the other always senses when it's no time for jokes.
text: By day you're strict and composed: the Emperor at work gives responsibility, order, leading roles. In the evening the Fool binds you — games, fooling around, a lightness in which you let yourselves be children. The Moon guides the switch between these worlds: each senses the other's mood and knows when a joke will rescue and when it will wound.

The one who chaired meetings all day comes home with a frozen face. Usually they're greeted by a cushion thrown from behind the door, and a minute later you're pelting each other with cushions all over the flat. But today the other understands from one look that it's not the time. The cushion stays on the sofa, and on the table appear tea and a quiet question: “Bad day?” **Play lifts the strictness of your day, and when play is out of place, the other senses it by themselves.**

A joke can hide real anxiety. If every difficulty is answered with play, serious conversations get put off, and the one who leads starts leading at home too — even the rules of the game. The Moon guesses the mood, but not the reasons. Cushions fly about the flat, and what worries you never gets said.

items.title: Like minds found in silence

captions.R1: Shared beliefs, a meeting of minds

items.meaning: You're kindred spirits who came to shared views each by your own road, and it matters not to close the door on new ones.
text: The Hierophant stands at two of your points. In success he brings recognition from experts: an academic degree, the title of master, a place in a professional circle where your opinion carries weight. Between you he connects through like-mindedness — similar views on what is right, shared principles, endless topics for conversation. And you arrive at these views as the Hermit teaches, separately: first each thinks it through alone, then it turns out you think the same.

Sunday morning. Each reads their own book without disturbing the other, and until lunch the only sound in the flat is the rustle of pages. Then one puts the book down: “Listen, the author's writing about what we argued over on Wednesday.” The conversation stretches into the evening, and by supper you share a conclusion each reached by their own road. **You're kindred spirits not by habit but by choice: each came to your shared views alone, in silence.**

Over time shared views wall you off from others. Two experts sure they're right easily start looking down on everyone else — colleagues, friends, relatives — and then on any thought unlike yours. New people don't come to you, nor do new ideas. Everything on the shelf has been read and agreed upon, and nobody has brought home a new book in years.

items.title: A candle for the anniversary
items.meaning: Shared customs and a quiet faith bind you, with more feeling in them than rules.
text: There are two Hierophants in your couple: one at work, the other between you. In success he makes you keepers of knowledge — teachers, mentors, people others come to for advice. Between you he binds through shared customs and faith in the same values. And the understanding between you comes from the Moon, intuitive: much in your rituals rests not on words but on feeling.

On the eve of one partner's important exam, the other does what their grandmother once did: slips a small coin into the jacket pocket and says nothing. The examinee finds it at the door of the exam hall and smiles: you needn't believe in the coin, it's enough to believe in the one who put it there. **Your rules rest not on fear but on a quiet faith in what you do together.**

A ritual sometimes outlives its meaning. Rules that were once about love become “the done thing”, and breaking them is frightening — what if something happens. Two experts teach each other the right way, and an anxious instinct prompts bad omens. The anniversary candle is lit every year, and nobody remembers why any more.

items.title: Knowledge without a lectern
items.meaning: One partner's authority doesn't make the other a pupil: at home you're equals and help each other grow, like a garden.
text: You're respected as experts: the Hierophant in success gives authority, students, a place in a professional circle. At home that authority doesn't turn into a hierarchy, because Justice holds you — an honest partnership of equals, where one partner's knowledge gives them no extra vote. And the Empress teaches you to help each other grow, the way you'd tend a garden.

One of you decides to apply for a master's degree — at the very place where the other has long been teaching. The teacher doesn't lecture in the kitchen or correct notes without being asked.
