Instead you divide the year fairly: who takes on the household during exams, who runs the money. In the evenings sandwiches and tea appear on the table, and the student asks questions when they choose to. **One partner's knowledge doesn't become power: it's shared fairly and used to help the other grow.**

Knowledge can make a partner a pupil for ever. The habit of teaching moves home, a fair division turns into a tally of the other's mistakes, and care into guardianship over someone who “isn't ready yet”. The other wants to grow, but beside an eternal examiner it's frightening. They passed all their exams long ago, yet at home they're still being tested.

items.title: The rule and the person

captions.R: Knowledge and the rules of the profession
captions.M: Seeing the person behind the rule

items.meaning: Your principles are firm and your hearts soft: you keep the rule, but don't lose sight of the person behind it.
text: Knowledge and rules are the basis of your work: the Hierophant makes you people of the profession who teach, examine, uphold standards. Honesty isn't up for discussion, and Justice makes that principle shared. But nobody would call you cold, because you know how to talk like the Hanged Man — turning a situation round and looking at it through the eyes of the one who's struggling right now.

The one who teaches fails the son of old friends: the exam was honestly failed. In the evening the friends call, hurt. The other doesn't say “quite right” or “why be like that”. They say: “The mark is right. Now imagine how they feel. Maybe offer the lad extra lessons?” The lessons start on Saturday. **Justice isn't cold in your couple: the rule is kept, but the person is seen.**

Two people of principle can end up without friends. Rules become more important than relationships, honesty a reason to judge, and the ability to see the other side goes on putting up with your own rightness. Each gives way to the principle, not to the person. The rules are kept, and there's nobody to invite to a birthday.

items.title: More than one truth

captions.R: An expert's voice in your circle

items.meaning: You value knowledge and honesty, and a broad view helps you agree: there's more than one truth in the world.
text: Your status is knowledge: the Hierophant in success makes each of you the voice of your circle, the one people listen to and quote. Two experts under one roof isn't easy, but Justice keeps the peace between you: a fair division of credit, respect for the other's contribution, a word that is kept. And the World's language helps you agree — a broad view in which there's more than one truth and you can agree without surrendering.

You're doing a joint project for the first time — a course, a book, a study. The first question is whose name goes first, and you settle it in five minutes: alphabetical order, and the other way round next time. What you argue about afterwards is substance — at length, with quotations, sometimes into the night. And every time you finish with: “Your truth is true too; let's find where they meet.” **You never argue over whose credit is bigger: the fair split was agreed in advance, so you can argue about what matters.**

An argument about how to live can turn academic. Each is sure they know better, the division of credit becomes a score, and the broad view becomes a wish to convert the other. Friends wait for your opinion, while at home you still haven't agreed. The debate runs without a lunch break, and there will be no winner.

items.title: Listener number one

captions.R: The weight of knowledge, your circle's respect

items.meaning: Your peers' recognition matters, but what holds you is admiration for each other, voiced without exams or lectures.
text: Your status rests on knowledge: the Hierophant values diplomas, mentors and the respect of your circle, and each of you wants to be seen as a master of the craft. Strength, which you give each other, helps you go out to people with what you know: next to the other even the one who doubted grows bold. And the Lovers push you towards it — you name plainly what you like in each other, and do it often, for no reason.

Before the first big lecture one of you rehearses in the kitchen, stumbling on every slide. The other sits opposite, asks awkward questions, and at the end says: “You know, people will want to listen to you — even I do, and I don't understand half of it.” The next day there are a hundred people in the hall, but the speaker's eyes search for one. **Your respect for each other rests on admiration said aloud, not on titles.**

Admiration sours when home becomes a lecture hall. The habit of teaching moves from work to the kitchen, drive helps you insist on your own way, and soon one is explaining to the other how to speak, work and even enjoy themselves properly. Instead of “I like it” come grades, and any praise sounds like a pass mark. A lectern appears at home, and the same person always stands behind it.

items.title: Desires above your station
items.meaning: From outside you're a solid couple, inside hot and bold: beside each other you may want what's not “proper”.
text: From outside you're a solid couple: the Hierophant makes each of you a respected person in your circle — with a reputation, students, rules. But inside it's hot. Between you is Strength — passion, a mutual recharge, the feeling that beside the other you can be anyone. And you speak of that “anyone” boldly: the Devil lives in your common language, and desires unbecoming to your status are spoken aloud.

A respected lecturer, the author of two textbooks, confesses over a late supper: “All my life I've dreamed of playing drums in a rock band. Don't laugh.” The other doesn't laugh. A week later an electronic drum kit stands in the hall, and the neighbours learn that you rehearse on Thursdays. **Beside each other you allow yourselves desires your status says you shouldn't have.**

Solid status drives desires into the cellar. Position obliges, and secret “I wants” start living a life of their own — as irritation over trifles, jealousy, attempts to control the other. Lecturing is easier than confessing. In public you're respected people, while at home lies a secret list of desires that nobody reads aloud any more.

items.title: Learning from each other

captions.M: Understanding each other at a hint

items.meaning: You value knowledge and authority, and at home you swap roles: today one teaches, tomorrow the other.
text: You gain weight in your profession through knowledge: the Hierophant makes you mentors and experts people come to for advice. At home, though, two authorities don't argue over who's in charge — Temperance blends two different ways of life so that neither loses: both families' holidays, two cuisines, two sets of habits. You agree in the Hermit's language: briefly, thoughtfully, often at a hint.

By day one of you runs a seminar for beginners, who listen with bated breath. In the evening the same person stands at the stove, and the other, without looking up from a book, says: “Too early for the salt.” You both laugh: at work one teaches, at home the other. On Saturday the roles will swap again. **At home there is no teacher and pupil: each in turn knows more.**

The home starts to resemble a library when arguing seems indecent. One lectures, the other smooths things over and gives way, and both close up in their own thoughts. Everyone keeps the rules, people speak only in whispers, and whatever you want to say out loud is put off until later. Later rarely comes.

items.title: Sleep on it
items.meaning: Morning is wiser than evening for you: you gather arguments by day, and the decision comes after a night's sleep.
text: You know how to argue without shouting: Temperance leads you to a calm middle where both are ready to agree. You have plenty of arguments, because the Hierophant at work makes you experts — with reasons, references, experience. But the last word often goes to the Moon: when the arguments run out, you listen to instinct and put the decision off until morning.

The argument about whether to sell the country cottage has gone on for three evenings. Both have made every case, both are right in their way. One quotes a grandmother's old saying: “Things look clearer in the morning.” At breakfast each says what they feel, without arguments — and it turns out neither wants to let it go. You keep the cottage. **Contentious decisions are put off until morning in your couple: knowledge supplies the arguments, instinct the answer.**

An argument put off until morning may never wake up. If awkward things are always postponed and balance rests on silence, decisions drown in vague feelings and the right words in a habit of not arguing. You have a whole shelf of postponed conversations, each waiting for its morning.

items.title: The draft by the marking pile

captions.M: Growing what you've planned with love

items.meaning: One partner's knowledge becomes a shared dream, and you grow it tenderly, like a garden.
text: You're valued for knowledge: the Hierophant in success leads to work where you teach and are listened to. But knowledge wants more than a timetable and marked exercise books, and the Star connects you through a dream — one both can see and both are inspired by. And you grow it in the Empress's language: tenderly, with care, as you'd raise a child or a garden.

One of you has taught for fifteen years. One day the other listens to a story about a difficult pupil and says: “You should write your own course. Nobody else could explain it like that.” Now on Saturdays there are two laptops in the kitchen: one writes the lessons, the other draws pictures for them and brings tea and pastries. **Knowledge becomes a dream for you, and the dream a shared venture you grow together.**

The dream may stay “not serious”. The habit of living by the rules insists serious people don't do this, the fear of seeming naive dampens inspiration, and care turns into coaxing: “have a rest, don't torture yourself.” The course draft has lain for three years beside a pile of marked exercise books, and the pile keeps growing.

items.title: Authority on pause

captions.R: An expert's weight in your circle
captions.M: Giving way for the other's dream

items.meaning: One of you is a respected expert, the other a dreamer with a guesthouse in the mountains, and there was room for both.
text: You carry weight: the Hierophant at work gives authority, students, a place in your professional circle. But it isn't he who binds you — it's the Star: belief in each other's dreams, even the most unexpected. And when one partner's dream demands a sacrifice from the other, the Hanged Man comes to the rescue: the ability to give way, see the situation through their eyes, and not count it as defeat.

One of you has long dreamed of opening a guesthouse in the mountains. The other is a respected professor, and leaving means losing their department. That evening the professor is silent for a long time, then says: “You know, the department will still be there. But your dream might slip away.” Now you have a guesthouse, and the professor lectures online on Fridays. **For the other's dream you know how to put your own authority on pause.**

A pause for someone else's dream can turn into resentment. If the one who gave way starts missing their weight and recognition, lecturing and hints creep into conversation: “and I, for your sake…”. The other's dream becomes a debt, and the Star dims. The guesthouse is running, and more and more often the professor lectures the guests over breakfast.

items.title: Students from all over the world
items.meaning: You both know how to teach, and a shared dream carries your knowledge far beyond a single classroom.
text: Your knowledge wants to go beyond a single classroom. The Hierophant makes you mentors with something to pass on, and the Star — the shared dream that unites you — suggests where: to people you don't yet know. The World helps you talk to them — a broad, open view with which you speak to a neighbour or another continent alike.

An online course one of you recorded in the kitchen with a phone for a camera suddenly attracts students from twelve countries. The other translates subtitles and answers emails at night. On Sunday you run a live lesson together for the first time, and the chat fills with “thank you” in six languages. **Your knowledge becomes a dream, and the dream a venture without borders.**

You grow so used to teaching the world that you start teaching each other too, and the broad view turns into a certainty that you know what's best for everyone. Comparisons with others' successes erode inspiration. Students all over the world listen to you closely, while at home you stopped listening to each other long ago.

items.title: Traditions of your own
items.meaning: Both families are dear to you and work takes much time — so your celebrations are your own, invented by the two of you.
text: Your status rests on knowledge and service: the Hierophant gives you work where you teach, advise, keep the rules, and you're respected for it. Such work takes a lot of time, and at home Judgement awaits — family roots, shared holidays, a sense of family where everyone has their place. To keep one from eating the other, you need the Lovers' language: choosing rather than following out of inertia.

One partner's work increasingly falls on family holidays, and the relatives take offence. The two of you sit down and decide: the big holidays when possible, but there will definitely be a tradition of your own. Now every Friday you have a long breakfast, phones in another room, and no work can make you miss it. **You don't inherit your traditions, you choose them — so that both work and love fit in.**

Relatives can speak louder than you. Rules on how to live come from the elders, work demands its share, and your own “I want” gets lost between duty to family and duty to work. The parents' counsel takes the place of the couple's choice. The family calendar is drawn up by three generations, and there isn't a single date in it just for the two of you.

items.title: An awkward wish

captions.R1: A big family and its memory

items.meaning: You respect your family, and wishes that won't suit them you first discuss honestly between yourselves.
text: Family matters to you: Judgement binds you through roots, a big family, shared celebrations and memory. Respect for rules is in your blood — the Hierophant at work makes you experts, mentors, people of tradition. And yet your wishes are honest: the Devil lets you own up to each other even about what the family would find awkward or wrong.

Both families are sure you'll buy a flat near your parents. One evening comes an awkward confession: “I want to move to another town, by the sea. I'm ashamed, but I want it.” The other breathes out: “So do I.” You think long about how to tell the family, and decide first to go and look, and only then to gather everyone for a family lunch. **Even the wishes most awkward for the family you first say honestly to each other.**

A wish kept quiet before the family starts steering things in secret. When the family's expectations weigh more than your “I want”, it comes out as resentment and stubbornness over trifles. Teaching each other “the right way” becomes easier than confessing. At family gatherings you're a model couple, and at home you argue about what was never said aloud.

items.title: A home that draws people in

captions.R1: A warm home people are drawn to
captions.M: Saying tender things in front of others

items.meaning: You're open and generous to people, and you save the warmest evenings for the two of you.
text: Your work runs on goodwill: the Lovers in success give charm, connections, creative professions, work where being liked matters. People are drawn to you, and the Empress gathers you around a home people want to come to: warm, generous, with the table laid. And in your common language the Lovers return: you say tender things to each other openly, even in front of guests.

Friday, guests again — one partner's colleagues, the other's friends, the neighbours. One guest later brings a client, another invites you onto a project, and half your work successes were born at this table. Around midnight, seeing everyone off, one hugs the other right there in the hall: “You're the most beautiful person in this house tonight.” **Success comes to you through people, and people come to your home — because it's warm there.**

An open house wears you out if it's open only to others. More and more guests, fewer and fewer evenings for two, and tender words said in front of everyone start to sound like a performance. Jealousy of the guests' attention, comparisons with other couples, resentment that the house works for everyone but you. The guests leave happy, and you're left with unwashed glasses and things unsaid.

items.title: A warm home, hot words
items.meaning: Your home is cosy and warm, and passion doesn't cool in it, because desires aren't kept quiet here.
text: Your charm at work is strong: the Lovers give connections, goodwill, work where being liked matters. You come back to a warm home — the Empress binds you through comfort, care, a nest where everything is arranged for two. And so that comfort doesn't turn sleepy, there's the Devil: in this home passion and desires are talked about without embarrassment.

Sunday, rain, pies in the oven, a cat on the windowsill — just like an advert for cosiness. And in the middle of it all one of you suddenly whispers something in the other's ear that makes them drop a spoon. The pies nearly burn. In the evening, over late tea, you laugh: so many years together, and still like the first month. **Comfort and passion live in the same home in your couple and don't get in each other's way.**

Jealousy smoulders longer in a warm home. The charm that brings in clients starts to worry, the wish to possess hides behind care, and bold words behind resentment. The Empress is jealous of others' attention, the Devil wants ownership. You haven't stopped baking pies on Sundays, but the hot words are heard less and less.

items.title: Chosen by heart, proved by deed

captions.R: Being proud of each other's success
captions.R1: A choice made by the heart

items.meaning: You choose both your work and each other with your hearts, and show love by deeds rather than words.
text: The Lovers repeat along this line, and each repetition has its role. In success they lead to work chosen for love and to pride in each other's status: you like who the other has become. Between you they connect through the choice itself — made once and confirmed every day. And you show love quietly, like the Hermit: not with vows but with what the other finds by the bed in the morning.

Two offers in one day: a prestigious one and one that lights up your eyes. The one who got them is silent for a week, agonising. The other gives no advice, only one evening leaves a sheet on the table: on the left the prestigious company's name, on the right the other one, and underneath: “On the right you're smiling.” The choice is made that same night. **You choose work, like each other, with your hearts, and then quietly prove the choice was right.**

Pride in your partner quietly turns into a demand. The one you were proud of must live up to it: keep up, shine, not disappoint. Love seeks an ideal, and the quiet language won't let you admit you have no strength left. The portrait in its frame looks better than the living person at the stove, and the comparison is heard more and more often.

items.title: A confession by playlist

captions.R: Work you love, and others' admiration

items.meaning: Your confessions come as songs, glances and notes, and the other always understands what they mean.
text: The Lovers twice over — at work and between you. In success they lead to work you love and to others' admiration: you're valued for your taste, charm and creative streak. Between you they connect through the choice itself — you chose each other and keep choosing again. And your confessions follow the Moon's laws: not head-on but through songs, glances and notes only the two of you understand.

A hard week for one of you ends with an untitled playlist appearing on their phone. Twelve songs, and in each a line about the other being there, about it all passing, about you being better than you think. The reply comes at night — also a song. Not a word about feelings has been said aloud all week, but both know everything. **You confess to each other not in plain words but in songs, glances and notes, and you hit the mark every time.**

Romance needs light. When feelings are only ever hinted at, the hints start being read differently: in the other's new song you look for who it's addressed to, in a late message from a colleague for a secret. Jealousy starts writing its own stories. The playlists keep arriving every week, and each one is now searched for evidence.

items.title: Quiet after the crowd

captions.R: Work where you have to be liked
captions.R1: A talk for two about what matters
captions.M: Warming up after a hard day

items.meaning: By day you give yourselves to people, and in the evening a quiet home and someone who understands without words warm you up.
text: Your success is tied to people: the Lovers at work give charm, a gift for being liked and building connections, a profession where you're on show all day. Such work drains you to the bottom, and the Hermit saves you — the thing that unites you: deep talks for two, respect for silence, the right not to put on an act. And love in your couple speaks the Empress's language: care, food, warmth.

All day one of you smiles at clients, jokes, persuades, keeps up appearances. They come home wrung out and sit silently on the floor in the hall. The other doesn't fuss: takes off their shoes, puts soup on to warm and turns on quiet music. An hour later the real conversation begins — about what actually happened that day. **After a day among people you have a home where you can be silent, and someone who understands that without taking offence.**

The one who spent all day with people shuts down completely at home, and the quiet after the crowd becomes a wall: the other, who waited all evening, gets only a “fine” and a back. All the charm goes to strangers, and at home there's only looking after a tired person. The other keeps waiting to hear about the day, then stops asking.

items.title: Listening in turn
items.meaning: One partner's work among people doesn't take away your talk for two: you both know how to yield the floor.
text: You know how to yield the floor gracefully — that comes from the Hanged Man, and in your couple it's the main way of coming to terms. The skill comes in handy, because the Lovers at work make you people who talk all day, are liked, listen to others. You come home for something else. The Hermit gives you deep talks for two, where you can finally be heard.

All day one of you cuts hair and listens to clients: weddings, divorces, renovations, gossip. In the evening they want only to talk — and the other yields: listens, nods, asks questions. And on Sunday the roles swap: the one who listened sits with tea in silence, and the other talks about their week until evening. **You know how to listen in turn: today one talks it all out, tomorrow the other.**

The listener's role quietly gets fixed on one. The one with the noisy job gets used to talking it all out, while the other gets used to staying silent and yielding, without noticing they haven't told anything themselves for a long time. A deep conversation becomes a monologue. One has been talking for ten years now, the other nodding for ten years.

items.title: An island of quiet
items.meaning: By day one of you belongs to people, by evening to quiet — and your right to that quiet is sacred.
text: Your success is tied to people: the Lovers give charm, taste and a gift for being liked, and the work often rests on connections and goodwill. The flip side of such a life is noise, and the Hermit saves you from it: you're connected by long quiet talks that leave you both calm. And the rules for combining noise and quiet you write in the World's language — agreements without pressure, where each has freedom.

A stage, a microphone, hundreds of people — one of you is asked to host events. The other dislikes publicity. You sit down and agree: work as much as you like, but two evenings a week belong only to you, and no guests at home without asking. On Thursdays you have a quiet dinner without phones, and no outside party gets in. **One partner's noisy success doesn't break your quiet, because you drew the borders between them together.**

The island of quiet empties unnoticed. One is invited everywhere, the other nowhere, and shared evenings turn into retelling other people's parties. Jealousy doesn't speak aloud but silently stores up grievance; agreements live on by inertia, though they've long suited nobody. On Thursdays dinner is still phone-free, only there's less and less talk over it.

items.title: A concession given as a gift

captions.R: Doing what you love, liked by people

items.meaning: You choose your work with your hearts, and you give each other concessions as gifts, not as debts.
text: You choose your work with your hearts: the Lovers in success lead you where it's interesting and where people love you, not where the pay is higher. The Hanged Man helps you afford such a choice — a readiness to see the situation through the other's eyes and give way if they need it more. The Hanged Man stands between two Lovers: you speak plainly about feelings and wishes, and a concession between you is never silent.

The dream job turns up in a small studio that pays half as much. The one invited hesitates: what will we live on this year? The other says: “Choose what makes your eyes light up. I'll cover us, and later you'll cover me.” The year is modest, but in the evenings you hear stories that make both your eyes light up. **You know how to give way to each other so that it sounds like a gift, not a debt.**

The lightness vanishes if a concession starts being expected. At some point the one who covered notices it is always them who gives way, and instead of a straight word a sigh appears. The Lovers, hurt by a one-sided gift, speak sharply and to the point: “For your sake I had to give up everything.” The gift, it turns out, came with a receipt attached — it just wasn't shown.

items.title: Turning jealousy over

captions.R1: Compassion and readiness to give way

items.meaning: Work among admiring people isn't dangerous for you, because you speak of dark things plainly and with compassion.
text: You're not afraid to talk about dark things: the Devil brings into the light jealousy, passion, the wish to possess — everything other couples hide. There's plenty to talk about, since the Lovers at work surround you with people, charm, others' admiration. And between you is the Hanged Man — compassion: you don't condemn the other's confession but try to see it through their eyes.

After a work party one of you is silent all the way home and there confesses: “I'm jealous. Of the way people looked at you at that party. I'm ashamed, but it's true.” The first doesn't make excuses or laugh. Sits down beside them: “Tell me what was happening to you in that moment.” The talk goes on into the night, and by the end the jealousy turns out to be a fear that can be calmed. **Jealousy isn't hidden in your couple but turned over: you look at it through the other's eyes and find what stands behind it.**

Admitted jealousy can become a weapon. If desires and fears are spoken too freely, they start being used: playing on pity, reproaching, demanding accounts. Compassion turns into concessions, honesty into leverage. Every confession is remembered and later surfaces in a quarrel.

items.title: Home without witnesses
items.meaning: Charm opens doors for you, attraction keeps you close, and the most important things you say to each other quietly.
text: Your success rests largely on charm and connections: the Lovers make you both people for whom doors open easily, and each is proud of how the other is valued. Others' attention doesn't drive you apart, because the Devil sits between you — a strong attraction that needs no explanation. And the most important things about each other you say, as the Hermit bids, not in public but in private.

At the office party one of you is surrounded by colleagues, someone takes photos, someone asks for a dance. The other watches from the side and doesn't interfere. You leave early and walk home. Halfway there comes: “I like it when people look at you like that. But you're going home with me.” **Others' admiration doesn't frighten you, because the important things about each other you know without witnesses.**

Jealousy in your couple doesn't shout — it keeps silent, and that is its danger. Suspicion grows, the wish to hold on strengthens, and nothing is said aloud. The question nobody asked, the other fills in alone and answers alone too. After every party — a long silence at the wheel on the way home, and both pretend they're just tired.

items.title: A date with a stranger
items.meaning: You still get to know each other anew, and the attraction only grows stronger for it.
text: The attraction between you doesn't fade: the Devil gives a pull that stays almost as strong over the years as at the start. The Moon warms it — you know how to remain a mystery to each other, speak in hints, play. And in public you're charming: the Lovers at work make you both the people colleagues, clients and audiences are drawn to.

Every few months you play a game: you arrive at a bar separately and get acquainted again, as strangers. One invents a new name, the other a profession. The bartender only realises what's going on by the third cocktail, when you leave together, holding hands. **The attraction between you doesn't fade, because you know how to remain a mystery to each other.**

Playing at mystery can turn into real secrets. The charm people like at work starts causing unease at home, mystery turns into things left unsaid, and attraction into a wish to possess. The Moon happily makes up whatever's missing. The game of strangers goes on, but now each checks whether the other is playing it a little too well.

items.title: Instinct honed on each other

captions.R: Taste and charm in your work

items.meaning: You're valued for taste and a feel for people, and at home that feel becomes care that comes before you're asked.
text: You're valued for taste and charm: the Lovers give creative professions, work with people, a knack for guessing what someone will like. You hone that instinct at home, where the Moon binds you — understanding at a hint, shared fantasies, a subtlety that can't be explained. And your care is like the Empress's: generous and ahead of any request.

Clients of one of you, a florist, often ask: “How did you guess what she needed?” They learn the guessing at home. The other understands at a glance when they're sad and, without asking, puts on the table a bouquet of whatever was left in the workshop and a plate of hot soup. **The feel for people your clients value, you hone on each other.**

Charm at work can cause alarm at home. Clients, compliments, long conversations — and the instinct that once sensed joy now senses threats. Care becomes a way to hold on, and hints a way to reproach. The other guesses everything except one thing: where the truth ends and their own fantasy begins.

items.title: A scene from a long film

captions.M: Patiently looking from the other side

items.meaning: The work you love brings rejections and applause, and you live through them together, like scenes in one long film.
text: The work you love brings you both rejections and applause: the Lovers lead to creative professions where charm and taste matter and success is unpredictable. The Moon holds you — shared waking dreams, fantasies, an understanding that's hard to explain to outsiders. And the Hanged Man helps you wait out rejections: patiently, turning the situation over and looking at it from an unexpected side.

The fifth casting in a row — rejected. The actor comes home in silence and sits on the windowsill. The other sits beside them: “Let's pretend it's a film. What scene is this?” After a moment the actor smiles: “The one where the hero loses before the finale.” — “There you are. And the finale hasn't been shot yet.” The next day they go to the sixth. **You live through rejections in the work you love together, and can see in them not a verdict but a scene from a long film.**

You can dream and wait forever. If every failure is turned into “the scene before the finale”, the finale can be awaited for years, and the Moon will paint ever more beautiful pictures of the future. The one waiting alongside starts sacrificing their own for someone else's dream. Your film has been shooting for ten years now, and there's still no finale.

items.title: Rehearsal in the kitchen

captions.R: The charm of stage and audience

items.meaning: You understand each other in imagined worlds and in the real one — as long as the play doesn't cross the line.
text: Audiences love you: the Lovers at work give charm, the stage, creative professions where being liked matters. Between you lives the Moon — a shared imaginary world, games, fantasies, understanding at a hint. And so that play doesn't get mixed up with life, you have the World: you agree openly on each one's freedom and on where the lines are.

The night before a premiere. The one playing the lead can't sleep, and you rehearse in the kitchen until three: the other reads all the other parts, mixing up the voices and laughing. By morning the lines are word-perfect. And just before going on, the actor gets a message: “Remember who you are when the curtain closes.” **You understand each other in imagined worlds as well as in the real one, and don't confuse the two.**

The play can cross the line. The stage brings partners, admirers, scripted kisses, and the Moon starts painting what isn't there. Each interprets the agreements on freedom their own way, and jealousy hides behind “it's just work”. On stage a kiss is work, and at home nobody mentions it for three days.

items.title: Friends on every continent

captions.R1: A shared view of the wide world

items.meaning: You have friends on every continent, and the closest is the one you look through the photos with after a trip.
text: Your charm fits in anywhere: the Lovers in success give connections, goodwill, work with people and a gift for being liked in any country. The world is big for you, and the World also unites you through a shared view of life — a love of roads, new people, wide horizons. And you speak once more in the Lovers' language: from the heart, openly, choosing each other among all these people.

From your travels you bring back not fridge magnets but people: an architect from Lisbon who later becomes a client, a couple from Tbilisi you now share family dinners with. On the evening after yet another return you look through the photos, and one says: “You know, the best thing in them is you.” **Your world is big, and the main place in it is beside each other.**

Breadth blurs closeness. There are so many people around that no time is left for two, freedom becomes the right not to come to agreements, and the attention once shared is spread across a hundred acquaintances. Jealousy smoulders but is never voiced. Hundreds of friends all over the world, and not a single close conversation in a month.

items.title: Wanting a lot, together

captions.R: Charm that opens up the world
captions.R1: A pull towards roads and new people

items.meaning: Your world is big and your wishes honest: you're not shy of wanting a lot and saying so aloud.
text: You're not shy of wanting a lot: the Devil makes your talk of wishes, passion and ambition honest and bold. There's no shortage of wishes, because the World binds you through a love of open space — new countries, people, roads. And at work the Lovers help you: charm, connections, a knack for being liked that opens doors in any corner of the world.

Morning in a hotel in a strange city. Over breakfast one of you suddenly says: “In five years I want us to have a house by the sea, our own business and six months of travel a year. And I want you — just as I do now.” The other doesn't laugh, but takes out a pen and starts writing on a napkin: “Then let's do the sums.” **Your boldest “I want” is spoken not in the half-dark but over breakfast, and there's no shame in it.**

Freedom and passion get on badly with jealousy. The charm that opens doors opens them to other people's attention too; open space turns into a right not to account for yourself, and the wish to possess into quiet control. Talking about passion is easy, about jealousy harder. The napkin with the plans was lost long ago, and “who are you spending your evenings with there?” is heard more and more often.

items.title: A patch for each of you

captions.R1: Clear roles and a safe rear

items.meaning: Your shared decisiveness doesn't turn into a fight: roles are assigned, and love gets spoken amid the schedules.
text: You move towards goals decisively: the Chariot in success gives drive, speed and readiness to take on the hard things. To keep two drives from getting in each other's way, the Emperor gives the couple clear roles: who answers for what, whose patch is where, who covers the rear. And love in your couple speaks the Lovers' language: among schedules and plans you don't forget to say warm things to each other.

Everything at home is divided: one handles money and paperwork, the other trips, repairs and celebrations. Nobody meddles in the other's patch, and nobody does the other's part for them. So when one has a crunch, the other takes over some of their tasks without question, and on Friday evening you still hear: “I love you. Let's go for a walk.” **Your roles are clear, and that's exactly why you're free: each knows their patch, and there's love enough for both.**

Clear roles harden over time. The one used to answering for the main things starts deciding for two, the rivalry for the last word goes on without a declaration of war, and warm words drown in schedules and lists. Each does their part well and doesn't see that the other is lonely. The house runs to a precise timetable, and there's no slot in it for “talk”.

items.title: Each to their own summit
items.meaning: Your two races to the top don't collide: roles are set out, and ambitions are spoken about plainly.
text: Your ambitions are no joke: the Chariot at work drives you both to the top — posts, records, companies of your own. Two such races could collide, but the Emperor binds you through clear roles and order: each has their own patch, their own summit and their own responsibility. And the Devil gives you honesty in talk — you speak about a wish for power, money and first place plainly, without shame.

An evening of reviewing the year. One of you says: “Next year I want to make partner at the firm. And I'll be honest: it matters more to me than a holiday.” The other nods: “And I want to open a second branch. Let's write down who takes on the home and when.” The table comes out honest, and the holiday moves to autumn — by mutual agreement. **Ambitions aren't hidden in your couple but shared out: each has their own summit and their own patch.**

The struggle for dominance can go underground. If one partner's ambitions start to matter more, order begins to serve one, and honest talk about wishes turns into bargaining: “last year I gave way, now it's your turn.” Two leaders now compete not with the world but with each other. The table of roles hangs on the wall, and each secretly rewrites it in their own favour.

items.title: Silence at the summit

captions.R1: A road walked side by side

items.meaning: Each of you drives your own work, and your shared route is roads and hikes where few words are needed.
text: The Chariot stands both in your work and between you, but it drives differently. In success it makes each of you a doer: your own projects, your own goals, your own momentum, and nobody expects the other to live for their career. Between you is the same Chariot — a shared road: hikes, trips, sport, any movement where you are side by side. And you hardly need to talk on the way: the Hermit teaches you to understand each other by your stride and to be silent in a way that doesn't weigh.

Saturday, climbing to a pass from dawn. Almost the whole way you walk in silence, each thinking their own thoughts: one has a launch on fire, the other negotiations. At the summit you sit on a rock, share sandwiches, and someone says: “You know, it's time to go freelance.” The other nods: “About time.” You come down with a plan. **Your main decisions are born on the road, where you can be silent side by side for a long time.**

Two chariots side by side easily start a race. Who grows faster, who earns more, whose goals matter more — the rivalry runs without words, and the silence that once brought you close now hides a score. Each pulls the other onto their route or demands that they give way. The prize in such a race is the right to decide, and there are always two losers.

items.title: Pulling over in time

captions.R1: Driving side by side, ready to defend
captions.M: Sensing when it's time to stop

items.meaning: Speed is shared between you, and what holds you is an instinct that tells you when the other needs to stop.
text: A double Chariot means two kinds of momentum. In success each races in their own contest: projects, deadlines, goals nobody will reach for you. Between you the same Chariot becomes moving side by side and readiness to defend: if one is attacked, the other steps in at once. The Moon teaches you to understand each other without words, and its instinct tells you when it's time to slow down.

For the second week one of you has been putting on a brave face, answering “everything's fine” and working till late at night. The other says nothing, but on Saturday morning turns the car not towards the office but towards the woods: “You're not going anywhere today.” The passenger is angry at first, then falls asleep right there in the car and wakes up a different person. **You sense the other's tiredness before they admit it, and pull over in time.**

At speed you can't see what's on the other's mind. Two races run in parallel, each busy with their own, and the instinct that used to guide you now throws up only anxiety: it seems the other has drifted away, is hiding something, competing. There's no time to ask — back on the road. The headlights shine far ahead, but it's dark inside the car.

items.title: A note on the fridge
items.meaning: You race after success and catch luck, and come back to where care doesn't have to be earned.
text: You know how to build up speed: the Chariot in success loves its own work, several projects at once and jobs where you can see the numbers grow. The Wheel of Fortune often gives you a following wind: the right person, a lucky order, a season that takes off. All the more important, then, where you come back to. The Empress makes care the couple's language: a dinner that's waiting, a blanket on the sofa, a talk about how the day went.

A good week: a big order came by chance through an acquaintance, and the one running the business works till late at night. At home the kitchen light is on, something warm is in the oven, and on the fridge there's a note: “Proud of you. Eat and sleep.” In the morning the other finds a reply under it: “Couldn't have done it without you.” **The race for success always ends at home for you, where care doesn't have to be earned.**

A good season speeds you up so much that home becomes a stopover. Work eats the evenings, luck promises “a bit more and we'll rest”, and care turns into service: feed, wash, don't get in the way. The one who waits stops growing themselves and feels more and more like an appendage to someone else's success. The fridge is full, and the note on it is the only conversation of the day.

items.title: Speed that knows how to wait
items.meaning: Used to speed, you also know how to wait out a lull — without cursing fate or each other.
text: At work you strain to race ahead: the Chariot gives momentum, decisiveness, impatience with standstills. But your following wind is shared and comes when it pleases: the Wheel of Fortune gives you both the feeling that luck visits the couple rather than one, and that it has its own rhythm. The Hanged Man helps you adapt to that rhythm: in a lull, don't drive on — wait and look around.

One partner's project is frozen indefinitely, and the one used to racing paces the flat. The other suggests something strange: “Let's not start anything this month. Let's just look at what's around us.” The month goes on walks, books and meetings with old acquaintances. At one of those meetings a new venture appears. **Your speed knows how to wait: when the wheel stands still, you don't drive on but build up strength together.**

Waiting wears out the one used to racing. The lull drags on, one partner's impatience turns into irritation with the other, and the other's patience into an excuse for doing nothing. Each blames now fate, now the partner. The engine idles, and the fuel burns away for nothing.

items.title: A map on the floor

captions.R: Racing to where there's more to do

items.meaning: Your careers race ahead, luck throws up turns, and you agree in a way that leaves room for both.
text: The Chariot takes you where there's more to do: new cities, new projects, a readiness to pull up stakes for a strong offer. Chance often throws up the turns, and the Wheel of Fortune makes them a shared story: luck knocks for one, and life changes for both. You come to terms in the World's language — broadly, without pressure, respecting that each has their own view and their own road.

An invitation comes for a contract abroad. You spread a big map on the sitting-room floor and sit over it until midnight: where the other will find work there, which language to learn, how long to go for, how often to come back. You decide only when the other has their own “why” too. **The world is big for you, and you agree with room to spare: so that both find work in the new place.**

A big world sometimes turns out to be one person's world. One partner's momentum sets the route, luck writes off the other's doubts, and the shared dream of change sounds like an order: “but we both wanted this.” The other follows, learns foreign languages, makes acquaintances, but never finds work of their own. Dozens of stamps in the passport, and not one route of their own.

items.title: Boxes in a new place
items.meaning: You pull up stakes easily for work, and in every new place each of you finds their own “I want”.
text: Your work moves fast: the Chariot gives momentum, decisiveness and a readiness to go where the offer is better. Such momentum means leaving a lot behind, and Death makes this a shared skill — letting go of a city, a flat, an old circle, without looking back. And the Lovers make sure no voice gets lost on the road: each says aloud what they want.

The last evening in an empty flat. You sit on boxes, eat pizza straight from the carton, and one asks: “What do you want there — for yourself, not for work?” The other answers at once: a workshop in the box room and a dog. The first thing you look for in the new place is a flat with a box room. **A move for one partner's work never takes away the other's voice.**

Momentum is dangerous when it becomes a habit. The other is expected more and more often to put their goals aside for the shared route, and consent is given in the heat of the moment, before it has had time to ripen. Moves follow one after another, and the other lives among boxes they never unpacked: why bother, if you'll soon be on the road again.

items.title: Selling what you grew fond of

captions.R1: Letting go of the past together

items.meaning: You part easily with houses, cars and habits for a new path, and say honestly what you were sorry to lose.
text: You move forward without stopping — the Chariot gives drive, speed, a readiness to change route for the goal. Movement demands letting go, and Death binds you through the ability to do it together: to say goodbye to the old without drama. And the Devil gives you honesty in this — he lets you admit aloud what you've grown attached to before you part with it.

A new stage demands a move to another town, and for that you'll have to sell the house you spent five years building. In the evening one admits: “It's not the house I'm sorry for. I'm sorry for me in this house — the one who built it.” The other nods: “Me too. Let's say goodbye.” You spend the last evening on the veranda, remembering every board, and in the morning you hand over the keys. **You can honestly admit what you've grown attached to — and let it go for a new path.**

You can also let go of what held you together. If for the sake of movement you part with everything you've grown fond of, sooner or later it's the turn of shared habits, friends, rituals. Speed won't let you feel regret, Death won't let you look back. You've had three houses already, and you haven't lived in any of them longer than it took to build.

items.title: A quiet minute before the dash

captions.R: Racing to the goal without stopping

items.meaning: You move fast, and the strength of the union lies in storms weathered together and a quiet minute before each decision.
text: Your pace is high: the Chariot in success likes quick decisions, dashes, business trips and projects where you must get there before others. Speed doesn't scare those with shared storms behind them — and the Tower is about exactly that: sudden troubles you came through together without falling apart. But before every dash you need a pause. The Hermit gives it without fuss: a minute on the balcony, a walk alone, and only then an answer.

Friday, nine in the evening, the phone rings: on Monday one of you has to be in another city for three months, rescuing someone else's project. The other says nothing, goes out onto the balcony and stands there a long time. They come back with a list: who'll finish the renovation, when you'll call, which weekends they can visit. “Go. We survived the neighbours' flood — we'll survive this.” **Speed doesn't scare you, because you have storms behind you and decide after a quiet minute for two.**

Speed turns against you if you start deciding on the move. A minute of quiet seems a luxury, decisions are made in the car between calls, and quarrels are finished over the phone. A harsh word thrown out in haste is remembered for a long time. The road is one, but the silence in the car is such that you can hear the indicator ticking.

items.title: Anxiety nobody mocks
items.meaning: You sense the other's anxiety and don't laugh at it: you both know the price of storms.
text: You have shared storms behind you: the Tower binds you through trials lived through hand in hand — sudden, heavy ones, after which you trust only whoever was there beside you. That's why you're especially sensitive: the Moon teaches you to notice the other's anxiety in small things and not brush it aside. And at work you still race ahead: the Chariot gives decisiveness and speed that don't fade even after blows.

At night one of you wakes from a nightmare: they dreamed again that the business was collapsing. The other doesn't say “it's only a dream” or laugh. They switch on the bedside lamp, hold them and recount what happened after the last collapse: how you clawed your way out, what you built afterwards. In the morning the one who had the nightmare drives to work at the usual speed. **You sense the other's anxiety from afar and don't brush it aside: you both know what storms cost.**

Storms you've come through teach you to fear any weather. Sensitivity to anxiety turns into constant expectation of disaster, speed into flight from it, and sharp words on tense days are remembered for a long time. Fear starts deciding where to drive. In every cloud on the horizon you see a storm and turn off to where there won't be one.

items.title: A picnic after the win
items.meaning: You're as good at winning as at celebrating — with a blanket in a meadow and your favourite strawberries.
text: You know how to win: the Chariot gives drive, speed and a taste for achievement. Your victories don't stay in reports, because between you is the Sun — joy, warmth, the knack of celebrating. And the Empress's generosity turns every victory into treats and presents that don't have to be earned.

The tender is won on Friday afternoon. The one who ran it calls the other from the car, and by evening a blanket is already spread in a meadow outside town: favourite cheeses, strawberries, a bottle saved for a special occasion. You lie on the grass until dark, and on the way home you're already discussing the next goal. **Victories are celebrated at once in your couple, generously and as two, so you want to win the next one too.**

The race for victories can leave the house without its owners. The next goal is always more important, celebrations are postponed, and generosity turns into expensive presents instead of time. The one who runs less fast feels like a spectator of someone else's success. The trophies on the shelf multiply, and the picnics are put off until next season.

items.title: Standing aside
items.meaning: You have warmth enough for two, so one partner's victories don't take the place of the other's.
text: You know how to win: the Chariot leads you both to heights, competitions, achievements. There's no rivalry between you, because the Sun gives warmth and joy for two — one partner's success warms the other. And to keep it that way there's the Hanged Man: the ability to give up your turn when the other needs it more.

After winning a major architecture competition, one of you is immediately invited to the next, even more prestigious one. They decline. The other has been preparing a project for that very competition for a year, and two wins in one family in a season, the first reckons, had better not get in each other's way. The other wins, and in the front row at the ceremony sits the one who declined. **The winner in your couple knows how to stand aside so the sun reaches the other too.**

If it's always the same one standing aside, the sun starts to burn. A concession repeated too often stops being generosity and becomes an unspoken sacrifice; the competitive streak looks for an outlet, and out comes rivalry. Victories are counted no longer together but against each other. There are two trophies on the shelf, and each knows whose stands nearer the edge.

items.title: A finish in a strange city

captions.R1: A joy that warms you both

items.meaning: A finish in a strange city, dinner in an unknown café — your victories are celebrated on the road and as two.
text: Your joy is shared, and the Sun makes it the main thing that unites you: warmth, celebration, a love of life. There are plenty of reasons for it, because the Chariot leads you both to victories — at work, in sport, in anything with a finish line. And you like to celebrate on the road: the World makes your view broad, and your best days happen in strange cities and countries.

A marathon in a strange city. One of you runs, the other waits at the last kilometre with a flag and a flask. The finishing time is a personal best. In the evening you wander unfamiliar streets, eat something odd in a small café and laugh at the runner trying to get down the stairs. **One partner's victory is a celebration for two, and your best celebrations happen on the road.**

A celebration can turn into an exhibition of achievements. The next record, the next country, the next medal — the race replaces the joy, and the one waiting with the flask becomes the support staff of someone else's victories. The light goes to one. The medals hang on the walls, and you can't remember what you talked about on the last trip.

items.title: Two tickets to anywhere

captions.R: Racing to the goal at full speed
captions.R1: Friendship and readiness to set off

items.meaning: You race to your goals in earnest, with lightness and friendship between you — as long as it doesn't hide the big talk.
text: You race towards your goals in earnest: the Chariot in success gives drive, career momentum and readiness to work as long as it takes. This momentum doesn't turn you into two worn-out runners, because between you stands the Fool — friendship, humour, readiness to set off, the knack of dashing somewhere with no plan. And what you want you say plainly: the Lovers dislike hints.

Friday, eight in the evening, both dropping after a week of deadlines. One of you opens a ticket site and jabs at the map at random: “Tomorrow at seven a.m., somewhere we've never been?” The other is already looking for a rucksack. Saturday is spent in an unfamiliar city where nobody knows you and nothing needs deciding. **Your momentum at work is balanced by lightness between you: with you two it's never frightening and never dull.**

Lightness can become evasion. Work is serious, rest is fun, and serious things between you — the status of the relationship, the future, what hurts — aren't talked about: why spoil the mood. The Chariot races, the Fool jokes, and the straight conversation keeps being put off. You discuss everything under the sun except who you are to each other.

items.title: A jump on the count of three
items.meaning: Speed, friendship and a thirst for thrills are shared between you, and it matters that these aren't all that holds you.
text: The thrill is shared: the Chariot at work loves speed and risk, the Fool between you turns risk into a game and a friendship where anything can be done with a laugh. And the Devil honestly names what fires you both up: a thirst for thrills, the rush, the feeling of being on the edge. You don't pretend a quiet life is enough for you — and there's a lot of closeness in that admission.

You mark your anniversary with a parachute jump. In the plane one goes pale, the other laughs and counts: “One, two…” — and on “three” you're both already falling. On the ground you lie on the grass for a long time, unable to get up, roaring with laughter. That evening one admits: “I want us to still be jumping like this in twenty years.” **Thrill and lightness are shared: you admit honestly what you want, and you're not afraid of wanting the risky.**

The thrill can become an addiction to excitement. Ordinary days start to seem bland, each next risk has to be bigger than the last, and lightness won't let you stop and ask why. Quarrels get sharper too. The rush holds you together, and in quiet weeks you don't know what to talk about.

items.title: A deal that sounds like love
items.meaning: Your rules are shared and fair, and you agree on them with tenderness, not by the rulebook.
text: You build your careers by the rules: Justice means an official job, a fair division of duties and clear agreements. These rules aren't foreign: behind them stands the Hierophant — shared values and a way of life you assembled from two families. And the Lovers make sure people can be heard behind the rules: even about dull things you agree warmly, respecting what each of you wants.

A second degree, evening lectures, exams — one of you decides to go back to study. At a family council you divide up the year: who takes over the dinners, which expenses to put off, how many evenings remain shared. At the end what you hear is not “agreed” but “I'm proud of you”. **A fair deal between you sounds like a declaration of love, not a tenancy agreement.**

The agreement goes stale when the rules begin to live apart from the people. One teaches how things should be done, the other monitors compliance, and what was invented for love becomes a rulebook. It feels awkward to take offence aloud — everything is by the rules, after all. The code of household rules grows thicker every year, and the words “I'd like” can no longer be found in it.

items.title: Bold desire, honest yardstick
items.meaning: Your rules are strict and your desires bold, and you speak honestly even about those that don't fit the rules.
text: Reputation is your main capital: Justice in success gives honest work, official status, respect for keeping your word. The Hierophant unites you — shared principles, an idea of the right way to live. And for all your correctness you don't hide desires: the Devil in your conversations lets you talk about the boldest of them — money, power, passion.

At night, after a glass of wine, one of you confesses: “I want to earn three times as much. I'm ashamed, but I want it.” The other doesn't wince: “Then let's work out how to do it honestly.” By morning there are three ideas on a sheet, all three within your rules. One of them eventually starts to work. **Even the boldest desires are spoken aloud in your couple, and tested by one yardstick — honesty.**

Principles and secret desires get on badly. A desire you're ashamed to admit looks for roundabout ways: a stash, jealousy, manipulation. The rules grow stricter, and the living “I want” quieter. In words you lead a proper life, in your thoughts quite another, and both stay silent.

items.title: One yardstick for two
items.meaning: You keep your word and take nothing extra, and your honesty is shared — even when it goes unspoken.
text: Justice appears twice in your line, in different roles. In success it demands that status be earned: no dubious side jobs, no borrowed credit. Between you it binds through trust in the spoken word — if it's said, it's done. And the Hermit teaches you how to agree: you don't decide in the heat of the moment; first each thinks it over alone, then comes back with a ready answer.

An offer of lucrative side work comes in, but the scheme is murky. The other asks a single question: “Will you be at peace with it?” — and stays out of it. The evening passes in silence; at night nobody raises the subject either. At breakfast comes a short “no”, and the other nods as if they knew all along. **Your decisions ripen in silence but are made by one yardstick for two.**

The trouble with two just people is that each is sure they're right. Admitting a mistake is hard; it is easier to brood over a grievance alone, pass a verdict and never voice it. The other learns of the sentence from the chill in a voice and goes off to do some weighing of their own. For months a quiet trial runs in the house: two judges, and not a single defence lawyer.

items.title: A nose for the dishonest
items.meaning: Spotless work and honesty at home give you footing, and instinct helps you notice what goes unsaid.
text: Justice has two jobs in your couple. In success she demands work without a single blemish: an honest reputation, official contracts, no dubious schemes. Between you she's the foundation: the honesty everything else rests on. And the Moon sharpens instinct: you sense what's unsaid and notice something is wrong with the other before they say so.

For the third evening running one of you checks their email with a stony face. The other doesn't interrogate — puts tea beside them and asks just one thing: “Is it something dishonest?” A direct hit. At work they're being asked to sign a report with fiddled figures. You spend the night discussing how to refuse, and in the morning comes a calm “no”. **You sense unfairness in each other from afar and name it before it can poison the evening.**

A nose for the dishonest can turn on your own. The Moon paints what isn't there, Justice hurries to a verdict, and soon a late night at work looks like evidence and silence like a confession. Admitting your own fault is hard, the other's easy. The other runs a quiet investigation where there was never any crime.

items.title: Backing the one who's right
items.meaning: You achieve things honestly, and there's a law between you: whoever brings in more doesn't get more say.
text: You win your successes honestly: Justice gives clear rules and a sharp sense of when something is unfair. Unfairness still happens, and then the Strength between you comes to the rescue: next to the other you can be angry, tired, and still stay strong. And you express love the Empress's way — with care you can touch: a hot dinner, a blanket, a bill paid on time.

The promotion goes to someone's acquaintance rather than to the one of you who earned it. In the evening the other doesn't argue over who's right but puts dinner on the table, pours tea and waits for the anger to talk itself out. In the morning you write to management together — calmly, point by point, with figures. **The other's care restores your strength, and cool reasoning helps you put it to use.**

Care turns bitter when it becomes payment. Contributions start being compared, the one who earns less is looked down on slightly, and the one who brings in more gets more say. Protection turns into guardianship, guardianship into the right to decide. Dinner is served on time, only it is put on the table the way a bill is.

items.title: A truth you have strength for
items.meaning: You defend the truth to the end, and draw patience and courage for a long fight from each other.
text: You don't swallow injustice: Justice at work makes you both people who stand up for what's yours, by the law and to the end. Such disputes can be long, and Strength helps you bear them — courage you share when one runs short. And the Hanged Man conducts your talks about hard things: patient ones, with the ability to wait and look at the matter from the other side.

An employment dispute with a former employer has dragged on for a second year: hearings postponed, lawyers changing, money running out. One evening the one bringing the case says they'll drop it. The other doesn't argue or press: “It's your call. But if you carry on — I'm with you, however long it takes.” They carry on, and win. **You're ready to pursue justice for a long time, because you give each other the strength to wait.**

The fight for the truth can eat years. Principle becomes more important than life, drive turns into stubbornness, and the other's patience into an unspoken sacrifice. Each new dispute begins before the last has ended. Your file of documents is already thicker than the family album, and the other opens both less and less.

items.title: Flags on a shared map

captions.R: Proving your status by the rules
captions.R1: Topping up strength when it runs out
captions.M: Setting goals on a grand scale

items.meaning: You think in decades and countries, prove your status by the rules — and neither goes towards a goal alone.
text: You prove your status by the rules: Justice demands documents, certificates, honest work and recognition no one can dispute. It's a long road, and the Strength between you helps you travel it — one tops up the other's strength when theirs runs out. And you set goals with the World's sweep: not for a year but for a decade, and not within one city.

The exam for an international certificate is being sat for the third time. The night before, the one sitting it is hunched over textbooks with red eyes, saying they can't go on. The other takes the textbook, asks twenty questions in a row, and for each right answer sticks a flag on the world map above the desk — wherever that certificate is recognised. By midnight there are forty flags. **You set big goals and pursue them honestly, and the other tops up your strength.**

A big goal weighs on the one who walks more slowly. The rules start being bent to suit one, drive turns into “come on, stop whining”, and the shared sweep becomes someone else's plan that's simply easier to carry out. Each pulls towards their own goal. The map with flags still hangs on the wall, only all the flags were placed long ago by one hand.

items.title: A spreadsheet that balances

captions.R1: A quiet evening and a shared rhythm
captions.M: A choice not based on salary

items.meaning: Each of you earns your status honestly, and you both have an equal say at home — whatever the salary.
text: Each of you earns your status yourself, honestly: Justice likes an official job, clear agreements, everything by the rules. Differences in success still happen, and Temperance smooths them out — a calm shared rhythm, quiet evenings, the ability to agree without shouting. And the Lovers keep this evenness from turning cold: you speak plainly about feelings and decide even small things together.

After a promotion one of you starts earning noticeably more. You rebuild the budget: not half and half, but in shares. The one who brings in less admits: “I feel awkward.” The other answers: “I'm not with you for the salary — not then, not now.” **A difference in income never becomes a difference in the right to a say.**

Honest accounting easily slides into petty accounting. You start recording everything: who bought the bread, who paid for the taxi, whose turn it is to wash up. Discontent is muffled for the sake of peace and saved up until the first quarrel, where it comes out all at once. The spreadsheet in your shared file balances to the penny, but your conversations are running a deficit.

items.title: An evening without rules

captions.M: Allowing yourselves a little too much

items.meaning: Honesty and order six days a week, and the seventh evening is for everything you want.
text: Rules are held in honour by you: Justice at work gives honest work, order, a reputation as people who do everything properly. Temperance gives you measure in everything — a shared rhythm without extremes. And so that measure doesn't turn into boredom, there's the Devil: in conversation you let yourselves own up to wanting a little too much — and sometimes indulge it.

You have a “Friday without rules”: once a week, no lists, budgets or early starts. You order food you don't usually eat, watch films until three in the morning and tell each other everything you've kept to yourselves all week. On Saturday you wake at lunchtime, laugh about the night before and become people of order again. **Once a week your rules are cancelled, and that's what makes them bearable.**

Strict rules with a loophole can fall apart entirely. If the evening without rules stretches into the weekend and then the week, measure is lost, and honesty about wishes becomes an excuse for any excess. The one who loves order starts to control, the one who loves freedom to hide things. Your Friday without rules stopped being a Friday long ago.

items.title: A dream in an envelope

captions.R: Honest work and a clean reputation
captions.R1: A shared dream on the horizon

items.meaning: You work honestly and unhurriedly, and you're united by a shared dream that mustn't stay sealed in an envelope for ever.
text: Your reputation is clean and your success honestly earned: Justice likes an official job, planning ahead and a backup plan. This life doesn't turn dry thanks to the Star — a shared dream on the horizon, which makes such careful work worthwhile. You speak of it in private, without witnesses and without grand words: the Hermit guards what matters from stray ears.

Every year on the anniversary of the day you met, you each write a note with one dream and put it in an envelope. This evening you open the old ones. Three out of five say the same thing: a small house by the water. You're silent for a long time, then get out the savings spreadsheet and, for the first time, count not “for a rainy day” but “for the house”. **Your honest work rests on a dream that only the two of you know about.**

The dream risks staying in the envelope for ever. The backup plan crowds out the main one, fear of change passes itself off as prudence, and every year there's a reason to wait a little longer. Nobody says it aloud — everything seems sensible. The envelopes pile up in a box, while the house by the water lives on as a photo in your phone.

items.title: Poems under a sober suit
items.meaning: Behind your strict rules hides a shared dream, and one day it's worth showing it to more than each other.
text: The dream in your couple doesn't show at once: the Star binds you through the other having spotted in the first what they hid even from themselves. There was reason to hide it, since Justice at work gives strict work by the rules — contracts, figures, reputation. And you prefer to talk about the dream quietly, as the Moon bids: in hints, in an undertone, as of a secret that belongs only to two.

By day one of you is an auditor in a sober suit. At night, when nobody sees, they write poems in a notebook. The other found the notebook by chance and told nobody. Only sometimes, leaving for work, they leave a note on the table with a line from it and one word: “More.” The notebooks multiply. **Under one partner's sober suit the other spotted a dream — and guards it like a secret for two.**

A dream kept secret risks never coming into the light. Strictness whispers that it isn't serious, secrecy becomes a convenient hiding place, and inspiration a habit of creating what no one ever sees. The other tires of being the only reader. There are six notebooks now, and nobody but the two of you has ever seen any of them.

items.title: Arbiter for the whole family

captions.R: An honest name in your trade
captions.M: Caring for the one who cares for others

items.meaning: One of you is the honest arbiter for all the relatives, the other the one who looks after the arbiter.
text: Everyone knows your honest name: Justice at work makes you people of contracts, order and a word that's kept. The relatives know it too — Judgement binds you through roots, a big family, shared celebrations and shared problems. And the Empress runs the caring in such a big family: generous, homely, able to look after the one who looks after others.

All the relatives come to one of you for advice: how to draw up a contract, how to divide the country cottage, who should pay for the roof repair. The calls start first thing on Saturday. At some point the other takes the phone, switches it to silent and lays the table for breakfast: “The cottage can wait till Monday. You can't.” **One partner's sense of justice serves the whole family, and the other's care protects them.**

A family arbiter risks being left without days off. Honesty obliges you to help everyone, relatives get used to sorting out their affairs with someone else's hands, and the other's care turns into a battle with those relatives. Less and less room is left inside the couple. A hundred unread messages from relatives on the phone, and not one conversation for two all week.

items.title: Giving up your share

captions.M: Giving way for the sake of peace

items.meaning: For peace in the family you can give up what's yours, and you always decide it together.
text: For peace in the family you know how to give way: the Hanged Man teaches you to see a dispute through the other side's eyes and not cling to your own at any price. Family for you is something to cherish: Judgement binds you through kin, roots, shared memory. And honesty doesn't desert you even then — Justice at work makes you both people of documents and clear agreements.

Your parents' country cottage is being divided. By law one of you is entitled to half, but a brother and his family live there every summer, while you go once a year. You sit down together and work it out: here's our share, here's what it's worth, here's what matters more. You decide to give your part to the brother for a token sum — and have it all drawn up by a solicitor, honestly and without grudges. **Your honest reckoning sometimes ends with you giving away your share yourselves.**

A concession to the family is sometimes paid for by the couple. For peace in the family it's usually the same one who gives way, and the other starts to feel the family matters more than they do, and honest reckoning turns into a hidden tally. Resentment goes silent. You gave the cottage away honestly, only every summer one of you looks at other people's photos from there a little longer than necessary.

items.title: A table with room for everyone
items.meaning: Your family is big, with old grievances, and you know how to bring it to one table without lecturing.
text: At work you're honest without compromise: Justice gives clear rules, official status, a reputation as people of their word. That honesty is needed at home too, because Judgement weaves you into a family line — a big family with its own stories, grievances and celebrations. And the World teaches you to make peace among relatives: broadly, with respect for each side and no attempt to prove who's right.

Two branches of one partner's family haven't spoken for ten years over an old inheritance dispute. You decide to hold a shared celebration on neutral ground. One of you honestly divides the costs, the other phones everyone personally. At the table it's awkward at first; by evening they're singing. **Old family grievances are settled in your couple honestly and broadly — so that everyone fits at one table.**

The peacemaker's role can become a duty. The relatives get used to you settling every dispute, honesty requires you to take part in every conflict, and your own peace is left untended. Grievances against relatives spill over into the couple. All the relatives have made up, and the two of you argue over who did more for the peace.

items.title: A cocoon of warmth

captions.R1: A warm home as your shared centre

items.meaning: A quiet study and a warm kitchen are the two poles of your home, and neither lives without the other.
text: Your work needs quiet: the Hermit in success gives mastery, depth and work that needs solitude. That quiet isn't cold, because everything in your life revolves around home — the Empress stands twice: she both connects you and sets your language. Home is your shared centre, and care is expressed with your hands: food, warmth, things made for each other.

All day over a difficult book without looking up — that's how one of you works. Towards evening the other sets dough to rise, and by seven the flat smells of bread. The translator comes out of their room following the smell, sits at the table, and only then does the conversation begin — about the book, the day, what you'd like to buy for the new kitchen. **The quiet of work and the warmth of home don't argue in your house: one feeds the other.**

Working at home, living at home, caring for each other at home — and cosiness gradually becomes a cocoon, while the world outside the door starts to seem unnecessary. Generosity turns into a habit of overfeeding, attention into guardianship, and quiet into isolation. The house is warm, well fed and calm, and there hasn't been a single guest since last spring.

items.title: Years of renovation

captions.R1: A home that grows with you

items.meaning: You finish your home over years, unhurriedly and together, and you both have the patience for it.
text: Your craftsmanship is unhurried: the Hermit at work gives hands that know how and a head that doesn't rush. The main thing you make with those hands is your home: the Empress binds you through a nest that grows along with you. And it grows slowly, and the Hanged Man teaches you both to bear with the unfinished and to see it not as a mess but as a path.

You bought the old wooden house five years ago, and it still isn't finished: there's no floor upstairs, and the veranda has no railings.
