The Moon supports such a path — the fine instinct that binds you: the other senses tiredness before it shows in words. And you answer in the Lovers' language — with tenderness, direct and open.

For the third week the one who works for a charity comes home silent. The other asks nothing, but on Friday there are candles on the table, a favourite meal and a note: “You're doing something important. And I admire you.” The evening passes without a word about work, and on Monday the one serving the cause has strength again. **Your self-sacrifice at work doesn't go unnoticed: the other senses it and answers with tenderness.**

A silent sacrifice breeds guesswork. The one giving themselves to the work doesn't complain — and the other starts filling in the gaps: they've drifted away, stopped loving, are hiding something. The tired one feels misunderstood and goes even deeper into work. One endures, the other guesses, and both are unhappy in silence.

items.title: Changing for the other

captions.R: Work where you give a lot
captions.R1: An instinct that brings you close

items.meaning: You say honestly what you want from each other, and you're ready to change when the request comes without reproach.
text: One of you has the kind of work where you give a lot: the Hanged Man brings night shifts, service, sacrifices for the job. The Moon binds you — an instinct that tells you when the other is struggling, even if they say nothing. And the Devil makes your talk honest: what you want from each other, you say plainly, without reproach and without games.

For three years one of you has worked nights, and the other falls asleep alone. They kept quiet for a long time, then said plainly: “I want to fall asleep next to you. Not because that's how it should be, but because I miss you.” The one working nights promises nothing, but a couple of months later moves to day shifts, losing money. **For the other's sake you're ready to change, if they honestly say what they want.**

A readiness to change can become a demand to change. If one is used to giving way and the other to asking, requests multiply, sacrifices pile up, and the Moon whispers that love is measured in concessions. The wish to be close turns into a wish to hold on. The one who moved to day shifts looks at night vacancies more and more often.

items.title: Meaning instead of profit

captions.R: Serving a cause bigger than yourselves

items.meaning: A cause bigger than you doesn't compete with love: the other understands such a choice without long explanations.
text: At work you're ready to serve a cause bigger than yourselves: the Hanged Man gives a calling to help, to wait and to give more than you receive. Such a path can be borne if beside you is someone with the same view, and the World unites you through exactly that — a broad shared picture of life where money isn't the main thing. You hardly need to explain your choices to each other: the Hermit gives understanding without unnecessary words.

One of you leaves a big company for an international foundation that pays three times less and sends people where help is needed. Friends don't understand. The other says nothing, just packs a warm jumper into the suitcase and a book you both once loved. In the margin, a note: “I understand.” **You're ready to give up profit for meaning, because you see the world with the same breadth.**

A lofty meaning doesn't feed you if one pays the bill for it. The one serving brings home tiredness and a small salary, the one who stayed carries the household and says nothing — how can you argue with a good cause? Silent understanding turns into silent resentment. A village far away has been saved, and at home there's no money to fix the leaking tap.

items.title: Years without finds

captions.R1: A shared view of what matters

items.meaning: You serve work that's in no hurry to answer, and you can support each other through long, empty seasons.
text: At work you're ready to serve and wait: the Hanged Man leads to work where recognition comes late or not at all. A shared view of what matters helps you bear it — the World binds you through a philosophy in which success isn't the only measure. And the Moon tells you when to offer support: each senses when the other's patience is running out.

The sixth season of the dig, and again not a single significant find. The archaeologist comes home tanned and silent. The other doesn't ask “well, did you find anything?”. They put on the table the site plan sent in spring and say: “Show me where you dug. And where you'll dig next year.” At night the two of you mark new squares on the plan. **Years without finds don't become years of bitterness for you: you both know what you're digging for.**

You can wait for a find all your life. If service to the work bears no fruit and a shared view justifies any wait, the one waiting alongside starts to feel a hostage to someone else's dream. The Moon gives hints, but not all of them. The site plan is dotted with squares, and the family calendar holds not a single holiday for two.

items.title: A bridge under the change

captions.R1: A support that lets you take risks

items.meaning: One of you dares to change, the other builds a reliable bridge beneath it, and the decision ripens unhurried.
text: Big changes at work don't frighten you: Death in success closes one chapter and opens another — leaving a profession, the end of a long project, a fresh start. You can take the risk because there's something to lean on: the Emperor gives the couple reliability — a plan, order, the certainty that the other will back you up. And such decisions ripen as the Hermit's do: slowly, in silence, without pressure.

The decision to leave their profession ripens in one of you for six months. The other never hurries or dissuades them. But when “it's decided” is heard on a Sunday, a spreadsheet lands on the table: how many months you'll last on one salary, which expenses to put off, when to check that everything is going to plan. **Change isn't a leap into the void for you: one dares, and the other builds a bridge beneath them.**

The one who builds the bridge may start deciding where to walk on it. Support turns into control: deadlines, reports, “it was agreed” — and the one changing their life begins to feel led on a leash. Grievances go unspoken, decisions undiscussed. The spreadsheet on the fridge lays out someone else's new life month by month.

items.title: The key to a closed shop

captions.M: Guessing when to hold each other

items.meaning: You meet the end of a venture calmly: one keeps order, the other guesses when it's simply time for a hug.
text: You have to close ventures more than once: Death at work puts full stops where others drag things out to the last — a shop, a project, a profession. In such times there's something to lean on: the Emperor binds you through order, rules, reliability, in which even an ending goes to plan. And you live through grief quietly, and the Moon tells the other when it's time not to talk but simply to hold you.

The last day of the bookshop one of you has run for twelve years. From the morning the other sorts the paperwork, arranges for the shelves to be taken away, makes a list of who should get the remaining books. In the evening you lock the door together, and the owner holds the key in their hand for a long time. The other says nothing — just hugs them right there on the doorstep. **Grief isn't discussed in your couple; it's lived through side by side — in order and in silence.**

Order can become a way of not grieving. If an ending is at once turned into a to-do list, sadness goes underground and surfaces later — as irritation, sleepless nights, sudden tears. The one who keeps order doesn't let themselves stop. The shop key lies in a desk drawer, and each time either of you sees it, you quickly push the drawer shut.

items.title: A shared table in a new place

captions.R: Starting work from a clean slate
captions.R1: Moving side by side on your own paths

items.meaning: You're not afraid to start your work over, and the union holds because a home grows up around you wherever you are.
text: Your professional histories are full of sharp turns: Death closes one venture and lets you start another from a clean slate. The Chariot helps you stay together on the turns — moving side by side, each on their own path but heading the same way. And the Empress makes sure there's a home on the road: you can create comfort anywhere in a single evening.

A new city, a rented flat, nothing of your own but suitcases. On the very first evening one of you finds a tablecloth at the market, the other buys a lamp and a pie. By night the kitchen light is on, it smells of baking, and the rented place is already a little bit yours. In the morning each goes off to start their own thing. **Wherever you start over, the first thing you have is a shared table.**

The imbalance builds up in the one who makes the home each time. Changes come without a pause, the momentum leaves no time to look around, and the homemaker's strength goes into the home rather than their own growth. One starts a venture again, the other sets out the crockery again. The flats change, but one of you never got to settle into their own work.

items.title: A pause between chapters
items.meaning: After every closed chapter you don't rush straight on but give yourselves a pause and choose the road together.
text: You know how to put full stops at work: Death closes professions, projects, stages without long regrets. After that you travel on together — the Chariot binds you through movement, shared resolve, a readiness for a new road. But between the end and the beginning you always have a pause: the Hanged Man teaches you not to hurry and to look at the crossroads from the other side.

One partner's contract has ended, and by Monday there are already two new offers. The one used to racing is ready to sign. The other suggests something strange: “Let's not decide anything for a month. Let's just live.” The month goes on walks, books, long breakfasts. By its end it turns out neither offer is needed, but a third one nobody had thought of is. **Between an end and a beginning you leave a pause, and the new road turns out truer for it.**

A pause can drag on if the momentum is lost. A month turns into six, rest into bewilderment, and the other's patience into a quiet anxiety nobody mentions. The one who loves speed starts to dash about. The map of the new road has long lain on the table, and nobody dares set out on it.

items.title: The road after an ending

captions.R: Drawing a line and starting anew
captions.R1: Driving side by side, each after their own

items.meaning: Every ending is a reason for you to get in the car and drive side by side, each after their own dream.
text: Side by side, but each after their own — that's how you move through life, and the Chariot makes this movement your bond. There are plenty of stops on the way: Death at work regularly closes chapters — a job, a project, a whole stage. And behind every closed door you look for a wider horizon: the World gives you a habit, after an ending, of not sitting still but looking beyond your own town and country.

One partner's contract has ended, the other has long dreamed of a long holiday. You buy an old van and drive across half a continent with no route. Each has their own aims: one is writing a book about roads, the other photographs mountains. At night by the campfire you tell each other what you saw that day. **The end of one chapter is the start of a road for you, one you drive side by side.**

Taking to the road straight after an ending takes you away from grief but doesn't rid you of it. If every ending is drowned at once in new impressions, the sadness doesn't go anywhere — it follows you and breaks out as irritation. Each races after their own, and the talks by the fire get shorter. The horizons change every day, and what was left behind is never discussed.

items.title: New business card, same choice

captions.R1: Turns of fate shared by two

items.meaning: You change professions and lives, and the union holds because after every turn you choose each other again.
text: Your careers rarely run in a straight line: Death closes one venture and opens another — a change of profession, leaving a stable company, starting from scratch. The Wheel of Fortune lends these changes a sense of shared destiny: the turns happen to you together, and your meeting too feels no accident. And the Lovers ask one thing — after every change, say “yes” to each other once more.

Over dinner one of you announces: I want to leave the bank and train as a carpenter. A pause. The other says: “It's scary. But I'm curious to see the new you.” Then the talk turns to money, timing and what you'll have to give up for a year. You make the decision together, though only one will change their life. **Every change of work comes with a second choice for you — choosing each other anew.**

Change wears you out when one of you sets its rhythm. Decisions are made in the heat of the moment, the swings grow wider, and the one who holds on to the familiar is being remade for the new life. The other tires of getting used to a new person every couple of years and quietly stops asking. It is hard to live beside someone with a new business card every year if you don't know whether there's room on it for you.

items.title: I want more

captions.M: Owning up to a hunger for more

items.meaning: Your professions and lives change decisively, and every change begins with an honest talk between you.
text: Your professions change decisively: Death closes one line of work and opens another without long regrets. These turns are often lucky — the Wheel of Fortune binds you through a sense of shared luck that catches you at the crossroads. And every change begins with an honest admission: the Devil lets you say aloud “I want more” and not be ashamed of it.

For eight years one of you has been a teacher and loved it. But one evening they say: “I want to earn three times as much. And I want thousands to listen to me, not thirty.” The other doesn't wince: “Then let's look for where that's possible.” A couple of months later a chance acquaintance invites them to an online school, and the new life begins with the first webinar. **Changes in your couple begin with an honest “I want more”, and luck has caught that wish more than once.**

The wish for more has no built-in stop. If after every success you want still more, changes come without a breather, and luck starts to seem compulsory. The one who holds on to the familiar can't keep up and stays silent. You've had five professions already, and not once have you managed to stop and enjoy it.

items.title: A list for New Year's Eve
items.meaning: You accept change in your partner rather than demanding they stay the same — and let go of the outworn without scenes.
text: Death stands twice in your line, and that isn't gloomy: it's the knack of ending things in time. At work it closes chapters — projects, posts, professions you've outgrown. Between you it gives a rare quality: accepting change in your partner easily and not demanding they stay the same. And you say goodbye to the outworn the Hermit's way — without unnecessary words or scenes.

You spend New Year's Eve not at a table with guests but the two of you in the kitchen. Each has a slip of paper: what it's time to part with — a post, a grievance, a habit, a project. You read the slips to each other silently, passing them across the table in turn, then tear them into tiny pieces. In the morning both wake up lighter. **You know how to part with the outworn together, without drama, and so you have room to grow.**

If you let go of everything, nothing will be left to put down roots. A double Death loves change so much that it stops cherishing the constant: work, city, friends, habits change faster than you can get used to them. Saying that the other needs something to lean on isn't done. You always have a new life, and not one shared habit older than a year.

items.title: Curious about change
items.meaning: You change often and deeply, and the other notices the new before it's put into words, and meets it with interest.
text: Death appears twice for you, and both times it means change. At work it changes professions, projects, whole stages of life. Between you it gives a rare gift — accepting change in your partner and not demanding they stay the same. And the Moon helps you sense these changes: you notice the new in the other before they've had time to mention it.

In a year one of you has changed almost completely: left the bank for ceramics, grown their hair, stopped eating meat, started getting up at five. Friends cautiously ask the other whether it's hard. The other laughs: “It's interesting. I'm waiting to see who you'll become next.” And they're the first to notice when a new shape of bowl appears in the studio that the potter hasn't mentioned to anyone yet. **Change in your partner stirs curiosity in you, not fear.**

When everything changes, it's easy to lose sight of what stayed the same. If changes come without a breather, shared habits and landmarks dwindle, and the Moon starts whispering anxiety: what if the next change takes the other away altogether? Curiosity gives way to wariness. You're still waiting to see who the other will become, only more and more often with apprehension.

items.title: A garden where an end was

captions.M: Planting the new and tending it

items.meaning: After every ending at work you plant something new — in the garden, in the home, in each other.
text: Endings at work do happen to you: Death closes chapters, professions, projects. Collapses happen too — the Tower binds you through troubles you came through together and after which you hold on to each other all the tighter. And after every ending you do the same thing: the Empress teaches you to plant the new and tend it until it grows strong.

On the day one of you closed their workshop, you don't sit at home. You drive to a nursery and buy saplings: two apple trees, a cherry, a lilac bush. Until dark you dig holes by the house, muddy and tired, then sit on the porch with tea, looking at the thin twigs in the ground. In spring the cherry has its first blossom. **After every ending a garden begins in your couple: you plant something new where just now it was empty.**

A garden after every trouble can become the only thing you talk about. If every loss is buried in the earth along with saplings, grief goes unlived, and care becomes a way of not noticing the other's pain. Changes come, collapses happen, and the garden keeps growing. You have twelve apple trees now, and for each you remember which trouble it covered over.

items.title: Not an end but a pause

captions.R1: Storms after which you're still together
captions.M: Seeing it all from another angle

items.meaning: You meet endings and collapses together and can see in them a pause before something new.
text: Your work knows real endings: Death in success closes a venture completely to make room for the new. The Tower helps you live through it — the shared memory of storms after which you found yourselves together rather than apart. You have a special way of talking about hard things, like the Hanged Man: turn the situation upside down and look at it from the other side, where an end turns out to be a pause.

One morning the one who has worked for ten years without holidays can't make themselves get up for work. The other doesn't panic or try to persuade. Sits down beside them: “Let's look at it differently. This isn't a collapse, it's the pause you haven't had in ten years.” The resignation letter is written that same day, and six months of quiet become a new start. **You know how to turn the hardest things upside down: to see a pause in an end, and a beginning in the pause.**

A habit of enduring easily grows into a habit of suffering. After many storms it's easy to start taking pride in endurance and waiting for the next; the upside-down view becomes an excuse: “that's how it's meant to be, we're used to it.” Accusations hide behind patience. You recall the hard past more often than the good present.

items.title: A map wider than the end

captions.M: Looking for a way out beyond the horizon

items.meaning: When your profession was no longer needed at home, you learned a language and went where it was needed.
text: Endings at work don't frighten you: Death closes chapters — a profession, an industry, a stage — to make room for the new. The Tower helps you live through them, binding you through shared collapses: together you've climbed out from under the rubble more than once. And you look for a way out widely, as the World teaches: beyond your town, your country, your usual ideas.

The industry you've both worked in for fifteen years winds down within a year: plants close, specialists are needed by no one. In the evening you spread a map on the table and sit silent for a long time. Then one puts a finger on a country where your profession is needed like air. “We don't know the language.” — “We'll learn it.” For six months you study the language in the evenings, then move. **The end of a whole industry wasn't the end of your road: you simply looked at the map more widely.**

When everything starts over too often, no roots remain. If every collapse is solved by moving, the old life isn't mourned, the new one doesn't take root, and grievances built up in crises travel along with you. Moving becomes the answer to any trouble. In the new place you're spreading out the map again, though the boxes aren't unpacked yet.

items.title: A fresh start as a celebration

captions.R: Starting over with a clean slate

items.meaning: Your professions change but your joy doesn't: you meet every new beginning together, and with a celebration.
text: You have to start from a clean slate more than once: Death closes old ventures and opens new ones, sometimes quite unlike the last. It doesn't become frightening — between you is the Sun, warmth and the knack of celebrating life in any of its chapters. “I'm proud of you” and “I love you” are said plainly and often in your couple: the Lovers bid it so.

The first day at a new job after a change of profession. The one starting is so nervous they can't eat breakfast. In their jacket pocket they find a note: “You glow when you start something. I'm proud of you.” In the evening there are balloons at home, a cake and friends gathered to mark “the first day of a new life”. **Every new start is a celebration for you, not a jump into cold water.**

A festival of change can tire whoever loves constancy. The one who starts again and again gets used to applause, while the other claps and doesn't notice they haven't started anything themselves for a long time. The Sun shines on one, pride is voiced in one direction. The other rejoices at the partner's latest beginning, while standing still themselves.

items.title: A joke instead of panic
items.meaning: You meet change as friends and fellow travellers, and each thinks the most serious things over alone first.
text: Your working paths change sharply: Death in success closes one chapter and opens another — a change of profession, city, circle. The Fool keeps you from being frightened by such changes, making you friends and fellow travellers: with humour, lightness, readiness to start from scratch. And serious things you think over like the Hermit — each alone first, in silence, and only then together.

Over dinner comes: “I want to give up law and train as a chef.” The other laughs till they cry, then says: “Great, I'll have a personal chef. Think about it for a week, and if you don't change your mind — go for it.” For a week you both think in silence, each your own thoughts, and on Sunday you send in the application for the course. **Change comes easily to you, because the other meets it not with fear but with a joke and quiet.**

Ease with change can hide flight. When things are hard, it's simpler to drop everything and start again than to sort things out; a joke relieves the tension, but it relieves you of the conversation too. Each thinks things over alone and shares conclusions less and less. Every new life starts with a clean slate, and the old debts are handed down into it.

items.title: Weighed twice
items.meaning: You live without a race, by shared views, and weigh every decision twice — first apart, then together.
text: You don't like chasing other people's successes: Temperance leads to fulfilment without strain — work within your strength, income within your means, time left over for living. You take the measure for this not from outside but from a shared view of what is right: the Hierophant unites you through customs and a habit of learning from each other. And important matters are settled by the Hermit's law — first separately, then together.

An offer to head a department comes to one of you on a Monday. You don't answer straight away: for a week each carries the question within. On Saturday, on your usual long walk through the same park, you compare conclusions — and they match almost word for word. The post can wait a year; peace matters more right now. **Your decisions are weighed twice, alone and together, so you rarely regret them.**

Evenness sets hard when nobody raises the difficult thing first. Discontent is hidden, you cling to the established order, think everything over separately and never bring it to each other. Life goes on properly and quietly, but without a living voice. The clock in the sitting room ticks the same on a happy evening and an anxious one, and you can no longer tell the time by it.

items.title: Tea at nine

captions.R: A steady path without a race

items.meaning: Your calm path and shared customs rest on a feel for each other, not on rules.
text: You have many customs, and the Hierophant makes them what binds you: shared views, habits, little rituals by which friends know you. You leave time for them because Temperance at work leads you on a steady path, without a race or overtime. And the customs rest on instinct: the Moon tells you when to keep a ritual and when to drop it, because today the other needs something else.

Every evening at nine you have tea — the same blend, the same cups, a chat about the day. But today the other comes home from work and goes silently into the room. The first doesn't put the kettle on. They bring a blanket and sit beside them in the dark. Tea will be tomorrow; today what's needed is quiet. **Your customs rest on instinct: you know when to keep a tradition and when to drop it for the other's sake.**

A custom is a handy stand-in for a conversation. If the ritual is kept at any cost, it's easy to hide behind it what's hard to talk about: the tea is drunk, “how was your day” is asked, and the real answer is never heard. Instinct says something's wrong, but calm is dearer. You drink your tea at nine faithfully, and it has long tasted of silence.

items.title: Gentle justice

captions.R: Growing at a measured pace, without envy

items.meaning: You share the load fairly and gently, like bread at the family table — no scales, no tally.
text: Your careers move at a measured pace: Temperance gives growth without envy or racing. To keep anyone from pulling for two, Justice works between you — the certainty that the load is shared fairly. And this calculation doesn't turn dry thanks to the Empress: your love is expressed through comfort, good food and a home always ready to take in whoever is tired.

On Sunday you cook for the week ahead: one chops, the other minds the pots, an old concert plays on the radio. One had a hard week and, without a word, gets the lighter jobs — peeling potatoes, filling the containers. Nobody writes it down or brings it up later. **Your justice is gentle: the tired one gets less to do, and it never becomes a debt.**

Equality wobbles when only one of you grows. The one who “fell behind” starts being quietly compared with the first, contributions start being weighed, and they talk themselves out of protesting for the sake of peace. The shared home grows and gets lovelier, while one of its owners feels like a guest in it.

items.title: Giving way by rota
items.meaning: You take the big career steps in turn: today one waits, tomorrow the other.
text: Your careers grow without spurts: Temperance gives calm growth that leaves time for life too. You share this growth fairly — Justice binds you through a rule of turns, where nobody gets ahead at the other's expense. And the Hanged Man helps you wait your turn: patiently, without resentment and without counting who waited longer.

Two years ago the promotion went to one of you, and the other waited, taking on more at home. This year it's the other's turn: they're going off to do a master's degree, while the first turns down business trips and takes over the household. Friends wonder how you split it all. You shrug: “By turns. We wrote it down.” **Giving way goes by turns in your couple, and nobody forgets whose turn it is.**

A rota of concessions can turn into a ledger of sacrifices. If every concession is written down, it stops being a gift and becomes a debt the other must repay. Temperance muffles resentment, Justice weighs it. The rota book balances perfectly, and not one page holds a heartfelt “congratulations, this is yours”.

items.title: Taking turns, half and half

captions.M: Sharing the world half and half

items.meaning: An even path and honesty in every clause give you a world with no boss and no subordinate.
text: You've nowhere to hurry: Temperance leads you both along an even path, often in similar professions and at similar levels. In your couple sharing is done honestly — Justice sets a rule with no boss and no subordinate. And you share the big world half and half too: the World at the point of common language makes the rules of your life shared, free and devised by both.

You choose holidays in turn: this year one decides, next year the other. This time it's the turn of the one who loves mountains, and the other, a lover of the sea, goes without a single sigh. But on the way back they're already discussing their choice for next year and showing photos of the island you'll go to. **Your justice is simple: take turns and split it half and half — and so there are hardly any arguments.**

Taking turns can kill spontaneity. If everything is divided by the rules, an unexpected “let's do it right now” starts to look like a breach of the agreement, and balance like boredom. Wishes adapt to the schedule. Holidays to a schedule, dinners to a schedule, and even a surprise has to be agreed in advance.

items.title: Growing without overtaking
items.meaning: There's no race between you: you grow level, and one partner's gentle strength supports the other rather than presses.
text: Overtaking each other doesn't interest you. Temperance keeps both your careers steady, often in similar fields, with a balance between work and home. The fire doesn't leave this evenness, because Strength sits between you: one charges the other without pressing, and tension goes into closeness rather than argument. Where to direct the shared charge is decided by the Lovers — with a direct “I want” and a choice made together.

A recruiter calls: a post with a noticeably higher salary — and working Saturdays. You count more than the money: “Do we have enough? And what do we want from this year?” You decide to say no, keep your Saturdays, and ask for a rise where you are. It comes by spring, without the Saturdays. **You grow more slowly than you could, but never at each other's expense.**

Evenness rests on someone's concessions more often than it seems. One always agrees, smooths things over, puts their own plans off, and the other's gentle strength quietly turns into pressure. Pressure is called care, giving way is called love, and it's hard to argue with such words. From outside the scales hang perfectly level, only one pan is always being held down by hand.

items.title: Saying the bold thing
items.meaning: Calm doesn't stop you dreaming daringly: beside each other you dare what you long kept quiet about.
text: Your life is steady: Temperance at work gives calm growth, stability, a reserve for a rainy day. But steady doesn't mean bland — Strength binds you through energy you share and courage you give each other. And the Devil makes your conversations honest: sooner or later your boldest wish gets said aloud.

For twelve years one of you has worked as an accountant, and everyone's sure they like it. One evening, staring at the ceiling, they say: “I want to open my own brewery. I want it so much it's embarrassing.” The other sits down beside them: “It's not embarrassing. We have a year's reserve. Let's try.” By spring the first batch is being bottled in the garage. **A bold wish doesn't stay in your head: the other gives you strength to say it, and your steady life the reserve for the risk.**

Calm muffles a wish but doesn't cancel it. An “I want” put off for years for stability's sake comes back as irritation, a craving for small pleasures, secret spending. Strength turns into pressure, Temperance into boredom. The rainy-day reserve grows, and the brewery remains talk after a glass of wine.

items.title: A still pond
items.meaning: Your work, rhythm and quiet are shared, and it matters that this evenness leaves room for hard conversations.
text: Temperance sets both your careers and your relationship. At work it gives level growth: often similar professions, similar standing, work without racing or envy. Between you it connects through a shared rhythm — calm, without sharp swings, with the knack of settling things by talking rather than quarrelling. The Hermit adds quiet: you're happy being silent together, and the silence between you is rest, not coldness.

Wednesday evening. You both got home from work at the same time, as nearly always, had supper, and now each is in their own armchair with a book. In two hours perhaps ten sentences have been said, all about trivial things. But when one gets up to put the kettle on, the other, without looking up, holds out their cup. **You grow level, and the silence between you is rest, not coldness.**

Still water grows weeds. Two calm people easily stop talking about what worries them: one gives way so as not to disturb the peace, the other doesn't ask so as not to cause worry. Passion turns into habit, and one evening it's unclear why you're together, beyond its being convenient. The pond by the house is pretty and quiet, only nobody has swum in it for a long time.

items.title: Heard in the silence

captions.R: A steady path in similar work

items.meaning: You live to one calm rhythm and sense when, in that quiet, the other needs to talk.
text: You have twice the usual Temperance: at work it gives a steady path, often in similar professions; between you, a shared calm rhythm where storms hardly ever happen. In such quiet it's easy to overlook what matters, but you have the Moon: a fine instinct that catches the slightest change in the other's mood.

An ordinary evening, tea, books. The other notices the first turning the same page for the third time and not once smiling at a joke in the series. Asking nothing, they close their book and say: “Let's go for a walk.” On the second lap round the block, a conversation begins about what has been sitting inside all evening. **Your silence isn't cold: in it you can hear when the other needs to talk.**

Still water and moonlight together lull you to sleep. If calm becomes the main thing, hard things stop being talked about, and instinct starts running idle: it notices but doesn't dare ask. One gives way so as not to disturb, the other stays silent so as not to break the peace. Walks round the block happen less and less, and pages get turned over more and more.

items.title: Watercolours in a café
items.meaning: Watercolours from a “just for me” folder reached a café's walls, because the other believed in them before the artist did.
text: You work calmly and without strain: Temperance gives a steady path that leaves time for life. That time goes on what binds you — the Star, a belief in each other's quiet talent that nobody outside sees. And you nurture it as the Empress does: carefully, warmly, without hurrying or demanding.

In the evenings one of you paints watercolours and hides them in a folder: “just for me”. The other secretly picks the twenty best, orders frames and makes an arrangement with the little café on the corner. On Saturday you go there for breakfast, and the artist sees their work on the walls. First they're cross, then they blush, and by evening one of the paintings has sold. **One partner's quiet talent grows in warmth: the other doesn't hurry it but nurtures it, like a flower.**

Care can become a hothouse nobody is let out of. If you look after someone's talent for too long, they get used to having everything done for them, and the carer to deciding what to show the world. Temperance fears risk, the Star criticism. The watercolours hang in the corner café, and they've never gone beyond that corner.

items.title: A sailboat on the screensaver
items.meaning: You share one dream between you, and you choose the road to it without debts or haste.
text: Your careers are even: Temperance gives work within your strength, income within your means and a life without racing. Above this evenness shines the Star — a shared dream that gives the calm work its meaning. You prefer to reach it patiently. The Hanged Man teaches you to wait, look at things from another side and not force your way to the dream before you're both ready.

You share one dream — a sailboat of your own and summers on the water. One of you tires of waiting and suggests taking out a loan right now. The other doesn't argue but asks: “Let's look at it from the other side. One more year and we'll buy it debt-free, and sleep soundly.” The first thinks overnight and agrees. **You neither rush your dream nor bury it: you grow it patiently, looking at it through both your eyes.**

Patience quietly turns into an eternal “later”. An even life draws you in, the dream is put off another year, then another, and each gives way to the other without noticing there's nothing left to give way on. The Star dims from waiting. The laptop screensaver has shown the same sailboat for three years, and the calendar has no date under it.

items.title: The steady light of a dream

captions.R1: A dream that shines for both
captions.M: Thinking of a world without borders

items.meaning: Calm work gives you time and money for a shared dream, and the dream gives calm work its meaning.
text: You work calmly: Temperance gives a path without strain, income within your means, time for life. Above this calm life the Star shines for you — a shared dream that inspires you both. And the dream is broad: the World sets the scale of your conversations — about travel, other countries, a life without borders.

A map of the world hangs over your table, and once a year you stick a new flag in it — the country you'll go to. You save a little at a time, without sacrifices, from every pay packet. This autumn it's the twelfth flag: Japan, which you saved two years for. On the plane one says: “You know, I thought we'd never get there.” **Your dream of the wide world doesn't blaze like a fire but shines steadily — and that's why it comes true.**

A steady light risks never becoming a flame. If you save a little at a time and go only where it's safe, the biggest dream — to leave for a long time, to live in another country — stays on the map. Temperance fears risk, the Star is shy of wanting more. There are more and more flags on the map, and the main one has never been put in.

items.title: A slip that weighs less

captions.R1: Family and all you've lived through together

items.meaning: Calm life, family and years lived together weigh more for you than any mistake, and “I love you” comes before reproach.
text: Work doesn't eat up your life: Temperance gives calm growth and time for what matters more than a career. What matters more for you is Judgement — family, shared events, all you've lived through together, which binds the union tighter every year. And you know how to forgive the way the Lovers teach: openly, with a direct “I love you”, without hidden scores.

Because of a crunch at work one of you forgets the other's aunt's milestone birthday — the one day they'd been asked to remember. In the evening they come home contrite. The other sighs, then hugs them: “So what. You remember everything else for years. Tomorrow we'll go together and you can apologise with a cake.” **Mistakes are forgiven quickly in your couple, because all you've lived through together matters more than one slip.**

Forgiving is easy if slips don't pile up in silence. But calm likes to smooth things over, and small grievances are forgiven aloud while staying inside. Relatives add their opinion, and forgiveness becomes a family matter discussed behind your backs. Every slip is forgiven, but each of you knows the list by heart.

items.title: A home chosen by two

captions.R: A grip that brings in money
captions.R1: A shared home and its abundance

items.meaning: Money won by grip settles in your home, where every door handle was chosen by both of you.
text: You know how to earn: the Devil in success gives grip, a hunger for high income and readiness for hard but generously paid work. Where that money goes is decided by the Empress, who connects you — into the home, the garden, children, everything that grows. And you decide in the Lovers' language: together, aloud, and even in small things nobody chooses for the other.

A year of hard work — and at last a house of your own. You walk through empty rooms with paint samples and argue over every wall: “This one's too cold”, “And that one's like a hospital.” Choosing the colour of the kitchen handles takes three evenings. Now guests say the house looks like both of you at once. **Big money turns not into status for you but into a home where every detail was chosen by two.**

Money won by grip easily becomes a leash: whoever earns more starts to see the house as theirs and to decide what goes in it, while the other becomes dependent — can't buy without asking, can't move things without permission. Wishes are no longer spoken plainly; they're begged for. The house is completely finished, and one of its owners lives in it like a tenant.

items.title: Wanting luxury honestly
items.meaning: A flat overlooking the river, wine on Fridays, a grand piano — you both want the good life and don't hide it.
text: There are two Devils in your couple: one at work gives grip, a pull towards big money and a readiness to work hard for it; the other in conversation gives the nerve to own up to wishes without shame. The Empress binds you: an abundant, beautiful, warm home into which everything you earn flows.

Over dinner one of you says: “I want a flat overlooking the river, good wine on Fridays and a holiday at least twice a year. Yes, it's a lot.” The other laughs: “I want the same. And a grand piano.” You don't pretend that little will do, but sit down and work out how much you need to earn and how. Now the piano stands by the window overlooking the river. **Luxury isn't shameful in your couple: you both want it, say so honestly and earn it honestly.**

If the wish for luxury is stronger than everything else, the home turns into an exhibition. Grip demands more, the Empress's generosity more beautiful, and the wish to possess moves from things to a person: money becomes a way to hold and decide. Talk about wishes comes down to purchases. The piano stands by the window, and there's no time to play it.

items.title: Grip and a quiet “I love you”
items.meaning: Money and influence come easily to you, and love holds because you speak of your wishes quietly but hold nothing back.
text: Your ambitions are serious: the Devil loves big money, influence, hard but generously paid work. To keep all this from becoming the main thing, you need a counterweight, and you have one: the Lovers — the choice of each other itself, made in earnest, with open eyes. You prefer to speak of it under your breath, in the Hermit's language: the most important things in private, without witnesses, and not always in words.

The quarter was hard, the bonus big. The one who got it could have brought home an expensive present, but instead books two days in a cabin with no signal. There, by the stove, the other finally says what they've kept inside for six months: what they really want. Nobody interrupts. **Money and influence don't become a leash for you as long as wishes are spoken quietly but honestly.**

A larger income gives one of you leverage, and decisions about your shared life are more and more theirs. The other responds with silence and an unspoken grievance, and the first tries to smooth over the chill with purchases. An expensive present lies where a conversation should have been, and the presents in the house keep multiplying.

items.title: Without the armour
items.meaning: At work you wear armour, but at home it comes off: the other sees what you really want.
text: Love in your couple is chosen in earnest, and the Lovers make that choice the centre of the pair. The centre is needed, because the Devil at work gives grip and high stakes, and with them armour that's hard to take off in the evening. The Moon helps it come off: the other senses what's hidden and sees under the armour what colleagues don't.

The one leading a big deal comes home and cheerfully talks about the negotiations: all's well, the numbers are growing. The other listens, then asks quietly: “Now tell me what you really want.” A long pause. “I want this to be over, and for us to go to the sea.” Tickets to the coast are bought that same night. **Through the business armour the other senses what their partner really wants, and loves them without it.**

Armour grows on fast. If at home too you have to keep up appearances, the other stops guessing and starts suspecting; grip turns into control, love into bargaining. Work secrets become the couple's secrets. The armour no longer comes off even at night, and there's nothing left underneath to guess.

items.title: Time you didn't sell

captions.R1: A long talk about what matters

items.meaning: You earn a lot, and closeness holds because expensive presents never stand in for a conversation.
text: The stakes at work are high for you: the Devil gives grip, a craving for big money and a readiness to work hard for it. The counterweight is the Hermit: he connects you through long talks about what matters and the ability to be together in silence. And you show care the Empress's way, through things you can touch — a present, a well-kept home, a full fridge.

After handing in a big project, the one who carried it comes home not with a shopping bag but with a printout: two days at a lake, phones in a drawer. There you barely leave the cabin and talk as you haven't since spring. You drive back in silence, but it's a good silence. **The most precious thing you bring home is the time you didn't sell to work.**

Care cheapens when it starts being bought. Work without days off, attention replaced by presents, conversations put off until “things get easier” — and each withdraws deeper into their own. The house is furnished, the fridge full, the presents expensive. Such a house has everything except the people who live in it.

items.title: A decision through others' eyes
items.meaning: Your decisions are heavy and your talks nocturnal: the other helps you see those they'll affect.
text: You have a lot of power at work: the Devil gives influence, money and decisions other people depend on. Such a load can easily harden a person, but you have your night-time talks — the Hermit connects you through depth, the ability to talk about what matters without witnesses. And the Hanged Man suggests how to talk: turn the decision over and look at it through the eyes of those it will affect.

Tomorrow one of you must make twenty people redundant. At night they can't sleep and go into the kitchen. The other follows, puts the kettle on and asks: “Tell me who these people are.” An hour goes on talking about each one. In the morning the list looks different: three are found places in other departments, the rest get good references. **Power at work doesn't harden you, because at home there's someone who helps you see the decision through others' eyes.**

When there's a lot of power, quiet at home is easily taken for agreement. The one used to deciding stops asking, and the one who can see the other side tires of showing it and silently gives way. Deep talks become rare, sacrifices habitual. Decisions are still made at night in the kitchen, only the other is no longer invited.

items.title: How much do we need
items.meaning: You earn well and know your figure for “enough”, beyond which freedom begins.
text: Your appetite for money is sound and large: the Devil at work gives grip, zest, a readiness to work hard for good income. The Hermit balances it — a shared wisdom and a habit of asking yourselves awkward questions. And your goal isn't wealth for its own sake but freedom: the World turns money into space, time and the right to choose how to live.

The year has been profitable, and the one who earns more is already planning the next dash. On an evening walk the other asks one question: “How much do we really need? To stop chasing.” You count for a long time — a house, trips, a reserve — and arrive at a figure. It's written on a sheet and stuck on the fridge: when you reach it, you stop. **Your appetite for money is balanced by a question you ask each other in quiet: how much do we really need?**

The figure for “enough” can keep moving away for ever. Grip dislikes stop signals, and when little is left to reach the goal, a new one appears; wise talks are put off, and the freedom it was all for stays somewhere ahead. The sheet on the fridge has been rewritten four times already, and each time the figure is bigger.

items.title: A refusal worth more than money

captions.R: High stakes and a strong grip
captions.R1: Giving something up for the other

items.meaning: Grip and big money never outrank love for you: you decide on every major contract together.
text: Your grip is strong: the Devil in success pulls towards big money, influence, hard and highly paid work. The Hanged Man helps you stay in this without losing each other: you're connected by a readiness to give something up for the other and see the situation through their eyes. And in the Lovers' language wishes are named honestly, and the choice is made anew each time.

On the table lies a contract many dream of: three times the money, but you'll have to live at work. The other says plainly: “I want you, not your salary. But it's your call.” The contract goes to someone else. Back in the old job, the one who turned it down soon gets a promotion, and the evenings are still yours. **You know how to give up the surplus for each other's sake, and that refusal binds you more firmly than money.**

Money and sacrifice are a dangerous mix. The one who earns starts buying the right to decide, the one who gave way demands gratitude for their sacrifice, and love becomes something to trade. Wishes are no longer named directly; they're pursued by roundabout ways. One pays for everything, the other gives thanks for everything, and both consider themselves in debt.

items.title: Two grips side by side
items.meaning: Big deals fire you up, and so do you each other, while your most secret “I want” is spoken only in private.
text: The Devil is in both your work and your feelings. At work he gives the thrill of big deals, a pull towards money and influence, a readiness to work flat out for results. Between you he turns into passion: an attraction that doesn't cool for years, and a shared hunger for more. And the most secret things you tell each other in private — the Hermit makes your language quiet and very personal.

The deal you've both worked on for six months closes at eleven at night. Instead of a restaurant — an empty office, a bottle from the corner shop and a view of the city at night. At some point one says what they hadn't admitted even to themselves: “It's not enough. I want more.” The other laughs: “Me too. But let's want it together.” **Your pull to each other and your pull to big work feed each other, as long as neither becomes a chain.**

Two grips side by side squeeze each other too. The wish to possess moves from business to the person: where were you, how much did you spend, who did you talk to. Money and status become ways to hold on, and the secrets you shared become leverage in an argument. The keys to the house, the car and the accounts hang on one key ring, and it's always in the same pocket.

items.title: A look across the table
items.meaning: In negotiations you understand each other from a look, and at home that look means something else entirely.
text: The Devil works on two fronts for you: at work he gives power, big deals, the thrill of high stakes; between you, an attraction that doesn't fade over the years. You understand each other through signals: the Moon makes your language subtle, almost invisible to outsiders — a look, a pause, a raised eyebrow.

You negotiate as a pair, like business partners. Across the table is a difficult client, and at some point one of you raises an eyebrow, barely noticeably. The other instantly changes tactics and calls a pause. The deal closes on your terms. In the evening, in the lift, the same look means something else entirely, and you ride home in silence, holding hands. **The thrill of the deal and your thrill for each other feed one another, and you understand it all from a single look.**

Strong attraction and secret signals can become a trap. If everything is settled with looks, things unsaid pile up, and the wish to possess moves from deals to a person: who called whom, why were you late. The Moon suggests suspicions, the Devil control. A look across the table is enough for a deal, but at home words would be more honest.

items.title: A secret present

captions.R1: A mystery that draws you in

items.meaning: You love secretly preparing for each other what the other only dreamed of, and you don't spare money for it.
text: The stakes at work are high for you: the Devil gives grip, a taste for risk, income that allows a lot. The Moon binds you — mystery, things left unsaid that draw you in, and the ability to guess the other's dreams. And you love spoiling as the Empress does: generously, lavishly, with surprises prepared for months.

For six months one of you secretly saves and arranges: a violin maker, a contact at a music college, a date. On their birthday the other gets an envelope with an address. At the workshop a violin made for them awaits, and a place on lessons — though they only once, years ago, let slip that they'd dreamed of playing. **Your surprises are thought out to the last detail: the other secretly prepares what you only dreamed of.**

Where there are many surprises, real secrets appear too. Secret spending becomes a habit, money a way to impress and hold on, and the Moon confuses a mystery with a secret. The one being spoiled starts to feel obliged. The surprises are as lavish as ever, and about what they cost and where the money comes from you stay silent.

items.title: Waiting and coming back
items.meaning: One partner's closed-door deals don't break your trust: they tell their worst fears to the one who waited.
text: The stakes at work are high for you: the Devil brings power, big money and dealings you can't always talk about. Between you is the Moon — a secret attraction, understanding without words, a shared world closed to outsiders. And you talk about hard things like the Hanged Man: patiently, able to wait and look at the situation from the other side.

The one who works on confidential deals is barely home for a week and can't say what they're doing. The other doesn't pry. When the deal closes, the first comes home at night, sits on the edge of the bed and tells all they can — including what they were afraid of. The other listens until dawn. **Work secrets don't become the couple's secrets, because the other knows how to wait and the first how to come back.**

Where there are many secrets, it's easy to start manipulating. Knowing each other's weaknesses becomes a lever, waiting a way to play on pity, and attraction a convenient leash. The Moon throws up suspicion, the Devil a wish to control. Each knows things about the other that could be used, and both remember it.

items.title: Plans whispered at night
items.meaning: You first whisper your boldest plans to each other at night, then build them on a grand scale.
text: Your boldest plans are born at night: the Moon binds you through shared secret dreams, fantasies nobody but you knows about. You know how to build them, since the Devil at work gives grip, a pull towards big money and the nerve for high stakes. And the World sets the scale: you're used to thinking not about the next street but about whole countries.

Two in the morning. You lie in the dark, and one whispers: “What if we bought that crumbling hotel on the coast? Restored it, made it the best on the whole shore.” The other is silent for a minute, then whispers back: “And opened another in the mountains.” In the morning you laugh at your night-time plans, and a week later you're driving to view the hotel. **Your big stakes are born of shared fantasies that nobody but you knows about.**

Dreams of the big can drift into fantasy. If night-time plans gather ever new details but aren't tested against figures by day, grip turns into a gamble and scale into chasing a mirage. What's private becomes a secret from the other. You already have five coastal hotels in your dreams, and one big loan at the bank.

items.title: Money turned into roads

captions.R1: A shared philosophy and the road

items.meaning: You earn with zest and spend on journeys after which you see the world the same way.
text: You earn with zest: the Devil in success gives a pull towards big money, grip and readiness for hard but generously paid work. You spend it on what unites you — on the World: roads, new countries, experiences after which you look at life in a similar way. And your main choice is in the Lovers' language: each other, not the figures in a report.

The annual bonus arrives in December. You spread a map on the floor and choose not a car or a renovation but a route: a month in the mountains you've long meant to visit. On the last night, at a pass, one says: “This is what all the work is for — not the money, but us, here.” **Money turns into roads for you, and roads into a shared view of life.**

Big money easily becomes a goal in itself. The grip demands more, there's never time for the road, and a rare trip becomes a display of what you can afford. The wish to possess moves from things to the person. The holiday has been put off for the third year — first you have to earn a better one.

items.title: A plan on the day of collapse

captions.R: Standing firm after a sudden blow
captions.M: Saying “I love you” on a hard day

items.meaning: You meet sudden blows at work together: one holds the plan, the other the words of love, and the walls hold.
text: Blows at work come to you without warning: the Tower in success can bring down a business, a post, an agreement a whole year rested on. The Emperor helps you stand firm — the reliability between you: a plan, order, the feeling that the other has your back. And to keep reliability from turning cold, there are the Lovers: on a hard day you aren't shy of saying the warmest things to each other.

One partner's business collapses within a week: a partner pulled out of the project and took the clients. That evening the other sits beside them with a notebook and calmly lays out three months: what we live on, whom we call, what we sell. And on the last page, under the figures, writes: “And remember that I love you, even bankrupt.” **When one partner's work collapses, the other builds walls of plans and calm around you both.**

Protection easily turns into guardianship. The one holding the plan starts deciding for two, irritation after the blow breaks out as orders, and words of love are heard less and less, giving way to instructions. The other feels not like a partner but a ward. The fortress is splendidly built, only one person decides who may leave it.

items.title: A fear named aloud

captions.M: Owning up to fear and desire

items.meaning: After collapses you want to keep everything under control, and you honestly tell each other so.
text: You've already lived through wrecks at work: the Tower brings down income, a post, plans — suddenly and without asking. After that you want support, and the Emperor binds you through exactly that: order, protection, a plan for a rainy day. And the Devil gives you honesty: the shameful — fear and the wish to control everything — can be spoken aloud between you.

A year has passed since one partner's business collapsed, and the other notices them checking the accounts every evening and getting angry at any unplanned expense. Instead of a row, the other asks: “Are you afraid it'll all collapse again?” A long pause. “Yes. And I want to hold everything in my hands, even you.” You laugh, and the laughter takes away half the fear. **Fear after a collapse doesn't turn into secret control in your couple: it's spoken aloud.**

Protection against new troubles easily becomes a cage. If fear isn't named, it hides behind rules, order turns into surveillance, and the wish to hold everything in your hands into a wish to hold your partner. Rows flare up over trifles. The home is protected from every trouble but one: it has grown cramped.

items.title: Getting up after the collapse

captions.M: Waiting out the storm in quiet

items.meaning: Sudden collapses at work don't break you: you absorb the blow in silence and set off again together.
text: Your work sometimes collapses without warning: the Tower brings down a post, a project or a whole industry in a day. After such a blow many couples get stuck in the ruins, but the Chariot leads you out — a habit of moving even when the road isn't yet visible, and moving side by side, though each on their own path. But you don't set off at once. First you need quiet: the Hermit gives you both time to understand what happened, without panic or unnecessary words.

The morning after the redundancy. The pass is handed in, the laptop too, and the one made redundant goes for a long run. The other doesn't call every half hour or send job listings. In the evening there's a sheet on the table divided in two: “what I'll do” and “what you'll do”. A week later each has their own column of tasks, and both lead the same way. **A collapse isn't the end of the road for you: after a pause for quiet, you set off again.**

After a blow it's easy to drive off in different directions. Irritation looks for an outlet and is taken out on the one nearest; one throws themselves into the first job that comes along, just not to stand still, the other withdraws and stops sharing. Each drives their own cart, and at the first fork they part — not because of a quarrel, but because nobody asked which way the other was turning.

items.title: Turning by instinct
items.meaning: A collapse at work is a reason for you to set off, and your shared instinct tells you which way to turn.
text: Blows at work come to you without warning: the Tower brings down a project, a post, an agreement in a single day. You don't know how to stand among ruins — the Chariot binds you through a habit of moving on together, at once, even without knowing exactly where. Where — the Moon often suggests: after a blow you make decisions by instinct and are surprisingly often right.

One partner's start-up closes suddenly: the investor has pulled out. Three days later you're already in the car with no particular destination. At a fork the other says: “Right. I don't know why.” Right leads to a small town where in a café you get talking to the owner of the local printing works, who's looking for exactly that kind of person. **After a blow you don't stand still but set off — and your shared instinct suggests the direction.**

After a blow instinct can speak in the voice of fear. If every decision is made by instinct, anxiety easily passes itself off as intuition, and movement as flight. Grievances built up in the crisis remain unspoken. You turn right, then left, and no longer remember what you were driving away from.

items.title: A pie for the neighbours

captions.R1: Luck that comes to you both
captions.M: Keeping the home warm in a storm

items.meaning: You wait out sudden collapses at work in a warm home, and that's exactly where luck finds you.
text: Your work never lets you get bored: the Tower in success brings sudden turns — closed projects, a change of management, an unexpected departure. But not everything collapses: the Wheel of Fortune holds you — the feeling that luck comes to the two of you and that after a slump a rise is sure to follow. And the Empress helps you wait for it — a language of warmth you speak in good weeks and bad: the home stays cosy, the table laid, the doors open.

A call on Friday: the project is closed, the team disbanded. On Saturday you bake a pie for the neighbours anyway, because you promised long ago to have them round for tea. At the table the neighbour mentions in passing that his department is looking for someone — and two weeks later the jobless one has a new pass. **Luck finds you where you keep on living, rather than waiting for it at a closed door.**

After a couple of collapses it's easy to start waiting for the next. The habit of preparing for the worst turns care into anxiety: stockpile, economise, don't risk, don't invite guests — what if it happens again. The one who brings in the income feels like the only support, and every setback at work becomes a family catastrophe. The larder is stocked for a year, and every conversation is a forecast of the worst.

items.title: Temporary means temporary
items.meaning: In a hard year one of you can step back for a while, and you both trust the next turn — until “for now” drags on for years.
text: Collapses at work come to you suddenly: the Tower brings down what seemed solid — a project, a post, a contract. A faith that unites you helps you stand firm: the Wheel of Fortune — the feeling that after a downturn a rise always comes and that your luck is shared. And the Hanged Man teaches you to wait out a downturn: sometimes step back, accept less, look at the situation differently — and not count it as defeat.

After the firm closes, one of you takes a simpler, worse-paid job than they could get: the rent must be paid, and finding a good post will take months. “It's temporary,” they say. The other nods and helps search, without rushing or pitying. The right post turns up by spring, and the simple job is left without regret. **In a hard year one of you is ready to step back for a while, and both know the wheel will turn again.**

A temporary retreat easily becomes permanent. Fear of another collapse keeps you in a safe position, faith in luck turns into waiting for everything to change by itself, and a concession into a habit of settling for little. You both stop talking about what you'd planned. “For now” is in its fifth year, and nobody mentions it any more.

items.title: A collapse that was a door
items.meaning: After a collapse you look beyond your own corner, and luck has found you there more than once.
text: Life doesn't stand still for you: the Tower at work brings down what seemed eternal — a post, a company, a whole industry. But luck often waits for you in the rubble: the Wheel of Fortune unites you through a shared luck that comes to the couple rather than to one. The World helps you see it — a broad view that takes you beyond your familiar corner: another city, another profession, another country.

One partner's company closes its local office within a week. A few days later a letter comes from a former colleague: Tbilisi is looking for exactly that kind of specialist. You sit on the floor among boxes and wonder whether the world isn't wider than it looks from your window. In the evening one says: “Listen, maybe this isn't a collapse but a door?” **A collapse often turns out to be a door for you: luck throws up a way out, and a broad view lets you step through it.**

You can get used to running away from every collapse. If every crisis is solved by moving, nobody thinks about the causes, and the broad view becomes a way of not seeing what needs fixing. Luck starts to seem fate's duty. Each crisis ends with a new address, and the old problems follow in the luggage.

items.title: A send-off for the old business

captions.R: Surviving the collapse of your work
captions.R1: Seeing out the old together, starting anew
captions.M: Saying “thank you” to the past aloud

items.meaning: You see off the collapse of a venture together, with gratitude, and only then begin something new.
text: The Tower in success can be cruel: a business with years invested in it can fall in a month. Death helps you hold on, and in your couple it is wise: together you can see off what has ended, not cling to the wreckage and not pretend nothing happened. And the Lovers won't let you stay silent: you say aloud how much it hurts and how dear the past was.

One partner's café closes after four years. On the last evening you invite the most loyal regulars, finish off the stock, recall funny stories, and at the end take down the sign together. At home it stands in the hall until spring, then goes off to the country cottage. The new venture begins without bitterness. **You don't hide the end of a venture: you see it off together, with gratitude, and only then move on.**

A farewell can become flight. If you start something new straight after a crash without mourning the old, the bitterness doesn't go anywhere: it surfaces as irritation, sharp words, reproaches of “it's all your fault”. And the one who changed faster starts to hurry the other. The new is begun, the old unmourned, and it comes back in every quarrel.

items.title: Owning up to attachment

captions.R1: Saying goodbye to the past together

items.meaning: A wreck at work gave you a reason to name honestly what you were attached to, and let it go together.
text: Wrecks at work do happen to you: the Tower brings down a post, a company, a familiar life in a single day. Death helps you live through them, binding you through the ability to let go of the old together and not cling to the wreckage. And the Devil helps you name what held on too tightly: work, status, money, a habit of being needed.

The company one of you gave ten years and every weekend to is closing. For the first week they pace the flat, unable to settle. Then they admit: “It looks like this job swallowed me whole. It's not the job I'm sorry for — I'm scared of who I am without it.” The other sits down beside them: “Let's find out. Together.” Over the next six months you learn to live without crunches, and it turns out you can live like that. **A collapse gave you a reason to admit honestly what you'd grown too attached to.**

An old attachment can return as soon as things pick up. A new job, the first successes — and the one who owned up disappears into the office again, while the other is afraid to remind them. The changes prove superficial, and the honesty a one-off. The collapse is survived, the lesson named, and the weekends are going on work again.

items.title: Building instead of panicking
items.meaning: You get through collapses at work by building something together with your hands, and in quiet work find a new path.
text: Two Towers on one line aren't double trouble but two different roles. In success the Tower brings sudden crashes: a profession you were counting on disappears, a company falls, the familiar way of life has to be rebuilt from scratch. Between you the same Tower becomes a support — trials you came through hand in hand, and the ability to build anew, literally and figuratively. You say little meanwhile: the Hermit gives you both time to think it through before speaking.

The spring when one partner's business closed is spent at the old country cottage. Together you strip out rotten boards, pour a foundation for a veranda, paint the windows. There's hardly any talk — just “pass me that” and “hold this”. And by June, sitting on the new step, the one left without work suddenly says what they want to do next, and the other nods: they'd seen it coming. **You recover by building: while your hands are busy with shared work, a new path takes shape in your heads.**

Getting used to collapses makes you jumpy. After a couple of crashes it's easy to start waiting for the next: snapping over trifles, seeing a threat in every call, taking it out on the one nearest. A harsh word at such a moment is remembered for ever, and the silence after it stretches for weeks. You walk around the house tapping the walls and hear cracks even where there are none.

items.title: Spotting the crack

captions.R: Surviving a wreck and getting up

items.meaning: Troubles have taught you to spot cracks early and shore up the walls in time — at work and between you.
text: Two Towers on the line mean both troubles and the experience of surviving them. At work the Tower brings wrecks you have to rise from; between you, a shared memory of troubles after which you stayed together. That experience has made you sensitive: the Moon sets your subtle language, in which each spots a crack before it becomes a collapse.

One partner's new job is going brilliantly, but one evening the other asks: “Doesn't anything about this boss bother you?” They stop to think: it does, but they've been pushing the thought away. Together you recall how the last crash began and find three similar signs. Soon you have a backup plan, and when the company starts to shake, there's no panic. **Troubles have taught you not only to fear but to sense: you spot the crack before it becomes a collapse.**

A nose for trouble easily becomes an expectation of trouble. If after every collapse you look for signs of the next, you see cracks everywhere: in the boss, in friends, in the other's silence. Irritation breaks through suddenly, and fear passes itself off as wisdom. You shore up the walls so often that living behind them becomes cramped.

items.title: A month of thawing out
items.meaning: A blow at work is met not by a hunt for culprits, but with the sea, long breakfasts and sunshine.
text: Wrecks at work do happen to you: the Tower brings down a job, a project or income suddenly and painfully. But after the blow the Sun meets you — the warmth, love of life and joy that bind you. And the Empress restores your strength: with care, food, comfort, time given without conditions.

One partner's company closes, and they come home drained. The other doesn't push them to look for something new or send job ads. Instead they announce: “You have a month's holiday. Sleep as much as you like, we'll walk by the sea, I'll cook.” The month passes in walks, long breakfasts and sunshine. By its end the one who lost their job sits down to their CV of their own accord. **After a blow the other doesn't hurry you to find something new but first warms you up, and strength returns faster.**

You can warm someone up for too long. If care becomes constant and sunshine a way of not thinking about difficulties, the one being warmed gets used to being looked after, and the one caring to pulling everything alone. The Sun dislikes heavy conversations. The month of thawing out stretches to six, and nobody mentions the CV any more.

items.title: Sunshine in the worst year

captions.R1: A warmth that doesn't go out

items.meaning: In the worst year friends still gather and soup is still on the stove: the warmth between you doesn't depend on luck.
text: The warmth between you doesn't go out even in the worst year. The Sun in your couple is joy, hospitality, a love of life, and it shines when work is dark: the Tower at work sometimes brings down a post or income suddenly and without explanation. You know how to wait out such storms like the Hanged Man — patiently, seeing the trouble as the other sees it, and not looking for someone to blame.

The year one of you lost their job and the savings went on debts, you remember not as the worst. On Fridays friends still gathered at yours — only instead of a restaurant there was soup and board games. The one out of work once said: “I thought you'd be angry.” The other answered: “And I thought it was harder for you than for me right now.” **The sun between you shines even in the worst year, because you know how to wait out a storm and not blame each other.**

Trouble hides behind a habit of smiling. If the party continues at any cost, real difficulties stop being talked about: guests, laughter, a warm table — and not a word about how frightening it is. One partner's patience turns into a silent sacrifice. In the family photos everyone is smiling, and out of shot lies an unpaid bill.

items.title: The world didn't fall

captions.M: Seeing the world wider than trouble

items.meaning: The warmth between you doesn't depend on luck at work, and even after a collapse you find a reason to gather friends.
text: Joy restores your strength: the Sun binds you through warmth, love of life, a knack for gathering people around you. Strength is needed, since the Tower at work every so often brings down what seemed solid — a post, an income, a project. And so that trouble doesn't block out everything, there's the World: you can look beyond your failure and see that life is far bigger than it.

A week after one partner's project collapsed. The other won't let them sit at home: on Friday you have dinner with friends, on Saturday a two-day trip to a neighbouring country. On an old square, among tourists and street musicians, the one who lost the project suddenly laughs for the first time in a week: “You know, the world didn't fall.” **After a collapse you don't hide but go out to people and the world — and the light comes back.**

A party after trouble can be a way of not noticing it. If every failure is drowned in gatherings and trips, the causes go undiscussed, and the one who's hurting smiles so as not to spoil the mood. Trips replace talk. The photos from your trips are bright, and the conversation about what happened has never begun.

items.title: Laughing among the ruins

captions.M: Saying “I love you” on the worst day

items.meaning: You meet sudden blows with laughter and tenderness — as long as a joke doesn't stand in for a conversation.
text: Blows at work can be sudden for you: the Tower in success brings down plans, contracts and posts without asking. The Fool holds you up — the ability to laugh among the ruins, to stay friends in trouble and start from scratch without drama. The Lovers teach you not to be shy: on the worst day you say “I love you”, and the word sounds like support, not consolation.

The company where one of you worked for six years closes within a week. That evening you sit on the floor with pizza, and the one who was laid off suddenly starts imitating the director announcing the news. You both laugh till you cry.
