Then the other takes their hand: “I love you. And you'll find something better.” **Laughter isn't a way of brushing things off for you, but a way of standing firm.**

A joke mustn't replace a conversation. If every blow is met with laughter, sooner or later there'll be nothing to laugh about — and you'll never have learned to talk seriously. The pain goes inward, irritation breaks out suddenly and at the wrong target. You still laugh together, only each of you cries alone in the bathroom.

items.title: A premiere for one spectator
items.meaning: Others see your talents, and what holds you is that home remains the first stage for each of you.
text: You are noticed for your talent: the Star brings recognition through creative work and experience, sometimes fame in your field. This talent grows on shared soil: the Hierophant gives you a common respect for knowledge, a habit of learning from the same masters and arguing about the same books. And the Lovers give you the courage to praise each other directly and often, without waiting for others' verdicts.

Before their first solo exhibition one of you shows the other the works, hung on the sitting-room wall. The other is silent for a long time, then takes one down: “This one looks better by the window.” On the opening night the hall is packed, and the artist keeps searching the crowd for one person. **Strangers' recognition is welcome, but your real premiere happens at home, before an audience of one.**

The footlights are shared unevenly: one stays on stage, the other is for ever in the stalls. The partner becomes a fan, advice becomes lecturing, and praise goes only to the one in view. The other claps ever more quietly and no longer remembers when they last stepped into the light themselves.

items.title: I want to be recognised

captions.M: Owning up to a thirst for fame

items.meaning: The wish for fame isn't hidden in your couple but honestly checked against what you believe in together.
text: Talent needs an audience: the Star at work leads to the stage, recognition, renown. Wanting it isn't shameful for you — the Devil lets you honestly own up to a thirst for fame, money, attention. And your yardstick is shared: the Hierophant binds you through values, a belief in what's right, and against that yardstick you check every wish.

One night one of you admits: “I want people to recognise me in the street. It's silly, but I want it.” The other doesn't wince or lecture: “It's not silly. Only let's agree what you won't do for it.” Until morning you draw up a list: don't lie, don't sell what you don't believe in, don't sacrifice family Sundays. **Even the wish for fame isn't shameful in your couple: it's spoken plainly, then checked against what you believe.**

A thirst for fame and preaching modesty get on badly. If one wants recognition and the other turns shared values into a moral, the wish goes underground and bursts out as a grievance: “you don't support me”. The Star compares itself with the famous, the Hierophant lectures. The list of rules lies in a drawer, and each reads it their own way.

items.title: The truth about what matters

captions.R1: Telling the truth about what matters

items.meaning: Your talents grow when the other tells the truth about what matters and tactfully keeps quiet about the rest.
text: The Star brings you recognition for talent: writing, music, projects where the author's hand shows. Justice keeps you close — an honesty you're not shy of: what you like and what you don't is said plainly. But not everything is said, and not all at once. The Hermit teaches you to choose your words: think first, then say one important thing, and keep quiet about the trifles.

The song is finished at three in the morning, and the author hands the other the headphones. The other listens twice, takes them off and says: “The chorus is the best thing you've got. The second verse isn't true.” The author grumbles, goes out onto the balcony, and by morning rewrites the verse. At the concert it's this very song the audience calls for again. **The other's honest opinion means more to you than any applause.**

Honesty wounds if it's measured out by your own standard. The one who criticises judges the other's work by their own taste and doesn't notice where it stings; the one criticised starts comparing themselves with others and doubting everything. Showing work becomes frightening, and the author withdraws. Manuscripts pile up in a drawer, because showing them is now scarier than leaving them unfinished.

items.title: Both names in the credits
items.meaning: You write together, share the fame equally, and hide lines in your songs that only the two of you understand.
text: Fame is shared honestly in your couple: Justice binds you through a rule that shared work is always signed with two names. There's plenty to share, since the Star at work gives talent, an audience, recognition for creative work. And the most personal things you hide in plain sight: the Moon teaches you to speak in hints, and in what thousands see there are words only you understand.

You write songs together: one composes the music, the other the words, and only one goes on stage. The album credits carry both names, in large type, side by side. And in the third song there's a line about “a cup by the window at four in the morning”, and only you know it's about your first sleepless night over a shared lyric. **Your songs hold lines only the two of you understand, and the credits hold both names.**

Secret dedications breed jealous questions. If you look for the addressee in every line, the Moon will soon suggest the wrong one; if you start counting the fame, Justice will turn it into bookkeeping, and the Star into a contest over who matters more. The songs come out one after another, and at home you hear more and more often: “Who's that one about?”

items.title: A light that recharges at home
items.meaning: One partner's talent grows in warmth: the other shields it from others' verdicts and won't let it burn out.
text: Your talent gets noticed: the Star in success takes you before the public, brings renown in your field and recognition for what you do with heart. Publicity is draining, and Strength comes to the rescue — you are each other's source of energy and shield against others' verdicts. And the Empress turns love into care: with spoiling and a warm home you nurture both yourselves and what you've set out to do.

A new series of one partner's illustrations goes viral, and along with the praise comes a wave of nasty comments. The other takes away the phone, wraps them in a blanket and puts their favourite pie on the table. “You'll read them tomorrow. Tonight you're a genius, full stop.” By morning the criticism looks smaller, and there's more strength for new work. **The light others see recharges at home — from the other's strength and care.**

One partner's renown can turn the other into staff. The one in the spotlight gets used to being recharged and doesn't notice the other tiring too; the one recharging gives all their care to someone else's talent and forgets their own. In the social-media photos it's always one of you, and it's the other who cooks the food in them.

items.title: The thirty-first letter
items.meaning: One partner's talent waits long for recognition, and all that time the other keeps their faith alive.
text: You have talent, but recognition is in no hurry: the Star at work promises light, but reaching it doesn't happen at the first attempt. The Strength between you keeps you from losing heart — one tops up the other's courage when theirs has run out. And you look at rejections like the Hanged Man: you turn them upside down and see not a verdict but a pause before the next attempt.

The thirtieth letter from a publisher — another rejection. The author of the manuscript puts it in the box with the others and says that's it. The other sits beside them: “Look at it differently. Thirty people have read your work. Two wrote that they were sorry. Let's send a thirty-first.” The thirty-first comes back with a contract. **Rejections don't put out talent in your couple: the other gives strength, and you have patience enough for two.**

Over time patience turns into the pose of the unrecognised. Rejections become proof that the world is unfair, the other's push becomes pressure, and waiting a convenient way not to risk again. The Star dims from comparisons with the lucky. The rejection letters are stored in a box, like trophies.

items.title: Holding hands, not holding back
items.meaning: Your talent is ready for the wide world, and you draw the courage for that step from each other.
text: Your talent wants to go out into the wide world: the Star at work promises recognition, and the World in your plans sets the scale — exhibitions abroad, international competitions, an audience without borders. Going out there is frightening, and the Strength between you comes to the rescue: the other gives courage when yours runs short, and doesn't pull you back.

An invitation to a photo exhibition in Berlin arrives along with panic: weak English, barely enough money for the trip, the work seems not good enough. The other sits down, takes their hand and says: “You're going. I'll come with you and translate as best I can.” At the opening the photographer stands by their pictures and smiles. **You have the courage to take your talent into the wide world, because the other holds your hand and doesn't hold you back.**

A big stage can demand ever more. Fame calls further, the other's strength turns into constant pushing, and freedom into a life between airports with little room left for the couple. The Star starts comparing itself with the better known. More and more photos on gallery walls, and fewer and fewer photos of the two of you.

items.title: Two talents in one blend
items.meaning: Your talents are unalike, and that's exactly why they sound stronger together — and you're not shy of praising each other.
text: The Star in success brings your talent before people: exhibitions, publications, the stage, recognition for creative work. You have more than one talent between you, and Temperance helps blend different worlds — artist and engineer, dreamer and practical mind — so that a third, better thing emerges. And the Lovers add courage: you're not shy of praising each other plainly and in front of everyone.

An exhibition opening. One of you painted the pictures; the other spent three weeks calculating the lighting and fixings so the huge canvases wouldn't fall. When the speeches begin, the artist steps up to the microphone and the first thing they say is: “Without this person nothing here would be hanging.” The hall laughs and applauds you both. **Your union is a blend of two different talents, and it sounds better than either alone.**

The blend separates if one talent is declared the main one. The one in view gets used to the light, the one backstage to the shade, and it's always the same one who gives way. Praise is heard less and less, comparisons with others' successes more and more. The exhibition booklet carries one name, and the fixings go uncredited.

items.title: A hundred days on tour

captions.R: Talent that asks for a stage
captions.M: Not being ashamed of greedy wishes

items.meaning: One partner's talent asks for big stages, and your knack for agreeing without strain keeps you from losing each other.
text: Talent asks for a stage in your couple: the Star calls to performances, an audience, recognition. Talent has a big appetite, and the Devil lets you own up to it honestly — you want fame, money, every stage in the world at once. And Temperance helps you find a measure between wishes and life together: it binds you through the ability to agree without strain.

An agent offers one of you a tour of two hundred days a year. They admit to the other: “I want them all. All two hundred. I want them greedily.” The other answers just as plainly: “And I want to see you more than on video calls.” At night you do the sums and argue, and by morning you settle on a hundred days, with the other coming along for twenty of them. **Even your greediest dreams of fame you discuss calmly, and find a measure that suits you both.**

Measure can give way to hunger. If appetite grows with every success, agreements get revised in one direction, and it's always the one at home who gives way. Temperance muffles discontent, the Star doesn't notice the other's shadow. A hundred days become a hundred and fifty, and nobody remembers what was agreed that night.

items.title: Two lamps over two desks

captions.M: Working side by side in silence

items.meaning: Two desks, two lamps, one silence: you create side by side and inspire each other without words.
text: The Star burns twice in your line and shines differently each time. In success it brings recognition for creative work: each has something to show the world. Between you it inspires: beside each other you understand who you want to be and bring out what would otherwise have stayed in drafts. You don't say much meanwhile — the Hermit gives you both the right to create in silence.

Two desks face each other, each with its own lamp. Evening after evening you work in silence, each on your own thing: one on a novel, the other on a series of engravings. Around midnight someone turns the screen or the sheet round: “Look.” The other looks for a long time and says one word, which is enough to last until the next evening. **You shine for each other, not at each other: inspiration is shared, and each has their own stage.**

Two stars side by side start comparing brightness. Who has more followers, whose exhibition was noticed, who was invited and who wasn't — nobody says it aloud, but the silence over the desks grows tense. Praise comes less and less, and showing your work to the other becomes ever more frightening. You count the likes under your partner's work before you've even looked at the work itself.

items.title: A shared source
items.meaning: Two creative people, you inspire each other and draw your ideas from shared dreams and half-tones.
text: The Star shines twice for you: at work it gives creative work that gets noticed, between you an inspiration in which each becomes bolder and brighter beside the other. You draw it from one source — the Moon makes dreams, images and half-hints your shared language, and from them ideas later grow.

In the morning one of you tells a dream: a city where houses grow like trees. The other listens, then takes out a sketchbook. By evening you have a draft for a children's book: one writes the text, the other draws. The book comes out, and on the last page there's a note in small print: “Dreamed by one, made up by two.” **Your inspiration comes from one source — shared dreams and half-tones you both know how to see.**

Two stars under one moon start to be jealous of the light. Whose idea, whose dream, whose name in bigger type — the Moon suggests grievances nobody voiced, and the Star compares itself with the other. Your source is shared, but more and more often you go to drink from it by turns.

items.title: Gran's recipe book

captions.R1: The family where it all began

items.meaning: Your talent grew from the family table, and from the first success you share it with those who fed you and believed.
text: Your talent gets noticed: the Star at work leads to recognition, readers, an audience. It grows from the family — Judgement binds you through roots, relatives who believed first, and a memory that nourishes the work. And you give thanks as the Empress teaches: with food, warmth, a laid table for everyone who was there for you.

One partner's blog of Gran's recipes unexpectedly gathers hundreds of thousands of readers, and a publisher offers a book. You take the first copy to the village. Gran leafs through it for a long time, finds her cabbage pie and cries. In the evening you bake that pie for all the relatives, and there's more laughter round the table than in the last ten years. **Your talent grew from the family table and returns there — with gratitude.**

The family may start to consider the success its own. If the relatives decide the book belongs to the family rather than the author, gratitude turns into a debt: share the fee, the recipes, your time. The Star tires of the claims, the Empress feeds everyone and forgets herself. The pies are baked every Sunday, but baking them for the relatives is no longer such a joy.

items.title: First stage: the family table
items.meaning: The first stage for your talent is the family table, and you have patience enough to wait for the big one.
text: Family is your first audience and main support: Judgement surrounds you with relatives who believe and support you, big celebrations, shared roots. This audience matters, because the Star at work gives a talent that needs a stage, and the big stage doesn't appear at once. The Hanged Man helps you wait for it: patience, the ability to wait without belittling yourselves while you do.

One of you writes songs, and the first listener of each is a grandmother, the second the whole family at the festive table. At an aunt's milestone birthday they sing a new one, and at the end even the uncle who always grumbles wipes his eyes. The other says quietly: “See? One day a whole hall will cry like that. We'll wait.” **Your talent grows among your own, and you have patience enough to wait until everyone hears it.**

The family's approval can become the only stage. Your own always like it, while going out to strangers is frightening, and waiting turns into a convenient excuse. The Star compares itself with the successful and hides. Your concerts happen only at family celebrations, and every year the same song is sung there.

items.title: A talent with roots

captions.R: Talent going out into the world
captions.M: Keeping your roots in the wide world

items.meaning: Your talent goes out into the wide world, but it has one set of roots — the family who believed first.
text: Your talent has one set of roots: Judgement binds you through a family who believed in you first, when nobody else did yet. And the talent goes far — the Star at work brings you before an audience, and the World widens the conversation to the scale of the whole planet: tours, exhibitions, other countries. You can see the world broadly and still remember where you came from.

The night after a concert in another country. The hall gave a standing ovation, but the first call after leaving the stage is not to the producer but to a grandmother who watched the livestream in her village. The other stands beside you holding the phone while Gran cries and tells how all the neighbours gathered at hers to watch. **The further your fame travels, the more often you ring home.**

The wide world can draw you away from those who believed first. Tours, interviews, new circles — and calls home grow rarer, family celebrations are skipped “for work”. The relatives take offence in silence, and the broad view turns condescending. You're listened to on three continents, and Gran learns your news from the internet.

items.title: Test tubes in the kitchen

captions.R1: A warm home as your shared support

items.meaning: One partner's work runs on instinct and imagination, while your home is clear, warm and always laid for a meal.
text: Your main support is home, and the Empress stands here twice: she unites you through comfort and prosperity, and she sets the language you love in — generous, delicious, caring. You need this support, because your work can be foggy. The Moon leads to work on instinct and imagination, where it's unclear what will take off and what won't, and income comes unevenly.

The house always smells of resin, or citrus, or something mysterious from test tubes: one of you composes perfumes. The other doesn't grumble: they've set aside a corner of the kitchen for experiments, put up shelves, and in the evenings is the first to sniff the new blends. A failed scent is discussed over dinner, a successful one celebrated with a pie. **The uncertainty in one partner's work is balanced in your couple by a home that's always clear and warm.**

The fog at work hides behind cosiness. When home is good, you don't want to look at where money comes from and where it goes: the Moon dislikes clarity in accounts, and the Empress is used to spending on joy. Worries go unmentioned so as not to spoil the evening. The house smells of pies, and in the letterbox bank letters pile up that nobody opens.

items.title: A pen name in a warm home
items.meaning: One partner's work lives in the shadows, but at home they can drop the mask — the other is quietly proud of them.
text: One partner's work lives under another name: the Moon at work leads to pursuits not spoken of aloud — pen names, closed projects, creative work in the shadows. Home is the shelter for this secret: the Empress binds you through comfort, care, a nest where the mask can come off. And the Hanged Man teaches you to keep quiet and wait — patiently, without resenting how much can't be shared.

The detective novels the whole country reads are written by one of you under a name that doesn't exist. Only the other knows. They patiently listen to the author's night-time doubts, bring tea before deadlines and keep quiet at parties when friends argue over who's behind the pen name. And at home a shelf holds every print run, signed with the real name. **One partner's secret is safely hidden in your warm home, and the other keeps it patiently and with pride.**

Another's secret is hard to keep when you can't talk about your own successes either. If the couple's whole life is subordinate to one secret, the keeper stops being visible, and patience turns into sacrifice. The Moon paints grievances, the Empress hides them behind care. The books sell in millions, and the other has long forgotten when they last boasted about anything.

items.title: Out of the fog, hand in hand

captions.R: Work with a lot of fog in it
captions.R1: Love as support when nothing is clear

items.meaning: There's fog in your work at times, but you find your way out holding on to plain words of love.
text: Your work often doesn't run in a straight line: the Moon in success leads to unusual professions, night shifts, creative work where it's unclear what will come of it. Uncertainty frightens, but the Lovers hold you, and hold you twice: love itself as support when everything around is shaky, and the couple's language — plain words about feelings. You clear the fog at work with clarity between yourselves.

A novel is being written at night, and the author doesn't know if it's any good. At breakfast the other finishes a chapter and talks not about style but about what they felt: “I was frightened for the hero. So it's working.” The author carries that sentence around all day and in the evening sits down to write again. **Where there's fog at work, the other's plain “I'm with you” leads you out.**

In the fog it's easy to mistake a shadow for a threat. Late nights, a closed laptop, calls nobody mentions — and the plain language of love gives way to suspicion. You want to love perfectly, but doubts won't allow it. At night each mentally reads things in the other's phone that aren't there, and in the morning is angry about what never happened.

items.title: A sketch made for oneself
items.meaning: Your love has no locked doors: you know each other's secret wishes and don't use them against each other.
text: One partner's work lives at night: the Moon leads to creative work where much is hidden from outside eyes and inspiration arrives after midnight. But there are no secrets between you. The Lovers bind you through a love chosen consciously and in earnest. And the Devil gives your conversations boldness: you don't hide secret wishes but name them aloud.

The tattoo studio stays open until late, and one of you is the last to leave. On your anniversary the other comes to the studio as a client, sits in the chair and hands over a sheet: a sketch the artist drew for themselves three years ago and showed nobody. “How did you know?” — “It was lying on your desk once. I want it. On me.” **What's most personal isn't hidden in your couple: the other knows even the sketches the first drew for themselves.**

Whoever knows another's secrets holds power. If you know everything about each other's wishes, it's easy to start using it — to pressure, demand, be jealous of what the other dreams of. The Moon confuses closeness with control, the Devil passion with possession. You have no locked drawers, but each of you checks more and more often what's in the other's.

items.title: One lantern for two

captions.R: A career path full of the unclear
captions.R1: Deep talks about your innermost things

items.meaning: You go through what's unclear at work together, and deep talk helps you see what the fog hides.
text: There's a lot that's unclear in your work: the Moon in success means unusual professions, intuitive decisions, work where the result now shows, now vanishes. You find clarity together. The Hermit connects you through deep talks about your innermost things, and at the point of common language he gives understanding at a glance. Two people with lanterns in the fog see more than one.

An odd project nobody around understands suddenly seems a mistake, and its author doesn't know whether to go on. You don't argue at the table but go for a night walk through the empty village. You walk slowly, under a single streetlamp. The other asks three questions, and by the end of the street the doubt has turned into a decision. **You don't hide one partner's doubts: you take them out on a night walk and examine them together.**

The fog thickens when each wanders through it alone. The Moon throws up fears and invented stories, and the habit of silence prevents you from checking them. Each retreats into their own thoughts and fills in the gaps for the other. Each has their own lantern, and they shine in different directions.

items.title: A night at the observatory

captions.R: Work in the quiet of night
captions.R1: A depth that brings you close

items.meaning: One partner's night work doesn't part you: the other comes where it's quiet, and words are hardly needed.
text: The night is shared in your couple. The Moon at work leads one of you to night work, where instinct and patience matter, and its subtlety also sets your way of talking: with looks, half-hints, silence. The Hermit binds you — depth, respect for the other's solitude, and conversations after which the world seems a little clearer.

Observatory shifts are at night, and one of you has no others. Once a week the other drives over by midnight with a flask and sandwiches. You sit under the dome, where only a red lamp glows, and hardly talk — one watching the screen, the other the sky. Around three the first points to a new dot on the monitor: “Look, a comet.” **The night is shared in your couple: one works, the other is beside them, and words are hardly needed.**

Night life can cut you off from the day. If your contact comes down to looks under the dome, daytime problems are left without an owner, and the Moon fills the silence with guesses: it seems the other has drifted away, that they're bored with you. The Hermit hides grievances. Under the stars you still understand each other, but by daylight less and less.

items.title: Dinner in a container
items.meaning: Your rhythms differ, but your care is one: dinner in a container finds whoever comes home at night.
text: Your care finds its way even at night: the Empress makes it the main way you speak of love — food, warmth, things left out for the other. At night — because the Moon at work leads to unsociable hours: night shifts, creative work till dawn, jobs where the schedule never matches anyone else's. And the Hanged Man teaches you to adapt to each other: give way, wait, see life through the eyes of the one whose rhythm is different right now.

One partner's night shifts as a dispatcher end just as the other leaves for work. You meet in the hall for five minutes. But something is always waiting on the table: dinner in a container with a note, “heat it up, don't eat it cold”, and in the morning a flask of coffee. At weekends you both shift your sleep and finally have breakfast together at noon. **Different rhythms don't part you: one adapts, the other notices, and care finds its way even at night.**

It can always be the same one who adapts. If the night schedule matters more, the other gives up evenings, friends and their own plans, and gets only notes in return. The Moon hides tiredness, the Hanged Man keeps quiet about the sacrifice. You live in one flat and meet only in doorways.

items.title: Waiting beside you in the fog

captions.R: Finding your way in the fog

items.meaning: Searching for yourself isn't shamed here: the other sympathises, doesn't hurry, and spots what's already working.
text: Your working path can be foggy: the Moon leads through periods of doubt when it's unclear what to do or where to go. At such times it matters who's beside you, and the Hanged Man appears here twice. Between you he's sympathy without reproach: the other doesn't hurry or shame you. And he also sets the way you talk: look at the fog from another angle, where uncertainty isn't failure but searching.

For the second year one of you doesn't know what they want to do: they left their profession and try one thing, then another. Friends advise them to “get a grip”. The other advises nothing. Just sometimes in the evening asks: “What did you enjoy today?” — and writes the answers in a notebook. After a few months a pattern emerges in the notebook. **One partner's hazy time isn't hurried in your couple: the other waits beside them and helps look at the fog from another angle.**

Fog and patience together can drag on for years. If you wait without a deadline, the search becomes a way of life, and the other's sympathy a silent sacrifice nobody notices. Resentment builds, but talking about it would be cruel. The other waits, the first searches, and both have forgotten what exactly for.

items.title: Your own measure of success

captions.R: A path that isn't clear yet
captions.R1: Patience and a view from the other side

items.meaning: One partner's creative path stays unclear for a long time, and the other patiently defends it before the family.
text: Other people's yardsticks of success don't stick to you. The World gives your conversations breadth: you look at life on a bigger scale than “a senior post by forty” and “a flat by fifty”. Breadth is needed, because your working path can be unclear — the Moon leads through creative work, unusual pursuits, periods when it's not clear where things are going. The Hanged Man helps you wait for clarity: patience and the ability to look at uncertainty from the other side.

At a family lunch an aunt again asks when one of you will “find a proper job”. They've been writing screenplays for three years and taking whatever work comes along. While they search for words, the other answers calmly: “We measure it differently. What matters to us is that it's interesting and there's enough to live on. So far there is.” The aunt shrugs, and under the table the screenwriter squeezes the other's hand. **Others' yardsticks don't stick to you: you look at life more broadly and patiently wait for the unclear to become clear.**

A broad view can justify anything. If every uncertainty is called a search and every wait wisdom, fog at work becomes a way of life. The one who waits endures in silence and tires of defending the other before the family. To the question “what do you do?” one of you has a new answer every year, and the other repeats it ever more reluctantly.

items.title: The night shift

captions.R1: An attraction that needs no reasons

items.meaning: One partner's night work and the strong pull between you get along, as long as you speak plainly about desires.
text: Your work can be unusual and closed: the Moon in success chooses night professions, creative work, work where much is hidden from outsiders. Such a life could pull you apart, but between you is the Devil — an attraction that needs no explaining, a strong and gripping passion. And to keep the secrets of work from becoming the couple's secrets, there are the Lovers: you speak openly about desires.

A nightclub, a shift until morning — that's one partner's job. Sometimes the other arrives towards the end of the shift, sits in a corner and watches the partner work: how they're loved there, how people are drawn to them. You drive home through the empty city, and on the way comes: “I like the way they look at you. But this night is ours, so let's hurry.” **Your attraction isn't afraid of the dark, because you talk about desires in the light.**

One partner's night life can wake the other's jealousy. The secrets of the job gather conjecture, the wish to hold on to the partner becomes control, and checks and suspicion replace a straight conversation. The attraction remains, but now it pulls not towards the person but towards power over them. One comes home towards dawn, the other pretends to be asleep, and both lie with their eyes open.

items.title: Attraction with boundaries
items.meaning: You're drawn to each other strongly, even a little alarmingly, and that's why you agree on boundaries so honestly.
text: A double Devil is strong: he binds you through a magnet that doesn't weaken, and he also makes your conversations frank — about desire, jealousy, the fear of loss. At work one of you has the Moon: night work, creativity on instinct, a world where much is hidden from outside eyes and where it's easy to get lost.

The city's nightlife is one partner's work: photo shoots until morning. The other admits: “I'm so drawn to you it frightens me. I'm starting to be jealous of every photo.” You don't hush it up but sit down and agree: two evenings a week the other goes along to the shoots with them, and you tell each other about new acquaintances yourselves, without being asked. **Even the strongest attraction you can discuss aloud and set honest boundaries for.**

Where attraction is stronger than reason, secrets become dangerous. If agreements start being broken, the Moon throws up suspicions, and the double Devil turns passion into control: checks, interrogations, attempts to hold on. One partner's night work becomes a field for the other's jealousy. The boundaries are written down, only each checks whether the other has crossed them.

items.title: Stories people make up
items.meaning: Night, instinct and silence are your shared element, and in them you find what others pass by.
text: The Moon is in both your work and your feelings. In success it leads to unusual professions where instinct and imagination matter, and where few understand what you're really doing. Between you it connects through shared fantasies, secrets, a world invented for two. And you keep an understanding silence, like the Hermit: much between you needs no words.

Two in the morning, an empty city after rain. You wander with cameras, photographing streetlights reflected in puddles, and barely speak. Sometimes one stops and silently points at something; the other nods and takes the same shot from the other side. In the morning the photos show two different cities, and both are yours. **You understand each other in what others find strange, and you don't need to explain it.**

A double Moon easily paints what isn't there. The secrecy that shielded you from outsiders starts working inside: each keeps quiet about their fears, and the other fills in the gaps. The world invented for two fills up with suspicion. The neighbours make up stories about you, and you make them up about each other.

items.title: A world of half-tones
items.meaning: A world of half-tones is home to you: you create by instinct and understand each other almost without words.
text: The Moon stands at all three of your points, and each time its role is different. At work it leads to work built on instinct and imagination — creativity, night hours, pursuits that are hard to explain. Between you it gives understanding without explanation. And in conversation it becomes a language of half-hints, images and dreams in which you both feel at home.

Night, a workshop where one of you is shaping something in clay that has no name yet. The other sits in the corner with tea and asks nothing. Around three the sculptor steps back and says: “It looks like…” — “Like that dream about the river,” the other answers. “I see it.” In the morning the figure gets a name, and the name was thought up by both of you. **Your world is full of half-tones, and neither of you is afraid in it, because you see the same thing in the dark.**

A triple Moon easily confuses feeling with truth. If everything is understood without words, guesses become certainty, fears facts, and secrets a habit. Each fills in for the other, and what's filled in isn't always kind. The workshop is as quiet and beautiful as ever, only more and more often you sit in different corners of it.

items.title: Candles for the whole world

captions.R: Work built on instinct and fantasy
captions.R1: A shared love of the world

items.meaning: Candles that smell of rain, made in your kitchen, now burn in twenty countries, every one packed by your hands.
text: Your work is unusual, built on instinct and fantasy: the Moon leads to creative pursuits where scent, colour and mood matter. The World sets its scale, binding you through a love of the wide world and a conviction that a border is no barrier. And above all you create comfort: the Empress makes care for people your shared language.

One of you started making candles in the kitchen, just for the house. The scents came out strange: “rain in a pine forest”, “Gran's attic”. The other posted photos online, and orders came in — first from your own town, then from Germany, Japan, Chile. Now the kitchen has become a workshop, and in the evenings the two of you pack parcels and write cards by hand. **One partner's small, strange venture became a bridge to the wide world, and your home its warm workshop.**

A dreamy business may never learn to count. The Moon dislikes figures, the Empress loves giving, so orders go out with gifts, and money comes in hazily. The workshop crowds out the home. Your candles burn in twenty countries, and there's no room left in your kitchen for supper.

items.title: Homesick

captions.R: An unclear path in foreign lands
captions.R1: A shared view of the world

items.meaning: You live broadly and not always clearly, but you meet each other's homesickness and doubts with patience.
text: Your path at work can be unclear: the Moon leads through periods of doubt, unusual pursuits, work where it's hard to say what will come of it. Unclarity isn't frightening when you see life the same way, and the World binds you through exactly that — a shared broad view, a love of open space, a readiness to live in any country. And you meet hard moments as the Hanged Man does: patiently, able to see the other's feelings through their eyes.

You've been living in another country for three years, and all seems well. But one evening one of you admits: “I miss home. The snow, Mum's cooking, our own language in the shops.” The other doesn't say “but we decided together”. They sit down beside them and ask: “Which of those can we set up here?” By New Year you have a real tree and dumplings for twenty guests. **One partner's homesickness doesn't become a reproach: the other sees it through their eyes.**

A broad life sometimes rests on one partner's sacrifice. The move was the first one's dream, while the other endures, adapts and stays silent, and the Moon keeps adding new reasons to their longing. Patience turns into submission. The tree is up, the dumplings made, and the homesickness hasn't gone anywhere — you've just stopped talking about it.

items.title: Legends at the map's edges

captions.R1: A shared picture of the world

items.meaning: You see the world with the same breadth, and one partner's instinct takes you where others don't look.
text: The World appears twice in your line: it binds you through a shared picture of life, and it sets the tone of your conversations — broad, free, without pressure. What would seem strange to others fits easily into this picture: the Moon brings unusual pursuits into your work, instinct, imagination, an interest in what hides at the edges of maps.

One of you collects legends and records them in remote villages — it pays almost nothing, but it makes books that thousands later read. The other travels along, takes photos and keeps a diary. In the evenings in strangers' homes you listen to old women telling of water spirits, and then argue till late about what's true. **One partner's unusual work fits into a shared picture of the world, where the strange doesn't frighten but beckons.**

A shared picture of the world can close itself off from others. If you're both sure you see life rightly, other people's doubts stop being heard, and unusual ideas stop being tested. The Moon throws up mysteries, the World certainty. Your world grows ever wider on the map and ever narrower in conversation.

items.title: A summer party
items.meaning: Your home is known as a place that's always warm and well thought out, and much of your success rests on it.
text: People know you and are glad to see you: the Sun brings recognition and the ease with which any door opens. All of it rests on a strong home — the Emperor binds you through order, reliability, roles shared out. And the Empress creates the warmth in this home: generous hospitality, a laid table, care for everyone who crosses the threshold.

Every July you throw a big summer party for all your friends. A month ahead one of you draws up a plan: who's coming, where the marquee goes, who's in charge of the music. A week ahead the other starts baking, marinating and making jam as gifts for the guests. On the day there are forty people, everything runs like clockwork, and in the evening the two of you dance under the fairy lights. **Your parties always succeed, because one is in charge of order and the other of warmth.**

A model home risks becoming a shop window. Hospitality turns into a display of success, order into control, the food into a duty “not to let the side down”, and the party stops delighting the hosts. The Sun expects admiration, the Emperor compliance. The guests leave enchanted, and you wash the dishes in silence until morning.

items.title: The protector's step back

captions.M: Stepping back and letting them risk it

items.meaning: One of you is in the spotlight and takes risks, the other holds the fort and knows when not to step in.
text: One of you is often on stage: the Sun brings recognition and the attention of many. Attention is dangerous, and the Emperor binds you through reliable protection — order, backup, a shoulder to lean on. And so that protection doesn't become a cage, there's the Hanged Man: the ability to step back and let the other take the risk themselves.

The one in the spotlight is offered a daring project: a live broadcast with no script, where you can get things badly wrong in front of everyone. The other, who always checks everything, wants to say “no”. They think it over for a long time that night, and in the morning say: “I'd be scared. But it's your stage. Go — I'll be in the wings.” The broadcast comes out uneven, alive and the most talked-about of the year. **The protector in your couple knows how to step back and let the other take the risk themselves.**

You can step back until you stop being noticed. If the protector always retreats to the wings, the Sun gets used to shining alone, and care turns into invisible work nobody thanks you for. Order rests on one person. Broadcast follows broadcast, and the credits never carry the name of the one standing in the wings.

items.title: The spotlight and a safe rear
items.meaning: One has the stage, the other the rear, and gratitude for that rear is heard as often as the applause.
text: Behind every bright success of yours stands a reliable rear: the Emperor binds you through order, protection and a division of roles in which one can shine without thinking about the household. There's someone to shine — the Sun at work gives visibility, recognition, status. And you write the rules of this life as the World teaches: together, on a grand scale, and with each one's right to revise them.

Before the performer's world tour, the other lays a spreadsheet on the table: cities, flights, hotels, fallback options, who meets you at the airport. “Are you coming?” — “Only to three cities. The rest of my time is booked in advance.” The tour goes off without a single hitch, and in the pauses between concerts you meet in those three cities. **One partner's light rests on the other's reliability, and you agreed the rules of this life on a grand scale.**

A reliable rear can turn into invisible staff. The Sun gets used to everything being organised, the Emperor to not being thanked, and the broad agreement turns out to suit mainly one. The one keeping order dissolves into someone else's schedule. In the tour photos one is always in the frame, the other always behind the camera.

items.title: A route with no hotels

captions.R1: The road where you're side by side

items.meaning: Each of you succeeds in your own field, and no victory gives the right to choose the route for both.
text: The Sun in success makes you a bright couple: each succeeds in their own work, and one partner's successes gladden the other rather than sting. You recharge in motion — the Chariot brings you close on the road, on trips, in sport — wherever you're side by side, though each drives their own cart. And where to go is decided by the Lovers: you choose the route together, not whoever is more successful at the moment.

A holiday for you is always the road: a car, a map, not a single hotel booked in advance. At a petrol station in the middle of nowhere you argue whether to turn off towards the river or drive on, and a tossed coin decides, because you both want each equally. That evening on the riverbank one says: “All year I wait for just this — you and the road.” **Your successes shine on both, and you recharge on the road, where decisions are made together.**

The sky is too small when there are two suns in it. Each is used to being at the centre, and one partner's success quietly starts competing with the other's: whose work matters more, whose holiday can be moved, who should support whom. Victories are claimed, grievances pile up, and more and more often you go on holiday in separate cars — it's easier for work that way.

items.title: A convertible after the deal
items.meaning: You celebrate success with speed and passion — a convertible, a night-time road and each other.
text: Your victories are loud: the Sun gives them a shine and a confidence visible from afar. You celebrate them in motion — the Chariot binds you through speed, the road, a thrill in which you're side by side. And you don't hide passion: the Devil lets you speak openly about desire, and want each other as strongly as you want victories.

The deal you both worked on for six months is signed on Friday evening. On Saturday you buy the old red convertible one of you has dreamed of since youth. At night you drive along an empty coast road, music at full blast, wind in your hair. At a lookout point one says: “I want to live like this forever.” The other kisses them by way of an answer. **Success smells of petrol and wind in your couple: you celebrate it with speed and passion.**

The speed you love easily turns into a race against each other. Who'll earn the next car first, who'll win more, whose victory shines brighter — the Sun loves first place, the Chariot the race, the Devil possession. Night drives become a race, not a ride. You now have two convertibles, and you drive them separately.

items.title: The price of luck

captions.M: Knowing the price of luck, as two

items.meaning: People call you lucky, and you know the price of your luck and discuss it only with each other.
text: Your success is visible: the Sun gives you both bright fulfilment, status and a confidence that shows from afar. Friends call you lucky, and partly it's true — the Wheel of Fortune binds you through shared turns, where luck comes to the couple rather than to one. But only you know the price of this luck, and you speak of it quietly, in the Hermit's language.

A Saturday dinner at friends'. Someone remarks with envy: “Well, you two are always lucky.” You smile and change the subject. At home, getting ready for bed, one asks: “Are we really just lucky?” The other remembers the nights before the launch, the rejection after which you had to start again, the year without a holiday. You sit in the dark for a long time. **You meet others' talk of your luck with a smile, and discuss its real price between the two of you.**

Shared luck sometimes turns into a contest. The Sun likes to be at the centre, and whoever is luckier at the moment quietly claims the shared victory; the other says nothing but remembers. The wheel turns, roles change, and the score continues from the other side. There are two stages in the house, and neither has enough audience.

items.title: Unease at the top

captions.R1: Luck that comes to you both

items.meaning: At the height of your luck you listen not only to the applause but to each other's quiet unease.
text: Luck comes to you as a pair: the Wheel of Fortune binds you through a sense that fortune smiles on the couple, not one partner, and that your turns are shared. There's brightness enough: under the Sun, work brings you both a name and attention. And yet the most precious thing in your couple is the ability to listen to the vague: the Moon makes you both alert to the other's unease even on the happiest day.

The best year of one partner's career: bonuses, offers, interviews. At the celebration dinner the other suddenly notices the hero of the evening staring out of the window. At home they ask: “What's worrying you?” — “I don't know. It's too good — it can't last.” You don't laugh at this, and the next day you set part of the bonus aside and take on no new loans. **Even in your best year you heed the other's vague feeling and prepare a way out.**

Unease at the top can poison joy. If every success is met by waiting for the reckoning, the celebration becomes torture, and the Moon paints disasters that aren't there. The Sun is hurt that its joy wasn't shared, and luck starts to be feared. On your best days you sit in the kitchen counting what could go wrong.

items.title: A celebration and a farewell

captions.M: Laying the table for both occasions

items.meaning: Bright successes and changes go side by side for you, and you can rejoice for one without forgetting to comfort the other.
text: You live through changes together, and Death makes that your shared strength: if something has ended, we say goodbye together and move on together. You have plenty of changes, because the Sun at work brings bright successes, and success always has a reverse side — something leaves to make room. The Empress teaches you to mark both: with a generous table, warmth, care.

On the same evening one of you wins an award for the best project of the year, and the other has their last day at a job they held for eight years. You lay the table for both occasions at once: champagne for the success and a favourite pie for what has ended. The toast to the award comes second. The first is to eight years that weren't wasted. **One partner's joy and the other's farewell fit at one table in your couple — and neither cheapens the other.**

One partner's light can make the other's ending invisible. The Sun loves to be at the centre, and someone else's loss beside your own success seems trivial; the table is laid in honour of one. The one who's sad right now smiles so as not to spoil the evening. The champagne is drunk, and nobody ever cut the farewell pie.

items.title: Stepping down from the top

captions.R: Being in view and on top

items.meaning: You can step down from the top for the other's sake and meet a new beginning without regret.
text: You don't cling to the past, even when it was brilliant: Death teaches you to renew yourselves together, close chapters and start new ones. You have plenty of brilliant past, because the Sun at work gives bright success, status, visibility. And the Hanged Man helps you make room: he shows the situation from the other side, where stepping down from the top isn't a loss but a release.

The one leading a successful project sees that the other has been offered a dream job in another city. They leave their post of their own accord, without drama, and hand over to a successor. At the farewell party colleagues ask if they're sorry. They laugh: “The important thing comes with me, and everything else we'll start again.” **At the top you know how to make room, because you know that after an end something new always begins for you.**

Stepping down from the top can become a sacrifice that gets brought up. If one gave things up and the other gained, in a hard moment you'll hear “I gave up everything for you”. The Sun misses the spotlight, and changes begun for the other's sake feel like someone else's. The new has begun, only the one who made way is still looking back at the summit.

items.title: Leaving at the peak

captions.M: Starting at the other end of the world

items.meaning: Success isn't a place you must stay for you, but a chapter after which you can start again anywhere.
text: Applause is familiar to you: the Sun brings the stage, recognition and sold-out halls. But you won't cling to success — Death binds you through an ability to renew yourselves together, to close even the most brilliant chapters. And you're ready to start the new anywhere: the World makes your view broad, and the other end of the world is no further for you than the next town.

Twenty years on stage, full houses, tours. At the farewell concert one of you announces they're leaving, and the hall gasps. Soon the two of you open a small music school in a seaside town on another continent. Twelve pupils, laughable pay, and you're both happier than you've been in a long time. **Leaving at the peak and starting again at the other end of the world is something you manage together and without regret.**

A new beginning far away can bring back the stage you left. The Sun finds it hard without applause, and on quiet evenings the one who left starts to pine, while the other blames themselves for supporting it. The wide world shrinks to a small school. The pupils sing well, and the one who once shone on stage rewatches old concert recordings more and more often.

items.title: A light that remembers the dark

captions.R1: Dark times you came through together

items.meaning: You don't forget the dark times you came through together, and you say your thanks for them aloud — even from a stage.
text: The Sun in success gives you brightness: status, recognition, prosperity visible from outside. But that isn't what holds you. The Tower binds you through dark times you came through together — sudden troubles you lived through hand in hand and came out of stronger. And your language is the Lovers': you say your gratitude to each other aloud, even in front of everyone.

The evening of an industry awards ceremony. One of you goes up on stage, says the expected words, and at the end looks into the hall: “And a special thanks to you. For the year when we had nothing but each other.” The other sits in the fifth row remembering a rented room and one winter coat between two. **Your present light knows the price of the darkness you came through together.**

Success erases the memory of hard years. The Sun loves the centre of the stage, and the one in view starts to count the victory as theirs alone and the other as part of the furniture. In a quarrel threats to leave, said in the heat of the moment, surface. In interviews the success story begins from the year when everything had already come right.

items.title: Vanity owned up to
items.meaning: Your success was earned through shared storms, and your honesty goes as far as the awkward: envy and pride are said aloud.
text: Today people admire you: the Sun has given your work shine and status. That shine came through storms — the Tower binds you through trials you weathered together, after which you know each other's worth. And your honesty goes as far as the awkward: the Devil lets you own up even to vanity, jealousy of someone else's fame, a wish to be first.

After the ceremony where one of you received an award, the other is silent for a long time in the taxi, then says: “I'm very proud of you. And I'm a little hurt it wasn't me they praised. There. Now it's said.” The winner laughs and takes their hand: “And I like that it was me they praised. I'll own up too.” You laugh all the way home. **Even vanity isn't hidden in your couple: said aloud, it doesn't get the chance to spoil the celebration.**

Owning up to vanity doesn't cancel it. If you only name envy and pride without noticing how they grow, the Sun starts drawing attention to itself, and sharp words in a quarrel hurt more, because you know exactly where to aim. The storms you weathered together start being divided into “mine” and “yours”. The confessions are just as honest, only it's harder and harder to laugh at them.

items.title: A quiet morning after a loud day
items.meaning: Your home is noisy and welcoming, and the best minutes are morning coffee on the porch without a single word.
text: The Sun appears twice in your line. At work it gives both of you bright fulfilment: success, status, recognition that's hard to miss. Between you it becomes joy — guests, celebrations, travel, warmth enough for everyone. But the most precious things in your couple happen without witnesses: the Hermit at the point of common language leaves you quiet hours just for two.

Once again the house is full in the evening: friends, colleagues, friends' children, music till midnight. In the morning, when the guests have all gone and the dishes are still unwashed, you sit on the porch with coffee in silence. One rests their head on the other's shoulder, and for twenty minutes nobody says a word. **There's plenty of light and people around you, and the warmest things in your couple happen in silence.**

Brightness dazzles you too. Two successful people easily turn life into a shop window: celebrations, trips, achievements — and quiet mornings grow fewer and fewer. Each is used to being at the centre, and criticism of each other sounds sharper than you'd like. Your photos are happy, but the conversation off camera doesn't flow.

items.title: The shadow behind the party
items.meaning: You're a bright, much-loved couple, and you can hear in each other what the party hides.
text: The Sun is with you both at work and between you: both successful, both in the public eye, and at home there's warmth enough for all your friends at once. But behind bright light each has a shadow, and the Moon comes to your rescue. It sets a quiet language in which you hear in each other what doesn't show in photos: tiredness, doubt, the fear of one day burning out.

The party for your shared studio's anniversary is in full swing: music, toasts, a hundred guests. One of you laughs loudest of all, and only the other notices that the laugh is half a tone higher than usual. Late at night, when the guests have gone, they sit down beside them: “What's wrong?” — “I feel the best is already behind us.” The conversation lasts till dawn. **Two bright people in your couple can be quiet too: you hear the other's fear and doubt through any party.**

Light likes to be looked at, and the Moon hides what doesn't sparkle. If you're both used to shining, admitting weakness becomes shameful, and rivalry — who's brighter, who's more successful — smoulders under the smiles. Instinct says something's wrong, but pride gets in the way of asking. In photos you're still the happiest couple in the crowd.

items.title: Party hats and cake
items.meaning: Your home is known as the place where people celebrate with childlike fun and everyone who comes is fed.
text: People look at you: the Sun makes your work visible and your names recognisable. You celebrate success like children — the Fool binds you through mischief and a friendship in which nothing is funnier than serious people. And your table is generous, like the Empress's: feed everyone who comes, and give them some to take home.

The evening after one of you receives an award. Instead of a restaurant — a house full of friends, paper party hats on everyone, a distinguished professor included, and a cake with “Our genius” written on it in wobbly letters. The prize-winner blows out the candles, laughs loudest of all, then spends till late packing leftover cake into tubs for the guests. **You celebrate success like children: with cake, silly hats and friends who are always welcome.**

An endless party tires the hosts. If every success becomes a party and every piece of hard news is smothered in cake, the serious has no place, and generosity no bottom. The Sun gets used to applause, the Fool to carelessness. There's a whole box of party hats in the cupboard now, and never time to talk just the two of you without guests.

items.title: A parody in the kitchen
items.meaning: Your fame is met at home with parody and laughter, and that keeps you both grounded.
text: Fame does come your way — with performances, interviews, being recognised in the street: that's how the Sun shines. The Fool brings you back down to earth — laughter, friendship, a lightness in which nobody at home puts on airs. And the Hanged Man teaches you to see yourselves from outside: turn the picture over and see how you look through the other's eyes.

After one partner's TV interview, the other meets them in the kitchen in a jacket worn back to front, with a spoon for a microphone: “Tell us, how did you become so great?” The star takes offence at first, then laughs till they cry. In the evening they rewatch the interview and admit: “You know, there really was a bit too much self-importance.” **Beside the other your fame becomes a reason to laugh, and that's the best protection against conceit.**

A joke can wound if it's always the same one laughing. If the one in the shadows answers every success with a parody, resentment can be heard behind the laughter, and the one in the spotlight starts hiding their victories from the other. Seeing yourselves from outside becomes painful. The spoon-microphone lies in a drawer, and nobody wants to take it out any more.

items.title: Refusing to grow serious
items.meaning: People know you as successful, and you still slip away from the reception to catch a night ferry.
text: Your success is visible: the Sun at work gives status, recognition, a life others look at from outside. It hasn't made you more serious: the Fool has made you friends and mischief-makers, and you still laugh at what one is supposed to frown at. And you look at life like the World — without borders: roads, countries, people, the freedom to choose how to live.

After the award ceremony everyone goes to the reception, while you slip out by the service entrance, change in the car and drive to the night ferry. In the morning you wake in another country with the award in a rucksack and your phones switched off. The agent is horrified, while you have breakfast on the waterfront and work out how you'll tell this story. **Success hasn't made you more serious: you still laugh and take off down the road.**

The lightness of successful people can become carelessness. If serious things can always be put off, commitments start falling through and actions start hurting those who counted on you. The Sun gets used to being forgiven everything. You still run off together, only now more and more often from conversations that should have happened long ago.

items.title: A third tradition

captions.R: Work that keeps the family going

items.meaning: From the customs of two families grows a third — your own, with pies and rules for two.
text: You have many customs, and the Hierophant makes them what binds you: shared views, celebrations, rules you keep not out of fear but out of love. Family matters to you too — Judgement at work often leads to work tied to the family and its legacy. And all of it is expressed in the Empress's language: a laid table, pies, care for everyone you love.

For one family New Year means Gran's dumplings and a trifle; for the other, roast goose and singing round the guitar. In your first years you dashed between two homes. Now you have a third tradition: on the thirtieth of December you gather both families at yours, make dumplings, roast a goose and sing round the guitar. **You keep both families' customs and add your own — and so a third tradition grows.**

When the rules multiply and the family grows ever more demanding, customs become a duty that eats up the celebration: whoever cooks becomes the staff, and faith in tradition turns into fear of breaking it. The relatives judge who made the most effort. The celebration goes perfectly, and the two of you fall asleep at the table without having talked.

items.title: A duty to the family

captions.R1: A way of life you share

items.meaning: You neither accept family expectations on trust nor reject them at once: each first tries them on the other.
text: A family business often awaits an heir in your couple: Judgement leads to work tied to kin, to the elders' expectations, to a duty you don't choose. Shared values help you decide such questions — the Hierophant binds you through a way of life and an understanding of what's right. And you weigh them as the Hanged Man does: seeing the situation not only through your own eyes but through the other's.

One partner's father is retiring and expects his child to take over the family printing business. That would mean moving to a small town and giving up their own work. In the evening the other says neither “accept” nor “refuse”. They ask: “If this were mine rather than yours, what would you advise?” The answer doesn't come at once, and it's unexpected: you'll take on the printing business together, but on your own terms. **A duty to the family isn't settled behind the other's back: you look at it through both your eyes.**

A duty to family can become a sacrifice nobody asked for. If one decides “for Dad's sake” and the other silently follows, the way of life becomes a prison, and the concession a reproach that will ripen with time. The family approves, and the two of you stay silent. The printing business runs, and the one who moved for it looks more and more often at the train times to the city.

items.title: Roots taken out into the world

captions.R: Work that grows from your family

items.meaning: You're heirs who don't hide the family legacy in a chest: in your hands an old recipe gets a new life.
text: Family heritage isn't dust on a shelf for you. Judgement leads to work that grows out of the family: a craft passed down, a calling heard in childhood. The Hierophant teaches you to cherish it — shared values and a respect for customs you both hold. But tradition isn't locked in a chest for you: the World makes your talk about it open and broad, and there's room in it for the new.

A family recipe for herb honey has been handed down three generations on one partner's side. You both decide it's time to show it to the world: new packaging, a website in two languages, the first fair abroad. Every jar carries the family's story, and the last line of the label has your two names side by side. **Your family business isn't a museum: you cherish its roots and take it out into the wide world.**

One family's tradition becomes a cage for the other. Relatives start deciding how to run the business, customs turn into rules, and talk about the future into a dispute over whose roots matter more. The other, who came into the family with roots of their own, feels like a guest. At family dinners only the business is discussed, and they sit at the table like the family's hired hand.

items.title: The last word belongs to two

captions.R: A calling tied to your family
captions.M: Deciding as two, not as a clan

items.meaning: Family and its affairs mean a lot on your path, but you decide honestly and as two, not at the family table.
text: Your path is closely woven with family: Judgement in success leads to a calling tied to your family line, to a family business, an inheritance, opportunities through relatives. Where relatives are involved, honesty is needed, and Justice keeps it between you: in shared affairs nobody grabs more than their share, and agreements are kept even with relatives. But the last word belongs to the Lovers — to the choice the two of you make.

One partner's parents invite you into the family business: good money, but also relatives' constant presence in your life. At Sunday lunch everyone already assumes you've agreed. At home the two of you sit down and honestly list what you gain and what you lose. You answer a week later, and the answer is yours, not the family's. **Your relatives' voice is heard, but the last word stays with the two of you.**

A family business can eat the family. Relatives decide who's in charge in the couple, an honest division turns into a dispute over shares, and the choice of two becomes a vote where you hold two votes out of ten. Arguing with relatives is awkward, and the grievance turns inward, into the couple. At Sunday lunch with the parents, things get decided that you never discussed at home.

items.title: Straight about shares
items.meaning: Money in the family business is no cause for whispers behind backs: shares are discussed at the family council, aloud.
text: Your work is tied to the family: Judgement leads to a family business, an inheritance, working side by side with relatives. Where there's family and money, honesty is needed, and Justice binds you through exactly that: clear shares, contracts, nothing left unsaid. And the Devil helps you talk about money — plainly, without shame, calling figures and wishes by their names.

The family workshop is growing, and one of you carries almost all the production. At the family council they say what others keep quiet: “I want a bigger share. Here's why, here are the figures.” The relatives are shocked, but the other backs them: “It's fair, and it's better said now than whispered later.” The shares are revised, and no quarrel follows. **Even about money in the family business you speak plainly — and that's why you don't fall out over it.**

Plain talk about money can grow into haggling with relatives. If every figure becomes grounds for a dispute, the family business turns into a battlefield, and honesty into a demand. The wish to get your due starts to outweigh family ties. The shares are set out to the last penny, and now you come to family celebrations with a lawyer.

items.title: Answering the call
items.meaning: You both hear the calling, and you gather the strength to answer it from each other, in silence.
text: Judgement in success is a call: a vocation that has long sounded somewhere within and then demands an answer. Answering is frightening, and here the Strength between you helps — beside the other you grow braver, and their faith gives you strength to bear the change. Decisions on that scale you make slowly, like the Hermit: you carry them inside for a long time and only then say them aloud.

For years one of you talked of a workshop in their home town as a dream for “some day”. This autumn they're quieter than usual and take long walks alone. The other doesn't hurry them, just leaves an advert for premises to let on the table and goes to bed. In the morning: “I'm going to see it.” By winter there are workbenches standing there. **You answer the call with your whole hearts, and gather the strength to answer from each other.**

One partner's call can drown out the other's voice. The one who answered pulls the couple along — to roots, family, their own work — and the other, not daring to say it all feels foreign, silently agrees. Strength turns into pressure, silence into things left unsaid. One has come home to their roots, while the other came as a guest and still lives as one.

items.title: Born again in your calling
items.meaning: You help each other return to work you once gave up, and there's courage enough for two.
text: Judgement at work promises a second birth: a return to a calling you once had to give up, a new turn of an old love for the work. Going back is frightening, and here Strength comes to the rescue — the courage you give each other when your own runs short. And what to go back to the Moon often suggests: dreams, vague longings, scraps of phrases that the other remembers and won't let you forget.

Ten years ago one of you left the stage and never spoke of it again. But sometimes they dream they're dancing again, and in the morning they tell the dream, laughing. One morning the other doesn't laugh, but finds a studio taking on an adult group and silently puts the timetable on the table. The first class is on Monday. **Your second birth in work begins with a dream the other wouldn't let you forget.**

The dream of going back may stay just a dream. Fear of looking ridiculous, relatives saying “at your age?”, pressure from a partner who wants too much to help — and the dream hides again. The Moon mixes up wishes with fears. The studio timetable has been on the fridge for three years, and nobody takes it down.

items.title: Sundays in turn
items.meaning: You have two families and one family business, and Sundays are shared fairly: one for them, one for you.
text: Two families is a lot, and Temperance helps you keep the balance between them without leaving anyone out. Family isn't only at home for you: Judgement at work often ties your work to the family — one continues the parents' business, inherits a practice, carries a name people know. And your care is generous, like the Empress's: feed, warm, never forget a single birthday on either side.

Your Sunday lunches go strictly in turn: one Sunday with one set of parents, the next with the other. One of you bakes a pie for their family, the other for the partner's, and this isn't up for debate. And once a month a Sunday is declared nobody's: you go nowhere, the phones are silent, and the pie is baked just for two. **Two families and one family business get along in your couple, because you keep the measure together and the care goes both ways.**

Caring for relatives can eat up caring for each other. The family business demands more and more, the balance rests on concessions, and generosity goes to everyone except your own couple. Nobody's Sunday is postponed time after time. Both families are content and well fed, and the two of you haven't had a pie on your own for a long time.

items.title: A family business, in measure
items.meaning: You keep the balance between the family business and the couple, and don't let relatives decide everything for you.
text: Measure and patience are what hold your couple in the midst of a big family. Judgement at work often ties business to kin: a family firm, shared projects with relatives, responsibility to elders. Temperance gives you the skill of keeping balance — between family and couple, work and home. And the Hanged Man teaches you to give way, but wisely: see through the other's eyes, without giving everything away.

At the family bakery they're deciding who works over the holidays. One partner's father has already decided: you both. The one whose family it is wants to stay silent, as usual. The other says gently: “We'll come in the morning. But the evening of the thirty-first is ours.” The father grumbles but agrees, and you spend New Year's Eve together. **The family business doesn't swallow your couple, because you know how to give way — but not on everything.**

Peace in a family often rests on the same side always giving way. Balance is convenient when one person pays for it: someone always works the holidays, always agrees, always understands. Resentment builds silently. Everyone is happy except the one who gave way to everyone.

items.title: The old and the new

captions.M: Opening the business to the world

items.meaning: Your family business lives in balance: respect for the elders, freedom for you, and something new for the world.
text: A family business is no museum for you: Judgement leads to carrying on what the elders began — a farm, a craft, a family name. It can be carried on in different ways, and Temperance binds you through a knack for keeping the balance between generations without offending anyone. And the World helps you open the business to the world: a broad view in which the family craft goes beyond the home village.

The vineyard one partner's family has worked for three generations passes to you. The father wants everything to stay as it was. The three of you sit down and agree: the old varieties and the cellar are his; the new direction and sales abroad are yours. A couple of years later the father's wine still sells to the neighbours, and yours in three countries. **The old business in your family doesn't fight the new: you've found a measure that leaves room for everyone.**

Balance between generations rests on concessions, and they aren't always mutual. If the elders go on deciding while you smooth things over, freedom stays a matter of words, and the broad view a dream. One of you is always making peace, the other always waiting. The vineyard thrives, and you two are still asking permission to plant a new variety.

items.title: Returning to a calling

captions.R1: A star that guides you both

items.meaning: You give each other back forgotten callings and believe in them before their owner does.
text: Judgement at work is a call that sounds from far away: a childhood calling, the family trade, what you're drawn to even though you've long done something else. The Star between you helps you return to it — faith in each other and a shared hope that it's not too late to dream. And the Lovers find the words for that faith: “you can”, “I'm proud of you”, “let's try” are said plainly and warmly in your couple.

The piano from one partner's parents' flat has stood closed for fifteen years. One evening the other lifts the lid and asks: “Play something. I want to hear you play.” The fingers don't remember at once, but by the end of winter there's a small concert for friends at your home. **One partner's calling becomes a shared star for you, not someone else's business.**

A calling can turn out to be someone else's expectation. The family's voice is easily passed off as your own call — “everyone in our family is an engineer”, “Grandma dreamed of it” — and then the star shines not for you but for those waiting for a report. Inspiration turns into a demand, and “I'm proud of you” into “you must”. The music-school diploma hangs on the wall like a debt to a grandmother.

items.title: A calling with passion
items.meaning: Your callings come late and loudly, and the other doesn't silence that call but helps you answer it.
text: Judgement at work is a call you answer wholeheartedly: a calling that waited a long time, a second birth in your work. You give each other hope on this path — the Star binds you through belief in the other's dream.
