And you know how to want passionately: the Devil lets you admit that you need this work so badly it takes your breath away.

Midway through their career one of you decides to become a pilot. Friends smile politely, relatives shake their heads. In the evening they say to the other: “I want this so much I can't sleep. Is it madness?” The other answers: “It's a calling. Go.” Two years of training, exams, debts — and the first solo flight, which the other watches from the ground, head tilted back. **You own your calling aloud with all your passion, and the other doesn't ask you to say it more quietly.**

Passion for a calling can crowd out everything else. If the call matters more than anything, the other becomes a spectator, and the hope they gave turns into an obligation to believe. The desire swallows money, time, conversation. The plane is in the sky, and the other stands alone on the ground for longer and longer.

items.title: Five generations in the attic

captions.R: A calling that comes from the family

items.meaning: An old house, letters in the attic, a grandfather's tools — your roots don't drag you back, they give you strength.
text: Judgement is in both your work and between you. At work it gives a calling that stretches back through the family: a craft, a profession, a place tied to kin. Between you it becomes roots — shared celebrations, relatives, all you've lived through together, which holds more firmly than any promise. And you understand each other as kin do, without words: the Hermit leaves your conversations quiet and deep.

The old village house where five generations of one partner's family lived has long stood empty. You go there in summer and barely speak for a week: you sort out the attic, find letters, photographs, a grandfather's tools. On the last evening you decide the house will be your summer home, and the tools will move to your workshop in town. **Your family line doesn't drag you back but gives you support: you return to your roots in order to go further.**

The voices of ancestors can drown out your own. If every decision echoes with “what will the family say”, “that's not how we do things”, your own “I want” can no longer be heard. Grievances against relatives build up silently, because talking about them is awkward. Portraits of five generations hang in the house, and not a single photo of the two of you together.

items.title: A family secret

captions.R: Work that carries on the family line
captions.R1: Roots and all you've lived through

items.meaning: Family history is alive for you: you dig it up together and treat what you find with care.
text: Judgement repeats on your line: at work it leads to work that carries on the family line — a family craft, a family business, a legacy. Between you it's roots, memory, everything lived through together. And you guard the family's secrets sensitively, as the Moon bids: you find them, understand them, but don't bring them into the light without need.

Sorting through one partner's grandfather's papers, you find letters nobody in the family knew about: the grandfather had a first love and a whole life before Gran. You read them together, all night long. In the morning you decide: don't tell the family yet, keep the letters in a separate folder and maybe one day write a book about it. **Family secrets don't frighten you: you uncover them together, and with care.**

Old family secrets cast a shadow on the present too. If you look for hidden meaning in every find, the past starts to explain everything — your quarrels, choices, fears. The relatives take offence that something is being kept from them, and the Moon fills in what's missing. The folder of letters grows, and about your own secrets you've stopped talking.

items.title: A garden that waits

captions.R: Work on the big map of the world
captions.R1: A home that grows and waits

items.meaning: Wherever your work takes you, you have a garden that waits, and a quiet you long to come back to.
text: Your work lives on the big map: the World at work gives projects in different countries, long contracts, life in two cities. But you have one set of roots — the Empress gathers you in a home that grows, gets lovelier and waits for your return. And your homecoming is quiet, like the Hermit's: after the road you need quiet for two, not a crowd of guests.

A year's contract abroad is behind you. You open the gate, and the garden a neighbour has been looking after greets you with overgrown apple trees. On the first evening you barely talk: you walk through the rooms, touch things, drink tea on the veranda. Only before bed does one say: “You know, in any country I count the days to this veranda.” **Your world is big, but you have one set of roots — a home where everything grows and waits for you both.**

A home can become a museum you visit on holidays. If work keeps calling further away, the garden grows without its owners, and the quiet after the road becomes the only thing you share. One lives more and more there, the other here. The garden blooms for the neighbour who waters it.

items.title: Bridge built, heading home
items.meaning: One partner's big job is seen through far from home, and they come back to where they were chosen and awaited.
text: The World at work means completion for you: a big project seen through, a bridge built in another country, a cycle that has closed. After such work you come back to the main thing — the Lovers bind you through a choice you make for each other again and again. And between homecomings you grow the home as the Empress does: caringly, generously, so there's somewhere to come back to.

For three years one of you built a bridge in another country. On the day the first car drives across it, they're offered the next contract — an even bigger one. They call the other, who hears the wind on the line and a voice asking: “Tell me you're waiting.” — “I am. And the garden's in bloom.” By early summer they're home, in a garden that grew without them. **One partner's greatest success ends not with a new contract but with a return to your shared home.**

The one who returns may not recognise a home that grew without them. While one was finishing their big job, the other grew a garden, habits, new friends — and now each has to find their place anew. The Lovers expect everything to be as before, but the before is gone. The garden blooms, and the one who came back walks through it like a guest, afraid to touch anything.

items.title: A tree and lanterns

captions.R1: A love that chose someone different

items.meaning: You come from different worlds and know how to celebrate both: each sees the other's customs through their eyes.
text: Your life knows no borders: the World brings work with different countries, moves, a life where your native tongue is just one of several. You chose each other despite the difference — the Lovers bind you through love for someone unlike yourself. And the Hanged Man helps you get along: each is ready to see the other's custom through their eyes and accept it as their own.

One grew up where New Year is the main holiday, the other where the main one is a spring festival of lights. In the first years you argued over what to celebrate. Now you have two holidays: in winter a tree and a festive table, in spring lanterns and dumplings made to one partner's mother's recipe. Friends come to both and no longer remember who's from where. **Different cultures don't argue in your couple: each is ready to see the holiday through the other's eyes.**

It's usually the one who moved who gives way to the other's world. They take on the other's customs and put their own away in a cupboard, the wide world narrows to one, and love demands giving up roots. Homesickness hides behind a smile. There are two holidays on the calendar, but you only truly celebrate one.

items.title: Freedom by mutual agreement

captions.R1: A choice made again and again

items.meaning: A big world and plenty of freedom don't stop you choosing each other again and again.
text: The World stands at two of your points. In success it gives scale without borders: international projects, moves, work that leaves you missing home. In the common language it teaches you to agree broadly: without pressure, respecting each one's freedom, with duties split in half. And between the two Worlds stand the Lovers — the choice of each other, made anew every time.

Six months on another continent — that's the offer one of you receives. You don't argue but sit down to write an agreement: how often you'll call, when the other will fly out, what each does with the freed-up time, what needs no reporting. The last clause: “at any moment you can say: I'm not doing well, come.” **Freedom doesn't threaten love for you, because you write the agreements about it together.**

An agreement about freedom can turn out to be an agreement for one. The one who left uses it generously, the one who stayed cautiously, and equality becomes a formality. The broad view becomes an imposed one: “but we agreed.” Jealousy smoulders beneath words about trust. On paper everything is fair, but you live by it differently.

items.title: Distance that saves up words
items.meaning: Work sends you to different cities, and a plainly spoken “I miss you” shortens any distance.
text: Your work often knows no borders: the World in success calls you to business trips, rotation shifts, work in another country or with people from all over the globe. Distance doesn't frighten you, because your closeness is built the Hermit's way — deep talks, the ability to be alone without losing the connection. The Hermit holds you even a thousand miles apart. And your language is the Lovers: “I miss you”, “I love you”, “I'm waiting” are said plainly, without embarrassment.

The third week of a rotation shift. The evening call lasts two hours: not about the weather or work but about the book each is reading in their own city, and what stayed with them. At the end one says: “You know, I miss you more than last time.” The reunion ten days later feels as if you hadn't seen each other for a year. **Distance doesn't cool you; it saves up words you later say face to face.**

Two worlds may never come together. Each has their own life, acquaintances and routine, and solitude becomes a habit of living without the other. Calls turn into weather reports, plain words into routine phrases, and jealousy fills in the rest. A reunion after a separation lasts three days, and for two of them you're getting used to each other all over again.

items.title: Told on the first call
items.meaning: You travel the world a lot and trust each other so much that you even report temptations first.
text: Your work spans the globe: the World at work gives business trips, projects in other countries, life between airports. Your trust is deep and quiet all the same — the Hermit binds you through an understanding that needs few words and no constant calls. And your honesty is special: the Devil lets you talk even about temptations — about what pulled at you but didn't happen.

A conference abroad, late evening in the bar. A colleague openly suggests to one of you that they continue the evening alone together. They politely decline, go back to their room and the first thing they do is call the other: “I've just been propositioned. The answer was no. I want you to hear it from me, not from someone else.” A pause at the other end, then laughter: “Thanks for telling me. Good night.” **Temptations far from home don't become secrets in your couple: you tell of them on the very first call.**

Honesty about temptations can become grounds for interrogation. If every confession is met with suspicion, the confessions stop, and the Devil switches from honesty to control: “who are you with there?”, “why aren't you answering?”. The silence that was trust becomes a wall of silence. The calls from business trips get shorter, and the questions afterwards longer.

items.title: Through the waiting one's eyes
items.meaning: Your work runs on a big scale, and the talk at home is short and about what matters — including how the other waited.
text: Your work runs on a big scale: the World gives international projects, big ventures completed, recognition without borders. But you don't measure success by that alone. The Hanged Man teaches you both to see the situation from the other side — through the eyes of the one who stays home, waits, keeps the household going. You speak of this quietly, like the Hermit: few words, but each about what matters.

After six months on a big project abroad, the one who worked there comes home victorious: contract signed, bonus, interviews. On the first evening they don't talk about their successes but ask: “And what was it like for you — those six months?” The answer is long, and they listen to the end. **One partner's big success is always looked at from the other side too — through the eyes of the one who waited.**

One partner's scale easily overshadows the other's life. The World calls ever further, giving way becomes a habit, and the one who waits talks about themselves less and less — their quiet affairs seem small beside the big ones. Silence hides tiredness. One has a world map with flags, the other a calendar with crossed-out days.

items.title: Feeling the landing
items.meaning: You're often apart, but never coldly: you sense each other even from halfway round the world.
text: Your work knows no borders: the World at work gives long-haul flights, international projects, life across two time zones. Waiting isn't hard for all that, because the Hanged Man binds you through a rare ability to sense each other at a distance and not blame each other for being apart. And you understand each other by instinct: the Moon makes your language subtle, almost wordless.

Half of each month one of you spends in the sky: they're cabin crew. The other doesn't check the flight schedule, yet somehow wakes in the night at the very moment the plane touches down somewhere in Seoul. A minute later a message arrives: “Landed. Are you awake?” — “I am now. As if someone woke me.” **You sense each other at a distance, and so your waiting isn't empty but warm.**

Instinct at a distance stands in for a real conversation. If everything is clear without words, words stop being spoken, and each lives through their worries alone, hoping the other will sense them. Waiting becomes a sacrifice nobody mentions. You guess the landing time, but don't know what's on the other's mind.

items.title: Presents from half a world away
items.meaning: Spices from Morocco, a blanket from Scotland and a passion that partings don't cool — that's your homecoming.
text: Partings are part of the job for you. The World at work sends you to different countries — business trips, rotations, projects on the other side of the globe. Partings don't cool you, because the Devil gives an attraction that only grows stronger at a distance. And your care is the kind the Empress loves: bring, treat, wrap up, fill the house.

From every trip one of you brings something for the house: spices from Morocco, a blanket from Scotland, coffee from Ethiopia. The suitcase isn't unpacked yet, but the kitchen already smells of new spices, and the other is cooking dinner to a recipe sent from the road. Until morning you can't tear yourselves apart. **Your homecomings are always festive: passion doesn't cool from partings, and care is carried across half the world.**

Presents from different countries gradually start replacing presence. The less often you're together, the dearer the souvenirs and the less talk about how the other lives while the first is away. Passion at meetings is stormy, jealousy in separation quiet and bitter. The house is full of things from all over the world, and half the bed is too often left cold.

items.title: You both know how to wait
items.meaning: Distant contracts don't break your attraction: whoever waits doesn't count the days aloud, and whoever leaves comes back.
text: You both know how to wait, and it isn't a sacrifice: the Hanged Man makes patience and give-and-take your shared language. Waiting is needed, because the World at work sends you to different countries — contracts, expeditions, projects on the other side of the globe. And the Devil brings you back: an attraction that doesn't weaken with distance, and an attachment you both know about.

For six months one of you works on another continent. The other doesn't count the days aloud or write “when are you coming?”. And when it's the other's turn to leave — for a three-month placement — the first waits silently too. Your reunions after time apart are such that friends can't get hold of you for days. **Your attraction withstands distance, because you both know how to wait and to give way.**

Waiting nobody asked for turns into a bill. If it's always one who waits, patience becomes sacrifice, and attraction a wish to hold on: calls on schedule, reports, jealousy of the other's world. The Hanged Man stays silent, the Devil demands. Your reunions are as stormy as ever, and the farewells ever heavier.

items.title: Six months apart

captions.M: An agreement on each one's freedom

items.meaning: You live six months apart and six together — that's what you agreed, and your passion is only stronger for it.
text: The World stands twice for you: at work it gives work on several continents; in conversation, an agreement on freedom in which nobody belongs to anybody. Between them is the Devil, a passion distance doesn't hinder. Strong attraction and great freedom get along in your couple, because you wrote the rules of this life together.

From April to September one of you runs projects in Asia; from October to March you live together. Friends don't understand how that's possible. You don't always understand it yourselves, but every autumn, meeting the other at the airport, you feel what you felt in the first year. You review the agreement every spring, and so far it suits you both. **Your freedom is written into the agreement, but passion isn't — it turns up by itself every time.**

An agreement on freedom is tested by jealousy. If at some point one wants to hold on and the other to stay free, the broad agreement turns into an argument over who broke it. Passion turns into a wish to possess, freedom into coldness. Six months apart become seven, then eight, and nobody says it's no longer what you agreed.

items.title: Calling in the same minute

captions.R1: Sensing each other at a distance

items.meaning: Six hours' time difference doesn't stop you calling each other in the very same minute.
text: Between you there's something hard to explain to outsiders: the Moon binds you through an instinct that works even across thousands of miles. Handy, because the World at work sends you to different cities and countries — projects, business trips, contracts without borders. So that instinct doesn't lose its way, you need plain words, and the Lovers give them: you speak openly about love and about worry.

Six hours' time difference, no agreed times for calls. And yet again and again you dial each other in the very same minute, and both hear the engaged tone. You laugh and call back. This time the other says at once: “I dreamed you were unhappy.” — “Not unhappy. Just missing you.” **Distance doesn't stop you sensing each other, and plain words keep the instinct from losing its way.**

At a distance imagination starts working against you. The Moon fills in what can't be seen: someone else's party, new acquaintances, a chill in a message. Plain words are put off until you meet, and jealousy has time to grow. A photo from someone else's party is studied longer than the whole of yesterday's conversation lasted.

items.title: A jealous dream, said aloud

captions.R1: A bond that's like a dream

items.meaning: Your separations are long and your bond subtle, almost dreamlike, and you're not afraid to name even the fear of loss.
text: Your life runs on a big map: the World brings work in different countries, long trips, separations. The bond between you is almost dreamlike — the Moon makes it subtle, intuitive, full of images and premonitions. And everything dark that's born of separation you bring into the light: the Devil lets you speak plainly even about jealousy and the fear of loss.

A call across eight time zones. One of you, after a silence, admits: “For three nights I've dreamed you're there with someone. It's silly, but I feel awful.” The other neither takes offence nor laughs: “Thank you for telling me. Shall I tell you who I really spend my evenings with here?” And they do — about colleagues, dull dinners, counting the days. The dream doesn't come back. **Even jealous dreams are told aloud in your couple, and they lose their power.**

A fear once told easily becomes grounds for control: the confession turns into a demand for reports, honesty into checks, and the Moon suggests ever new suspicions. The wish to possess grows with each separation. One day instead of “I dreamed” comes “show me your messages”, and nobody tells their dreams any more.

items.title: Passports and one kitchen
items.meaning: Work carries you all over the world, and you meet in your own kitchen and spend the first hour in silence.
text: The World is in both your work and your relationship. At work it gives scale without borders: negotiations in different countries, projects in several languages. Between you it becomes a shared philosophy of life — the same attitude to freedom, the road, people. And when the big world finally lets you both go, the Hermit gives you the main thing: quiet for two, where you needn't speak any language at all.

One flies in from Singapore, the other from Berlin, and you meet at home at almost the same time. The suitcases stay in the hall. You silently make coffee, sit on the windowsill and look at your courtyard, which hasn't changed at all in these three weeks. The first words come only an hour later. **You both belong to the big world, and to each other in a quiet where no language is needed.**

Two big worlds may never intersect. If each has their own map, the shared philosophy becomes a reason not to agree — “we both believe in freedom, after all” — and quiet becomes a habit of living apart. Meetings get shorter. This year your passports have seen more countries than you've seen of each other.

items.title: A route by hunch

captions.R1: One big picture of the world

items.meaning: Your routes are born of hunches, and a shared picture of the world makes any country feel a little like yours.
text: The World repeats in your couple: at work it gives work without borders, between you one big picture of life in which any country can become home. And the Moon tells you how to choose the route. You trust your hunches and go where you're drawn, even if on the map it looks strange.

The holiday is a week away, and there are no tickets. In the evening one of you says: “For some reason I'm drawn to Georgia.” The other laughs: “And I wanted mountains. They have mountains there, right?” Three days later you're in a small village where you don't know a soul, and by the end of the week you've been invited to the neighbours' wedding. **Your routes are born of hunches, and that makes the world seem even bigger.**

A hunch can call you ever further from home. If every vague wish turns into a trip, life becomes an endless road with no room left for roots and ordinary days. A shared view of the world becomes a conviction that home is boring. You feel at home in a dozen countries and like strangers in your own flat.

items.title: Freedom in a firm frame

captions.R: A free path with no timetable

items.meaning: Work with no timetable coexists with a home that keeps one, and decisions are made after quiet thought.
text: Your work rarely runs to a timetable: the Fool gives freelance professions, orders whenever they come, ventures started from scratch on inspiration. You can afford such freedom because there's support at home: the Emperor gives the couple order, rules, a sense that the rear is secure. And you make decisions like the Hermit — without unnecessary words, after quiet thought.

Orders come to one of you in fits and starts, and the schedule jumps around. But at home there's a firm routine devised together: Monday for bills and plans, Wednesday a shared dinner with no phones, Friday no work at all. When a month turns out empty there's no panic: a reserve for exactly this was put aside back in spring. **Freedom at work is possible for you because there's a firm frame at home that you built together.**

A frame can become a cage for the one who loves freedom. Order demands accounts, rules sprout new rules, and the one who lives without a timetable starts to feel watched. Talking about it isn't done, and discontent goes inward. The freelancer accounts for every tenner spent.

items.title: A safety net under the leap
items.meaning: One of you takes risks on instinct, the other spreads a safety net in advance, and the home doesn't shake.
text: Your work loves freedom and risk: under the Fool come projects without certainties, flexible hours, decisions “from scratch”. The risk doesn't bring the home down, because at home the Emperor rules — order, reserves, clear rules you came up with together. And when to take a risk and when not, the Moon often tells you: you decide on instinct, and your instinct is shared.

The offer is risky: leaving a stable contract for a project of your own. The one taking the risk says: “I feel we have to.” The other answers: “So do I. But first we put aside six months to live on.” Three months go on building the cushion, and only then is the resignation handed in. The project goes hard, but the home doesn't shake. **Your risks always come with a backup: one leaps on instinct, the other spreads the net in advance.**

Where one takes risks and the other insures, secrets easily appear. The one who leaps starts hiding debts so as not to hear “we told you so”; the one who insures starts controlling every expense. Instinct gives way to suspicion. The net is spread, only under it there's now a pile of unpaid bills that one of you knows about.

items.title: A home on wheels

captions.M: Comfort at any point on the way

items.meaning: Your work and life are on the road, and you carry comfort with you — a blanket, a saucepan and care for each other.
text: Your work has no address: the Fool at work gives freelance professions, remote orders, life without an office. You chose the road together — the Chariot binds you through movement, shared routes, a readiness to set off for places you've never been. And you carry home with you: the Empress makes care your shared language, and comfort appears at any point on the way.

Your home is a converted van. In the morning you both work at a fold-down table with a view of the mountains; by lunchtime you move on to a lake. In the evening soup simmers on a little stove, on the bed lies a blanket knitted by one partner's grandmother, and on the window sits a pot of basil that has travelled with you for over two thousand kilometres. **Even on the road you have a home: a blanket, a saucepan and someone who'll feed you.**

Nomadic life can rest on one partner's care. If one works and drives while the other cooks, does the washing in roadside launderettes and looks for places to park, freedom quickly becomes unequal. The Fool dislikes chores, the Chariot dislikes stopping. The basil on the window is still alive, and the one who waters it dreams more and more often of a flat with a bath.

items.title: A breather on the road
items.meaning: A month by one lake in the middle of a long road — you know how to fit the route to the other's tiredness.
text: Your free work is on wheels: the Fool leads to work without an office or schedule, with a readiness to up sticks in a single evening. Your road is shared — the Chariot binds you through movement, routes, the thrill of new places. And so that the road doesn't wear you out, there's the Hanged Man: the ability to stop for the other's sake and give way when they need a breather.

Three months on the road, and somewhere among the northern lakes the other suddenly says: “I'm sick of new places. I want to live in one house for a month and see the same lake every morning.” The first is still full of plans for the north, but puts the map away. You rent a cabin on the shore for a month. Every morning the same lake, and after three weeks it's the other who takes out the map. **On the road you know how to stop in time if the other needs a breather.**

Stopping for one can become a permanent halt. If it's always the one who loves the road who gives way, their thrill turns to longing and freedom to a feeling that life is passing them by. If it's always the one who tires, it turns to exhaustion. The map lies in the glovebox, and each waits for the other to take it out.

items.title: Home is where the signal is

captions.R: Working with no office or schedule
captions.R1: The road as a shared home
captions.M: Measuring life on a world scale

items.meaning: You live light and on the move, and the shared route matters more to you than any address.
text: You work without ties: the Fool in success gives a free schedule, remote orders, the knack of earning where others only holiday. The Chariot brings you close — the road as a shared home: you're both quick to set off, and moving side by side holds you together. And you measure life in the World's language — broadly, without borders, with the feeling that the whole world is open to two.

Monday morning: laptops on a café table in a city where you've been for three weeks, the internet barely breathing, the sea outside the window. One curses the connection, the other is already looking for a co-working space on the next street. By lunch the work is done, and in the evening you look at the map for where to move on next month. **Home is where you both are, and work is wherever there's a signal.**

When things are hard, it's easier to move than to sort it out. Debts and unfinished business stay in the last city, talk of the future is put off until the next stop, and any quarrel is settled by a change of scenery. There are roots nowhere. The suitcases have been half unpacked for three years now.

items.title: A net beneath the leap
items.meaning: You leap into the unknown boldly because chance loves your couple, and you decide with your hearts, together.
text: Your careers rarely go to plan: the Fool drops the secure for the interesting and isn't afraid to end up at zero. Such a leap is survivable for the lucky, and the Wheel of Fortune gives you exactly that feeling of shared luck: chance loves your couple and throws up people, orders, coincidences. You decide in the Lovers' language — with your hearts and together, and you laugh at your fears together.

Monday. One of you comes home jobless — they quit, because they couldn't take any more. The other looks at them, laughs and opens a bottle: “To freedom. What shall we do?” The first commission comes ten days later, from someone you happened to chat with in the post-office queue. **You're not afraid to start from zero, because beside you is someone who laughs with you, not at you.**

Lightness is costly if one pays for it. The leaps repeat, debts and missed deadlines are put down to luck, and decisions are made on the spur of the moment, on a wave of delight. The one holding the net tires of laughing and starts counting. One leaps, the other catches every time — and the net is already full of knots.

items.title: A crazy wish, said aloud

captions.R: Free work without a safety net

items.meaning: Your craziest wishes are spoken aloud, and luck somehow loves exactly those.
text: Your craziest wishes are spoken aloud: the Devil makes the “I want” in your conversations bold and unashamed. They come true surprisingly often, because the Wheel of Fortune binds you through shared good luck — chance loves your couple in particular. And at work the Fool gives freedom: projects without a safety net, decisions from scratch, a readiness to leap where others don't even look.

Dinner, a glass of wine, and one of you says: “I want to open a bar on the roof of this building.” The other laughs — and then asks: “Why not?” A week later it turns out the roof is up for rent, and the upstairs neighbour knows someone with a licence. By summer the bar is open, and in the evenings you can't move for people. **A crazy idea spoken aloud over dinner stands every chance of becoming a business in your couple.**

Wishes without brakes lead to debt. If every crazy “I want” is instantly turned into a venture, sooner or later luck turns away, and freedom turns into loans and open commitments. Admitting a failure is harder than admitting a wish. You've had three rooftop bars already, and only one of them is still open.

items.title: Closing without drama

captions.R1: Letting go of the outworn together

items.meaning: Your freelance ventures start easily and end honestly — after a quiet evening alone with yourselves.
text: You let go better than many: Death, which unites you, makes parting with the outworn calm and even bright. This skill comes in handy given the way you work. The Fool leads to free work with no schedules or certainties — easy to start and just as easy to end. And you say goodbye to it like the Hermit: without noise, after a quiet evening alone with yourselves.

The podcast one of you ran for five years has stopped bringing joy. The decision to close it isn't discussed over the kitchen table. The other simply notices that recording has been put off for three weeks and one evening says: “Maybe it's time?” The answer comes after a long pause: “It's time.” You record the last episode together, with laughter and thanks to the listeners. **You don't cling to what has served its time: lightness lets you drop it, and quiet lets you say goodbye properly.**

The habit of dropping things can reach what matters. When any venture can be closed in an evening, the hard ones get closed before they can bear fruit; responsibility frightens, and the way out is always the same — start again. Each decides alone and announces the decision ready-made. In the cupboard stands a box of started and abandoned projects, and its lid no longer shuts.

items.title: Soup from whatever there is
items.meaning: You've started from zero more than once, and there was always soup, a table and faith in each other.
text: You've started from zero together more than once: the Tower has bound you through troubles lived through, which you came out of holding on to each other. The troubles aren't accidental, since the Fool at work leads to ventures at your own risk — freelancing, projects without contracts, schemes nobody believes in. And the Empress keeps you warm: in any crisis you'll find food, warmth and a table where the two of you can sit.

A client disappears without paying for three months' work. The one who was cheated sits in the kitchen staring at the wall. The other opens the nearly empty fridge and half an hour later puts on the table a soup made from whatever was there — potatoes, an onion, the last of the chicken. “Eat. We'll think tomorrow.” The soup turns out to be the best of the year. **When the ground goes from under your feet, you have a shared table at which to start again.**

Lightness without a cushion makes each blow heavier. If there's no reserve and risk is a habit, crises follow one another, and care turns into eternal rescue: the other feeds, consoles and carries, while the first jumps again. Not everyone finds it funny any more. Each new failure is met with the same soup from leftovers, and nobody feels like joking about it any more.

items.title: Experience already paid for

captions.R: The freedom to start from scratch

items.meaning: Falls you've lived through together made you wiser, not angrier, and in a failure you look for a lesson, not a culprit.
text: The freedom to start from scratch is in your blood: the Fool leads to risky projects, businesses of your own, leaps without a safety net. Leaps sometimes end in falls, and the Tower binds you through exactly those — collapses lived through together, after which you only grew closer. And you talk about falls as the Hanged Man does: turning them over and finding a meaning in trouble that isn't visible at once.

One partner's own studio closes after two years: the clients didn't come, the debts stayed. In the evening the other doesn't say “we told you so”. They take out a sheet of paper and suggest writing down everything this failure has taught you. The list comes out long: how not to hire, how to do the sums, whom not to trust. The sheet goes into a frame. **Falls don't turn into reproaches in your couple: you look on them as experience already paid for.**

Patience with the other's leaps isn't endless. If one keeps starting from scratch and the other keeps finding meaning in the failure, the one who bears it sooner or later tires of being wise. The Fool doesn't count debts, the Tower gets you used to disasters. There are three framed lessons on the wall now, and the next leap is discussed as if they weren't there.

items.title: Travelling light after a fall

captions.M: The world as a shared home

items.meaning: Collapses lived through together made you light on your feet: you no longer fear losing things, and the world is open to you.
text: You're not afraid of starting from scratch: the Fool gives freelance projects, decisions without a safety net, a light attitude to losses. This lightness was hard-won — the Tower binds you through collapses you lived through together, after which you stopped clinging to walls. And the World has made your view broad: home for you is wherever you both are, even at the far edge of the map.

After your shared business went under and you had to sell the flat, you sat on your suitcases in an empty room for a long time. Then one said: “You know, I have nothing left to lose. Let's go and see the world.” For two years you've worked remotely from different countries: a month in Georgia, winter in Thailand, spring in Portugal. You own two rucksacks' worth of things. **Having survived a collapse, you stopped fearing loss, and the world opened up to you.**

Lightness after loss turns into reluctance to build. If any home seems temporary and any venture something that will collapse anyway, you stop investing in anything long-term. Freedom becomes a way of promising nothing. You still own two rucksacks' worth of things, and the talk about where you want to grow old keeps being put off.

items.title: A midweek picnic
items.meaning: Your free schedule turns into midweek picnics and declarations of love for no reason at all.
text: You have no boss: the Fool chose free work for you, your own projects and a schedule you draw up yourselves. This freedom isn't lonely — the Sun binds you through joy, warmth and love of life that you know how to share. And love sounds light and frequent in your couple, as the Lovers bid: confessing, praising, saying “how good that you exist” costs you nothing.

Wednesday, midday, sunshine. Both of you have work, but neither has a boss. One texts the other: “Picnic in the park in an hour?” — “Already packing the basket.” For two hours you lie on the grass, eat strawberries and make plans for the summer. Then each finishes their work by evening, and nobody regrets the lost time. **Freedom at work turns into joy for two in your couple, not a lonely race.**

Carefree is fine until the bills arrive. If every sunny day matters more than an order, money starts running out unexpectedly, and light declarations don't help you agree who'll be earning. The Sun dislikes anxious conversations. The midweek picnics carry on, only now the basket gets packed with whatever's left.

items.title: Living brightly
items.meaning: Dawn in Istanbul on a whim, work from anywhere — you allow yourselves a bright life and aren't shy about it.
text: You have no bosses: the Fool leads to freelance work, your own projects, life without a timetable. This freedom is sunny — the Sun binds you through joy, love of life, a warmth everyone around can see. And your wishes are bold: the Devil lets you want the vivid — passion, luxury, adventure — and say so plainly.

Friday, midnight. One of you, lying on the floor among cushions, says: “I want to watch the sunrise in Istanbul. Tomorrow.” The other is already opening a ticket site. Twelve hours later you're sitting on the roof of a little hotel overlooking the Bosphorus, drinking strong tea and kissing until the sun comes up. On Monday you both work from the same hotel. **Your joy is bold: you want to live brightly and hide it neither from each other nor from the world.**

A bright life without brakes is expensive. If every “I want” is granted at once, money goes out faster than it comes in, and freedom turns into debts and missed deadlines. The Sun dislikes counting, the Fool answering for things. You've seen a couple of dozen sunrises in different cities, and once again there's nothing to pay the rent with.

items.title: Freedom for two
items.meaning: A life without bosses and complete trust hold you together — as long as you do agree about the future.
text: The Fool is in both your work and between you. At work he gives a life without timetables or bosses: freelancing, your own projects, the ability to start from zero without fear. Between you he becomes friendship and complete trust — the kind where nothing needs checking or proving. And you share silence like the Hermit: being quiet together isn't awkward for you but calm.

Tuesday, eleven in the morning. One works on the balcony, the other in the kitchen, and in three hours you haven't said a word to each other, except that someone silently put a cup of coffee on the windowsill. At lunchtime you suddenly decide to drop everything and drive to the lake — because you can. In the evening both finish their work late into the night, content. **You're both free and give the other freedom, and your closeness is the silence of two friends who aren't bored by quiet.**

Two freedoms side by side easily become two lonelinesses. If nothing is promised and nothing discussed, the relationship turns into a cohabitation that's comfortable but leaves unclear who you are to each other. The serious conversation keeps being put off: why, everything's fine. You share a flat, a fridge and the internet, but you've never shared a decision about the future.

items.title: A barge full of books
items.meaning: Freedom, friendship and shared fantasies make your life light — as long as one of you sometimes looks at the bills.
text: Two Fools on one line make freedom squared: dream work with no timetable and no certainties, and between you a friendship where nothing needs proving. And you speak the Moon's language: fantasies, plans that look more like fairy tales, games only the two of you understand. You're two dreamers who find it easy to be together.

Sunday morning, the bed strewn with maps and notebooks. You're working out how you'll live on an old barge and take tourists along the river with a bookshop on deck. The idea seems mad, but by lunch you already have a name for the barge, a menu and a list of books. In the evening one of you does, after all, open a spreadsheet and look up what a barge costs. **You're two dreamers, and you're not ashamed to dream things up together.**

Fantasies with nothing under them end in debt. If neither likes doing sums, dreams multiply and reality piles up in the letterbox; freedom turns into uncertainty, and lightness into a way of not noticing problems. Each hopes the other will sort it out. The barge was bought long ago in your dreams, and the rent is two months overdue.

captions.J: Raise them in warmth and plenty

items.meaning: For the young ones you create a home with plenty of everything: food, care, attention, celebrations and time.
text: You raise the young ones the way generous gardeners raise a garden. The Empress fills your tandem with care: a warm home, good dinners, celebrations remembered for years, arms always ready to hug. You share the care so that the child gets it from both of you and sees parents who delight in growth — theirs, your own, the family's. Plenty turns cramped when there is too much of it: the child is spoiled, decided for, shielded from every difficulty, and for each other you have only the time after they have fallen asleep. A garden where everything grows for one shoot forgets the people who planted it.

captions.J: Hold the home like a solid wall

items.meaning: You hold the home together firmly: roles are assigned, rules are clear, and the young one knows someone has their back.
text: Your parenting tandem runs like a well-ordered household: roles are assigned, the schedule is clear, decisions are made rather than left hanging. The Emperor gives the child the main thing — the feeling of a wall at their back: the parents won't lose their heads, they'll protect and sort things out. You support each other with deeds, not words: one does the pick-up from training, the other cooks dinner, and nobody tries to take all the credit. The wall becomes a fence when rules matter more than people: strictness without explanation, “because that's how it is”, two commanders fighting for the last word. The child grows up safe, but without a say.

captions.J: Speak to the young ones with one voice

items.meaning: Together you keep a shared code of rules, and the young one sees two mentors, not two camps.
text: You set the rules for the young ones together and never argue in front of the child: what is decided is decided by both. The Hierophant gathers your parenting tandem around a shared code — what time to be home, what is not up for debate, why elders are listened to. If one of you says “no”, the other will not overrule it behind their back but will talk it over in private first. The child sees two mentors with one voice and has no need to hunt for the one who will give in. The tandem grows heavy when the shared voice turns into a sermon in chorus: two-part lectures, “we know better”, and the child has no one left to bring their disagreement to.

captions.J: Show the young ones what love looks like

items.meaning: The young ones learn love from you not through words: they see how you look at each other, argue and make up.
text: You give the young ones the main lesson without even planning it: they watch how you treat each other. The Lovers keep you a couple first, even as parents — a kiss in the hallway, a shared joke at dinner, an honest “sorry” after an argument. You split duties evenly, and the child has no idea which of you is “in charge of upbringing”: both are. The tandem wobbles when the child becomes a witness or a judge of your quarrels: asked to pass on that dinner is ready, asked to choose whom to spend the weekend with. The love they were meant to see turns into a play in which they have been handed a role.

captions.J: Take the young ones along on the road

items.meaning: You parent as a team on the move: the young one rides with you rather than waiting until the adults are free.
text: As parents you work like a crew: each has their own task, and in a hard moment you stand back to back. The Chariot does not leave the child at home waiting for the adults to finish their business but takes them along — hiking, building the country cottage, to competitions where one of you shouts louder than the whole stand. The child sees two people pulling in one direction and standing up for their own no matter what. The crew starts to rock when the parents begin to compete — whose decision counts more, who is the better parent — and the child grows up feeling that they too are being driven to a finish line nobody asked them about.

captions.J: Be fair judges, not wardens

items.meaning: Your home runs on fair order: promises are kept, and the rules are the same for all, yourselves included.
text: As parents you negotiate like lawyers and keep your word like sentries. Justice divides duties fairly between you — who does the school run, who checks homework, who sorts out squabbles — and the child sees that “chores first, then screens” applies to the adults too. Promises are kept, punishment fits the offence, and both sides know how to apologise. Order becomes a barracks when every slip is met with a report: a hearing for every bad mark, a verdict for every misstep, two adults sitting as a full court. The child stops coming to you with the truth: they already know its price.

captions.J: Light the way with your own experience

items.meaning: You don't lead the young one by the hand but hold up a light you found alone, so they can make the way themselves.
text: Each of you first thinks a hard question through alone, and only then shares a conclusion tested on yourself: “look, you can get through here.” This is the Hermit's light: found without hints and raised high so the child can see where to step. You leave each other this silence and do not interrupt each other's thinking. Silence stops being a support when each shines only in their own window: you decide separately, don't share conclusions even with each other, and the child sees two lights but does not know which one to walk towards.

captions.J: Take over from each other in turn

items.meaning: You take turns like rowers: whoever is strong leads, and a slump is weathered by the two of you.
text: The weight of parenting passes from one of you to the other like a ship's watch. The Wheel of Fortune turns now to one, now to the other: one has a hard year at work, and the other does more with the child; next time it's the other way round. You don't count who has done more shifts, you step in when you see the other is spent. The child sees that a slump is no disaster: parents move, change jobs, rebuild their lives and stay on the same side. The support shakes when the wheel spins your moods too: today you are both kind and allow everything, tomorrow both irritable, and the child wonders what they did wrong, though it has nothing to do with them.

captions.J: Be a support that doesn't crush

items.meaning: You are a strong parenting team: both of you can take a blow, and neither pulls the young one to their side.
text: In parenting you hold each other up the way two people carry a heavy load: if one's hands falter, the other takes the weight. Strength makes you confident as parents: you stay calm when the child screams in a shop, and you don't panic when they bring bad news home from school. One of you can hand the lead to the other where the other is stronger, and the child sees adults with enough composure for any storm. The support starts to crush when strength is turned against each other: an argument about upbringing becomes a duel in front of the child, and they learn not composure but that whoever is louder is right.

captions.J: Care without dissolving into sacrifice

items.meaning: You give the child endless attention — as long as it is not at the expense of yourselves and each other.
text: You can do what few parents manage: stop and look through the child's eyes. The Hanged Man makes you patient, sensitive parents — ready to hear for the hundredth time about a falling-out with a friend, to give way when giving way is possible, to cover for each other without counting or reproach. The child sees grown-ups who know how to feel for others. Care becomes sacrifice when you give the child everything and leave nothing for yourselves or each other: the holiday cancelled, your own interests abandoned, no couple any more — only parents. Later the sacrifice sounds like a reproach, and the child grows up feeling they owe someone.

captions.J: Change as the young one grows

items.meaning: You don't cling to old rules: you change along with the child and help them through changes.
text: Your parenting starts afresh every few years: the toddler gives way to the schoolchild, the schoolchild to the teenager, and you boldly let go of rules that worked yesterday. Death gives your tandem the courage to change: you don't cling to how things were, and you help the child through a move, a new school, a first loss — honestly, without “don't cry, it's nothing”. You back each other decisively and without needless words. Changes wound when there are too many in a row: a new home, new rules, new jobs for you both — and all without a conversation. The child needs something that stays the same, and best of all if that is you.

captions.J: Reach agreement calmly, without shouting

items.meaning: Calm and united, you raise the child in a home where arguments are quiet and a middle is always found.
text: As parents you don't argue in raised voices in front of the child — not because it is forbidden, but because you know how to agree in other ways. Temperance keeps your parenting calm: decisions about the child come after a talk, grievances don't pile up, and one's strictness is balanced by the other's gentleness. The child grows up in an even climate and learns that disagreement is no disaster. The balance becomes a show when one always gives way for the sake of peace and the other doesn't notice. The child sees not agreement but polite silence, and remembers that feelings are best kept to oneself.

captions.J: Keep order without keeping them on a leash

items.meaning: As parents you are a strong, passionate couple: discipline at home and freedom the child gains as they grow.
text: Even as parents you remain first of all a couple — passionate, strong, with desires of your own that you don't hide from the child behind a screen of “we're just parents”. The Devil gives your tandem discipline and grip: a routine, order, clear rules, and within them the certainty that the child is safely protected. You talk honestly with them about hard things and don't pretend the world is safe. The grip becomes a chain when the child is drawn into your game: used to hold on to each other, guarded jealously from the other parent, won over with presents. The child ends up not protected but caught between two fires.

captions.J: Stick together when everything falls apart

items.meaning: In a storm you are a rock: the child knows that whatever collapses, you will stand beside them.
text: When something collapses — the flat floods, the nursery closes, the car breaks down in the middle of the motorway — you don't panic but stand side by side and deal with it. The Tower makes you strongest as parents when trouble strikes: decisions come fast, roles are shared out without words, and the child learns that a disaster is a task, not the end of the world. Together you make, mend and build, and the child is there with a screwdriver. The tandem cracks when the storm breaks between you: rows in front of the child, harsh words, a slammed door. A child remembers what is said at such moments longer than you do, and goes on waiting for the next thunderclap.

captions.J: Inspire each other and the young ones

items.meaning: You inspire by example: the child sees parents who are on fire with their work and believe in each other.
text: In your home the child sees two people who are on fire. The Star makes you inspiring parents: one rehearses for a concert, the other finishes an article, and both find time to come to the school play. You are not shy of tenderness in front of the children, you back each other's dreams, and the child learns that grown-ups have dreams too, and that they come true. The light becomes a shop window when the family lives for photographs: perfect celebrations for show, the child compared with friends' children, discontent hidden behind a smile. The child learns not to dream but to look the part.

captions.J: Sense the young one without words

items.meaning: You understand each other at a glance and sense what the child feels before they say it.
text: You discuss parenting matters with glances: one notices the child came home from school not quite themselves, the other is already putting the kettle on and holding back the questions. The Moon makes you perceptive parents: you hear what goes unsaid and know how to support without needless words. Your home is a little magical — with bedtime stories, made-up games and the right to fantasy. Perceptiveness turns into anxiety when you stop speaking aloud: decisions about the child are made through hints, grievances with each other are hidden, and the child feels the tension in the house without knowing where it comes from.

captions.J: Warm the young ones and be proud of them aloud

items.meaning: Together you are two suns: the child grows up in warmth, protected and sure that you are proud of them.
text: In your home the child is warmed from both sides. The Sun makes your tandem generous and dependable: celebrations on a grand scale, pride spoken aloud — “look what they've drawn!” — and the certainty that behind them stand two people who are always on their side. Between yourselves it is the same: each has their own work, and both rejoice when the other shines. The warmth becomes too much when it turns into smothering: every step watched, the child's wins claimed by the parents, their failures grieved more loudly than they grieve them themselves. It is hard to grow up under two suns when you also need some shade.

captions.J: Connect the young ones to their family line

items.meaning: You hold on to each other and to the family: the child grows up among generations, not just with you two.
text: You stand by each other whatever happens, and as parents all the more: if one gets something wrong with the child, the other does not bring it before the family court but helps put it right. Judgement ties your tandem to the family line: grandparents close by, family stories told at the table, and the child knows where they come from and who were the people whose surname they bear. You forgive each other's slips and make the big decisions together. The tandem loses its voice when the family decides for you: the elders say how to raise the child, which school to pick, whom to become, and you only pass it on. The child sees not two parents but messengers of someone else's will.

captions.J: Open up the wide world to the young ones

items.meaning: You raise children as equal partners: duties are split in half, and with you the young one sees how big the world is.
text: You share parenting half and half — no “that's not my job” and no keeping watch on each other. The World makes you one well-joined team: shared views on what matters, lots of talking, agreements that suit both. You open up the world to the child — trips, other languages, people from different countries at your table — and they see that their parents calmly accept both them and people unlike themselves. The whole closes in when your shared view becomes the only right one: other families “live wrong”, the child's friends are “the wrong crowd”, and any disagreement meets joint re-education. The wide world shrinks to the walls of your home.

captions.J: Be elders who are fun to be with

items.meaning: As elders you are light and playful: the young one sees two friends with whom trying new things isn't scary.
text: With you, the child isn't afraid of mistakes and has fun starting things. The Fool turns your tandem into a gang: a trip to another city on a whim, dinner in a tent on the balcony, a game invented on the way home from school. You laugh at failures, yours and others', and the child understands: life doesn't fall apart over a broken cup or a lost match. You give each other freedom too: each parents in their own way, without the other's supervision. Lightness turns into emptiness when neither takes on the boring part: who signed up for the club, who remembers the parents' evening, who will say “no”. The child has fun but has no one to lean on.

captions.O: Teach them to care and to grow things

items.meaning: Care is what you teach the young ones: to grow a flower, feed a guest, make a home warm with their own hands.
text: On the child's windowsill grows their very own tomato plant, and they water it themselves. The Empress teaches care in the most practical sense: feed the cat, bake a pie for grandma, decorate the room for a holiday, grow something from seed to fruit. The child sees that things bloom under their hands and grows up generous. The lesson turns sour when care flows only one way: everything is done for them, every difficulty is kept away, and their wishes are granted before they have said them. The child learns not to grow things but to receive — and for a long time cannot see why the world is not like their parents' home.

captions.O: Teach them order and responsibility

items.meaning: You teach the young ones order and responsibility: their own place, their own job and their own word, which they keep.
text: You give the young ones a framework. The Emperor brings an order a child can grasp: everything has its place, everyone in the family has their duties, and a child's word weighs as much as an adult's — so long as it is kept. You teach them to plan — a money box for a bike, a timetable for the week — and to stand up for their own. The child sees how the world works and feels at home in it. The framework becomes a cage when order rests on fear: orders without explanations, punishment for any deviation, “not up for discussion”. The child learns not responsibility but obedience — and rebels at the first chance.

captions.O: Hand over the keys to your way of life

items.meaning: You pass on to the young ones not bans but the keys to a shared “us” — until the form matters more than who receives it.
text: You teach what you believe yourselves and pass it on from hand to hand. Upbringing under the Hierophant is a way of life: a family saying before a journey, holidays of your own, a patient “here's why we do it this way” for every “why”. The child receives not a list of bans but the keys to a shared home. The handover grows heavy when the form matters more than the one receiving it: “because you must” comes without a “why”, the question “what for?” is called cheek — and instead of a key the child is left holding a lock.

captions.O: Teach them to choose with the heart

items.meaning: You show the young ones how to love themselves and choose with the heart: friends, pursuits, people they feel good with.
text: Before they know their times tables, the young ones learn from you to choose without fearing their choice. With the Lovers, raising a child starts with acceptance: you are loved not for top marks but because you're ours; want to try music school — go ahead, and if you don't like it, you'll pick something else. You talk with them about feelings, friendship and how to tell that someone is dear to you, and don't hide how people make up after a quarrel. The lesson goes wrong when your dream chooses for the child: they must be beautiful, gifted, “top of the class”, and love quietly becomes a reward for measuring up. Then they learn to choose not with the heart but by reading your face.

captions.O: Teach them to set a goal and reach it

items.meaning: You teach the young ones to set a goal and go for it: fall, get up and hold course even when it is hard.
text: You put the reins in the young ones' hands. The Chariot's way is a goal and movement: they pack their own rucksack, choose their own club, sort things out with the coach themselves. You teach them to finish what they start, to get up after a fall and to be glad not only of the medal but of the distance covered. At home the child has chores, and at weekends a road where they choose the next stop. The lesson turns into a race when the goal is set for them: a schedule down to the minute, one club after another, “you can do better” — and the child rushes not where they want to go but where they will be praised.

captions.O: Teach them to answer for their actions

items.meaning: Honesty and responsibility are your lessons: broke it — own up, promised — do it, hurt someone — put it right.
text: The main thing you pass on is the link between an act and its consequence. In your parenting Justice teaches simple, durable things: if you broke it, say so yourself; if you promised, do it; if you hurt someone, put it right, don't just apologise. You explain why a rule is the way it is and live by it yourselves, so the child doesn't look for loopholes. Truth is never punished in your home: nobody is scolded for owning up. The lesson grows heavy when justice is confused with severity: every slip is examined like a court case, a mistake becomes a stain, and the child grows up judging themselves before anyone asks.

captions.O: Teach them to find answers on their own

items.meaning: You teach the young ones to think for themselves: you give not an answer but a question, a book and time for quiet.
text: When the child asks a question, you answer with one: “What do you think?” — and wait without prompting. The Hermit raises an independent mind: books on the bottom shelf, the right to be alone, the habit of getting to the heart of things rather than grabbing a ready answer. You respect their silence and their odd passions, be it beetles, stars or old coins. The lesson cools when independence replaces involvement: “you'll work it out” is said where the child needs a hand, and their stories are heard with half an ear, without looking up. They learn to cope alone — and stop coming to you.

captions.O: Teach them to keep steady at fate's turns

items.meaning: From you the young ones learn not to fear change: a loss is not the end, luck is noticed, and turns are met with curiosity.
text: You teach the young ones to live at the turns. The Wheel of Fortune brings flexibility to your parenting: a move is an adventure, not a tragedy; losing a competition is a reason to try again; an unexpected chance is something you notice and catch. You tell them how you yourselves fell and got up, and give thanks aloud for a lucky day, so the child sees that luck goes to those who are ready for it. The lesson wobbles when the rules themselves become changeable: allowed yesterday, forbidden today, tomorrow depends on the mood. Then the child learns not to catch luck but to read the weather at home.

captions.O: Teach them to master their own fire

items.meaning: The young ones learn not to fear their strength and anger but to steer them — gently, without breaking their character.
text: You don't put out the fire in the child but teach them how to handle it. Parenting under Strength means self-control without fear: you can be angry, but you can't bite; stubbornness is good if it leads to a goal; scared means we'll go and look together. You show by example how to cool down without slamming a door and how to push through a hard thing when you want to quit: a club where you fall and get up, a long climb uphill, a sum on its second evening. The lesson hardens when the gentle hand turns to iron — “stop crying”, “pull yourself together”, “you have to be strong” — and the child learns not to master feelings but to hide them from you.

captions.O: Teach empathy and seeing the other side

items.meaning: You teach the young ones compassion: to look through another's eyes, to wait, to help with no thought of reward.
text: The most frequent question in your home is “and how does it look from their side?”. The Hanged Man brings compassion and patience into your parenting: “let's take a pie round to the neighbour, she's on her own”, “let's wait, sometimes it's better not to rush”. The child grows up able to put themselves in another's place and to give without expecting a reward. The lesson warps when parental care turns into a sacrifice that keeps being brought up: “all the nights we lost sleep over you”, “we gave everything, and you…”. Instead of compassion the child absorbs guilt and spends a lifetime giving to make up for it.

captions.O: Teach them to let go and begin again

items.meaning: You help the young ones learn to let go: to say goodbye to what has ended and greet the new without fear.
text: Everything comes to an end, and with you the child learns this without fear. Death teaches the art of letting go: outgrown toys are passed on to little ones; a friendship that has ended stays a good memory; when moving house you say goodbye to the old room rather than leaving it in silence. You talk honestly about change and give them time to be sad. The lesson wounds when change crashes down without warning: a new city, a new school, new rules — all in one summer, with no conversation. The child learns not to let go but to get attached to nothing: it will be taken away anyway.

captions.O: Teach balance and the art of agreement

items.meaning: You give the young ones a sense of measure: to agree, to wait, to mix hot with cold and find the middle.
text: Above all you teach the young ones a sense of measure. Temperance keeps your parenting free of extremes: sweets are fine, but not instead of dinner; screens, yes, but after a walk; fell out with a friend — cool down and talk. You show how to find the middle: hear both sides, don't decide in the heat of the moment, let a decision settle overnight. The child grows up calm and able to reach agreement even with someone who shouts. The lesson turns bland when there is so much measure that no room is left for strong feeling: anger is forbidden, crying awkward, delight “too loud”. In the end the child masters not balance but keeping everything inside.

captions.O: Teach them to want boldly and live untethered

items.meaning: Under your roof the young learn not to be ashamed of their desires, and that no one belongs to anyone — not even to parents.
text: Desires are no cause for shame in your home. The Devil's kind of upbringing speaks honestly about strong wants: if you want something, say it aloud and go for it, but know the price and keep your word. You don't pretend the world has no temptations; you explain how they work: why adverts promise happiness, how to tell your own dream from one pushed on you. Above all, you show that a person is not a thing and belongs to no one, not even their parents. The lesson darkens when love is bought or kept on a leash: a present instead of a talk, control of every step, “after all we've done for you”. The child learns not freedom but bargaining.

captions.O: Teach them to rebuild after a collapse

items.meaning: Your lesson for the young ones: don't fear wreckage — what breaks, we take apart, understand and build stronger.
text: In your home something broken is not the end but the start of work. The Tower's lessons are resilience and hands-on work: together you fix the bike, rebuild the den after a downpour, and take a failed exam apart brick by brick to see where the crack was. You don't hide the truth from the child, even an awkward one, and don't pretend everything is fine when it isn't. The lesson turns destructive when the explosion happens inside the home: a harsh word in the heat of the moment, a ban flung in anger, a shout after which all is forgiven but not forgotten. The child remembers what was said in a storm longer than anything said in calm.

captions.O: Teach them to believe in their own star

items.meaning: You teach the young ones to believe in their own star: to dream aloud, to try and not be afraid to show their gift.
text: Dreaming aloud is allowed in your home, even expected. Under the Star, raising a child means faith in their light: a drawing hangs on the fridge as if in a museum, a song is heard to the end, and “I want to be an astronomer” is met not with laughter but with a book about the stars. You notice what sets them alight and add fuel — a club, a mentor, a trip to an exhibition. The lesson fades when the child starts being compared — “look at the neighbours' boy”, “you could be like your sister” — or is handed the job of fulfilling a dream you never fulfilled yourselves. The light kindled for them begins to shine in someone else's direction.

captions.O: Teach them to trust instinct and not fear the dark

items.meaning: With you, the young ones learn to trust instinct, to dream and not to fear the dark — in their room or in themselves.
text: Bedtime stories in your home are long, and the child makes up half of them. The Moon makes you guardians of imagination: you take their dreams seriously, believe their “I think that boy is lying” and teach them to listen to themselves. Fear of the dark is never laughed at — you go into the room together, with a torch, and check every corner. The lesson clouds over when your own anxieties move into the house: things left unsaid in front of the child, “you don't need to know”, scary stories about the street and strangers. The child learns not to listen to instinct but to fear what lies beyond the door.

captions.O: Teach them to delight in themselves and share warmth

items.meaning: You raise confident, generous young ones: glad to be themselves, sharing warmth and unafraid to be noticed.
text: In your home joy is the main teacher. The Sun teaches confidence without boasting: you are good just as you are, not for a medal; you may be proud of yourself and laugh out loud; your warmth is worth sharing — treat someone, invite them over, be glad for a friend. You praise specifically and from the heart, and parties for small victories are remembered longer than presents. The lesson dries up when the warmth becomes conditional: “you have to come first”, “average marks are a disgrace”, harsh criticism for a slip. The child learns not to shine but to measure up — and dims when they can't.

captions.O: Pass on the family memory and the art of forgiving

items.meaning: You pass on the family's memory and the art of forgiving: know your roots and don't drag old grudges along.
text: Your young ones grow up among family stories. Judgement makes memory part of upbringing: albums, tales of the great-grandfather who built a bridge, a pie recipe that has survived three house moves. You teach them to know their roots and be proud of them, but above all to forgive: to admit a mistake, to apologise first, not to nurse a grudge for years. The lesson grows heavy when memory turns into a debt: “everyone in our family has been an engineer”, “that's how we lived, and so will you”, “don't disgrace the family name”. The child is given not roots but a chain, and the call of their own path drowns in their ancestors' voices.

captions.O: Teach them to feel at home in the wide world

items.meaning: You bring up the young ones to feel at home in the wide world: openness, languages and people unlike you.
text: The world map above the child's bed is not decoration in your home but a plan. The World opens the horizon for the child: languages, travel, books about faraway countries, guests from other cultures they learn to talk to without shyness. You show that people unlike us are not a threat but a source of interest, and that it feels good to finish what you start: a thousand-piece jigsaw, a model ship down to the last mast. The lesson narrows when your view of the world becomes the only one: the child's hobbies are criticised, their friends chosen for them, and the wide world turns out to be the parents' world.

captions.O: Teach them the freedom to try and to fail

items.meaning: You encourage the young ones to meet the new without fear: to try, to get it wrong, to laugh at failure and start again.
text: “Give it a go: if it doesn't work, that's fine too” is the main rule of your upbringing. The Fool teaches the young ones freedom: to pick a club themselves and drop it if it isn't theirs; to take an alarm clock apart to see how it ticks; to go to a camp where they know no one. You laugh at failures together and don't make a tragedy of a grazed knee. The lesson grows shaky when freedom has no shores: no rules, “do what you like”, adults' promises shifting with the mood. The child gets room to roam but nothing to lean on, and any freedom starts to frighten.

items.title: A reserve for the wheel's turn

captions.M: To dream of a home with plenty of everything
captions.N: To build order and a safe rear
captions.D: To stand firm on money's swings and not blame fate

items.meaning: Your task is steadiness on fate's swings: save at high tide, don't panic at low tide, and don't blame each other.
text: You dream of a full house and know how to build, and the main test is holding steady when the wheel turns. The Wheel of Fortune brings the couple streaks — profit, then a lull; luck, then a downturn — and arguing with it is useless. The Emperor gives you order and the ability to secure your rear, the Empress a desire for abundance and growth. Together they can build a house that will withstand any streak, as long as you don't confuse stability with standing still.

A good year: one of you lands a big contract, and right away you want everything — a car, a renovation, a holiday by the ocean. The other gets out a notebook: “Let's put half into an account we don't touch.” Grumbling, a compromise, a slightly more modest holiday. A year later the contracts dry up, and that very half calmly carries you for eight months. **The wheel takes nothing from those who build a reserve at high tide instead of only celebrating.**

The wheel rocks you when you spend everything at high tide and look for a culprit at low tide. Loans are taken on a whim, problems are left to the last minute, and then each reproaches the other: “You were the one who insisted.” Other people's stability stirs envy and eats away at you. The Wheel needs not control but an agreement: what we do in a good year and what in a bad one, decided in advance and together.

items.title: Two masters in one house

captions.M: To want comfort and a full house
captions.N: To charge ahead and take charge
captions.D: To divide power and responsibilities without a fight

items.meaning: Your task is to share power: each has their own area of responsibility, and nobody runs the whole house alone.
text: Your house has two strong masters, and the main task is to divide the household so that you don't have to divide power. The Emperor demands order, clear roles and responsibility, but on his dark side he becomes a struggle for supremacy. The Chariot in the middle adds drive: each is used to taking charge and leading. And the Empress brings the wish for comfort, prosperity, a full house — which is what you're working for.

In the first years you argued about everything: who decides on the renovation, who runs the budget, who chooses the school. Tired of arguing, you sit down and divide up the “ministries”: finance and the car for one, the house and holidays for the other, and big things go to the “cabinet”. Arguments drop by two thirds, and each is surprised to see the other handle their area better than expected. **Order holds when power is divided into areas rather than conquered whole.**

The struggle for supremacy turns the house into a battlefield. Every small question becomes who's right, whose word is final; rules made by one get in the other's way, and there's no time to talk about feelings — there's a war to fight. Sometimes one gives up, turns passive and shifts everything onto the other. The Emperor is strong when he trusts: the other's area is their territory, and checking up on it means going to war again.

items.title: Leave home to put down roots

captions.M: To want a home and a harvest of your own
captions.N: To dare to move
captions.D: To break from the past and build a life of your own

items.meaning: Your task is to close an old chapter, leave your parents' homes and put down roots in a place of your own.
text: Your union begins with a farewell.
