Death in the couple's tail demands that you finish an old chapter: step out from under your parents' wing, leave your former life, let go of whatever keeps you in place. The Chariot gives you the resolve for it — a move, a new city, the step you have put off for years. And the Empress explains what it is all for: you want a home of your own, where everything grows by your rules and not someone else's.

For years you have lived in a room at one set of parents' place: convenient, cheap, soup on Sundays. One Sunday the other spreads printouts across the table — flats in another part of town, prices, routes to work. A month of persuading, tears in the family kitchen, boxes, and the first supper eaten on the floor among them. **Your home is born the minute you decide to close someone else's door behind you.**

The lesson gets stuck on the threshold. The old chapter is not closed: the parents still decide how you should live, turn up without calling, and the move is put off “until better times”. Or you rush ahead so abruptly that one of you has no time to say goodbye to the past and drags it along into the new home. Death does not tolerate half-measures: the old must be truly let go, or the new has nothing to grow on.

items.title: A big step with a light tread

captions.M: To want a family and a full house
captions.N: To decide fast and race ahead
captions.D: To think about responsibility before serious steps

items.meaning: Your task is serious steps with open eyes: decide lightly, but think about responsibility in advance.
text: You commit to big things easily, and the couple's task is to think about consequences before the leap, not after. The Fool gives you the courage to begin: move in together within a week, get a dog, buy a house in another town. The Chariot in the middle adds speed, the Empress a dream of a full family and a warm home. Only beginning is easy; then come the everyday days nobody prepared for.

You buy an old house out of town two weeks after seeing the advert. The first winter — no proper heating, debts for repairs and quarrels from the cold. In spring you sit down and for the first time count everything to the penny: what we'll do ourselves, what we'll put off, how we'll live if there isn't enough. The house takes two more years to finish, but without surprises. **Courage bears fruit when a plan follows the leap.**

Lightness becomes carelessness when serious things go unsaid. Decisions are made on emotion, debts appear unnoticed, and when the time comes to settle the bills — literally and figuratively — one of you wants to run. Mutual reproaches, mood swings, rules only one of you keeps. The Fool needn't become cautious: it's enough for him to look where he's jumping.

items.title: Setbacks stay at the door

captions.M: To want a warm, well-fed home
captions.N: To live through ups and downs
captions.D: Not to vent setbacks on loved ones; to restore strength

items.meaning: Your task is to shield home from your races: not to take setbacks out on loved ones, and to restore strength, not drain it.
text: Home is your rear guard, and the main lesson is not to turn it into a place for dumping irritation. The Chariot demands movement and victories, and the Wheel of Fortune in the middle promises that victories will alternate with defeats. Every bad day is easy to bring home and take out on those closest. And the Empress explains where you're running to: a warm, well-fed home where you're both happy.

After a disastrous meeting one of you comes in and picks on a trifle from the doorway: shoes left out again. The other is about to answer back but says instead: “Come here. What happened at work?” Ten minutes later in the kitchen there's the story, the anger, laughter — and nobody cares about the shoes. Since then you've had a rule: first “how was your day”, then everything else. **Home stays a refuge when setbacks are talked about, not taken out on loved ones.**

The Chariot becomes dangerous when strength is taken from loved ones instead of restored on your own. Tiredness turns into aggression, failure into a reproach to the partner, competition at work into a struggle for dominance at home. There's no rest, because there's “no time”. The Chariot needs a stopping place: time when nobody is racing anywhere and you can simply be together.

items.title: Replanting after the landslide

captions.M: To want a home with plenty of everything
captions.N: To live through a turn of the wheel
captions.D: To go through sudden shocks together, not apart

items.meaning: Your task is to come through sudden collapses together and grow your own again, without blaming each other.
text: You are to build where the ground sometimes shakes. The Empress gives the couple a longing for abundance: a home of your own, a full table, a growing business. The Wheel of Fortune reminds you that life moves in circles, and a rise gives way to a fall without warning. And the Tower in the couple's tail is the test of collapse: a sudden job loss, plans in ruins, the fall of the image you had invented of each other. The task is to live through it together and grow something new on the cleared ground.

You have just moved into a mortgaged flat, and a month later one of you loses their job. The first week is panic and reproach: “I told you it was too soon.” Then you sit down at the table and cut the budget; one takes on extra work, the other retrains within three months. A year later you remember that autumn as the time you truly became a family. **After a collapse what saves you is looking in one direction — at what can be rebuilt.**

A collapse becomes destructive when, in trouble, you look in different directions. One panics and seeks someone to blame, the other pretends nothing has happened. Different experience in your parents' families — for one, money in childhood was now short, now plentiful, for the other always steady — turns every downturn into an argument over who is right. A garden won't grow on land pulled two ways: after a collapse you will have to plant together.

items.title: Thanks to every turn

captions.M: To want a growing, full family
captions.N: To close chapters and begin new ones
captions.D: To meet change with gratitude, not complaints

items.meaning: Your task is to meet change with gratitude: let go of what you've lived and grow something new at every turn.
text: Your family grows through turns, and the couple's task is to meet them with gratitude rather than resentment at fate. The Wheel of Fortune brings a change of stages: moves, new jobs, additions to the family, the passing of elders. Death in the middle helps you close what you've lived through honestly, without clinging. And the Empress explains what it's all for: you want to grow living things — a home, a garden, a family that becomes fuller with every turn.

When the grandmother's old house is sold, one of you can't talk about it without tears for a week. The other suggests not saying goodbye in a hurry: together you go through the things, keep the three dearest, and on the last evening have supper in an empty room, remembering all that happened there. A year later the apple tree from the grandmother's garden, brought as a cutting, takes root on your plot. **Every turn brings a harvest if you say goodbye to the past with gratitude.**

The wheel grows heavy when every turn is met with a complaint. “Why us again”, “everything was so good” — and grievances instead of decisions, manipulation instead of conversation. One clings to the old, the other already lives the new, and misunderstanding grows between them. The Wheel doesn't need submission — it needs gratitude: for what was, and for what comes in its place.

items.title: Success that spares the home

captions.M: To want a big, warm family
captions.N: To dare to make big changes
captions.D: To shine at work without forgetting home and each other

items.meaning: Your task is success without losing your home: flourish brightly without giving work the people it was all for.
text: You want both great success and a warm home, and your lesson is not to let one eat the other. The Sun calls you to fulfilment, to work you can be proud of. The Empress in your wishes calls to family, comfort, abundance at a shared table. And Death in the middle says that for this you'll have to end something: an old job, an old rhythm, an old idea of who in the family is the breadwinner and who the keeper of the hearth.

One partner's business is finally taking off: orders, interviews, nights at the office. Six months later the other notices they've eaten dinner alone for the fifth evening running, and silently photographs the empty chair opposite. That evening they show the picture. The next day the first hires an assistant and crosses Sundays out of the calendar. **The sun shines brighter when success lights up the home too, not just the office.**

The light starts to burn when one partner's victories eat up the life of both. The one who shines claims shared credit and doesn't notice whose support holds them up; the one in the shade holds back their feelings and quietly fades. Changes that could rebuild everything are postponed: it's frightening to give up what has been achieved. The Sun needs the warmth of home just as the home needs the sun.

items.title: Firmness without cruelty

captions.N: To live through upheaval and stress
captions.D: Not to turn harsh; to get your way without pressure

items.meaning: Your task is firmness without cruelty: under stress and after losses, aim your strength at the work, not at each other.
text: Under the pressure of circumstances you turn hard, and the couple's lesson is to keep firmness without losing softness. The Emperor teaches you to reach goals without manipulation or domination, and to direct your drive into the work. The Tower in the middle brings stress and upheaval — renovations, moves, losses — in which it's easy to snap. There's something to endure it for: the Empress wants comfort, prosperity and a warm home.

The third month of renovation: dust, debts, the builders didn't turn up again. One of you snaps and shouts at the other over the tiles they chose. The other walks out, slamming the door, and comes back with two pairs of boxing gloves: “Let's be angry at the punchbag, not at each other.” It's funny, but it works: in the evenings you pound the bag in the basement, and over supper you talk normally again. **Strength builds a home when it's aimed at the work, not at each other.**

Harshness grows unnoticed. First a sharp tone “because there's no time”, then rules set by one, then pressure and manipulation to get your way. Feelings hide behind orders. The Emperor needs an outlet for his drive — sport, working with your hands, a shared project — and a habit of saying “it's hard for me” before “do as you're told”.

items.title: Nothing like the old pattern

captions.M: To want a home and family warmth
captions.N: To survive the collapse of old expectations
captions.D: To accept a different partner and say goodbye to the past

items.meaning: Your task is to say goodbye to old scripts and accept a partner quite unlike the pattern you're used to.
text: Your union is a new chapter, and the couple's task is to let it truly begin. Death demands a farewell to the past: to scripts learned in your parents' home and in your former life, to the expectation that someone close will behave the way you're used to. The Tower in the middle brings these expectations down abruptly, sometimes painfully. And the Empress in your wishes reminds you what for: you want a warm home where new things grow rather than old ones repeat.

One of you grew up in a home where the father decided everything, and learned early to adapt. The partner answers every question with “What would you like?” — and for the first month this is maddening: it seems the other doesn't care. At night the understanding comes: the anger isn't at this person but at the old habit of waiting for someone else to decide. In the morning the first says, for the first time, what they want. **The new chapter begins when you stop reading other people's lines into your partner.**

The past destroys the present when it hasn't been let go. The partner's difference seems a mistake, crises seem proof that “it's all going wrong again”, and your own mistakes go unnoticed. Relatives compare you with other couples, debts and grievances trail behind from the old life. Death doesn't ask whether you're ready: it closes the door. A new one can only be opened by the two of you.

items.title: From zero, but not empty-handed

captions.N: To survive losing what you had
captions.D: To become independent and answer for shared money

items.meaning: Your task is to start from zero boldly but responsibly: become independent and stop trusting to luck.
text: You know how to start from zero — what's left is to learn not to start from zero every time. The Fool gives lightness: lost it — we'll find more; it fell down — we'll build again. The Tower in the middle brings sudden losses: a job, a home, what you'd built up. The Empress, meanwhile, wants prosperity and comfort. The lesson is to make sure the next storm finds you prepared rather than careless.

For the second time in five years you're left with no money: the first time a workshop went under, the second one of you quit without discussing it with anyone. Sitting on your suitcases at your parents', for the first time you talk seriously about money: a cushion, work of their own for each, no “we'll sort it out later”. The first sum saved is laughable, but you celebrate it as if you'd bought a flat. **Lightness becomes strength when a reserve and a shared rule stand behind it.**

Carelessness costs dearly when nobody looks after tomorrow. Loans are taken lightly, jobs dropped lightly, and in trouble the parents help, and this becomes a habit. One reproaches the other for immaturity while not keeping their own rules. The Fool needs self-sufficiency — financial and moral — or freedom turns into dependence on others' help.

items.title: Not rushing each other

captions.M: To want a family, children, a home
captions.N: To be successful and happy
captions.D: To agree on status and roles, and not rush your partner

items.meaning: Your task is a shared course without hurrying: agree where you're heading, and don't rush the one who needs time.
text: You want a lot and all at once — a home, a family, success — and the couple's main lesson is not to rush each other. The Chariot demands a clear course: who you are to each other, where you're going, what each one's role is. The Sun in the middle and the Empress in your wishes paint a beautiful goal — a happy, warm, full family. But each moves towards it at their own pace, and one partner's haste easily becomes pressure on the other.

Six months into the relationship, one of you is already choosing names for future children, while the other is still getting used to the idea of a shared flat. First come the grievances: “What, are you having doubts?” Then an honest conversation: what “soon” means to each of you, what each is afraid of. You agree on steps for the year ahead, and the other, given time, is the one to suggest speeding up. **The course becomes shared when you choose the pace together.**

Haste turns into a race for a picture. One hurries, the other brakes, and every step — a wedding, a move, a child — becomes an argument about timing, not about wishes. The status of the relationship hangs in the air, roles go undiscussed, and tiredness builds up. Knowing the goal isn't enough for the Chariot: it needs an agreement on who steers and at what speed to drive.

items.title: When the shiny facade falls

captions.M: To want well-being and a full house
captions.N: To shine, succeed and be seen
captions.D: To survive the fall of an image and stay together

items.meaning: Your task is to live through the collapse of a glossy picture and discover that the real warmth is still there.
text: You build a beautiful house, and the task is for it to stand when the facade falls. The Empress and the Sun give the couple a pull towards well-being: success, prosperity, a warm home to be proud of. The Tower tests what stands behind the shine: one day an invented image collapses — of the partner, of a career, of the “perfect family” — and it becomes clear what really holds you together.

One partner's business, once written up in the local news, folds within six months. Friends vanish, the car is sold, at a family celebration the relatives awkwardly look away. But at home, that very first evening, the other puts beans on toast on the table, as in your student days, and says: “Well, now we can see who's really with us.” **Your warmth is tested not by the shine but by what remains once it has flaked away.**

The collapse wounds more deeply when you lose your composure. One blames the other for the failure, the other goes to extremes — work, spending, resentment. Trouble drives you into separate corners, and what collapses then is not the facade but closeness itself. The Tower doesn't punish: it clears the ground. But building something new on it — more honest and more modest — is a job for two.

items.title: Jump when the wheel calls

captions.N: To take risks lightly, without a safety net
captions.D: To step past the fear of change together, not risk blindly

items.meaning: Your task is courage with open eyes: catch a chance together without jumping blind or hiding from change.
text: Fate keeps offering your couple chances, and the main exam is how you catch them. The Wheel of Fortune brings turns that won't wait: an offer, a meeting, an opportunity that vanishes in a week. The Fool is ready to jump without looking, the Empress to grow something big from the leap. The task is to step past the fear of change together and not mistake courage for carelessness.

Friends are selling a small bakery in the next town, and you have ten days to decide. One of you is already baking croissants in their head, the other doesn't sleep for two nights. On the third day you drive there together, spend all day in the bakery, count the takings, talk to the suppliers. You sign — with a six-month cushion and an exit plan. **A chance becomes luck when one brings courage and the other a lantern.**

The Wheel punishes two kinds of imbalance. The first is jumping blind: borrowing for a dream, dropping something reliable for a pretty idea, then blaming fate and each other. The second is being so afraid that you close in on yourselves: no new people, no ventures, complaints that life is passing you by. The Wheel needs sincerity: say honestly what you want and what scares you — and decide together.

items.title: Joy that has work to do

captions.M: To want abundance and a warm home
captions.N: To live lightly and not plan ahead
captions.D: To fulfil yourselves and not hide problems behind fun

items.meaning: Your task is to turn lightness into achievement: shine through deeds, not just a smile, and talk about problems aloud.
text: Being with you is light and fun, and the couple's task is to make that light warm something. The Sun in the tail demands fulfilment: each has their own calling, their own success, their own pride, and an honest talk about what isn't working. The Fool brings lightness and a habit of living without plans, the Empress a dream of a full house. Your lesson runs between “I want it all” and “it'll sort itself out”: abundance grows only for those who take it in hand.

For years you have joked that one day you'll open a café, sketching menus on napkins in other people's cafés. At a birthday party a friend asks: “So when?” — and for the first time you don't laugh. A week later you're touring empty premises with a tape measure, and the napkin menu has been typed up properly. **Your sun rises when the dream you used to laugh at becomes real work.**

The sun sets when problems are hidden behind fun. Failures are turned into jokes, money isn't discussed, expectations of each other grow, and nobody starts doing anything. Or one carries everything and claims the victories, while the other remains an eternal party in someone else's life. The Sun needs not only warmth but work: without it lightness becomes idleness, and abundance empty promises.

items.title: A promise that is kept

captions.M: To want a love that holds a choice
captions.N: Rules brought from your parents' homes
captions.D: To keep your word, admit fault and not judge each other

items.meaning: Your task is an honest pact between lovers: keep your word, admit fault and don't turn the rules into a courtroom.
text: Your union is tested by promises, and the examiner is Justice: keep your word, admit your fault, don't blame the other for what you both did. The Hierophant brings the rules of your parents' homes — what is proper, when to marry, who is responsible for what. But beneath all the rules, say the Lovers, lies a choice: you are together because you want to be, not because that is how things are done.

For three years you have promised yourselves to marry “after the renovation”, “after the move”, “when there's money”. Over supper one of you finally says: “Let's admit it: we're just scared. Of what, exactly?” The conversation is hard and honest, with a list of fears on the back of a gas bill. A month later you give notice of marriage — no lavish wedding, just the way you want it. **Your pact grows stronger when it honestly names both what you promised and what you fear.**

Justice hardens when it becomes a courtroom. Each measures by their own yardstick and shifts the blame, and broken promises pile up like overdue bills. One takes everything on and starts to control, the other withdraws from any family question. Rules adopted “because that's how it must be” weigh on you both. The scales level out when each first admits their own share, not the other's.

items.title: Your own star, not a script

captions.M: To want a love of your own choosing
captions.N: The rules and scripts of your parents' families
captions.D: To dare your own dream and not dim your partner's

items.meaning: Your task is not to live out your parents' script but to make room for each one's dream, and for a shared one too.
text: A ready-made script lies before you, and your task is to dare to write your own. The Hierophant brings your parents' rules and examples into the couple: how one ought to live, what work to do, when to have children, what to save for. The Lovers remind you that you chose each other yourselves, not on someone else's prompting. The Star in the couple's tail sets the main condition: find and fulfil your dream — and don't stand in the way of your partner's.

For ten years one of you has worked as an accountant, “like Dad”, and secretly draws at night. The other stumbles on a folder of sketches and, instead of “what's the point?”, says: “Show this to people.” You hang the first three drawings in the café round the corner, and relatives who grumbled about a “frivolous pastime” come to see them in their best clothes. **One partner's dream comes true when it becomes a matter of honour for the other.**

The dream fades when the rules win. You live “as you should”, not as you wish: a steady job, a renovation like everyone's, holidays where the parents go. Dreams stay in a drawer so as not to look naive, and if one does dare, the other mocks the idea and points to their “respectable” relatives and to those who “live properly”. Sometimes one dream gets in the other's way, and instead of support comes an ultimatum. The Star doesn't light up on schedule: it needs someone to say “let's do it”.

items.title: Strength that knows how to yield

captions.M: To say “I like this” and “this hurts”
captions.N: To share fairly, without keeping score
captions.D: To tame stubbornness and respect the other's strength

items.meaning: Your task is two strong characters learning not to win but to reach terms — honestly and with love.
text: You have been given two strong characters and the task of not breaking each other. Strength is the main task here, and its test is pressure: each has their own rightness, and giving way feels like weakness. Justice shows where to look for balance — in an honest agreement where duties and respect are split equally. And the Lovers supply the language for such an agreement: saying plainly what you like, what hurts and what you want, rather than waiting for the other to guess.

The question of who walks the dog at the weekend threatens to become yet another “you only ever think of yourself”. Then one of you stops and puts it differently: “I'm angry because I need a Saturday too. Let's split it fairly.” The other breathes out, and five minutes later you have a rota for the month ahead. **Your strength grows not by beating the other but by naming what is yours and hearing what is theirs.**

The test drags on when strength goes around words. Instead of “that hurt” — a jibe; instead of a request — a demand; instead of an agreement — a silent tally of who did how much. Each waits for the other to admit they were right first, and gathers evidence. Passion becomes a fight, justice a courtroom, and love a trophy. What needs taming here is not your partner but your own wish to always win.

items.title: Reopening an old case

captions.M: To want to choose your love yourselves
captions.N: To admit your own share of the blame honestly
captions.D: To forgive the past and not live by the family's verdict

items.meaning: Your task is to review the past honestly, forgive, and choose each other yourselves, not by your relatives' will.
text: Your couple is reviewing old cases. Judgement in the couple's tail brings up the past — parental grievances, old mistakes, the family's view of whether you suit each other — and demands a fresh verdict. Justice sets the order: first admit your own share honestly, then judge the other. And the Lovers remind you what it is all for: you want to choose each other without looking over your shoulder for anyone's approval.

For years one partner's family has kept its distance: “not our sort”. The other puts up with it for a long time, then snaps, and the quarrel with the family becomes a quarrel between you. The turning point comes when the first says aloud to their parents for the first time: “This is my choice, and I answer for it,” — and the other admits they too said more than they should have. **The family's verdict loses its force when you both answer for your choice — before your relatives and before each other.**

The case drags on when the review becomes an endless trial. Everything is dragged up: who said what at the wedding, whose mother gave whom a look, who failed to call first. Each sees themselves as the prosecutor, never the accused, and forgiveness is put off until the other admits their guilt. While the family rather than you decides about the couple, the verdict simply hangs over you — neither acquittal nor conviction.

items.title: Say it aloud, don't stockpile

captions.M: To want a love with nothing left unsaid
captions.N: To hold back hurt until it bursts out
captions.D: To agree on your own ways and voice your wishes aloud

items.meaning: Your task is a shared way of life where wishes are spoken aloud, not stored up as grievances until a silent war.
text: Your couple's main lesson is to reach agreement in words. The Hierophant in the tail sets the task of building your own ways: deciding what your family will be like, what rules you live by and what you tell others. Strength shows what happens if you don't agree: the unspoken builds up and breaks out as silent pressure, barbs and stubbornness. And the Lovers add jealousy and uncertainty — they grow exactly where the main thing has not been said.

It has long bothered one of you that the other stays at work until late at night, but it feels awkward to say so: after all, they're doing it for the family. Instead of words — a slammed cupboard door, answers through gritted teeth, a suspicious glance at the phone. The turning point comes the evening the first one finally says: “I'm lonely in the evenings,” — and it turns out the other is tired of it too. **Jealousy and resentment lose their ground the moment a wish is spoken aloud.**

Things stall when rules replace conversation and silence replaces rules. Each is sure the other ought to understand anyway and takes offence when they don't. Work crowds out the family, all the relatives know your business, and you tell each other less and less. Words said in the heat of the moment wound for a long time, so for you it matters especially to talk calmly and in good time — while the words can still be chosen.

items.title: Fire tempered with patience

captions.N: Passion and a strong temper
captions.D: To find measure: don't stifle feelings or always give in

items.meaning: Your task is balance: hot feelings and strong characters learn to blend rather than put each other out.
text: You have been dealt the job of mixing fire with water. Temperance in the couple's tail is the task of finding measure where it is hard to keep. Strength brings a hot temper and passion, the Lovers a longing for an ideal love, beautiful and without rough edges. Together they either flare up or demand the impossible, and your work is not to put out the feelings but to pour them from vessel to vessel until the water is the right temperature.

A conversation about visiting family for the holidays boils over in a minute: one is ready to slam the door, the other to give in silently, as they have three times before. Then suddenly the one who always yields says: “No. Let's find an option where nobody loses.” Half an hour of talking — and you spend the first days of the holidays with one set of parents and the last with the other. **Your measure lies where neither passion nor giving way wins alone.**

The tilt begins when only one of you holds the balance. One keeps damping things down, softening, yielding, and the other doesn't notice the scales tipped long ago. What is held back builds up and one day spills out — out of all proportion to the cause. Or both chase an ideal picture and are ashamed of ordinary quarrels, hiding them even from themselves. Temperance doesn't ask you to stay even all the time: it asks you not to keep inside what the two of you could blend together.

items.title: Honest scales of give and take

captions.M: To want a love between equals
captions.N: To give way for the sake of peace
captions.D: To share the load fairly, admit fault and forgive

items.meaning: Your task is honest balance: share the effort equally, admit fault and forgive, rather than give way in silence.
text: Your lesson is honest balance in love. Justice in the couple's tail watches the scales: who puts in how much, who admits mistakes, who forgives. Temperance teaches you to give way and smooth things over, but it risks a tilt: one always yields and the other gets used to it. The Lovers remind you that love between equals is not bookkeeping but a choice each of you makes freely.

Time after time one of you forgives the lateness, the forgotten promises, the cancelled plans: “oh, it's nothing.” At last they stop smiling and say honestly: “I'm hurt. And I don't want to pretend I'm not any more.” The other gets defensive at first, then admits: “You're right. I took advantage of your gentleness.” **The scales even out when the truth about the tilt is spoken by the one used to keeping quiet.**

The tilt grows unnoticed. The one who yields saves up grievances and one day presents the bill for everything at once, while the one who was yielded to can't understand where the trial came from. It can also go the other way: one takes on all the responsibility and starts controlling the other's every step, as if they were a debtor. Justice between lovers is not exact accounting but a readiness to admit your own share and forgive the other's.

items.title: Love with no shop window

captions.N: To seek the middle ground patiently
captions.D: To live for real, not for show, and not remake your partner

items.meaning: Your task is a real union instead of a pretty display: accept each other as living people and stop living for an audience.
text: It is easy for you to build a beautiful shop window, and your task is not to move into it. The Star here tests the union for authenticity: do you live for yourselves or for those who are watching? The Lovers bring a dream of love as in the films, Temperance brings patience and a knack for smoothing things over. Together they risk smoothing away everything alive for the sake of a perfect picture, and the lesson is the reverse: to love the real person and show the world the real union.

For your anniversary, friends expect beautiful photos from you: you have always been “that couple”. Instead, for the first time in ten years, you spend the evening at home in pyjamas, eat pizza out of the box and honestly tell each other you are tired of being perfect. No posts — and the warmest anniversary in years. **The Star shines brightest where you no longer have to live up to anything.**

The shop window demands sacrifices: discontent is smoothed over, quarrels are hidden, a partner's hobbies that don't fit the picture are quietly frowned upon. One fits the other to an image, the other puts up with it and adapts, and both compare themselves with other couples. Outside, everything is flawless; inside, there is tiredness and much left unsaid. The Star doesn't ask for glitter: it needs the honesty that turns a dream from a stage set into a shared cause.

items.title: Strength without rose tints

captions.M: To want to admire each other
captions.N: To dream of an ideal partner
captions.D: To respect the other's strength and speak without pressure

items.meaning: Your task is respect without rose-tinted glasses: accept the other's strength and weakness, and speak plainly, not press.
text: Your task is to learn to respect a living person, not an ideal. Strength demands that you tame your pressure: your demands, your wish to have the best, the most successful, the most attractive person at your side. The Star adds a great dream of a partner, the Lovers the wish to admire them. Together they easily turn love into an exam in which one is always sitting it and the other is always unhappy with the mark.

For years one of you has nudged the other: change jobs, take up sport, dress differently — “I only want what's best.” The other puts up with it, then explodes: “Do you love me or the person I could be?” The talk goes on late into the night, and for the first time the first says plainly what they are really afraid of: that people will see you as failures. **Your strength lies in each one's right to be themselves, and in an honest word instead of pressure.**

Expectations turn into a struggle when they go unsaid. One presses with hints and comparisons, the other defends with stubbornness, and you talk in different languages. Work eats up your time, chores are divided unfairly, and tenderness gives way to demands. Strength is tamed by gentleness: not remaking but accepting — and saying from the very start what you like and what you don't.

items.title: Your own call, not a yardstick

captions.N: Hoping after a loss
captions.D: To overcome the past and rewrite old relationship scripts

items.meaning: Choose each other, let go of the past and don't idealise love.
text: Everyone is happy to offer a yardstick for your love, and your lesson is to hear your own. The Lovers give the couple a picture of the right kind of love, which you can't help comparing with the real one. The real one doesn't match the picture, and every loss — a plan that fell through, a hard year — tests whether you can find the Star's hope, the kind that comes precisely after losses. And the last word belongs to Judgement: to the call from within that you answer with your whole being.

After lunch with the family someone drops: “normal people have already… by now” — and the phrase rides home with you. All the way you measure yourselves with someone else's ruler and keep falling short. Then, nearly home, one of you asks: “Do we actually even want that?” — and suddenly the ruler looks ridiculous. **You are led not by approval from outside but by a call you both answered from within.**

The lesson stalls when someone else's yardstick is taken for your own. Love is checked against a model — how couples you know live, how things are done at your parents' — and every difference sounds like a verdict: so there's something wrong with us. Hope is hidden so as not to look naive, and your own call drowns in other voices. The union sits an endless exam in which everyone gives marks except the two of you.

items.title: Your family, your own holidays

captions.M: To choose with the heart, not on advice
captions.N: Elders' voices and family grievances
captions.D: To build your own ways and keep relatives out of the couple

items.meaning: Your task is ways of your own: get on with both sides of the family, but decide about your family yourselves.
text: Between two family lines you are to create a third — your own. The Hierophant demands a way of life of your own: your own rules, holidays, decisions about how your home will run. Judgement in the middle brings the elders' voices — their expectations, grievances, conflicts that stretch across generations. And the Lovers insist that you chose each other yourselves, and nobody but you need approve that choice.

One partner's mother still considers the other “temporary”. At every celebration — a barb, in every family photo — a distance. For a long time you argue between yourselves over whose side to take. At last you decide differently: you start a celebration of your own — the first Saturday of summer, when you invite both families to your place, on your terms. A couple of years later people are hugging at that Saturday. **Your way of life grows stronger when you stop choosing between families and start building your own.**

Relatives enter the couple's borders when the borders haven't been drawn. One family teaches you how to bring up children, the other how to spend, and you argue not with each other but with other people's voices. One tries to remake the other to suit their family's demands, the other shuts down and keeps quiet. The Hierophant needs a charter adopted by the two of you: what we decide, what we consult the elders on, and what isn't discussed with anyone.

items.title: A bridge between two families

captions.M: To want a love everyone will accept
captions.N: The voices of two families and old grievances
captions.D: To reach accord and rebuild trust without hurrying

items.meaning: Your task is accord: joining two families and two histories, rebuilding trust and not rushing the reconciliation.
text: Each of you came into the union not alone but with your own family line, and your task is to join the two banks. Temperance sets you the main test — accord: finding the middle between two ways of life, two histories, two ideas of what a family is. Judgement brings the voices of the elders and past grievances, your own and your parents'. And the Lovers remind you that the bridge is built for love, not to please everyone.

Your first New Year together: one family celebrates noisily, with three generations at the table, the other quietly, with just the parents. Both mothers expect you and take offence in advance. You sit down and invent your own version: New Year's Eve with one family, New Year's Day with the other, and the evening after that yours alone. A few years on, this order becomes your family tradition. **Accord is born not from giving in to one side but from a third way the two of you invent.**

The bridge collapses when it is built in a hurry or for show. Grievances are smoothed over quickly, without being talked through, and trust, once cracked, stays cracked. One tries to please the relatives, the other to match the picture of a “proper couple”, and both suppress what they feel. Temperance needs time: reconciliation steeps like good tea, and whoever rushes it ends up drinking plain water.

items.title: Time for two amid the chores

captions.M: To want solitude amid the bustle
captions.N: To care, to raise, to feed
captions.D: To find time for the couple, and work of their own for each

items.meaning: Your task is not to dissolve in caring: find time for the two of you, and for each a pursuit of their own outside the home.
text: The Empress leads your couple twice: you both know how to care, raise, feed, and the main lesson is not to vanish in that care. Home, children, parents, garden — everything needs hands, and at some point you notice you're living like two housekeepers rather than a couple. The Hermit in your wishes quietly suggests what's missing: time for yourselves, a pursuit of your own, a quiet in which each can hear what they themselves want.

Your week is scheduled to the minute: the children's clubs, the market, the allotment, guests. Midweek you suddenly notice you talk only about shopping. The next day one of you arranges things with Gran and takes the other away for a whole Saturday — no phones, a café on the other side of town. You talk as if you hadn't seen each other for a year. **The garden blooms when the gardeners find time for each other too.**

Care turns into sacrifice when you both dissolve in it. One gives up work, the other hobbies, and a few years later each vaguely feels they've lost themselves. Irritation comes out in rows over trifles, and wishes go unspoken. The Empress needs each of you to find fulfilment separately, and the couple to have time that belongs to it alone.

items.title: Generosity that can say no

captions.N: To give, care and feed
captions.D: To learn to refuse and not dissolve in others' needs

items.meaning: Your task is generosity with boundaries: help without dissolving, and know how to say “no” to those used to taking.
text: You're a generous couple, and the main task is to learn to say “no”. The Hanged Man demands boundaries: don't give everything, don't sacrifice yourselves to the bottom, know how to refuse those used to asking. The Empress in the middle generously feeds, cares, nurtures — your own and strangers alike. And the Hermit in your wishes pulls towards modesty and quiet, which never exist in a house full of people asking.

For years your flat has worked like a free hotel: relatives come “for a week” and stay a month, friends borrow and forget to repay. Having seen off yet another set of guests, you sit in the empty kitchen, and one says: “We're good to everyone except ourselves.” A week later you refuse for the first time — politely but firmly. The world doesn't collapse, and the house becomes quiet and warm. **Generosity stays warm when it gets boundaries.**

Generosity becomes sacrifice when refusing is no longer possible. One carries the relatives, the other the friends, and there's neither strength nor money left for your own couple. Others' expectations grow, gratitude shrinks, and resentment builds within the union. It's important for the Hanged Man to understand: help that leaves you no room to breathe doesn't make the world better — it just shifts someone else's load onto your shoulders.

items.title: A big goal for two

captions.M: To want wisdom and an unhurried pace
captions.N: To grow and multiply your own
captions.D: To set a grand shared goal and not mock each other's plans

items.meaning: Your task is a big shared goal: don't think small, don't mock each other's plans, and grow your shared venture seriously.
text: Ordinary plans aren't enough for your couple, and the task is to dare a big shared one. The World demands scale: a goal that draws you both in — a journey, a venture, a dream worth stepping out of your usual circle for. The Empress in the middle gives the strength to grow and multiply, and the Hermit in your wishes patience and the wisdom to see things through. Only scale is frightening, and it's easier to laugh it off than to take it on.

Over dinner one of you says: “I want to build a small hotel by the sea.” The other laughs — and sees that the first isn't laughing. Instead of a joke they ask: “How much do we need, and when do we start?” Until two in the morning you work out on the back of an electricity bill how many years of saving it'll take if you start on Monday — and on Monday you start. **The union grows when the other takes one partner's dream seriously.**

The horizon collapses when a partner's plans are met with mockery. “You? Hardly”, “fantasies again” — and the person stops sharing. Life becomes Groundhog Day, conversations go in circles, and friends and new people seem superfluous. Each pulls their own way, with no agreements. The World needs a horizon: a union that sets no big goals starts to bore itself.

items.title: Love without a blueprint

captions.M: To want to understand love completely
captions.N: To choose again and again
captions.D: To let go of the ideal and accept each other's flaws

items.meaning: Your task is to love without a blueprint: drop the ideal picture of a relationship and accept a living person whole.
text: You carry a blueprint of the right kind of love in your heads, and the couple's task is one day to put it aside. The Lovers appear twice: love here is both the path and the main lesson. Your wishes, though, are coloured by the Hermit: a habit of thinking everything through alone, seeking the perfect answer, weighing every step. The result is a union where both want to do everything right — and for that very reason are often dissatisfied: with themselves, with the other, with how things are.

For three months you choose rings, because “it's for ever, we can't get it wrong”. Then six months on the venue. One evening, after yet another argument about napkins, one of you says: “Listen, why don't we just sign the register on Thursday and go out for pizza?” So you do — and it is the best day of your life. **Love comes alive when it stops sitting an exam in perfection.**

The ideal becomes a tyrant when a living person is forced to fit it. Every flaw in the partner seems proof of a mistake, every quarrel a failure, and you flare up over trifles. Parents add fuel: “now, at your age, we…” Insecurity hides behind demands, demands behind perfectionism. The Lovers teach the main thing: love doesn't need flawlessness, it needs acceptance.

items.title: The pull and the right to quiet

captions.M: To want a quiet of your own
captions.N: To choose with the heart, not out of fear
captions.D: To love without owning: let go of control and jealousy

items.meaning: Your task is an attachment that doesn't cling: strong feeling and each one's right to a silence of their own.
text: Your main lesson is to love strongly without holding on. The Devil gives the couple a powerful pull: you want to know everything about the other and never let them out of your sight. The Lovers turn that pull into a question of choice: are you together because you chose to be, or because you can't tear yourselves apart? And the Hermit reminds you that each of you needs a silence of your own — and that silence is the easiest thing to mistake for a threat.

In the evenings one of you vanishes into a workshop in the garage: soldering, thinking, saying nothing. At first the other is jealous of that door, texts every half hour, invents reasons to call them back. One evening they don't text at all — and near midnight the door opens by itself: the first one calls them in to see what they've made. **The lesson is learned when one partner's silence stops frightening the other, and closeness stops demanding a report.**

The lesson drags on when the pull and the silence go to war. The one who needs solitude hides ever deeper, because every withdrawal is met with an interrogation. The one afraid of losing holds on ever tighter: checking, jealous, hurt by every “I need some time alone”. Neither speaks of what they really want. The result is a union where one stands guard and the other thinks more and more about escape, though they never actually leave.

items.title: Solitude for two

captions.M: To want understanding without many words
captions.N: To cope on your own
captions.D: To share and help rather than hide in your shell

items.meaning: Your task is not to turn the union into two solitudes: share what you find and ask for help rather than withdraw.
text: The Hermit appears in your tail three times, and that speaks for itself: you both find it easier to think, decide and go through things alone. The wish, the path and the couple's main task all lead one way — inwards. Your lesson is not to let the union turn into two parallel solitudes: to learn to share what you have found, to ask for help, and to sense when the other needs support and when they need to be left in peace.

One of you is having a hard month: a project is on fire, sleep is short. Out of habit they shut themselves in the study and say nothing; out of habit the other leaves them alone, respecting their boundaries. A month later it turns out it was hard for both: one was waiting to be called, the other to be asked. Since then you have a rule: once a week each tells the other what is on their mind, even if “everything's fine”. **Your closeness begins where one of you dares to say: “I need help.”**

Silence becomes a wall when each retreats into their work, books and thoughts and stops calling to the other. There are no shared friends and no shared pursuits, and criticism replaces conversation: it is easier to point out flaws than to share feelings. One may overshadow the other without noticing, simply because their work is louder. A union of two wise people rests not on silence but on bringing each other what you find in it.

items.title: Two hermits in the fog

captions.M: To want quiet and a corner of your own
captions.N: To retreat into yourself from what is hard
captions.D: To stop hiding feelings and trusting guesses over words

items.meaning: Your task is to come out of two shells towards each other and voice your fears before the fog becomes a wall.
text: For both of you silence comes easier than speech, and that is your main lesson. The Hermit is doubled here: both the wish and the path to it lead into quiet, into your own corner, to answering hard questions alone. The Moon in the couple's tail shows what grows in such quiet: guesses, anxieties, grievances over things that never happened. The task is to learn to come out of your shells towards each other and name your fears aloud before they become the truth inside your heads.

For a week you barely talk: each has their own worries. One decides the other has cooled and starts answering curtly. The other notices the curtness, decides it is their own fault and closes up even more. At night someone cracks: “Are you angry with me?” — “I thought you were angry with me.” And both laugh with relief. **Your lesson is one question asked aloud that clears a week of fog.**

The fog thickens when tenderness is taken for weakness. Feelings are hidden, wishes go unspoken, and each builds their own version of events without checking it against the other's. You adjust in silence, get irritated in silence, and then quarrel over nothing — because the real thing was never said. The Hermit needs silence, and the Moon needs light: without conversation two wise people can live side by side for years and never know each other.

items.title: Time to plant your own garden

captions.M: To want quiet and a modest life
captions.N: To wait and put things off
captions.D: To grow up together and build your own prosperity

items.meaning: Your task is to grow up together: stop putting life off, step out of your relatives' care and grow your own.
text: Your task is to stop putting life off and start growing your own. The Empress, the main card of your task, demands maturity: your own home, your own means, shared values, practicality, the ability to weather feast and famine without panic. The Hermit and the Hanged Man pull the other way — towards modesty, waiting, sacrifice — and with them it is easy to live “temporarily” for years, under your relatives' wing, waiting for better times.

For seven years you have lived “temporarily”: half the boxes still packed, sleeping on an air mattress — why buy a bed if everything is about to change? There is always a reason to wait: a downturn, work, “Mum will be hurt”. One Sunday the other books a taxi to the furniture shop: “I want something of our own. Now, not later.” By evening a real bed stands in the bedroom, the boxes are finally unpacked, and you both marvel at how long you've wanted this. **Your garden begins when you stop waiting for permission to live your own life.**

Waiting drags on when it is comfortable. Parents decide for you, money comes and goes without a plan, and the wish for a home of your own is snuffed out with “it's too early”. One endures and sacrifices, the other retreats into their thoughts, and the shared garden stays a wasteland. The Empress has no patience for childishness: you may start small, but start now.

items.title: Life on pause

captions.M: To want to think a little longer
captions.N: To wait, give way, put things off
captions.D: To leave limbo and decide together

items.meaning: Your task is to take the union off pause: stop waiting for a sign, stop sacrificing silently, and finally decide together.
text: Your union easily hangs in mid-air. The Hanged Man appears twice here — as the path and as the main task: to come out of limbo, to stop putting decisions off, waiting for a sign from above and giving way in the hope that things will somehow sort themselves out. The Hermit adds a habit of thinking alone: each of you weighs things for a long time but says nothing aloud, and the pause stretches on for years.

You have lived together for five years, and the talk about the future is put off every time: “let's wait till after the holiday”, “when things are clearer at work”. Sorting out a shelf, the other finds an old notebook of the first one's with a list written three years ago: a house, a dog, a trip up north. None of it was ever discussed. That evening, for the first time, you talk everything through to the end. **The pause ends not when a sign comes but when a wish is finally said aloud.**

Waiting turns into sacrifice when one holds the union together with all their might while the other is still thinking. The one holding on tires and starts to reproach; the one thinking feels the pressure and withdraws even deeper. There are no shared goals, only silent patience and unspoken grievances. The Hanged Man teaches you to look at the situation from outside: sometimes it is enough to turn the question over — not “when will things be clear” but “what do we want now”.

items.title: From the cell to the wide world

captions.M: To want to live in your own quiet corner
captions.N: To give up the world for the union's sake
captions.D: To agree, and open the union to the world, not lock it up

items.meaning: Your task is not to lock the union in a cell: agree on a world of your own and leave room in it for friends and change.
text: You are both drawn to shut yourselves off from the world, and the couple's task is to build a world of your own, an open one. The World in the tail demands wholeness: agreeing on rules with room for both, accepting each other's hobbies and friends, letting new things into your life. The Hermit beckons to a quiet corner, the Hanged Man suggests giving up whatever is superfluous for the union's sake. Together they turn the couple into a cell for two — warm, but cramped.

For many years one of you acted in an amateur theatre and gave it up when you moved in together: “We're fine just the two of us.” A couple of years later the other finds an old poster and suggests going to see the old company's new play. Afterwards the first can't speak for half an hour, and a month later goes back on stage — and at the premiere the other sits in the front row. **Your world becomes whole when it finds room for what one of you once gave up.**

A cell becomes a prison when nobody is let in any more. One partner's friends seem superfluous to the other, plans are mocked, hobbies criticised, and each defends their own. There are no agreements, so you come together and drift apart again and again along the same script. The World needs an open door: a union held together only by isolation can't withstand the first draught.

items.title: A choice not made in a trance

captions.N: To be drawn to each other beyond measure
captions.D: To choose each other freely, without jealousy or control

items.meaning: Your task is a clear choice: love without losing yourselves, and hold on to each other without jealousy or control.
text: This is where you find out whether your choice is free. The Lovers in the couple's tail set the task of loving as adults: choosing a person with open eyes and not losing yourself in the process. The Devil gives the couple an attraction so strong that choice easily turns into a trance, and love into jealous possession. The Hermit in your wishes recalls the counterweight: each needs a life of their own, their own thoughts and the right to be alone.

At the start you weren't apart for a single day: shared friends, shared weekends, practically one phone between you. A year later one of you notices they can't remember when they last read a book or called an old friend. They say so plainly — and the other, to the surprise of both, breathes out with relief: they had been missing themselves too. **Your choice becomes free when each of you has a life of your own again.**

Attraction blinds when insecurity hides beneath passion. One is jealous of friends, of work, even of a book; the other adapts and gradually dissolves. Outbursts of anger alternate with stormy reconciliations, and the ideal picture of love doesn't match what happens at home. The Lovers need clarity: a love that demands you give yourself up is not a choice but captivity.

items.title: A chain forged by two

captions.M: To want freedom and a footing within yourself
captions.N: To cling to each other too tightly
captions.D: To free yourselves from power and dependence on each other

items.meaning: Your task is to break the grip: be together by choice, not from fear that neither of you would cope alone.
text: The doubled Devil sets you a single task: to undo the chain that two people forge so easily. The attraction here is enormous: money, a shared home, habit and the fear of being alone hold you to each other, and all of it is easy to mistake for love. The Hermit in your wishes points the way out: each of you needs a footing within yourself — your own income, your own work, your own quiet — so as to stay together by choice, not out of necessity.

One of you hasn't worked for a long time: that was decided once — “why bother, I'll provide”. They quietly sign up for a course and six months later land their first commission. The other is angry at first — “what, aren't you getting enough?” — and then notices it has become easier to breathe at home: the reproaches are gone, and so is the fear. **The chain comes undone when each can stand alone — and still chooses to stand side by side.**

The grip tightens when wishes go unspoken. One controls the money, the other the time and the social circle, and both hold each other with whatever they can: guilt, promises, the threat of leaving. Every attempt to break free ends in a return to the same circle. The Devil shows a simple thing: a union held together only by fear of loss drags you both down. Freedom doesn't destroy such a couple — it makes it real for the first time.

items.title: A shared trail for two loners

captions.M: To want understanding and a path of your own
captions.N: To fear not being understood
captions.D: To nurture each other's interests and find a shared pursuit

items.meaning: Your task is a shared trail: take an interest in the other's world, don't snuff out their passions, find a pursuit for two.
text: Each of you walks your own trail and feels at home on it. The Hermit stands at both ends, in your wishes and in the outcome, and leads inwards — to your own pursuits, your own questions, your own quiet. The Moon in the middle adds fear: what if the other doesn't understand, laughs, finds it strange? So you keep your worlds to yourselves. The task is not only to respect the other's silence but to take an interest in it and look for a road you can walk together.

For years one of you has watched the stars through a small telescope on the balcony, while the other politely keeps out. One August night the first finally calls: “Come here, you have to see this.” Saturn with its rings — and the other stands on the cold balcony for two hours, asking questions. The next morning the other finds where in the mountains the meteor shower is best seen and silently shows the screen. **The path becomes shared when one dares to invite and the other to take an interest.**

Silence is dangerous when indifference hides behind it. The other's passions seem odd and quietly fade — from silence, a shrug, “you and your hobby again”. In hard times each hides in their own shell instead of helping. There are no shared pursuits, few shared friends, and the union runs on habit. The Hermit would do well to remember: boundaries deserve respect, but if you never cross them, you'll never know the other.

items.title: Off with the first-date masks

captions.M: To want depth and a corner of your own
captions.N: To fill in the gaps and believe illusions
captions.D: To show your real selves and let the made-up image go

items.meaning: Your task is to take off the masks you put on at the start and love each other as you are, not as imagined.
text: The double Moon wraps the union in fog, and getting out of it is your main work. At the start of a relationship it is easy to seem like someone else — braver, merrier, more confident — and then to keep up that image for years, irritable with fatigue. The Hermit in your wishes adds a habit of going through things alone: real feelings hide deep, tenderness seems a weakness, and guesses fill the emptiness.

For the first two years one of you posed as a lover of camping: that is how they won the other over by a campfire. In the third year they finally confess: “I hate sleeping in a tent.” The other laughs till they cry: “And I only went for your sake!” Since then you spend your holidays in small hotels by the sea — and rest properly for the first time. **The union grows stronger when the masks fall and it turns out that what's underneath is loved too.**

An illusion lasts as long as it is defended. Each adapts to the other's expectations, irritation builds, and aloud it's “everything's fine”. Grievances are born of invented stories, quarrels come from nowhere, and one no longer decides anything without the other's approval. The Moon asks for courage: show your real self, risk disappointing — and discover that this is exactly who is loved.

items.title: Values a home grows from

captions.M: To want wisdom and your own answers
captions.N: To build your own big world
captions.D: To reach shared values and grow prosperity together

items.meaning: Your task is shared values: agree what matters most to you, and grow your home and prosperity on that.
text: Each of you knows what you believe in, but the common ground on which something can grow is still to be found. The Empress demands shared values and practicality: deciding what you work, save and grow for. The World in the middle gives a broad view, the Hermit in your wishes — your own answers to the big questions. Without a common denominator each grows their own, and the shared garden stays empty.

One of you thinks money should go into education and travel, the other into the home and security. For years you argue over every big purchase. At last each writes on their own sheet “the five most important things in life”. Three items match: family, freedom, learning all your life. Since then you check every expense against those three words. **A shared garden grows on values you found together.**

Without shared values abundance doesn't hold. Money comes and goes, each spends on their own things, and “feast or famine” becomes the norm. One thinks the other impractical, the other thinks the first too down-to-earth. One partner's carelessness and the other's stubbornness keep you from agreeing. The Empress needs a shared answer to the question “what for?”: without it the harvest is gathered alone.

items.title: A world seen upside down

captions.M: To want to find meaning in silence
captions.N: To build one world out of two
captions.D: To stop sacrificing in silence and find a shared goal

items.meaning: Your task is a shared meaning without sacrifice: seeing the world through the other's eyes, not carrying the union alone.
text: You will have to see your union from an unfamiliar angle. The Hanged Man in the couple's tail is a test of sacrifice and pause: someone holds the relationship together with all their might, yields, waits, and yet no shared goal is in sight. The World shows what to arrive at: a shared picture in which two different views can live side by side. And the Hermit suggests the way — through silence and an honest talk with yourself: what do I really want from this union?

For years one of you has adapted: moving after the other, changing jobs, turning down trips. On a long walk they say it aloud for the first time: “I don't know where we're going. I'm just following you.” The other is stunned — they thought everything was shared anyway. You sit down on a bench and until dark you sketch on a napkin the world you want to see in five years. **You truly meet when sacrifice gives way to a shared design.**

Sacrifice leads to a dead end when it goes unspoken. One gives and waits for gratitude, the other doesn't notice and is surprised by the reproaches. Each lives in their own picture of the world and is sure it is shared. Expectations grow, nobody takes responsibility, and leaving is frightening. The Hanged Man asks you to stop and turn your view around: to see the union through the other's eyes and decide what you are building together, not who sacrificed what.

items.title: Two worlds, one map

captions.M: To want to live by your own understanding
captions.N: To hold to your own picture of the world
captions.D: For two worlds to agree, without re-educating each other

items.meaning: Your task is a pact between two whole worlds: hear the other, don't re-educate them, and stop going round in circles.
text: You both came into the union with finished worlds of your own — views, habits, answers to the big questions. The World appears twice, as the path and as the outcome: to join two wholes into one without destroying either. The Hermit reinforces this with the certainty that your own answer was found long ago and there's no need to revisit it. Hence the lesson: agree, listen, and don't turn love into re-education.

One of you lives entirely by rules: early rising, a strict budget, no spontaneous spending. The other has a guitar, friends till midnight and holidays decided the day before. For five years you argued over whose order was right and nearly split up three times. At last you sit down and write “our rules” on a sheet — just seven points for both, and everything else each decides alone. **A shared world comes not from one picture winning but from a short pact between two.**

Two worlds collide when each is sure they're right. A partner's hobbies are criticised, their friends seem superfluous, their plans laughable. One's strictness and the other's freedom never meet, and again and again you part and come back along the same circle without ever agreeing. The World needs neither isolation nor victory, but a map with room for two different countries.

items.title: A fortress with open windows

captions.N: To build a reliable fortress
captions.D: Not to close in on each other, and to let the world in

items.meaning: Your task is not to lock yourselves in each other: keep a reliable home, but let in friends, pursuits and change.
text: You know how to build a reliable home, and the couple's task is not to turn it into a closed circle. The Wheel of Fortune demands movement: new people, new pursuits, changes that arrive on their own schedule. The Emperor in the middle builds a fortress with rules and reserves, the Hanged Man in your wishes — quiet for two, far from everyone. Together they risk closing the gates, and the wheel keeps turning anyway — only now without you.

For a long time you hardly go anywhere: work, home, a series in the evenings. Friends stop inviting you. When redundancies start at one partner's work, it turns out there's nobody to ask for advice — all your connections have lapsed. After that you make a rule: once a month, guests or something new for the two of you. The first to come, to your surprise, are those same friends who'd stopped inviting you — with wine and a reproachful “at last”. **Luck comes in through open doors, not through locked gates.**

A fortress suffocates when nobody is let in. Your circle shrinks, change frightens you, and every turn of the wheel catches you off guard. One sacrifices their interests for “our quiet”, the other makes sure everything stays as it is. Grievances pile up, complaints about fate replace decisions. The wheel needs space: friends, new pursuits and a readiness sometimes to let go of control.

items.title: Time to step into the sun

captions.M: To want to wait and endure
captions.N: To live by the rules, “as you should”
captions.D: To talk about problems and start enjoying life

items.meaning: Your task is to step out of the shade of “that's how it should be”: talk about problems, act, and let yourselves enjoy life.
text: You know how to live “as you should” and how to endure, but you're only learning to allow yourselves joy. The Sun demands fulfilment, warmth and honest talk about what's wrong. The Emperor in the middle keeps strict order, the Hanged Man in your wishes a habit of enduring and putting your own needs off “for later”. Together they create a life that's proper, reliable and dull, where problems go unmentioned and joy is considered a luxury.

Your schedule has been the same for years: work, renovations, the allotment, reporting to your parents. One evening one of you admits: “I can't remember when we last laughed.” The other takes offence at first, then agrees. For the first time in years you spend your savings not on repairs but on a trip to the sea — and come back different people. **The sun comes out when you stop postponing life for the sake of doing things properly.**

Inaction hides behind order. Nobody talks about problems — “what's the point?” — and they pile up for years. One sacrifices their wishes, the other doesn't notice or doesn't want to. Fulfilment is put off, expectations grow, and the home grows cold, though everything is proper. The Sun needs not permission but a decision: to start enjoying life not some day, but now.

items.title: A wheel that changes hands

captions.M: To want to give way and step into the shade
captions.N: To race ahead and steer alone
captions.D: Neither crush nor turn passive: share the wheel

items.meaning: Your task is to hand over the wheel: one doesn't crush, the other doesn't fade into the shade, and two make decisions.
text: Driver and passenger are roles you slip into easily, and the task is to learn to hand over the wheel. The Emperor raises the question of power and responsibility: who decides, who answers, how not to turn care into suppression. The Chariot in the middle gives one the drive to lead for both, and the Hanged Man offers the other a comfortable role — give way, step into the shade, let the stronger one decide.

One of you is responsible for everything at home: shopping, holidays, repairs, even what to wear to friends' weddings. The other doesn't argue — it's calmer that way. The first is sent away on business for a month, and for the first time the other decides everything — from the gas bill to the leaking tap. Coming back, the first finds the house in perfect order and a person they don't recognise: confident, cheerful. **The wheel becomes shared when the one driving dares to let go of it, if only for a while.**

Suppression happens quietly. One decides because it's quicker, the other agrees because it's calmer — and a few years later the first burns out under the load while the second forgets how to want. Feelings aren't discussed: why bother, if everything is decided anyway. The Emperor needs honesty: power nobody challenges is sooner or later left with no one to talk to.

items.title: When your partner changes

captions.M: To want everything to stay as it was
captions.N: To surge ahead and change
captions.D: To accept change in your partner, not cling to who they were

items.meaning: Your task is to accept that your partner changes: not to keep them as they were, nor fear who they're becoming.
text: Sooner or later one of you will surge ahead, and the other will have to let go of the person they knew. Death demands accepting change in someone close — a new job, new views, a new rhythm — and not clinging to who they were when you met. The Chariot in the middle gives one the resolve to change, while the Hanged Man stirs in the other a wish for everything to stay as it was, and a readiness to sacrifice for that.

One of you suddenly quits the office to train as a landscape designer. For the first months the other takes offence: new friends, new jargon, evenings in other people's gardens. One Saturday they visit a site and see the first explaining to a client where to plant the lilac — absorbed, happy, in a way they haven't spoken for years. At home the other asks: “Will you teach me?” **Change in one doesn't threaten the union when the other doesn't cling to the old version.**

One partner's growth becomes a threat when the other won't accept it. Fear of loss makes you mock the new, put on the brakes, complain: “you've changed”. The one who's changing feels like a traitor and either gives up their own path or goes ever deeper into it, alone. Death needs you to let go of the old: the person you love has the right to become someone else.

items.title: Neither fleeing nor waiting

captions.M: To want to wait and adapt
captions.N: To rush ahead and take to the road
captions.D: To own your freedom and not flee from what is hard

items.meaning: Your task is freedom without flight: one shouldn't forever take to the road, nor the other forever wait on the platform.
text: Two roles easily take shape in your couple: the one who leaves and the one who waits. The Fool, the main card of the task, is freedom without shores: starting is easy, but as soon as things get serious, you want to run. The Chariot gives the escape its wheels: a new project, a trip, a dash. And the Hanged Man in your wishes offers the other the role of the patient one — to wait, give way, accept, anything not to lose.

Every time talk turns to a wedding, one of you finds an urgent business trip or a new course. The other waits and says nothing. This time it is they who buy a ticket — a week by the sea — and leave a note: “I need to think too.” When they come back, they find two cups on the table and someone who, for the first time, hasn't gone anywhere. **Freedom becomes shared when both answer for it — the one who leaves and the one who waits.**

Freedom turns into flight when you drive away from hard conversations. The one who runs even reproaches — “you're holding me back” — though they get jealous the moment the other is late. The one who waits sacrifices years in the hope that some day everything will change. Moods swing, there are no agreements. The Fool doesn't demand that you stay put: he demands that each pay for their own freedom rather than shift the cost onto the other.

items.title: A chariot for each of you

captions.M: To want to sacrifice for the common good
captions.N: To wait for a lucky turn
captions.D: Not to demand giving up goals; to save your strength

items.meaning: Your task is a goal for each: nobody abandons their path for the other, and both take care to restore their strength.
text: You need not one chariot but two, running side by side. The Chariot demands movement towards a goal — and each has their own: a career, a venture, a dream. The Hanged Man nudges one to give up their own for the other: wait, give way, adapt. The Wheel of Fortune throws lucky turns first to one, then to the other, and it matters that one partner's chance doesn't cancel the other's path.

One of you is invited to head a new branch just as the other is finishing studies they've given three years to. The usual script — the other drops everything. But this time you look for another option: for six months the first commutes back and forth, the other completes their degree, and then you decide together where to go. You are both tired, but nobody has been left on the roadside. **You travel faster when neither has to leave the road for the other's sake.**

The Chariot crushes when one partner's goal becomes the only one. The one who gave way stores up resentment and waits for gratitude; the one racing ahead demands new concessions and bristles at any “and what about me”. Strength is spent without being restored, tiredness turns into irritation, irritation into quarrels. The Chariot needs a rule: each has their own road, but the rest stops are shared and compulsory.

items.title: A storm seen differently

captions.M: To want to see trouble from a new angle
captions.N: To ride out a run of rises and falls
captions.D: To go through crisis together without rushing to extremes

items.meaning: Your task is to go through a run of crises together: don't flee to extremes, and see a collapse as a turn, not the end.
text: Your couple meets not one storm but a series, and everything depends on how you face them. The Tower brings sudden collapses — loss, disappointment, the fall of what seemed solid. The Wheel of Fortune turns the storm into a cycle: after a fall comes a rise. And the Hanged Man, where your line begins, suggests the key skill: to look at trouble from a different angle and find meaning in it, not only damage.

In a single year the cottage you rent burns down, one of you loses their job, and the other's promotion goes to someone else. For the first month you are both on edge. Then one suggests something strange: go away for a week to where nobody knows about your troubles, and don't talk about them aloud. On the fifth day, sitting on a stranger's jetty, you find yourselves discussing not what you lost but what it set free: you could live somewhere else, and differently. **A collapse becomes a turn when you look in it for a lesson, not a culprit.**

A crisis drives you apart when each saves themselves in their own way. One goes to one extreme — work, money, control — the other to another: the search for a higher meaning, books about fate, waiting for things to resolve themselves. The image of a partner who seemed reliable crumbles, composure is lost, and each looks their own way. The Tower doesn't ask permission, but how you go through the storm is up to you — together or apart.

items.title: Not afraid of the turn

captions.M: To want to wait it out and not risk
captions.N: To end what has outlived itself
captions.D: To step past the fear of change together into a new cycle

items.meaning: Your task is to step past the fear of change together: end what's outlived itself and enter a new cycle rather than wait.
text: Changes come to you on fate's schedule, and you prefer to wait them out — that's exactly the lesson.
