The Wheel of Fortune demands that you accept the turns and overcome your fear of them together. Death in the middle says it plainly: something has already ended, and pretending otherwise is useless. And the Hanged Man offers a comfortable position — wait a little longer, it might sort itself out.

You've both long felt cramped in the town where you live, and you've long been saying: “Maybe, some day.” One partner's company is closed, and the decision you kept putting off is made for you by circumstances. The first month is frightening. Already in the new city, walking along the waterfront, you both admit you'd have waited another ten years. **Fear shrinks when you step into the new together, not alone.**

Waiting becomes a trap when fear is stronger than desire. The outworn is kept because it's familiar; the new isn't started because it's unknown. Each is afraid in their own way, but talking about fear is shameful, and instead of conversation there's irritation and reproach. The wheel will turn anyway: the only question is whether you meet the turn holding hands, or each clutching their own.

items.title: Out of the shade, into the sun

captions.M: To want to live for the other
captions.N: To finish the old to begin your own
captions.D: For both to flourish without eclipsing each other

items.meaning: Your task is light for both: leave sacrifice and shade behind, end what has outlived itself and let each of you flourish.
text: You are to shine for two. The Sun sets the couple the task of fulfilment: each must find their own work and their own joy, without hiding behind the partner or eclipsing them. The Hanged Man, where your line begins, pulls the other way — to live for the other and give up your own. And Death stands between them like a mountain pass: to come out into the light, you will have to end the old role of the one who always stays in the shade.

For ten years one of you has run the home and kept the books for the other's business, while their own dream — teaching — sits on a back shelf. It is the other who brings in an advert for a training course: “It'll be hard for me without you. But it's worse for you without this.” A month later the first has their first students, and at supper you finally have two stories about the day instead of one. **The sun rises for both when the one in the shade dares to step out to their own work.**

The shade deepens when sacrifice becomes a habit. One dissolves in the other's affairs and silently waits for gratitude; the other grows used to the victories being theirs and doesn't notice whose hand held them up. Problems go undiscussed, expectations grow, and one partner's sun burns rather than warms. The Sun needs light from both sides: a union in which only one has found fulfilment fades sooner or later.

items.title: A foundation after the collapse

captions.M: To want to endure and not complain
captions.N: To survive a sudden collapse
captions.D: To build a reliable system and talk about feelings

items.meaning: Your task is a foundation after the collapse: a system that withstands a blow, and a habit of talking about feelings.
text: Your couple knows how to endure; what it has to learn is to build so that enduring isn't needed. The Emperor demands a reliable system: a stable income, pots for different contingencies, clear agreements. The Tower in the middle explains why: sudden blows happen, and what rested on luck collapses. And from the Hanged Man comes a habit of silently carrying the load instead of saying: “It's hard for me.”

In a single month you lose one partner's job and your rented flat, and the other says aloud for the first time in years: “I can't keep it all in any more.” You sit down and build a system: three pots — for a rainy day, for housing, for joy — and a rule that once a month you talk not only about money but about how each of you is doing. **A foundation is solid when it has both a reserve and the right to say that it's hard.**

Endurance without a system leads to new collapses. There's no money for a bad day, rules devised by one get in the other's way, and feelings are held in until they burst out. One becomes harsh and commanding, the other passive and silent. The Emperor builds reliably only when he listens: walls raised in silence collapse at the first tremor.

items.title: Change starts with yourselves

captions.M: To want the other to change
captions.N: To live through crisis and collapse
captions.D: To see your own mistakes and change yourselves

items.meaning: Your task is to change yourselves after a crisis, not wait for your partner to change: see your own share and start there.
text: After every crisis each of you wants the other to change — and that's the main lesson. Death demands change, but it begins with yourself: see your own mistakes, not only the other's, let go of old habits, live through the crisis as a trial, not a verdict. The Tower in the middle brings collapses that put the question point-blank. And the Hanged Man suggests turning your view around: what if it's not only about the other?

After a bad quarrel that nearly ended in a break-up, you both wait a week for an apology. At last one sits down and writes not a list of the other's mistakes but a list of their own. It turns out unexpectedly long. The sheet is silently laid on the table. The other reads it, leaves, and an hour later comes back with their own. **Change in a couple begins when each looks at themselves first.**

A crisis teaches nothing when it's always the other's fault. Each waits for the partner to change and takes offence when it doesn't happen. Fear of change keeps you in place: changing jobs, habits, the way you argue is frightening — reproaching is easier. Death makes no exceptions: if the old doesn't die in you, it repeats in every new crisis.

items.title: Freedom without “must”

captions.M: To want to sacrifice and endure
captions.N: To survive the collapse of obligations
captions.D: To build the union on trust, not on duty and checks

items.meaning: Your task is a union without “must”: hold together by trust and choice, not by duty, sacrifice and checks.
text: Obligations easily crowd out wishes in your couple, and the task is one day to burn the list. The Fool asks the main question of freedom: what holds you — desire or “must”? The Hanged Man teaches sacrifice and endurance, piling up debts that will later be presented. And the Tower in the middle brings this structure down — abruptly, in a single day, when patience runs out.

Years of reproaches — “I give up everything for you”, “and because of you I have to put up with this” — end in a row, after which you both sit in the kitchen in silence. In the morning one suggests a strange game: for a month, nobody owes anybody anything. Whoever wants to cooks; whoever misses the other calls. By the end of the month it's clear: you want and miss more often than you used to do things out of duty. **The union becomes light when what holds you is desire, not duty.**

Freedom without trust turns into chaos. One demands liberty for themselves while checking the other's phone, each has their own rules, and any serious decision prompts flight. It also happens the other way: sacrifices pile up until they collapse all at once, and after the fall you both discover you were held together only by obligations. The Fool needs freedom given without checks and faithfulness kept without chains.

items.title: A new goal after the finish

captions.M: To want rest and a pause
captions.N: To enjoy the success you've won
captions.D: To find a new shared goal and not get stuck in routine

items.meaning: Your task is not to stop at the finish: find a new shared goal and get moving again without overdoing it.
text: You know how to achieve, and the test comes after the victory. The Chariot demands movement towards a goal, and as soon as the goal is reached it asks: where next? The Sun in the middle gives the couple success and warmth, and the Hanged Man a pull to stop, take a pause, live without racing. A pause is needed, but if it drags on, the chariot stands still, passion fades and routine sets in.

You spent a long time building a house and finally moved in. The first months are bliss: a fireplace, a garden, guests. Then the evenings become the same, conversations short, and neither understands what's wrong. One Sunday one spreads a map on the table and asks: “Where do we want to go next?” A week later you have a new goal — walking a long coastal trail end to end — and training at weekends. **The union comes alive when a reached goal is followed at once by the next shared one.**

The Chariot gets stuck when one goal is reached and there's no new one. Each withdraws into their own affairs, passion fades, mutual demotivation grows: why try if things are fine as they are? The opposite tilt happens too: one drives themselves with new dashes without restoring their strength, while the other wants only rest. The Chariot needs a rhythm — a dash, a rest stop, a new route — all three together.

items.title: When the other is in the dark

captions.M: To want to carry your load in silence
captions.N: To look happy and successful
captions.D: To notice the other struggling and get through it together

items.meaning: Your task is to notice when the other is in the dark: see their trouble behind the bright picture and face it together.
text: Outside everything is sunny for you, and that makes it all the more important not to miss it when one of you is in the dark. The Tower brings sudden trials that must be lived through together, not hidden. The Sun in the middle keeps up the façade: successful, cheerful, all's well with us. And from the Hanged Man comes a knack for silently carrying your own load without troubling others — even the one beside you.

For months one of you smiles in public and jokes at home, but can't sleep at night: everything at work is falling apart, and it's shameful to talk about. The other only notices on finding, at three in the morning in the kitchen, a cold cup of tea and a person staring at the wall. They sit down beside them and don't leave till morning. A week later you're looking for a way out together — and you find it. **Trouble is easier to bear when the one beside you sees it behind the sunny façade.**

The danger of a façade is that the cracks can't be seen behind it. One hides how low they feel, the other doesn't notice or doesn't want to, because it's calmer that way. When the trouble breaks through, it turns out each was in it alone. The Tower asks for attention to small things: a tired voice, cancelled plans, a smile that doesn't reach the eyes.

items.title: Solutions instead of complaints

captions.N: To wait for things to sort themselves out
captions.D: To seek solutions instead of complaining and playing on pity

items.meaning: Your task is solutions instead of complaints: don't wait for things to mend themselves or press each other with pity.
text: When the wheel turns downwards, it's easier for your couple to complain than to act, and that's your main lesson. The Wheel of Fortune demands that you look for solutions: stop blaming circumstances and each other and start doing something. The Fool in the middle offers an easy “it'll sort itself out”, the Hanged Man the role of a sufferer who needs pity. Together they turn every downturn into a play where everyone waits to be rescued.

For three months one of you has been out of work and every evening tells how unfair the world is. The other sympathises, consoles, then tires and snaps: “Enough, let's do something.” The quarrel is hard, but in the morning you sit down together and make a list: ten companies, three acquaintances, one course. A month later the job is found. **The wheel turns upwards when a complaint gives way to a to-do list.**

A complaint becomes a lever when it's used to steer. Grievances and tears make the other give way, tantrums replace conversation, and someone else is always to blame — the boss, fate, the partner. Decisions are put off, problems grow. The wheel turns for everyone, but it lifts those who, finding themselves at the bottom, ask not “why me” but “what next”.

items.title: Playing fair as a pair

captions.M: To want more than the rules allow
captions.N: To stick to rules and laws
captions.D: To be honest about money and admit your fault

items.meaning: Your task is to play fair: wishes and money by law and conscience, debts paid on time, fault admitted.
text: Honesty with the world and with each other — that is what your couple is tested on. Justice demands clean accounts: debts paid on time, promises kept, mistakes admitted rather than shifted onto the other. The Devil in your wishes tempts you with the easy way: more, faster, round the rules. The Hierophant stands in the middle as a reminder of law and rules — external ones and those you adopted yourselves.

For a couple of years one of you “forgot” to declare their side income, and the other never asked: after all, the money went into the home. The letter from the tax office arrives on a Friday. You want someone to blame — whoever didn't remind, whoever advised, whoever invented these rules in the first place. Instead you sit down together and work out the debt with penalties; on Monday the first goes to pay it themselves, and that evening you laugh for the first time in a week. **The union grows stronger when the wish for more passes through honesty, not around it.**

Justice breaks down when the blame always lies with the other. One takes out a loan without consulting, the other learns of the debt from a bank letter, and instead of a conversation a trial begins. The one who thinks they're right controls every expense; the other withdraws and says nothing. Justice asks you to forgive, but also to settle your accounts: admit your share, put it right, and agree on new rules together.

items.title: A star with no pedestal

captions.N: To keep to your circle's rules
captions.D: To shine together without belittling or binding your partner

items.meaning: Your task is to shine together without rising above: don't measure each other by status or make your partner dependent.
text: You both like to dazzle, and the couple's task is to shine without climbing onto a pedestal. The Star demands that each be able to fulfil their dream and show themselves, without hiding in the other's shadow. The Devil kindles a craving for status and power, and the Hierophant in the middle a pride in your circle, family, the rules of “decent people”. Together these cards easily turn the union into a hierarchy where one is on stage and the other at its foot.

One of you comes from a family with a famous name, the other from a small town where the parents have a vegetable plot and a garage. In the first years, at family celebrations, the other is quietly corrected: wrong fork, wrong joke. At one such celebration the first stands up at the table and says: “I'm proud of where my person comes from. Everything we have, we made with our own hands.” From that evening something in the family changes. **The Star shines brighter when its light doesn't have to be won at the other's expense.**

Light turns into superiority when one starts measuring the other by status. Mockery of their hobbies, comparisons with “successful” acquaintances, money handed out to keep them close. The one belittled is afraid to pursue their dream, and the one belittling doesn't admit mistakes and puts the relationship on display. The Star needs simplicity: two people on one level, each with their own light.

items.title: Power split down the middle

captions.M: To want power and strong feelings
captions.N: To demand honesty and order
captions.D: To keep strength in check and share power fairly

items.meaning: Your task is to share power fairly: keep your drive in check and don't steer each other with money and rules.
text: You have a lot of strength, and the main thing is not to turn it against each other. Strength demands that you tame your force: anger, stubbornness, the wish for everything to go your way. The Devil in your wishes fuels the craving for power and strong feelings; Justice offers a way to share that power — honestly, by agreement, with equal rights. Otherwise one strong hand begins to steer the other: with money, rules, fear.

For a long time all your money sat on one partner's card: “it's easier that way”. The other had to ask for grocery money every time and felt like a child. After yet another “and what do you need that much for?” they don't shout but sit down and write out how much they put into the home in time and work. The list comes out long. A week later you have a joint account and two personal ones, with no reports. **Strength becomes shared when power over money and decisions is split fairly.**

Force turns into pressure when it isn't kept in check. One works without days off and believes they've earned the right to decide; the other carries the household and stays silent until they explode. Passion in quarrels turns into harsh words, and reconciliations change nothing. Strength needs a clear rule: argue as much as you like, but don't steer each other — not with money, not with fear, not with silence.

items.title: An inheritance without a feud

captions.M: To want your own, and more of it
captions.N: To demand a fair share
captions.D: To settle family accounts fairly and stay united

items.meaning: Your task is to go through family accounts honestly: inheritance, debts and old grievances mustn't set you two at odds.
text: Your families' past will one day present you with a bill, and you'll have to pay it honestly, without falling out. Judgement raises the theme of kin: inheritance, family debts, old grievances between relatives. Justice in the middle demands clarity: who's entitled to what, who owes what, where the line runs between a right and greed. And the Devil in your wishes tempts you to take more — at any price.

When one partner's grandfather's house is being divided, the relatives demand it be sold and argue over every square metre. The other is silent at first, then says: “I don't need those metres if they stop you speaking to your brother.” You propose a fair option — a valuation and a buyout in instalments, no court. The brother doesn't agree at once, but a year later he comes to your housewarming with a present. **Family accounts close in peace when fairness matters more to you than gain.**

The past destroys when you look for gain in it. Disputes over shares grow into lawsuits, grievances against relatives get transferred onto each other, and you start counting who contributed what. Nobody can admit a mistake. Judgement needs honesty and measure: take what's yours, give back what's not, and don't let old accounts divide those living now.

items.title: No sermons, no taming

captions.M: To want power over the other's feelings
captions.N: To press with temper and stubbornness
captions.D: To accept the other's opposite nature without remaking them

items.meaning: Your task is a union of opposites without lectures: don't remake each other by force, passion or morals.
text: You're very different, and keeping that balance without lecturing is your main lesson. The Hierophant puts the question of a way of life before you: how two people with different habits, views and ideas of what's right can live together. Strength in the middle pushes you to settle it by force — outlast, wear down. And the Devil, where it all begins, adds the temptation of power: to make the other convenient, yours, remade in your image.

One of you is an early bird who loves order and makes lists; the other lives at night and finds their keys only by making them beep. The first years are endless training: alarms, reminders, lectures on discipline. At last the first notices the other has become nervy and quiet, and scraps all the rules but two. A month later the keys still get lost, but there's laughter at home again. **Your way of life holds when the difference between you stops being a reason for re-education.**

Teacher and pupil are bad roles for lovers. The one who lectures is sure they know what's right and presses — with temper, passion, morals. The one being remade either shuts down or answers with the same force, and an argument over trifles becomes a war of world views. The Hierophant needs a shared charter that also records each one's right to stay themselves.

items.title: A measure for strong desires

captions.N: To push and not give way
captions.D: To find measure in passion, not rush, and rebuild trust

items.meaning: Your task is a measure for strong desires: don't rush, don't press each other, and guard your trust.
text: Your desires are strong, and they need measure. Temperance demands balance: don't rush, don't throw yourselves into extremes, mix hot with cold. The Devil in your wishes wants everything at once — passion, money, power. Strength in the middle adds pressure: push through, outlast, take what's yours. Without measure this mixture explodes; with measure it becomes an engine that carries you both.

You fell in love so hard that within a month you'd moved in together, within three taken out a mortgage, within six got a dog. In the second year it turns out you hardly know each other: habits, fears, how each copes with tiredness. Instead of breaking up you take a pause: every evening an hour of talk without phones, like the first dates you never really had. **Trust grows at the pace both can bear, not the pace passion wants.**

Without measure, passion turns into control. One wants to hold every detail of the other's life, the other resists, and every argument ends not in an agreement but in the stronger one's victory. Emotions are suppressed until they explode, trust cracks from one harsh phrase and is glued back in a hurry. Temperance asks for a slow fire: passion doesn't go out if you don't fan it into a blaze.

items.title: Responsibility without policing

captions.M: To want to hold everything in your hands
captions.N: To balance and smooth things over
captions.D: To answer for your own part without controlling the other

items.meaning: Your task is responsibility without policing: each answers for their own, and neither becomes the other's inspector.
text: It's easy for one of you to take everything on, and responsibility just as easily becomes policing. Justice demands honesty: each answers for their own part, admits their own mistakes, neither shifts their load nor takes over the other's. From the Devil comes the urge to hold everything in your hands; from Temperance in the middle, a habit of smoothing things over to avoid rows until the imbalance grows huge.

One of you handles all the accounts, remembers every deadline and checks whether the other has paid their share. The other stopped keeping track long ago — why bother, it'll be checked anyway. Then the first disappears for a month into a crunch at work, and it turns out the other copes perfectly well alone, only paying on the last day instead of three days early. Surfacing from the crunch, the first for the first time hands over half the tasks without checking. **Each of you needs your whole share of responsibility — without the other as a safety net.**

Over-responsibility quickly becomes control. The one who answers for everything gets tired and starts reproaching; the one answered for gets out of the habit and steps back from family matters. Debts and late payments crop up exactly where nobody feels in charge. Justice needs the ability to switch: to trust, to let go, to see that the other may have their own way of doing things.

items.title: Strength for all but each other

captions.M: To want success and strong sensations
captions.N: To burn with a dream and big plans
captions.D: To set priorities: work, rest and time together

items.meaning: Your task is to set priorities: to put your strength not only into dreams and careers, but into home and each other.
text: You have strength enough for everything — except each other, and that's the main lesson. Strength demands balance between work, rest and family, a fair share of chores and attention. The Devil in your wishes fires up ambition and a thirst for results, the Star in the middle — big dreams for which you'd sacrifice weekends and sleep. Your relationship ends up last in the queue.

You have two businesses, a marathon in spring, evening classes and a renovation. One Sunday you suddenly find the shared calendar booked up until June, with no slot for “us”. One of you takes the calendar and writes “us” in — as firmly as client meetings: Wednesday evening and half of Sunday. For the first weeks it feels strange, then it becomes the most precious item on the schedule. **Strength shows not in how much you get done, but in who gets your attention.**

Without priorities strength turns into a race. One slogs without days off, the other carries the home and stores up resentment, chores are shared unfairly, and irritation spills out in sharp words. Each is sure they're trying for the common good, and doesn't notice there's almost nothing common left. Strength needs humility: to admit you can't do it all, and to choose what matters more.

items.title: Love in spite of gossip

captions.M: To want strong feeling and status
captions.N: To hope and dream regardless
captions.D: To defend your choice before the family, not live for gain

items.meaning: Your task is to defend your union despite the gossip: choose for love, not for gain or the family's approval.
text: Many find your union strange, and the couple's task is to defend it without looking back at the gossip. Judgement puts relatives and society up for discussion: a difference in age, status, background, the family's opinion of your couple. The Star in the middle gives hope and the courage to dream regardless. And the Devil in your wishes tests what holds you: feeling — or status, money, gain.

One partner's relatives are sure the other is “after something”: you're just too different — in age, money, background. For years you justify yourselves, prove, explain how you met. At last you simply stop: quietly, without guests, you make it official, and come to the next family celebration together — calm, holding hands. A few years later the chief sceptic is the first to raise a toast to you. **The choice becomes yours when you stop asking permission for it.**

The test grows heavier when it has a false bottom. If the union rests not only on feeling but on gain — a flat, connections, money — the gossip hurts more, because there's a grain of truth in it. A false image built for the relatives cracks over time. Judgement needs honesty with yourselves: why are we together — and are we ready to answer that aloud?

items.title: The keys to your own life

captions.M: To want prosperity and strong support
captions.N: The voice of the family and family debts
captions.D: To leave your relatives' care and create your own ways

items.meaning: Your task is ways of your own: leave your relatives' care and money behind and decide about your family yourselves.
text: Strong families stand behind your couple, and the task is to become independent within them. The Hierophant sets the theme of traditions and relatives: how to live, where to live, on whose money and by whose rules. Judgement adds the voice of the family line, family debts and expectations. And the Devil lures with the easy way — accepting help that binds more tightly than any rules: money, a flat, connections, paid for later with obedience.

One partner's parents gave you a flat — and kept the keys. Every Sunday an inspection of the fridge, every purchase discussed at the family table. The other suggests: “Let's move to a rented place. Smaller, but ours.” The first resists for a long time, then agrees. A year later relations with the family are warmer than before: now they visit by invitation. **Your way of life becomes yours when you stop paying for it with your freedom.**

Care turns into power when obedience is expected in return for help. Relatives decide when you should have children and where to go on holiday, and you argue not with each other but with other people's rules. One tries to remake the other to fit their family's demands, the other shuts down. The Hierophant needs a charter of your own — not against the family but alongside it, written by the two of you.

items.title: A garden where both grow

captions.M: A secret fear of falling behind
captions.N: To grow, care and invest
captions.D: To grow together, not jealous of each other's growth

items.meaning: Your task is for both to grow: don't envy each other's success or leave one in the shade of shared abundance.
text: The Empress leads your couple twice, and the main task is for both to grow in the shared garden. You know how to create abundance, grow a home, a business, a family, but on the dark side this growth becomes unequal: one grows, the other gets stuck, and jealousy of the other's success poisons the harvest. The Moon mixes in a secret fear: what if I fall behind, what if I stop being respected?

In three years one of you has gone from sales assistant to manager, while the other kept the house all that time. At a party a friend jokes: “Well, you're the keeper of the hearth.” The other laughs, and that night can't sleep. The first notices and in the morning suggests: “Now it's your turn — study, your own business, whatever you like. We'll share the house.” **Abundance is real when both grow, not one at the other's expense.**

Unequal growth breeds quiet wars. The one who grew dismisses the one who “fell behind”, the one who fell behind is jealous of work, friends, successes. Household duties tilt, money becomes a measure of power. The fear of falling behind hides behind grievances, and nobody talks about it. The Empress needs a garden where each has their own bed: you can only grow what's shared if nobody stands in the shade.

items.title: Grown-ups with no rescuers

captions.N: To wait for care, as in childhood
captions.D: To take responsibility and not wait to be rescued

items.meaning: Your task is to grow up together: stop waiting for someone to come and fix everything, and take responsibility yourselves.
text: The secret hope that some day someone will come and fix everything — that's what your couple has to outgrow. The Hanged Man in the main task speaks of difficulty taking responsibility and inflated expectations — of the partner, the parents, fate. The Empress in the middle promises care, as in childhood. And the Moon hides real needs: you want them guessed rather than having to ask.

For years you've lived on loans from relatives: for repairs, for a holiday, “temporarily”. Every call from Mum comes with a question about what you're spending on. Putting the phone down after yet another such call, the other puts a notebook in front of the first: “Let's add up how much we owe and pay it back. Ourselves.” It takes two years, but every payment is a small victory. **Grown-up life begins on the day you stop waiting for rescuers.**

Waiting to be rescued becomes a way of life when it's comfortable. Parents decide for you, you resent their power and keep taking. One waits for the other to guess, the other for the first to ask, and both store up resentment. Playing on pity replaces asking. The Hanged Man teaches you to turn the picture over: support is found not outside but in each other.

items.title: Loving without self-doubt

captions.M: To want mystery and complete merging
captions.N: To doubt that you deserve love
captions.D: To love yourself within the couple and leave jealousy behind

items.meaning: Your task is a love that starts with yourself: stop doubting your worth and stop testing the other's feelings.
text: Believing that you are loved — that is the main lesson. The Lovers in the couple's tail, twice over at that, set the task of self-love within the union: while one doubts whether they deserve it, jealousy and control grow by themselves. The Moon in your wishes adds fog: you long for complete merging and wordless understanding, and every silence from the other seems a sign that the feeling is fading.

Burned once before, one of you takes a long time to believe they can be loved just as they are. Every evening there are careful tests: are you really not tired of me? On yet another such evening the other doesn't answer the question but silently puts a sheet of paper on the table with twenty reasons why they chose this person and nobody else. For years afterwards the sheet hangs on the fridge. **Jealousy retreats where a person finally believes they weren't chosen by mistake.**

Self-doubt quickly becomes suspicion of the other. Messages checked, questions asked, flare-ups over trifles, an ideal picture of the relationship that reality never lives up to. One tries to earn love, the other tires of proving it, and both are unhappy. The Moon and the Lovers need the same thing: stop guessing and say aloud what you're afraid of — then fear stops being in charge.

items.title: Obsession dressed as love

captions.N: Jealousy and doubts about your choice
captions.D: Not to hold on through fear; to voice secret desires

items.meaning: Your task is love without obsession: don't hold on through fear, and don't stay silent about what you truly want.
text: You're drawn to each other so strongly that love is easily confused with obsession. The Devil sets the couple a task of freedom: a person isn't property, and holding them through fear, guilt or dependence means truly losing them. The Lovers in the middle bring jealousy and doubts about your choice, the Moon in your wishes a longing for secret, complete closeness with no room for outsiders or the unknown.

Late one evening one of you admits: every time the other is late, they imagine the worst and stare at the phone for hours. The other could be offended by the mistrust, but instead asks: “What are you really afraid of?” The conversation goes into the past, to an old story of betrayal the first had never told. After that evening the “where are you?” calls grow fewer and fewer. **The grip loosens when a secret fear is spoken aloud and shared between two.**

Obsession grows in the dark. Desires are hidden, fears unnamed, and instead of conversation there's control: where were you, who did you talk to, why didn't you answer. You hold each other with whatever you can: intimacy, money, guilt. A union where one stands guard and the other makes excuses drags both down. The Devil lets go when what was hidden comes out into the light.

items.title: A secret worth sharing

captions.M: To want mystery and wordless understanding
captions.N: To retreat inwards and think alone
captions.D: To build trust: share and call out, rather than hide

items.meaning: Your task is trust: opening your secret worlds to each other instead of hiding them behind a silent wisdom.
text: Each of you has an inner world the other isn't let into straight away, and your task is to open its door. The Hermit stands both on the path and in the couple's main task: you tend to think alone, decide silently and respect each other's silence so much that you can miss the moment the other is struggling. The Moon, meanwhile, pulls towards mystery and wordless understanding — beautiful, but not always accurate.

For six months one of you has been writing a novel at night and showing it to no one. The other notices the light under the door but doesn't ask, out of respect. At last the first brings a printout: “Will you read it? I'm scared.” You read all night, and by morning you share a secret that brings you closer than any confession. **Closeness grows when a secret becomes shared rather than a wall between you.**

Silence drives you apart when it becomes a place to hide from problems. Each deals with hard things alone and keeps quiet about their fears, while the other guesses at reasons and takes offence at what they imagined. A partner's interests seem foreign and are quietly snuffed out by indifference. The Hermit would do well to remember that the lantern is not for its bearer alone: light that is shared shows the road to both.

items.title: A moon that has its phases

captions.M: To want mystery and depth of feeling
captions.N: To withdraw in order to recover
captions.D: Not to take distance for lack of love or believe your fears

items.meaning: Your task is to learn each other's phases: tell withdrawal from lack of love, and don't build stories out of fear.
text: Feelings in your couple have phases, like the Moon: now fullness and closeness, now a dark side when one withdraws. The Moon stands both in your wishes and in the main task — the union longs for depth, mystery, merging, and gets mood swings and fears instead. The Hermit in the middle explains what is going on: withdrawing is a way to recover, not a sign of lost love. The task is to learn to see the difference.

Every couple of months one of you seems to disappear: short answers, long walks alone, early nights. In the first years the other took fright every time and staged an interrogation. Now you have a signal — a cup upside down on the windowsill: “I'm in my burrow, it's not about you.” The other leaves a bar of chocolate beside it and waits. Three days later the cup stands the right way up again. **Your closeness rests on trust that a dark phase is always followed by a full one.**

Darkness frightens when it is explained by the worst. Distance looks like cooling, silence like a betrayal of feeling, and each has their own version ready, though nobody has asked anything. Tenderness is hidden so as not to seem weak, fears are shifted onto the partner, quarrels flare up out of nowhere. The Moon needs you to accept a simple thing: everyone has their own nights, and what they need is not an interrogation but a light in the window.

items.title: A dream of home without the fog

captions.M: To dream silently and fear to ask
captions.N: To wait and sacrifice your own
captions.D: To decide honestly together what your family will be

items.meaning: Your task is to bring your dream of family out of the fog: say honestly what you want and grow it together.
text: Each of you has a dream of home and family, and it's time to bring it out of the fog into the light. The Empress demands grown-up decisions: what your home, your prosperity, your family will be like, how you grow together. The Moon in your wishes hides dreams behind fear — what if the other doesn't want it, what if they laugh. And the Hanged Man in the middle offers a convenient way out: wait, give way, sacrifice your own, anything to avoid starting a hard conversation.

For years your couple has skirted the question of children: one thinks the other isn't ready, the other that the first doesn't want them. Relatives ask, you joke your way out. On the drive back from the country cottage, one finally says: “I'm afraid to talk about it, because I'm afraid of your answer.” The answer turns out to be nothing like what was feared. **Your shared home begins with the conversation you were both afraid of for so long.**

The dream fades when decisions are put off out of fear. One sacrifices their wish without asking whether the sacrifice is needed, the other lives on guesses. Relatives press, envy of others' well-being gnaws, and the practical steps — housing, money, plans — aren't taken. The Empress needs clarity: you can only grow what has been planted, and you plant with words spoken aloud.

items.title: Compassion, not pity

captions.M: To sense each other without words
captions.N: To sacrifice and endure
captions.D: To sympathise, not to play on pity

items.meaning: Your task is compassion instead of pity: to feel the other's pain without turning it into a lever or dissolving in it.
text: You have sensitivity to spare, and it has to be turned into compassion, not pity. The Hanged Man stands twice, on the path and at its end: in this couple it's easy to sacrifice, endure, dissolve in the other's pain — and just as easy to play on pity when you want your own way. The Moon in your wishes heightens sensitivity to the limit: every mood of the other echoes in you.

When one partner's years-long project collapses, the other lives their grief for a week: not sleeping, not eating, crying along with them. On the eighth day the first says: “I don't need us both to suffer. I need you beside me, holding on.” The other breathes out, puts the kettle on and suggests a walk — and it helps more than shared tears. **Compassion works when one holds on rather than drowning along with the other.**

Sensitivity turns into manipulation when pain becomes a way of getting what you want. Tears instead of a request, hurt silence instead of a conversation, “you don't care how bad I feel” — and the other gives in out of guilt. Or you both drown in feelings and can't help each other. The Hanged Man teaches you to turn your view around: real help is support, not a shared bog.

items.title: Breaking the charmed circle

captions.N: To endure, sacrifice, wait
captions.D: To leave the repeating script and settle conflicts in words

items.meaning: Your task is to break the circle: stop repeating the same heavy conversation and come to terms in a new way.
text: Your couple has its own charmed circle, and the main task is to get out of it. The World demands completion: agree, decide, close the question rather than return to it again and again. The Hanged Man in the middle prompts you to endure and wait, and the Moon to hope the other will understand without words. As a result the same quarrel repeats for years — to the same script, with the same lines.

Every December you quarrel about the same thing: where to spend the holidays. The same arguments, the same hurt, the same silence until Christmas. In the fifth year one of you gets out a notebook and writes down what you're really arguing about: not the trip but whose family matters more. For the first time the conversation goes deeper rather than round in circles, and by mid-December the decision is made without tears. **The circle breaks when you talk about what lies under the quarrel, not about the quarrel itself.**

The script repeats when the unspoken waits to be guessed. One endures and keeps quiet, the other doesn't understand what the hurt is about, and each new round adds tiredness. The illusion that “everything's fine with us” keeps you in place, and real agreements are never made. The World needs words: a conflict settled aloud doesn't come back.

items.title: Passion that chooses its words

captions.N: To flare up and hold on too tight
captions.D: To protect each other with words and choose trust

items.meaning: Your task is a passion that guards its words: don't wound in the heat of the moment, don't test, keep choosing trust.
text: You have passion enough; what you must learn is not to burn each other with words. The Lovers demand a careful love: honest, faithful, without blows to the sore spot. The Devil in the middle brings passion and a quick temper — peace one moment, war the next — and the Moon in your wishes adds secret fears: what if the other isn't the one, what if they leave? In the heat of the moment these fears fire off phrases that can never be taken back.

During yet another quarrel one of you throws out: “You're just like your father.” The other goes pale and goes out onto the balcony. An hour later the first goes out too and doesn't make excuses but says: “That was cruel. I'm scared when we fight, and I hit where it hurts most.” Since that evening, parents and the past are off limits in your quarrels. **Passion stays love as long as there are words in it you don't say even in anger.**

The storm becomes a habit when quarrels replace conversation. Scenes in front of friends, checking messages, jealousy born of invented stories, and after every storm a passionate reconciliation that solves nothing. Relatives on both sides are happy to add fuel. The Lovers need faithfulness in words too: in a quarrel you may be angry, but you mustn't betray trust.

items.title: Trust rather than checking

captions.M: To want to know everything about the other
captions.N: To worry and fill in the gaps
captions.D: To respect each other's boundaries and not hide in a shell

items.meaning: Your task is trust without surveillance: respect each other's boundaries, but don't hide behind them from what's hard.
text: The Moon stands twice on the way to your main task, and anxiety is a frequent guest in this couple. You want to know everything about the other, understand every pause, and any closed space seems a threat. The Hermit in the main task teaches the opposite: each has the right to their own corner, their own thoughts and their own quiet. The lesson is to respect those boundaries — and not to hide behind them when the other needs help.

Once one of you reads the other's messages while they're in the shower. Finds nothing — and that makes it even more shameful. In the evening they confess: “I get scared when you close up, and I do stupid things.” The other isn't angry but explains: “I don't close up from you, I close up to think. Let me tell you when I'm going into myself.” **In your couple a boundary isn't broken into but explained — and that's how trust grows.**

Anxiety corrodes when guesses replace questions and surveillance replaces trust. One closes up ever deeper because every pause is followed by an interrogation, the other grows ever more anxious because nothing is explained. Both need to know where the line is: don't go where you weren't invited, and don't vanish where you can't be found.

items.title: Solid ground under moonlight

captions.N: To live by instinct and guesswork
captions.D: To find firm footing: shared goals instead of illusions

items.meaning: Your task is solid ground underfoot: shared goals and a clear outlook instead of illusions, guesswork and shaky support.
text: The Moon stands three times in your tail, and this couple's world resembles a moonlit night: beautiful, mysterious, and nothing seen for certain. You're drawn to magic, to understanding without words, to living by instinct. The task is to find solid ground under this light: shared goals, clear agreements, support resting not on one shaky thing — looks, money, connections — but on what you're really building together.

For three years you live as if in a fairy tale: spontaneous trips, shared dreams, talks till dawn. At some point one of you asks: “What will we have in five years?” — and neither knows. Instead of taking fright, you sit down and for the first time draw up a shared plan: a home, work, a dream for two. The fairy tale doesn't vanish; it just gains a road. **Magic doesn't melt when solid ground appears beneath it.**

An illusion holds until the first trial comes. A union built on one thing — beauty, money, a shared crowd — wobbles when that support disappears. Adjusting to the other's expectations ends in irritation, and one no longer decides anything without the other's approval. The Moon needs a dawn: an honest look at who you are and where you're going, without masks or invented roles.

items.title: Jealous of the wide world

captions.N: To reach for the wide world
captions.D: To deal with jealousy and grow your own, not envy

items.meaning: Your task is to handle jealousy of the world, friends and your partner's success, and to grow your own rather than envy.
text: One of you has a wide world, the other anxiety, and jealousy can easily spread here like a weed. The Empress speaks of lessons in jealousy and temptation: of friends, work, success, other people's attention. The World in the middle opens wide horizons before the couple, where each has their own people and pursuits. And the Moon in your wishes suggests the worst stories about what happens where you aren't.

One of you has friends in five countries, evening calls, trips to conferences. Each time the other is silently jealous and imagines what goes on there. This time the first takes them along to a conference — and the other sees: ordinary tired people, coffee in paper cups, talk about work. The jealousy doesn't vanish at once, but there's no more fog in it. **Jealousy retreats when the other's world stops being a mystery and becomes a place where you're expected.**

Jealousy grows where your own life doesn't. The one who stays home is jealous and envious; the one who goes out into the world gets irritated and closes off. An imbalance in duties — one carries the home, the other “develops” — sharpens the grievances. The Empress needs each of you to have your own garden: when your own life is full, the other's stops seeming a threat.

items.title: A house with no locked rooms

captions.M: To want mystery and a world of your own
captions.N: To build a large shared world
captions.D: To make the union whole, with no secrets or illusions

items.meaning: Your task is a whole world with no locked rooms: give up secrets and illusions and show each other everything.
text: You're building a large shared world, and the couple's task is to leave no locked rooms in it. The World appears twice: both the path and the main lesson lead to wholeness — a shared picture of life where views, plans and friends come together. But the Moon, where your line begins, hides caches in this picture: about money, the past, fears. And the whole isn't whole while it has doors to which the other has no key.

For nine years one of you has secretly helped a younger brother with money — afraid the other won't understand. By chance the other sees a bank statement, and the conversation is hard. But having listened, the other says: “It's not the money that hurts. It's that in this you treat me as an outsider.” A month later you're helping the brother together. **Your world becomes whole when there's nothing left in it to hide from each other.**

The whole cracks when illusions hide behind a pretty picture. You tell friends what a harmonious couple you are, while at home you go round the same conversations. Secrets multiply, one partner's views are imposed on the other, and each stays in their own room behind a locked door. The World needs honesty: open all the doors, even those with a mess behind them.

items.title: A foothold on a turning wheel

captions.M: To want a wide and whole life
captions.N: To keep everything under control
captions.D: To find common footing amid change and not blame fate

items.meaning: Your task is steadiness amid change: accept that the wheel turns, and hold on to each other rather than to control.
text: Your couple's life rises and falls, and the task is to find a footing that doesn't depend on the turns. The Wheel of Fortune in the couple's tail brings changes and crises from time to time, and fighting the change itself is useless. The Emperor offers his answer: control everything, plan it all in advance, hold on tight. The World shows a better one: stability is not standing still but the ability to stay whole at every turn.

The fifth move in seven years. One of you, as always, draws up a forty-point spreadsheet and gets angry when something doesn't go to plan. The other suddenly says: “Let's keep three points: the bed, coffee and us. The rest will follow.” You laugh, and for the first time a move passes without a quarrel. **Your footing is not a plan but the certainty that at any turn you hold on to each other.**

The wheel breaks those who grab at its spokes. The harder one tries to keep change under control, the more painful each turn: complaints about fate, accusations against the partner, grievances and manipulation. Your circle shrinks because there is no strength left for friends. Steadiness comes when you stop looking for someone to blame and start looking for a solution — together, shoulder to shoulder.

items.title: Praise instead of nitpicking

captions.M: To want a broad, free life
captions.N: To demand order and control
captions.D: To warm with praise, not burn with criticism

items.meaning: Your task is warmth instead of nitpicking: delight in each other aloud and don't turn order into constant criticism.
text: There's order in your union; what you have to learn is warmth. The Sun in the main task demands joy and generosity: praising, thanking, being proud of each other's successes aloud. The Emperor in the middle pulls the other way — control, correct, demand that things measure up. And the World in your wishes reminds you that you both need freedom, without which even the most beautiful order becomes a strict school.

One of you is used to noticing only flaws: folded wrong, put in the wrong place, could have been better. A visiting friend says to the other: “What a beautiful shelf — did you make it yourself?” — and the first suddenly realises they've never once said that. Since that evening you have a new habit: at dinner each names one thing about the other that pleased them that day. **The Sun shines when praise is heard more often than criticism.**

Order burns when warmth is replaced by demands. Harsh criticism, inflated expectations, a guardianship in which the other can't do anything alone — and the light in the house dims. The one constantly corrected stops trying, the one correcting is angry at the inaction. The Sun doesn't need control: it makes things grow by warming them.

items.title: Order with room for surprises

captions.M: To want space and new impressions
captions.N: To move, achieve, win
captions.D: Not to freeze in rules, and to keep the passion

items.meaning: Your task is order with room for passion: don't freeze in rules, surprise each other, let each other go to friends.
text: You build a strong union, and the task is to keep it from getting dull. The Emperor demands order, rules, a reliable rear, but on his dark side turns into coldness and passivity: everything planned, everything under control, and the passion has gone somewhere. The Chariot in the middle and the World in your wishes pull you outwards — to movement, travel, new people. The main thing is not to let order lock you indoors.

Life is mapped out a year ahead: holiday in August, the country cottage at weekends, dinner at seven. On an ordinary Wednesday one of you comes home with two tickets for the night train: “We'll be back on Sunday, the rest can wait.” The other is cross at first — the plans! — then laughs and packs a rucksack. On Monday you're at work short of sleep and happy. **Order holds when there's room in it for one mad Wednesday.**

Order becomes a cage when the schedule matters more than people. One checks where the other was and with whom, the other answers with coldness. Friends, hobbies, sport take a back seat, because they're “not in the plan”. Passion fades, and the union runs on habit. The Emperor should trust: let the partner go to friends without a report, and sometimes break his own schedule.

items.title: The end of a two-city life

captions.M: To want a world without borders
captions.N: To be always on the road
captions.D: To end the stage of partings and dare to live one life

items.meaning: Your task is to end the stage of partings: stop living in two cities and dare to share one life.
text: The road is familiar to you; what you have to learn is to arrive one day. Death demands that a stage be finished: partings, life in two cities, an eternal “we'll decide later”. The Chariot in the middle keeps you moving — business trips, flights, meetings at stations. And the World lures with breadth: you both like life to be big. But a union that's always on the road risks never starting to live.

Every weekend you meet in one of two cities: one travels to the other, then the other way round. It's romantic, and on Monday both go back to their empty flats. One Sunday on the platform one of you doesn't board the train: “Let's decide today — who moves to whom, and when.” The ticket is wasted, but by spring you have a shared address. **A new chapter opens when you stop saying goodbye at stations.**

The stage drags on when separation becomes convenient. You needn't settle household questions, share a wardrobe or see each other tired. Crises are lived through alone, over the phone, and each sees the other's mistakes but not their own. Death dislikes endless in-between states: a stage you don't close yourselves will one day be closed by circumstances.

items.title: Freedom with an address

captions.M: To dream of a life without borders
captions.N: To race ahead without looking back
captions.D: To combine freedom with responsibility and not run away

items.meaning: Your task is freedom with an address: travel, take risks and live lightly, but don't run from serious steps.
text: You pull up stakes easily, and the couple's task is to learn to stay when things get serious. The Fool in the tail asks the main question: where is the line between freedom and flight? The Chariot gives you speed and a thirst for the road, the World a dream of life without borders. Starting is easy for you, but when it comes to shared decisions — housing, money, commitments — you badly want to leave again.

For years you have lived out of suitcases: a year in one country, six months in another, working remotely. Whenever talk turns to a home of your own, someone remembers a new place you “must see”. In yet another airport, under the departures board, one of you asks: “Are we ever going to arrive anywhere?” You laugh, cancel the return tickets and, for the first time in years, rent a flat for a year rather than a month, with a map on the wall marking just one place so far — home. **Freedom becomes real when it has an address you want to come back to.**

Freedom turns into flight when hard things are solved by leaving. Instead of a conversation — a new route; instead of a commitment — “we'll sort it out later”; and each keeps their own rules of freedom for themselves while being jealous of the other. Moods swing, agreements fall apart. The Fool teaches not to give up freedom but to take serious steps as boldly as a step into the unknown.

items.title: A route for two

captions.M: To want to see the whole world together
captions.N: To catch the turn of fate
captions.D: To choose a shared course and not fight over the wheel

items.meaning: Your task is a shared route: daring to move together without fighting over the wheel or losing your own goals.
text: Learning to travel together is your main task. The Chariot leads here: choose a common course, dare to move or make a big turn, and don't fight for the wheel. The Wheel of Fortune throws up occasions — a sudden offer, a change, luck that won't wait. And the World explains where you are drawn: you both want a wide life, a different horizon, the feeling that the whole world is open.

One of you is offered a job in another country, with two weeks to decide. For the first few days you argue: the other has a career, friends, plans. Then you sit down with a map and a list: what we lose, what we gain, what the other will do there. For the first time an argument turns into a plan in which the other has a column of their own: a venture they have long dreamed of and could start there. **The course becomes shared when one partner's goal doesn't cancel the other's.**

The Chariot skids when the team has two heads. One is ready to dash off at the first turn of the wheel, the other demands that everything be put off for the sake of their own plans. Rivalry for the lead eats up the strength needed for the road, and you are worn out without ever setting off. Or you do go, but so fast that you forget to restore your strength — and in the new place there are two tired people who can't remember why they came.

items.title: A new world on the old ruins

captions.M: To want a large, whole world
captions.N: To accept a sharp turn of fate
captions.D: To survive the upheaval of your life and keep each other

items.meaning: Your task is to survive a sudden break in your familiar life and build a new shared world on the ruins.
text: Sometimes fate turns your life over in a single day, and the couple's main question is what you do next. The Tower brings a sudden break: a move not of your choosing, the loss of a business or a home, an event after which the old world can't be put back together. The Wheel of Fortune promises that a sharp turn will be followed by a new cycle. And the World you reach for shows the goal: to build a new, whole world from the debris — not the old one, but yours.

You leave your home town with two suitcases: circumstances left no choice. The first year in the new place — a rented room, work outside your profession, quarrels born of helplessness. One warm evening you sit on the steps outside, and one of you says: “You know, I like the sunsets here.” From that evening you start building a life instead of waiting things out. **A new world begins the minute you stop mourning the old one and look around together.**

Upheaval drives you apart when each clings to their own piece of wreckage. One wants everything back, the other wants to forget, and you look at what happened from different worlds. Composure is lost, grievances about the past spill onto each other. The Tower leaves no choice about whether to fall, but it leaves a choice about how to build: each in their own corner, or one house for two.

items.title: Together on every turn

captions.M: To want a whole, gathered life
captions.N: To let go of turns already lived
captions.D: To accept your partner whole; seek solutions, not culprits

items.meaning: Your task is to accept each other whole at every turn of fate: with flaws, crises and new beginnings.
text: Your shared life moves in turns: a rise, a fall, the end of one stage and the start of the next. The Wheel of Fortune teaches you to accept this change rather than fight it, and to accept each other in any state — with flaws, in crisis, at rock bottom. Death helps you let go of the turns already lived, and the World explains what you both reach for: a whole life in which everything lived is gathered into one story.

When one of you hits a hard turn — debts, a collapsed project, empty evenings — the other doesn't rush in to rescue but simply stays close: brings dinner, listens, goes along to the banks. When the slump comes to the other, the first knows exactly what to do. **You hold on through the memory that each has already seen the other at their worst turn — and stayed.**

The turns hurt when complaints replace solutions. You blame fate and each other, grievances pile up, and every crisis becomes a hunt for who let whom down. Change frightens you, and you cling to the old even when it has outlived itself. Your circle narrows, fears grow. The Wheel needs one thing: stop arguing with the turn and look for what the two of you can do on this one.

items.title: Order without an iron fist

captions.N: To rebuild after a collapse
captions.D: To create rules that help rather than crush

items.meaning: Your task is order without an iron fist: build a secure base without crushing each other with rigid rules.
text: You know how to build; what matters is that the building doesn't crush those who live in it. The Emperor demands order, responsibility, a reliable income, but he also teaches the main thing: reach your goals without pressure and don't create rules that later stifle you. The Tower in the middle brings down whatever is built too rigidly. And the World, the couple's shared wish, reminds you that you both need space — otherwise any fortress becomes a prison.

When you nearly lose your flat, one of you brings in a strict regime: a spending spreadsheet, receipts for everything, nothing “just because”. For months it works, and then the other admits they're afraid to spend even on a coffee. You sit down to review the rules and keep three: the cushion is untouchable, big things are decided together, the rest is each one's freedom. **Order holds when the rules protect both rather than command one.**

Rules become a cage when one person sets them. The other either submits and turns passive or rebels, and then every argument is a fight for the lead. Feelings go unspoken, replaced by instructions. The Emperor is strong when he can hand over the wheel where the other is stronger and admit that not everything in life needs controlling.

items.title: Apart without panic

captions.M: To want to see the world, even apart
captions.N: To break off abruptly and start again
captions.D: To trust when apart, not break up in the heat of it

items.meaning: Your task is separation without panic: trust each other at a distance, and don't break up in a rage at the first storm.
text: You both need freedom, and you'll have to let each other go without fear. The Fool demands freedom without checks and calm during separations: business trips, travel alone, a life of one's own for each. The World in your wishes pulls you to the wide world, where sometimes you have to be apart. And the Tower in the middle suggests the worst scenario — an abrupt break-up on emotion, when separation seems like the end.

One of you leaves to work abroad for six months. The first weeks bring anxiety, jealousy of new colleagues, a row over video call in which “maybe we should split up” is said. The next day you call again and agree: no decisions in late-night conversations, a letter every evening, a meeting in three months. The six months pass, and the homecoming becomes a second honeymoon. **Separation doesn't wreck a union when trust is stronger than night-time fears.**

Freedom turns into a cliff edge when difficulties are solved by breaking up. Mood swings, jealousy of the other's life, the manipulation of “then let's split up” — and a week later a reconciliation as if nothing had happened. Each demands trust and doesn't give it. The Fool needs you to accept your partner as they are, and to remember that freedom is no excuse for slamming doors.

items.title: Two stars in one harness

captions.M: To want a big, bright life
captions.N: To shine and achieve success
captions.D: Not to compete for first place; keep the race out of love

items.meaning: Your task is two bright careers without rivalry: pull in one harness and don't turn the union into a race.
text: You're both strong and successful, and your love easily becomes a contest — that's what you need to avoid. The Chariot demands movement, victories, a goal, and tests whether you can race in one harness rather than against each other. The Sun in the middle gives each their own light and a taste for success, the World in your wishes a dream of a big, wide life. Chasing it easily eats up the time that should have belonged to the two of you.

You both get promoted in the same week — and instead of celebrating, spend half the evening establishing whose post is grander. In the morning one texts the other: “Listen, are we one team or two competitors?” That evening you celebrate together as you used to, and a month later you agree on the main thing: one evening a week with no work, no phones and no keeping score. **A union of two strong people holds when victories are counted as shared, not compared.**

The harness creaks when each pulls towards their own finish. One career demands a move, the other staying put, and someone must give up their goal, but nobody wants to agree. Envy of the partner's successes hides behind congratulations, and the relationship is put off “until the next project”. The Chariot needs balance: each has their own goal, but the road is shared, and it must have stops for two.

items.title: Happiness without bracing

captions.M: To want a world full of light
captions.N: To rejoice and shine
captions.D: Not to expect the worst; to hold on to each other

items.meaning: Your task is happiness without bracing for a blow: value the good days, and in the bad ones hold on to each other.
text: You have a lot of light, and that's exactly why one of you is sometimes afraid: what if it all collapses? The Tower teaches you to live with this fear: blows happen, but the habit of expecting the worst poisons even the sunniest days. The Sun in the middle and the World in your wishes give the couple joy, success, a big life — things worth protecting. Protecting them without freezing in fear of losing them — that's what you have to learn.

The hard stretch is behind you, life has settled, yet one of you just can't relax: checking the news on holiday, saying “touch wood” at every celebration. The other suggests a game: every time someone says “touch wood”, they must name aloud one thing they're grateful for today. The first week brings ten thanks a day, and after that “touch wood” is heard less and less. **Happiness lasts when it's noticed every day, not only when it's leaving.**

Fear of the worst wrecks the good by itself. One is constantly anxious and looks for a catch, the other tires of reassuring and withdraws. And when a blow does come, you meet it apart: one in panic, the other pretending all is well. The Tower doesn't ask whether to strike, but how you hold on is up to you: together, and seeing the good as well.

items.title: An anchor for two wanderers

captions.M: To want space and new horizons
captions.N: To live on a wing and a prayer, without plans
captions.D: To find shared stability without losing lightness

items.meaning: Your task is an anchor for two wanderers: find a shared footing without giving up freedom and luck.
text: You're both quick to set off, and you need an anchor that won't stop you sailing. The Wheel of Fortune demands shared stability: in a life where something is always changing, you need at least one fixed centre. The Fool in the middle suggests living on a wing and a prayer, the World in your wishes seeing the whole world and putting down roots nowhere. A wonderful life — until the first serious slump, when it turns out there's nothing to lean on.

For a long time you've lived like migrating birds: contract work, flats for six months, friends in every port. When one partner's contract suddenly ends and the other hasn't yet found a new one, it turns out there's neither a reserve nor a place to come back to. After that autumn you get two things: a cushion for six months of living and a small flat as a base. **Freedom doesn't suffer from an anchor if it's shared and chosen by both.**

The turns hit harder when there's nothing to hold on to. In a good streak everything is easy; in a bad one each blames circumstances and the other, moods swing, and the partner's feelings get lost against your own. Your circle is wide, but in trouble there's no one to call. The Wheel needs a centre: a few simple agreements and one place where you're both expected.

items.title: Warmth that doesn't smother

captions.M: To want freedom and the whole world
captions.N: To travel light, without obligations
captions.D: To warm, not mother, and talk about problems openly

items.meaning: Your task is warmth without smothering: enjoy and support each other without turning care into surveillance.
text: You both need space, but what you must learn is something else — to warm without burning. The Sun demands warmth and generosity: delighting in each other's successes, supporting each other in hard times, speaking honestly about problems. The World and the Fool in your wishes and on your path pull towards freedom — travel, lightness, a life with no one to report to. Beside them the Sun easily overdoes it: care turns into guardianship, and guardianship into a cage.

One of you leaves for a month on an expedition they've dreamed of since youth. For the first few days the other calls three times a day: have you eaten? Are you warm enough? Then they catch themselves and send one message: “I'm proud of you. Tell me everything when you're back.” On returning, the first talks until morning — and for the first time feels they were awaited at home, not kept watch over. **Warmth reaches the other when it carries pride and no surveillance.**

The Sun scorches when warmth becomes a condition. One looks after the other and expects gratitude for it; the other suffocates and escapes into freedom without explaining anything. Problems go unmentioned so as not to spoil the party, expectations grow, and one partner's victories are claimed or ignored by the other. The Sun needs honesty: say what worries you, what feels cramped, what is missing — before warmth turns into heat.

items.title: Who put in more

captions.G: Jealousy and competing over who gives the home more

items.meaning: It all starts with the question of who puts more into the home — and with jealousy of whatever thrives elsewhere.
text: You quarrel about the warmest thing of all — your home. The Empress here turns care into rivalry: who invests more, who earns more, who does the washing-up more often, who has “grown” and who is “stuck”. The one who has fallen behind feels like a lodger in their own home, and the one who has pulled ahead feels like the only adult.

A promotion comes through, and now one of you gets home at ten. The other has spent the whole day on the household, and by evening there is dinner on the table and hurt in their voice: “What do you care, they praise you at work.” The first snaps back: “And who pays the rent?” **You are both tired, but the one who takes offence is the one whose contribution to the home goes unseen.**

It is harder when advisers join in. One partner's parents remind everyone who the “main breadwinner” is, the other's friend advises them “not to put up with it”, and each brings other people's words home. Jealousy flares at anyone who gets attention: friends, work, even the children. A home that should feed you both becomes a field where each tallies up the harvest. Each of your contributions is worth naming aloud before it starts being presented as a bill.

items.title: An order instead of a request

captions.G: Deciding for both and demanding obedience

items.meaning: Trouble starts when one decides for both of you and the other is the last to know.
text: What makes you quarrel is power. In a quarrel the Emperor turns you both into bosses: decisions are made for two, rules are set without discussion, and disagreement is treated as mutiny. Feelings meanwhile are hidden behind a stony face — you can't tell whether the person is angry or just thinking, and that is even more maddening.

One partner comes home to learn that the other has already arranged to sell the car: “I've done the maths, it's better this way.” Maybe it is better. Only nobody asked, and the evening turns into a cold war: “Without me again?” — “You'd have mulled it over till winter.” **What hurts is not the decision but that it was made without the other.**

It gets really hard when both fight for the last word. Every small question — where to put the wardrobe, when to have dinner, whose parents to visit — becomes a battle for supremacy. The loser withdraws and stores it up, the winner doesn't notice they are commanding an empty hall. The Emperor is strong at order, but a home is not a barracks: rules that suit both are written by both.

items.title: A lecture instead of a talk

captions.G: Lecturing and remaking each other

items.meaning: Quarrels start with “I know better how it's done” — and with family advice that sounds louder than your own voices.
text: Your quarrels are like lessons where both want to be the teacher. When you clash, the Hierophant gives each of you a truth of your own about how to live, raise children, rest — and you are tempted to share it in a preachy tone. Add to that the voices of the family, with their traditions, advice and certainty that they know your household better than you do.

One of you is slicing bread, the other remarks: “You're holding the knife wrong.” A minute later it turns out the tea is brewed wrong too, the holidays are in the wrong place, and at the parents' house it was always done differently. Who started it no longer matters: each is defending not the knife but their own family and their right to be right. **Conflict flares up where one tries to re-educate the other and the other hears a verdict on the home they came from.**

Worst of all is when the argument spills beyond the two of you. One partner's parents start “explaining” to the other how things should be done, the other responds with coldness, and soon two families are at war, with the two of you on opposite sides of the table. Each is sure they are defending the truth, and neither hears the other. Lecturing wears you out more than shouting: afterwards you don't want to make up — you want to be silent.

items.title: A paradise tested by quarrels

captions.G: Looking for the serpent in paradise

items.meaning: You stand before each other unguarded, so any shadow in your paradise turns into a storm where every word hits home.
text: You quarrel in earnest not over chores but over love. The Lovers are two people open to each other with nothing in between, and words hit their mark: nobody knows the other's sore spot better than you. You long to keep the beginning untouched — and under every flower you imagine a serpent: a dry tone, a long pause, a forgotten “good night”.

In the afternoon one sends a photo of the doorway where you first kissed, and the reply comes three hours later: “ok”. By evening a whole story has grown out of two letters: so it has cooled, so it's no longer like the beginning. The question comes out sharper than intended, the answer sharper still. **What sets you quarrelling is not a trifle but the fear that the paradise you entered together is already over.**

A quarrel turns into a test: the temptation is strong to hurt deeper and see whether the other stays. You want to save that first openness, yet it is precisely what you spend: words said in the heat of the moment are not forgotten, and next time each approaches the other already shielded. The storm passes quickly, but after each one there is one more locked gate in paradise.

items.title: Two drivers on one sledge

captions.G: Each pulling the team their own way

items.meaning: You clash over who holds the wheel: who leads, who decides, whose goal matters more and who must give way.
text: Conflict begins where both of you want to lead. Here the Chariot gives two strong people one team of horses: each has their own goal, their own pace and the certainty that this is the way to go. While your roads coincide, you are unbeatable. Once they part, a peaceful evening explodes over nothing: who picks the route, who got behind the wheel, why we're doing it your way again.

You are driving to see friends, one at the wheel, the other navigating on the phone. “Turn right here” — “I know a shorter way.” Ten minutes later you are stuck in traffic, and the argument is no longer about the road: it's about you never being listened to, about your work mattering more than mine, about you always deciding alone. **Behind every argument about the road lies one question: who holds the reins.**

It is worse when rivalry moves into big decisions. One expects the other to put their plans on hold for the sake of their career and is hurt if they won't give way. A partner's wins provoke not joy but envy, their setbacks a silent “told you so”. Each pulls their own way, the harness creaks, and the cart stays where it is. One thing helps: agree on the route before you get into the car.

items.title: A court where both prosecute

captions.G: Keeping score of grievances and passing verdicts

items.meaning: Every row becomes a trial: who is right, who did more, whose promise was broken — and the score never adds up.
text: You rarely get as far as shouting — more often as far as a written record. In your conflicts Justice makes each of you keep score: who took out the bins more often, who was late last time, who promised and didn't deliver.
